I would like to speak about my hobby, it is repairing old bicycles. I do this since eleven years.

I start because my neighbour is leaving one bicycle in our shed when he moved away. It was very old and it was broken, and I don't know anything about bicycles. But I watched some videos and I try. After two months it was working, and this was a very good feeling for me.

model_answers.transcript:
The hobby I'd talk about is fixing up old bicycles, which I've been doing for about eleven years now.

It started more or less by accident. A neighbour moved out and left a bicycle in our shed — a heavy old thing with a bent wheel and no brakes to speak of — and rather than take it to the tip I decided I'd have a look at it. I knew nothing whatsoever about bicycles at that point. It took me two months, a great many internet videos and one very patient man in a bike shop, but eventually the thing worked. The back wheel alone took three separate attempts. I'm not sure I've been that pleased with myself since.

These days it's a Sunday morning job. A couple of hours most weeks, more if something's genuinely stuck. I pick bikes up cheaply, do them up over a month or two, and then give them away — I've handed on four so far, which is a good deal more satisfying than selling them would be. None of them costs more than about thirty pounds to start with.

The reason it's survived when other things haven't is that it's the exact opposite of my job. At work nothing is ever really finished and half the problems belong to somebody else. Whereas a bent wheel is a bent wheel. It's in front of you, it's yours, and when it's straight you can see that it's straight. That sounds like a small thing, and eleven years suggests otherwise.

The one that's lasted is fixing up old bicycles, which I've been at for something like eleven years.

It began by accident, as most of these things do. A neighbour moved out and abandoned a bicycle in our shed — heavy, bent wheel, brakes in name only — and instead of taking it to the tip I thought I'd see what could be done with it. I knew absolutely nothing. Two months, an unreasonable number of videos and one extremely patient man in a bike shop later, the thing rode. The back wheel alone took three goes. I don't think I've been quite so pleased with myself before or since.

It's a Sunday morning habit now. Two hours most weeks, longer when something refuses to move. I buy them cheaply, work on them across a month or so, and then hand them on — four have gone to friends, which beats selling them by a distance I can't really explain. I want to describe one tradition of my country that I did it. It is a bread day in the village of my aunt, before the spring holiday.

The village is small, maybe four hours from my city. All the families bring the dough to one big oven and they cook the bread together. This oven is very old, I think more than one hundred years.

model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd describe is a bread-baking morning that happens in my aunt's village every spring, the day before the main holiday. Every family brings their dough down to one communal oven and the whole thing gets baked together.

The village is tiny — four hours from where I grew up, three streets and an oven that's supposedly two hundred years old. I'd been going there as a child and doing absolutely nothing, and I finally took part properly when I was twenty-two. Until then I'd always found a reason not to. It starts at five in the morning, which was most of the reason.

By the time we got there at six the queue was already halfway down the lane. My job turned out to be kneading for the best part of an hour, which sounds straightforward and is not. After that you shape the loaves, and mine came out looking like something a child had made. The woman next to me rearranged two of them without saying anything at all, which was somehow worse than a comment. The oven itself was too hot to stand anywhere near for long.

At the time I was mortified, and I spent the walk back working out how soon I could reasonably leave. Looking back, though, I'm oddly glad about the whole thing. Not because of the bread, which was ordinary. It was more that my grandmother had stood in that queue, and until that morning that had been a story rather than something I'd done.

model_answers.label: The top of the range
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd describe is a bread morning in my aunt's village, held the day before the main spring holiday, when every household carries its dough down to one shared oven and the lot goes in together.

The village amounts to three streets and that oven, which is said to be two hundred years old and probably isn't. I'd been taken there every year as a child and had contributed nothing whatsoever. Not until I was twenty-two did I actually take part, largely because the thing begins at five in the morning and I had spent a decade finding that unanswerable.

We arrived at six to find the queue already halfway down the lane. My allotted job was kneading, for something close to an hour, which sounds undemanding and is the opposite of it. The dough had been sitting under a cloth in the back of the car since four. Then came the shaping, at which I was conspicuously poor. The woman beside me quietly reshaped two of my loaves and said nothing, which stung considerably more than criticism would have. None of it had been explained to me; you were simply expected to watch.

I was mortified at the time and spent the walk back calculating how early I could decently leave. What I feel now is harder to name. The bread itself was unremarkable. But my grandmother had queued in that lane, and up to that morning that had been a piece of family furniture rather than anything I had physically done.

I want to tell about a decision I made about three years ago. At that time I am working in a small company, only nine people, and another company offered me a job.

The other job was better. The salary was more, maybe twenty percent more, and the office was near to my home, only twenty minutes. So it was a good offer, and everybody told me to take it. My mother said take it, my friends said take it also.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a decision I made about three years ago, which was turning down a job that would have paid me quite a bit more.

At the time I was working for a small firm — nine of us, all in one room — and a much bigger company got in touch and offered me a role. On paper it was an easy call. The salary was around twenty per cent higher, the office was twenty minutes from my flat rather than an hour, and not one person I asked told me to stay.

What made me hesitate was my manager. She'd taught me most of what I actually know how to do, and she was still handing me work I wasn't quite ready for, which is how you learn anything. At the bigger place I'd have been one of about forty people doing the same job. So it came down to money against the person I was learning from, and in the end that's what tipped the balance.

Turning it down was harder than I expected, and for the first couple of months I did wonder whether I'd been sentimental about it. Then, about six months later, she put me in charge of a project on my own, and I'm now running a small team, whereas if I'd moved I'd probably still be doing the same tasks I was doing back then. Looking back, I'd say the useful part wasn't the decision itself — it was working out that I was choosing what I'd be taught, not just where I'd sit.

'On paper', 'tipped the balance', 'got in touch' — chunks carry the meaning, not adjectives.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
This was three years ago, and it was a decision to turn something down rather than to take it — an offer that was, on the face of it, plainly better than what I already had.

I was at a small firm then, nine of us in a single room, and a far larger company approached me. Twenty per cent more money, a twenty-minute commute instead of an hour, and not one person I consulted advised me against it. What nobody could see from outside was that most of the value of the job I was in sat with one person — the manager who'd trained me, and who was still quietly handing me work I hadn't earned yet. That is a rare thing, and it isn't advertised anywhere.

So the choice wasn't really money against loyalty. It was whether I was picking a salary or picking who I'd be taught by, and once I'd put it in those terms it more or less made itself.

It was still uncomfortable. For a couple of months I half-suspected I'd dressed up cold feet as principle. Then, six months in, she handed me a project of my own, and I've run a small team ever since. Had I taken the offer, I'd almost certainly have ended up competent and interchangeable, which is a worse place to be at that age than underpaid. What I take from it now is that the decisions people call good ones are rarely the ones with the better numbers attached — they're the ones where somebody managed to work out what they were actually choosing between.

annotations.span: I'd dressed up cold feet as principle

I'll talk about a change I made a couple of years ago, which was moving out of my parents' house and getting a place of my own.

Up until then I'd lived at home my whole life — my parents, my two sisters and my grandmother, all in one house. It was noisy in a way I actually liked, and to be honest most things were done for me. But I was twenty-four by then, most of the people I'd been at university with had already moved out, and I'd started to feel slightly stuck.

So in the September of that year I took the plunge and rented a small flat on the other side of the city, about ten minutes from where I work. It's one room and a kitchen, and the rent takes a third of what I earn, but it's mine.

The person it affected most wasn't me — it was my mother. She rang every single day for about a month, and I think she read the move as a verdict on the house rather than a decision about me, which it honestly wasn't.

As for the difference it's made, the obvious answer is that I've had to learn how to run a household, and that's true enough. But the thing I hadn't expected was how much better I get on with my family now that I see them once a week instead of every evening. In hindsight, the distance turned out to be the point rather than the price.

annotations.span: I took the plunge

annotations.why: Save it for the moment you finally did the thing you'd delayed.

annotations.span: As for the difference it's made

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd pick is moving out of my parents' house, which I did a couple of years back and which took me far longer to get round to than it should have.

I'd lived in that house since I was born — two parents, two sisters, a grandmother, and never a quiet room in it. I don't want to make it sound like an escape, because it wasn't; the noise was half of what I liked about the place. But at twenty-four I was still being looked after, and there comes a point at which being looked after starts to feel like being held still.

I rented a flat on the far side of the city that September, ten minutes from work, one room and a kitchen, with a rent that swallows a third of what I bring in. Modest, but entirely my own.

What I hadn't reckoned with was my mother. She phoned daily for a month, and I gradually worked out that she'd taken the move as a comment on the house rather than a decision about me — which is a distinction that is almost impossible to explain to somebody while they're upset.

The difference it's made isn't really the domestic competence, though I've had to pick that up. It's that seeing my family once a week rather than every evening has done more for how we get on than fifteen years of living on top of each other ever managed. Only with a bit of distance did any of us become particularly easy to like.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion at the close, where band 7 used an ordinary statement.
'Get round to', 'reckoned with', 'swallows a third' sit naturally, undisplayed.
It heads off the wrong reading of the story before making its point.

annotations.span: took me far longer to get round to than it should have
annotations.label: A phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Get round to' says delayed-not-refused in three words.

annotations.span: being looked after starts to feel like being held still
annotations.label: Reframes the situation in one image
annotations.why: One line of interpretation is worth thirty seconds of extra detail.

annotations.span: What I hadn't reckoned with was my mother.
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect together
annotations.why: Combining two structures in one short sentence is what sustained control looks like.

annotations.span: she'd taken the move as a comment on the house rather than a decision about me
annotations.label: Precision about somebody else's reading
annotations.why: Reporting a misunderstanding exactly is harder — and worth more — than describing an emotion.

annotations.span: Modest, but entirely my own.
annotations.label: A short sentence breaks the rhythm
annotations.why: Drop your pitch and pause before it; the contrast does the emphasis.

annotations.span: Only with a bit of distance did any of us become particularly easy to like.
annotations.label: Negative inversion after 'only'
annotations.why: 'Only after ___ did I ___' is the one inversion worth drilling for speech.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about my achievement. I finish a teaching qualification two years ago and I am very proud about this.

It was a part-time course, so I am working in the day and studying in the evening, and also on Saturday sometimes. It took two years. It was very hard because I am tired all the time and I don't sleep enough.

In the first year I failed my first lesson. A teacher came and she watched me for forty minutes and after she said it is not good enough. I was very sad and I want to stop the course. But my friend said to me, try one more time. So after three months I try again and this time I passed.

Not many people knew about it. I didn't tell my family because I think maybe I will fail again. Only my friend knew. My mother knew at the end when I finished and she cried.

It mattered because I never think that I can do this. In my family nobody is a teacher. So it was a very big thing for me. So this is my achievement that I am proud of.

Four sentences start with 'so', and the last one repeats the prompt.
'Hard', 'sad', 'big', 'proud' — nothing else does any evaluating at all.

annotations.label: Reported speech not backshifted
annotations.why: 'She told me it wasn't good enough.' Shift the verb back one step.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about finishing a teaching qualification, which I did about two years ago and which took me the best part of two years to get through.

It was a part-time course, so I was working during the day and studying most evenings and every other Saturday. That sounds manageable said out loud, but by around the fourth month I was permanently tired and I'd more or less stopped seeing anybody.

The part I'd point to is what happened in the first year. You have to be observed teaching a full lesson, and my first observation went badly — the assessor sat at the back for forty minutes and then told me, perfectly politely, that it wasn't good enough. I remember walking home afterwards and deciding I'd hand the whole thing in. A friend on the same course talked me out of it, and I did the observation again three months later and got through it.

Hardly anybody knew I was doing it, actually. I hadn't told my family, mainly because I'd convinced myself I'd fail and I didn't fancy explaining that twice. My mother found out on the day I finished, and she cried, which I wasn't remotely prepared for.

As for why it mattered — I think because nobody in my family had done anything like it, so I genuinely had no idea whether I could. Passing the second observation told me more than the certificate did. In a way the qualification is the least interesting part; what I came away with was evidence that I don't fold the first time something goes wrong.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect and a proper reported-speech backshift replace the present-tense slips.
'The best part of two years', 'talked me out of it', 'I don't fold' carry it.

annotations.label: Signposts the centre of the story

annotations.label: Reported speech, correctly backshifted
annotations.why: Report what people said rather than quoting; it shows more control.

annotations.label: Precise phrasal verb for persuasion
annotations.why: 'Talked me out of it' beats 'she said don't stop' in every way.

annotations.label: Understatement doing the emotional work
annotations.why: Spoken English hides feeling in dry phrases; copy the register.

annotations.label: A trailing clause adds a reaction

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd choose is a teaching qualification I finished a couple of years ago, taken part-time over two years while I was working.

On paper that's a single sentence. In practice it was most evenings and every other Saturday for the best part of twenty-four months, and by the spring of the first year I'd stopped being much use to anybody, including myself.

What made it an achievement rather than simply a slog was the first observation. Somebody sits at the back of your classroom for forty minutes and then tells you, very courteously, that what you did was not good enough — and there's no arguing with it, because they happen to be right. I walked home that evening having quietly decided to withdraw. A friend on the course sat me down and pointed out that I was treating one bad hour as a verdict on two years. Three months later I was observed again and got through it comfortably.

Almost nobody knew I was doing it. I hadn't told my family, on the grounds that failing privately is a good deal cheaper than failing in public, and my mother only learned about it the week I finished.

Looking back, the certificate is the least of it. What I came away with was a piece of evidence about myself I couldn't have obtained any other way — that a bad first attempt is information rather than a verdict. Had I withdrawn that evening, I'd have spent years believing something about myself that wasn't true.

'A slog', 'no arguing with it', 'the least of it' arrive without being shown off.

annotations.why: Turning your motive into a comparison sounds thought about, not rehearsed.

annotations.span: a bad first attempt is information rather than a verdict
annotations.label: Lifts the story into a principle
annotations.why: One general sentence at the end changes what the whole turn was about.

annotations.span: Had I withdrawn that evening
annotations.label: Inversion replaces the third conditional
annotations.why: Drop the 'if' and invert; it is the cheapest register lift available.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a mistake in my job. Last year I make eight hundred leaflets with the wrong date.

I work in the marketing and it was my second month there. My manager said, print the leaflets for our open day. So I write the text and I send it to the printer. But the top part I copy from the old leaflet, and there was the old date there.

Nobody see this. Not me also. The boxes come and we put the leaflets in the library and in two shops. After two days a woman call and she ask which date is correct.

I feel very bad. We must print again, it costs four hundred euro. My manager was not angry but she was disappointed.

Now I check everything two times. So this is my mistake.

what_caps_it.point: The talk ends around eighty seconds and the 'what you do differently' bullet gets one line.
Past and present alternate freely, and the order of events is never marked with a perfect.
'Very bad', 'not angry', 'disappointed' — three general words cover the entire consequence.

annotations.span: But the top part I copy from the old leaflet, and there was the old date there.
annotations.label: Names the exact cause
annotations.why: Keep this. A mistake card needs the mechanism, not just the result.

annotations.span: Last year I make eight hundred leaflets
annotations.label: A dated past event in the present
annotations.why: Say 'Last year I sent eight hundred leaflets to the printer.'

annotations.span: Nobody see this. Not me also.
annotations.label: No tense, and 'also' in a negative
annotations.why: Say 'Nobody spotted it, including me.' Negatives take 'either', never 'also'.

annotations.span: I feel very bad.
annotations.label: The flattest word at the key moment
annotations.why: Say what you braced yourself for, and what happened instead.

annotations.span: Now I check everything two times.
annotations.label: 'Two times' where 'twice' belongs
annotations.why: Say 'nothing with a date on it leaves my desk until somebody else has read it.'

annotations.span: So this is my mistake.
annotations.label: Closes on the card's wording
annotations.why: The last bullet asks what you do differently. It currently gets one sentence.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a mistake in my work. Last year I am organising a small event for our company and I made the leaflets with the wrong date on them.

I was working in the marketing department and it was my second month there. My manager asked me to print eight hundred leaflets for the event. I write the text myself, and I send it to the printer. But I copy the top part from the old leaflet from the last event, so the date was the old date.

Nobody sees this problem, also not me. The boxes came and we put the leaflets in the library and in two shops. After two days a woman phoned and she asked which date is correct. I felt terrible. We must print everything again and it costs about four hundred euros.

My manager was not angry but she was disappointing, I think. She said next time show me first.

Now I always check with another person before I send something, even a small email. So this is my mistake and what I learn from it.

what_caps_it.point: Five present-tense verbs sit inside a past story, and 'must' never becomes 'had to'.
'Disappointing' for 'disappointed', and every judgement is 'terrible' or 'small'.
Events arrive in the order they happened with no shaping, and the close repeats the card.

annotations.span: My manager asked me to print eight hundred leaflets for the event.
annotations.label: A number instead of 'many'
annotations.why: Keep this — one exact figure makes a story sound genuinely remembered.

annotations.span: Last year I am organising a small event
annotations.label: Present continuous after a past time phrase
annotations.why: 'Last year I was organising' — the time phrase decides the tense.

annotations.span: I write the text myself, and I send it to the printer
annotations.label: The narrative drops into the present
annotations.why: Wrote and sent. Choose the tense before you start and hold it.

annotations.span: Nobody sees this problem
annotations.label: Another present-tense slip
annotations.why: 'Nobody spotted it' — and 'spotted' is the more precise verb too.

annotations.span: We must print everything again and it costs about four hundred euros.
annotations.label: 'Must' has no past form
annotations.why: Use 'we had to reprint everything and it cost four hundred euros'.

annotations.span: she was disappointing, I think
annotations.label: -ing adjective describing a person
annotations.why: 'Disappointed' is how she felt; 'disappointing' is what caused it.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a mistake I made at work last year, which was sending eight hundred leaflets to the printer with the wrong date on them.

I'd been in the marketing team about two months, so I was still at the stage of trying to look competent. We were running a small open day, and my manager asked me to get the leaflets designed and printed. I wrote the text myself, and to save time I copied the header from the leaflet we'd used for the previous event — which of course still had the previous event's date sitting in it.

Nobody spotted it, including me. The boxes arrived, we dropped them off at the library and a couple of shops, and it wasn't until two days later that a member of the public rang up to ask which date was right. Reprinting cost about four hundred euros and, worse, we'd already put the wrong date in front of a few hundred people.

What I'd braced myself for was being shouted at. What actually happened was that my manager said, fairly mildly, that she'd rather have seen it before it went out, which was a good deal harder to hear than shouting would have been.

What I do differently now is dull but effective: nothing with a date, a price or a name in it leaves my desk until somebody else has read it. It takes four minutes. And I'd argue the real mistake wasn't copying the header — it was assuming that being quick and being careful were the same thing.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect, a cleft with 'it wasn't until', and a correctly formed 'would rather have'.
'Braced myself for', 'dropped them off', 'a good deal harder' replace bare adjectives.
Paired cleft sentences shape the aftermath, and the close names the real error.

annotations.span: I'd been in the marketing team about two months
annotations.label: Past perfect gives the mistake its cause
annotations.why: Saying how new you were explains the error without excusing it.

annotations.span: which of course still had the previous event's date sitting in it
annotations.label: A trailing clause delivers the punchline
annotations.why: Hang the consequence off the end of the sentence rather than starting a new one.

annotations.span: Nobody spotted it, including me.
annotations.label: Short sentence, self-implication
annotations.why: One four-word sentence after a long one resets the listener's attention.

annotations.span: it wasn't until two days later that a member of the public rang up
annotations.label: Cleft with 'it wasn't until'
annotations.why: Use it to make a delay feel like part of the story rather than a detail.

annotations.span: What I'd braced myself for was being shouted at.
annotations.label: Sets up a contrast before making it
annotations.why: 'What I expected was ___. What happened was ___' is a two-sentence structure worth owning.

annotations.span: she'd rather have seen it before it went out
annotations.label: 'Would rather have' about the past
annotations.why: The form is rare in candidate speech and immediately audible.

annotations.span: a good deal harder to hear than shouting would have been
annotations.label: A comparison instead of an adjective
annotations.why: Comparing two reactions says more than any single word for 'bad'.

annotations.span: What I do differently now is dull but effective
annotations.label: Announces the last bullet plainly
annotations.why: Name the bullet aloud and you will not run past it.

annotations.span: assuming that being quick and being careful were the same thing
annotations.label: Two gerunds carry the whole lesson
annotations.why: End on the idea, not on the event; it lifts the last ten seconds.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is small and entirely avoidable: about a year ago, eight hundred leaflets went to the printer carrying the date of an event that had already taken place.

I'd been in the team a couple of months and was still at the stage of wanting to look quick rather than careful. We had an open day coming up and, instead of building the leaflet from scratch, I lifted the header off the previous one and changed what I thought needed changing. The date was not on that list.

Nobody caught it — not the printer, not my manager, and least of all me. The boxes went out to a library and two shops, and it took a phone call from a member of the public, forty-eight hours later, to establish that several hundred people had been given the wrong information. The reprint came to roughly four hundred euros, which was the cheap part.

What I'd steeled myself for was being taken apart. What I got was my manager remarking, quite mildly, that she'd have liked to see it first — and mild disappointment turns out to be considerably more effective than anger.

Nothing with a date or a price on it now leaves my desk unread by somebody else. It costs four minutes. And the useful lesson had nothing to do with proofreading: speed and care had felt like the same virtue to me, and they are not remotely the same thing.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive with a perfect infinitive and an 'it took X to Y' structure carry the aftermath.
'Taken apart', 'the cheap part', 'steeled myself' land without being displayed.
The close separates the surface lesson from the real one instead of restating it.

annotations.span: The date was not on that list.
annotations.label: Understatement does the admission
annotations.why: A dry short sentence is more convincing than 'it was a terrible mistake'.

annotations.span: not the printer, not my manager, and least of all me
annotations.label: A three-part list with a fall
annotations.why: Level pitch on the first two, drop on the third; the rhythm carries it.

annotations.span: it took a phone call from a member of the public, forty-eight hours later, to establish that
annotations.label: 'It took X to Y' compresses the aftermath
annotations.why: The structure hands you a whole clause of detail inside one sentence.

annotations.span: What I'd steeled myself for was being taken apart.
annotations.label: Two idioms placed, not displayed
annotations.why: 'Steel yourself for' and 'be taken apart' are ordinary spoken English, not decoration.

annotations.span: mild disappointment turns out to be considerably more effective than anger
annotations.label: A precise comparative judgement
annotations.why: Comparing two reactions is a more interesting claim than describing one.

annotations.span: speed and care had felt like the same virtue to me, and they are not remotely the same thing
annotations.label: Closes on the real error
annotations.why: Separate the surface mistake from the belief underneath it; that is the band-8 move.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
Mine is a small one, and completely self-inflicted. A year or so ago I signed off eight hundred leaflets that announced an open day using the date of an open day we'd already held.

At that point I'd been on the marketing team two months and my main ambition was to look like somebody who got things done quickly. Rather than start the leaflet from nothing, I took the header off the last one and edited what struck me as needing editing. The date did not strike me.

It went past the printer, past my manager, and past me, which tells you how many pairs of eyes a wrong date can survive. The boxes were dropped at a library and two shops. Two days later somebody rang in, entirely reasonably, to ask which of the dates was the real one — by which time several hundred people were holding the wrong information. Reprinting came to around four hundred euros, and that was the affordable part.

I'd prepared myself for a proper dressing-down. Instead my manager said, without raising her voice at all, that she'd have preferred to see it before it went out. You can't defend yourself against it, which is exactly why it worked.

These days nothing carrying a date, a price or somebody's name leaves my desk until another person has read it. Four minutes. And what I actually had wrong was not proofreading at all — I'd been treating fast and careful as the same quality, and they have almost nothing to do with each other.

what_lifts_it.point: A sentential 'which' clause and a past perfect continuous, both delivered without a pause.
'Dressing-down', 'self-inflicted', 'the affordable part' — plain, exact and entirely spoken.
The manager's line is left to do its own work instead of being characterised.

annotations.span: which tells you how many pairs of eyes a wrong date can survive
annotations.label: 'Which' referring to the whole sentence
annotations.why: 'Which' can point back at everything before it, not only at the last noun.

annotations.span: I'd been treating fast and careful as the same quality
annotations.label: Past perfect continuous for a long-held habit
annotations.why: 'Had been treating' says it went on for years before the day you learned.

annotations.span: a proper dressing-down
annotations.label: The exact noun for being told off
annotations.why: 'Dressing-down' is what a speaker says; 'criticism' is what a report says.

annotations.span: and that was the affordable part
annotations.label: Ranks two costs in five words
annotations.why: Say which cost you could bear and the other one is implied.

annotations.span: You can't defend yourself against it, which is exactly why it worked.
annotations.label: Explains the effect in plain words
annotations.why: After a strong observation, a plain sentence convinces more than another strong one.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Add what happened in the room afterwards. Your manager's reaction is a whole missing paragraph.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Say what you did wrong in the first ten seconds. Delaying it costs you the middle of the turn.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Name what you expected to happen and what happened instead. That contrast is bullet four.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Follow your strongest sentence with a plain one. 'You can't defend yourself against it' is why the mild version landed.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my plan for the future. My plan is to go to work in another country. Maybe Ireland, maybe Canada. In two years.

I decide this last year. My cousin go to Ireland three years ago and he works in a hospital there and he is very happy. In the summer he come to my house and he told me it is possible for me also. So after this I start to think seriously.

Until now I do some things. I learn English and I do this exam. And I open a bank account and every month I put money, so now I have four thousand. Also I send the papers for the registration but they say it takes long time.

It is important for me because here the salary is low and I cannot save. And my mother is not happy. But I go anyway.

That is my plan.

what_caps_it.point: The turn stops near eighty seconds with the 'why it matters' bullet answered in half a sentence.
Nothing done so far is in the present perfect, so the plan and the progress sound identical.
'Very happy', 'low', 'not happy', 'long time' — the case for emigrating rests on four flat words.

annotations.span: Maybe Ireland, maybe Canada. In two years.
annotations.label: Commits to a place and a timescale early
annotations.why: Keep this. A plan with a date in it is far easier to talk about than an ambition.

annotations.span: I decide this last year.

annotations.why: Say 'I decided this last year.'

annotations.label: Progress up to now needs a perfect
annotations.why: Say "So far I've done three things." That is the tense this bullet runs on.

annotations.why: Say "there's nothing left at the end of the month."

annotations.why: Say 'they say it takes a long time.'

But I go anyway.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my plan for the future. My plan is to go and work in another country, maybe Ireland or maybe Canada, in the next two years.

I decided this last year. My cousin went to Ireland three years ago and he is working in a hospital there and he is very happy. When he came in the summer he told me it is possible for me also. So after this I start to think about it seriously.

Until now I did some things. I am learning English and I am doing this exam. And I opened a savings account and every month I put some money, so now I have maybe four thousand. Also I sent my documents for the registration, but it takes a very long time they say.

It matters for me because here my salary is low and I can't to save money. And I want to see another country before I am too old. My mother is not happy about this plan, she says it is very far. But I think in two years I will go.

So this is my plan for the next years.

what_caps_it.point: No present perfect anywhere, 'can't to save', and the story slips into the present.
The steps pile up with 'and' between them, and the ending repeats the prompt.
'Happy', 'low', 'far', 'very long time' — nothing more precise than that.

annotations.span: My plan is to go and work in another country, maybe Ireland or maybe Canada, in the next two years.
annotations.label: States the plan and the deadline together
annotations.why: Keep this — a plan with a time limit on it sounds like a plan, not a wish.

annotations.span: So after this I start to think about it seriously.
annotations.label: Past event told in the present
annotations.why: 'That's when I started thinking about it seriously.' Past trigger, past verb.

annotations.span: Until now I did some things.
annotations.label: Present perfect missing entirely
annotations.why: 'So far I've done three things' — unfinished time takes the perfect.

annotations.span: I can't to save money
annotations.label: 'Can' followed by 'to'
annotations.why: Modals take the bare verb: 'I can't save much'.

annotations.span: It matters for me
annotations.label: Wrong preposition after 'matter'
annotations.why: Things matter to a person. Learn the preposition inside the chunk.

annotations.span: So this is my plan for the next years.

model_answers.label: The target — same plan, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a plan I've had for about a year now, which is to go and work abroad — probably Ireland, possibly Canada — within the next two years.

The idea really started with my cousin. He moved to Ireland three years ago and he's been working in a hospital there ever since, and when he came home last summer he said, fairly bluntly, that there was nothing actually stopping me doing the same. I'd assumed the whole thing was complicated in a way it apparently isn't, so that conversation is what set it off.

So far I've done three things. I've been putting money aside every month since January — about four thousand at this point, which is roughly half of what I'd need. I'm doing this exam, obviously, which is the one part of it I can't hurry. And I've sent off the first stage of the registration paperwork, which everybody warns me will take the best part of a year to come back.

Why it matters is a bit harder to say, and I've been asked it before. Part of it is money, because what I earn here doesn't leave much at the end of the month. But if I'm honest the bigger reason is that I've never lived anywhere else at all, and I'd rather find out whether I can manage it at twenty-six than wonder about it at forty. My mother isn't keen, which I understand — she has never lived away from the town she grew up in. The plan is to go anyway, and to go on good terms.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect continuous, a reported-speech backshift and 'would rather' all appear correctly.
'Set it off', 'putting money aside', 'on good terms' replace bare, general verbs.
The three steps are counted out loud, and the close weighs two reasons against each other.

annotations.span: I'll talk about a plan I've had for about a year now
annotations.label: Puts a duration on the plan
annotations.why: Saying how long you've held it makes it sound worked on, not invented.

annotations.span: he's been working in a hospital there ever since
annotations.label: Present perfect continuous for an ongoing state
annotations.why: Use it for anything that started in the past and is still true.

annotations.span: he said, fairly bluntly, that there was nothing actually stopping me
annotations.label: Reported speech, properly backshifted
annotations.why: Reporting is safer and scores better than quoting people directly.

annotations.span: that conversation is what set it off
annotations.label: A phrasal verb naming the trigger
annotations.why: 'Set it off' works for any decision that began with one moment.

annotations.span: So far I've done three things.
annotations.label: Counts the shape before filling it
annotations.why: Announcing a number buys thinking time and keeps you organised.

annotations.span: I've been putting money aside every month since January
annotations.label: 'Since' plus a start point, in the perfect
annotations.why: 'Since' takes a point in time; 'for' takes a length.

annotations.span: Why it matters is a bit harder to say
annotations.label: Signposts the last bullet honestly
annotations.why: Admitting the answer is difficult is itself an answer, and it buys a clause.

annotations.span: I'd rather find out whether I can manage it at twenty-six than wonder about it at forty
annotations.label: 'Would rather X than Y' with two clauses
annotations.why: The structure hands you a whole comparison in one sentence.

annotations.span: to go anyway, and to go on good terms
annotations.label: A chunk closes the turn cleanly
annotations.why: 'On good terms' is exactly right and costs three words.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The plan I'd describe is a fairly ordinary one: to be working abroad inside two years — Ireland most likely, Canada if that falls through.

It crystallised about a year ago, and I can date it to a single conversation. A cousin of mine has been working in a hospital in Dublin since he left, and when he was home last summer he pointed out, not especially gently, that the only thing keeping me here was my own assumption that it would be difficult. He was right, which was irritating.

Since then I've been chipping away at it. Money first — I've put by roughly four thousand, which covers about half of what the move would genuinely cost. This exam, obviously. And the registration paperwork, the first stage of which has gone in and which I'm told will take the better part of a year to come back.

As for why it matters, the financial argument is the easy one and probably not the true one. What sits underneath it is that I've lived in one city my entire life, and I'd sooner discover at twenty-six whether I can manage somewhere else than spend my forties wondering. My mother would rather I stayed, and I don't think she's wrong to feel that; I just don't think it's a reason. Plans like this aren't really predictions — they're a way of committing to something before you've worked out how to justify it.

what_lifts_it.point: 'The first stage of which' folds two sentences into one relative clause.
'Falls through', 'chipping away at it', 'put by' sit naturally in speech.
The close defines what a plan is rather than restating this particular one.

annotations.span: Canada if that falls through
annotations.label: A fallback named in four words
annotations.why: 'If that falls through' is the exact phrase for a plan that might not happen.

annotations.span: He was right, which was irritating.
annotations.label: Dry aside instead of a feeling word
annotations.why: Understatement reads as fluent; 'I felt very motivated' does not.

annotations.span: Since then I've been chipping away at it.
annotations.label: One idiom summarises three steps
annotations.why: Use it for any long project made of small unglamorous actions.

annotations.span: the first stage of which has gone in
annotations.label: Relative clause with a preposition
annotations.why: 'The first stage of which' is one structure worth having ready.

annotations.span: I'd sooner discover at twenty-six whether I can manage somewhere else than spend my forties wondering
annotations.label: A long comparison held together correctly
annotations.why: Sustaining one complex sentence beats three short accurate ones.

annotations.span: they're a way of committing to something before you've worked out how to justify it
annotations.label: Defines the category at the close
annotations.why: Ending on what plans are, not on your plan, lifts the whole turn.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
Nothing very original: I'd like to be working outside this country within two years. Ireland is the front runner and Canada is what I'd do if Ireland didn't work out.

I can put a date on when it stopped being a daydream, because it was one conversation. A cousin of mine has been in a Dublin hospital for three years, and when he came home last summer he told me, in a fairly blunt way, that the only obstacle in front of me was my own belief that there was one. That was annoying and it was also correct.

Since then it's been slow, unglamorous progress. There's about four thousand put away, which sounds better than it is — it covers roughly half the move once you allow for two months' rent up front. There's this exam, which I can't speed up. And there's the registration, stage one of which is submitted and which apparently sits in a queue for the best part of a year.

Why it matters is the part I've had to think hardest about. Money is the answer people expect and it's not really the true one. The truth is I've never lived anywhere but here, and I would much rather establish at twenty-six that I can't cope somewhere else than sit at forty-five still wondering. My mother would prefer I stayed. She isn't wrong to feel that, and a feeling still isn't an argument. A plan of this sort isn't a forecast at all — it's a way of committing to something well before you can justify it.

what_lifts_it.point: Chained relatives and a self-referring noun clause, both arriving at conversational speed.
'Front runner', 'unglamorous', 'sits in a queue' — spoken register held for two minutes.
Concession and rebuttal land inside one sentence rather than across two.

annotations.span: the only obstacle in front of me was my own belief that there was one
annotations.label: A noun clause looping back on itself
annotations.why: 'Belief that there was one' points back at 'obstacle'; the loop is the point.

annotations.span: stage one of which is submitted and which apparently sits in a queue
annotations.label: Two 'which' clauses chained on one noun
annotations.why: Chain relatives instead of starting a new sentence; the list keeps moving.

annotations.span: slow, unglamorous progress
annotations.label: Two adjectives that refuse to flatter
annotations.why: Describe your own effort accurately and the plan starts sounding real.

annotations.span: which sounds better than it is
annotations.label: Undercuts the number as you give it
annotations.why: Qualify a figure in the same breath and you stop sounding boastful.

annotations.span: She isn't wrong to feel that, and a feeling still isn't an argument.
annotations.label: Concedes and holds in one sentence
annotations.why: Grant the position, then separate the feeling from the argument.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Say why it matters for thirty seconds. That bullet carries the band and it currently has one clause.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Present perfect for what you've done, future forms for what's left. Keep them apart and the answer organises itself.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Date the decision to one conversation. A plan with an origin is more convincing than a plan with a reason.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Separate the feeling from the argument when you concede: she isn't wrong to feel it, and a feeling still isn't an argument.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about an advice which my manager gave to me. It was my first job and I was twenty-three years old.

In that time I was very shy in the meetings. Before I say something, always I say sorry. Sorry, maybe this is a stupid question, or sorry, I don't know if this is correct. I do this every time, in every meeting.

One day after a meeting my manager called me to her desk. She was not angry, she was very calm. She said to me, why you are saying sorry before you speak? And she said, when you say sorry first, people don't listen to your idea, they only hear the sorry. It was a little bit hard for me but she is right.

After that I try to stop. In the beginning it was very difficult and I forget many times. But after some months it became more normal for me.

Now in the meetings I just say my idea directly. And I think people listen more. So this is the advice which changed something for me.

what_caps_it.point: 'An advice' in the first sentence, and every judgement is 'difficult', 'hard' or 'normal'.
The past narrative runs in the present, and the reported question keeps question word order.
The habit is described three times over, and the close repeats the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a piece of advice my first manager gave me, which I got when I was about twenty-three and which I still think about.

At that point I'd been in the job maybe six months and I was pretty nervous in meetings. What I'd got into the habit of doing was apologising before I said anything — sorry, this might be a silly question, sorry, I'm probably wrong about this. I wasn't even aware I was doing it.

She called me over one afternoon, perfectly pleasantly, and she asked me why I kept saying sorry before I opened my mouth, which I hadn't expected at all. Then she said something that landed: when you apologise first, people stop listening to the idea and start listening to the apology. Which was uncomfortable, because it was so obviously true.

What I did about it was fairly mechanical. For roughly two months I wrote the word 'sorry' at the top of my notebook before every meeting, purely so that I'd catch myself. I still slipped up constantly for the first few weeks, but by about the spring of that year it had more or less gone.

The difference it made wasn't really about meetings at all. It was that I'd been treating my own opinions as things that needed apologising for, and once somebody had pointed that out I couldn't stop seeing it. I'd say the best advice I've been given has all been like that — not new information, just somebody naming a habit I was too close to notice.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect, a fronted 'what I'd got into the habit of', and a correct reported question.
'Something that landed', 'slipped up', 'too close to notice' replace flat adjectives.
The advice sits quoted at the centre, and the close generalises about advice itself.

annotations.why: 'A piece of advice' is worth learning whole; the error version is very audible.

annotations.why: 'What I'd got into the habit of doing was ___' can carry any bad habit.

annotations.span: asked me why I kept saying sorry before I opened my mouth
annotations.label: Reported question in statement order
annotations.why: Report questions rather than quoting them; the word order alone earns credit.

annotations.span: Then she said something that landed
annotations.label: One verb does the whole reaction
annotations.why: 'It landed' beats 'it was very shocking for me' in every register.

annotations.span: What I did about it was fairly mechanical.
annotations.label: Announces the third bullet
annotations.why: Saying the bullet out loud stops you skipping the practical step.

annotations.span: I still slipped up constantly for the first few weeks
annotations.label: A phrasal verb for small repeated errors
annotations.why: 'Slip up' fits any habit you're trying and failing to break.

annotations.span: The difference it made wasn't really about meetings at all.
annotations.label: Separates the surface from the real change
annotations.why: 'It wasn't really about ___' is the single most useful evaluating move here.

annotations.label: Closes on a general claim
annotations.why: Say what good advice is, rather than repeating what yours was.

model_answers.transcript:
The piece of advice I keep coming back to came from my first manager, when I was twenty-three and roughly six months into the job.

I was nervous in meetings, and the way that came out was a compulsive apology in front of anything I said — sorry, this may be a stupid question, sorry, I've probably misunderstood. It was so habitual that I'd have denied doing it.

She took me aside one afternoon, entirely without malice, and asked me why I apologised before I had said a single word. Then she put it in a way I've never quite managed to forget: apologise first and people stop attending to the idea, because they're busy attending to the apology. It was an unpleasant thing to hear, mostly because it was unanswerable.

The remedy was crude. For a couple of months I wrote the word at the top of every page of notes, simply in order to catch myself in the act, and it took until roughly the spring of that year before it stopped surfacing altogether.

What she'd actually done, though, wasn't correct a verbal tic. She'd pointed out that I treated my own opinions as things requiring permission, and once that has been said to you it cannot be unsaid. Which is, I think, what separates advice worth having from the other kind. The useful sort tells you nothing you didn't know; it simply names a habit you were standing too close to see.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive perfect — 'once that has been said' — and a fronted 'what she'd actually done'.
'Compulsive apology', 'without malice', 'verbal tic' are precise rather than rare.
It divides what was said from what it did, then defines good advice at the close.

annotations.span: It was so habitual that I'd have denied doing it.
annotations.label: Result clause with a past modal
annotations.why: 'So ___ that I'd have ___' shows degree and hypothesis in one sentence.

annotations.span: entirely without malice
annotations.label: Three words replace a whole clause
annotations.why: Precision compresses; it does not decorate.

annotations.span: What she'd actually done, though, wasn't correct a verbal tic.
annotations.label: Fronting sets up the reveal
annotations.why: 'What X had really done was ___' delays the point and holds attention.

annotations.span: once that has been said to you it cannot be unsaid
annotations.label: Two passives carrying an abstract claim
annotations.why: The passive is the natural voice for things that happen to you.

annotations.span: The remedy was crude.
annotations.label: A four-word sentence resets the pace
annotations.why: After a long sentence, a very short one is heard as emphasis.

annotations.span: it simply names a habit you were standing too close to see
annotations.label: Defines the category at the end
annotations.why: Close by saying what the thing is, not what happened to you.

title: A time you had to wait a long time for something

how long the wait went on

How you felt, and how that changed.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a time when I wait very long in the airport. It was two years ago and I go home for Christmas.

My flight is at seven o'clock in the evening. When I come to the airport, on the screen it says delayed. Nobody tell us anything. After two hours they say the flight is cancelled and there is another plane in the morning.

So we wait all the night in the airport. The restaurants close at eleven. There was only one machine with chocolate. I sit on the floor with my bag.

Near me there was an old man from my city and we talk. He was very calm. More calm than me.

In the morning at eight o'clock we go in the plane. It was very long, maybe eleven hours.

I was very tired and angry. That's all.

The present simple runs through a story that is explicitly two years old.
'Very long', 'very tired', 'very calm' — the intensifier does all the work, three times over.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a time when I wait very long in the airport. It was two years ago and I am going home for Christmas.

My flight was at seven o'clock in the evening. When I come to the airport, the screen says delayed. Everybody is waiting and nobody tells us anything. After two hours they said the flight is cancelled and we have to wait for another plane in the morning.

So we waited in the airport all the night. There was no hotel and no food after eleven o'clock, only one machine with chocolate in it. I sat on the floor near my bag with an old man from my city and we talked about many things. He was very calm, more calm than me.

Finally at eight o'clock in the morning we went on the plane. It was eleven hours in total.

At the end I was very tired and angry, but also a little bit funny, because now it is a story I tell to my friends. So this is the time when I wait a long time.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a night I spent at an airport a couple of years ago, waiting for a flight home at Christmas.

The flight was supposed to leave at seven in the evening. By the time I got there the board already said delayed, which nobody seemed able to explain, and for the first two hours we just stood around watching it. Then they announced that the flight was cancelled and that we'd be put on something the following morning.

What made it hard wasn't the delay itself. It was that the airport more or less closed around us — the food places shut at eleven, there were no hotel rooms left within an hour's drive, and after midnight there was nobody at any desk to ask. So about sixty of us spent the night on the floor of a departure gate.

I ended up sitting next to a man in his seventies who was travelling to the same city, and we talked, on and off, for about seven hours. He was infinitely calmer about it than I was, which I found slightly annoying at three in the morning and rather admirable by six.

We finally boarded at eight, which made it eleven hours altogether. By that point I was too tired to be angry, and honestly the whole thing has turned into something I rather enjoy telling people about. Which is the odd thing about waiting — it's unbearable while it's happening and it becomes a story about ten minutes after it stops.

what_lifts_it.point: A reported passive, a cleft naming the real difficulty, and a comparative with a full clause.
'Stood around', 'shut at eleven', 'on and off' replace bare adjectives throughout.
One cleft reorganises the middle, and the close abstracts away from the night.

annotations.label: Names the event and the time at once
annotations.why: One opening clause fixes both the tense and the scale of the story.

annotations.span: the board already said delayed, which nobody seemed able to explain
annotations.label: A relative clause adds the frustration
annotations.why: Hang 'which nobody could ___' onto any fact to comment on it.

annotations.span: we'd be put on something the following morning
annotations.label: Reported passive, correctly backshifted
annotations.why: Use the passive when an organisation does something to you.

annotations.span: What made it hard wasn't the delay itself.
annotations.label: Cleft reorganises the whole middle
annotations.why: 'What made it ___ wasn't ___' turns a list of events into an argument.

annotations.span: the airport more or less closed around us
annotations.label: One image replaces three facts
annotations.why: A physical description of a situation reads as fluent, not decorative.

annotations.span: on and off, for about seven hours
annotations.label: A chunk describing intermittent time
annotations.why: 'On and off' fits anything that happened repeatedly but not continuously.

annotations.span: He was infinitely calmer about it than I was
annotations.label: Comparative closed with a full clause
annotations.why: 'Than I was' rather than 'than me' is a small, very audible upgrade.

annotations.span: slightly annoying at three in the morning and rather admirable by six
annotations.label: The same thing judged twice
annotations.why: Judging one thing differently at two times gives you a free contrast.

annotations.span: it's unbearable while it's happening and it becomes a story about ten minutes after it stops
annotations.label: Closes on a general claim
annotations.why: Ending above the anecdote is the cheapest lift available in Part 2.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The wait I'd describe is a night at an airport a couple of winters ago, for a flight that in the end left thirteen hours late.

It was due out at seven in the evening. The board said delayed from the moment I arrived, with no explanation attached to it, and there is a particular kind of standing about that airports produce — you can't leave, you can't settle, and you can't find anybody to ask. At around nine they cancelled it outright and told us we would be re-booked onto a morning service.

What made the night difficult wasn't the delay so much as the way the building shut down around us. The last food place closed at eleven. Every hotel within an hour was full. From midnight there was not one member of staff on that floor, which meant sixty-odd people were left waiting with nobody to be annoyed at.

I spent most of it beside a man in his seventies heading to the same city, who was so entirely unbothered that I found him irritating at three and rather impressive by six. We boarded a little after eight, thirteen hours after the flight had been due to leave.

I was well past anger by then, and past most other things as well. And it has since become one of those episodes I'm oddly fond of — which is the strange economics of waiting: it costs you everything while it lasts and pays you back afterwards, in stories.

what_lifts_it.point: An existential 'there is a particular kind of' and a 'so ___ that' clause do compound work.
'Standing about', 'sixty-odd', 'well past anger' are spoken rather than written register.
Three short sentences stage the collapse, and the close is a general claim.

annotations.span: there is a particular kind of standing about that airports produce
annotations.label: Existential plus a defining clause
annotations.why: 'There's a particular kind of ___ that ___' names an experience precisely.

annotations.span: you can't leave, you can't settle, and you can't find anybody to ask
annotations.label: Three parallel clauses in one breath group
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across the first two and fall on the third.

annotations.span: sixty-odd people were left waiting with nobody to be annoyed at
annotations.label: 'Sixty-odd' and a dry ending clause
annotations.why: Approximating with '-odd' is natural spoken English and costs nothing.

annotations.span: so entirely unbothered that I found him irritating at three and rather impressive by six
annotations.label: 'So ___ that' carrying a double judgement
annotations.why: One structure delivers degree and contrast at the same time.

annotations.span: I was well past anger by then
annotations.label: A state described as a place
annotations.why: 'Well past ___' is more precise than any adjective for exhaustion.

annotations.span: it costs you everything while it lasts and pays you back afterwards, in stories
annotations.label: An abstract close with a shape
annotations.why: Two balanced halves make a general claim sound considered rather than tacked on.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
The wait I'd describe is a night at an airport a couple of winters ago, for a flight that in the end left thirteen hours late.

It was due out at seven in the evening. The board said delayed from the moment I arrived, with nothing attached by way of explanation, and airports produce a particular kind of standing about — you can't leave, you can't settle, and there's nobody to ask. At around nine they cancelled it outright and told us we'd be re-booked onto a morning service.

What made the night hard wasn't the delay so much as the way the building shut down around us. The last food place closed at eleven. Every hotel within an hour was full. From midnight there wasn't one member of staff on that floor, which meant sixty-odd people were left waiting with nobody even to be annoyed at.

I spent most of it beside a man in his seventies heading for the same city, so entirely unbothered by any of it that I found him irritating at three and rather impressive by six. We boarded a little after eight, thirteen hours after we should have gone.

I was well past anger by then, and past most other things as well. And it's since become one of those nights I'm oddly fond of — which is the strange economics of waiting. It costs you everything while it's happening and pays you back afterwards, in stories, at a rate nobody would accept in advance.

what_lifts_it.point: 'So…that' across a long complement and an emphatic 'not one', neither of them laboured.
The closing metaphor runs three clauses without a single decorative word in it.
Band 8 named the paradox; this states it as a rule and then puts a price on it.

annotations.why: Keep the 'that' clause even when the 'so' phrase runs long; it holds the sentence.

annotations.span: there wasn't one member of staff on that floor
annotations.label: 'Not one' as an emphatic singular
annotations.why: 'Not one' is stronger than 'none' and takes a singular verb after it.

annotations.span: the strange economics of waiting
annotations.label: An abstract noun frames the close
annotations.why: Borrow a word from another field and the sentence after it writes itself.

annotations.span: nobody even to be annoyed at
annotations.label: Precise absurdity in six words
annotations.why: Say what you were deprived of rather than what you felt.

annotations.span: at a rate nobody would accept in advance
annotations.label: Extends the metaphor one step and stops
annotations.why: Push an image one clause further than expected, then end. Don't explain it.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Add the second half of the night. Between eleven and eight there is a whole minute of missing story.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Give clock times instead of 'very long'. 'Seven in the evening until eight the next morning' does the work for you.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Say what made it hard other than the delay — the shut cafés, the empty desks. Cause beats complaint.

I want to talk about a conversation with my neighbour. It was three years ago in the winter, in my building.

That day there was no electricity in all the street. It was six o'clock and outside it is already dark. So the people go out on the stairs with candles and telephones.

There I meet the man from the flat over me. Before this, four years, we only say hello in the lift. Nothing more. But that evening we talk two hours.

He tell me many things. He worked on ships twenty years and he saw many countries. And his wife died five years before, so now he is alone. I don't know nothing about this.

I want to talk about a conversation with my neighbour. It happened maybe three years ago in my building, in the winter.

That day there was a power cut in the whole street. It was about six o'clock and it was already dark outside. Nobody has light, so many people go out to the corridor and the stairs with candles and their phones.

I meet there the man who lives above me. Before this, in four years, we only said hello in the lift, that's all. But that evening we talked maybe two hours on the stairs.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a conversation I had with a neighbour about three years ago, which I still think about rather more than I'd have expected to.

It happened during a power cut, one evening in January. The whole street went dark at about six, and because nobody could do anything indoors, most of the building ended up out on the stairwell with candles and phone torches, waiting for it to come back on.

I got talking to the man who lives directly above me. Up until that evening we'd exchanged nothing but hello in the lift for four years — I couldn't have told you his first name. We ended up sitting on the stairs for the best part of two hours.

He'd spent twenty years at sea, on cargo ships, which I'd had no idea about, and he'd been to places I've only ever read about. And somewhere in the middle of it he mentioned, entirely in passing, that his wife had died five years earlier and that the flat had been very quiet since. He wasn't asking for sympathy about it; he was answering a question I'd put to him.

The reason it's stayed with me isn't really the sailing. It's that I'd lived twelve feet below somebody for four years and had never once found out a single thing about him, and it took a power cut to fix that. We talk properly now — not hello, actual conversations. Which tells you something faintly uncomfortable about how much of a conversation is simply circumstances.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect carries all the background, and 'I couldn't have told you' adds a past modal.
'Got talking to', 'entirely in passing', 'the best part of two hours' replace vague nouns.
The fourth bullet is named, and the close makes a claim rather than a summary.

annotations.label: Person and time in the first clause
annotations.why: Two facts in the opening let you spend the rest of the turn on content.

annotations.span: I got talking to the man who lives directly above me
annotations.label: The exact chunk for an unplanned start
annotations.why: 'Get talking to' means it wasn't arranged, which is the whole point here.

annotations.span: Up until that evening we'd exchanged nothing but hello in the lift for four years
annotations.label: Past perfect covering four years
annotations.why: One 'we'd ___ for ___' sentence does all the background at once.

annotations.span: I couldn't have told you his first name
annotations.label: Past modal proving the point
annotations.why: 'I couldn't have told you ___' is stronger than 'I didn't know him well'.

annotations.span: entirely in passing
annotations.label: Two words describe how it was said
annotations.why: Saying how something was mentioned is more informative than the mention.

annotations.span: that his wife had died five years earlier
annotations.label: Past perfect plus 'earlier', not 'before'
annotations.why: Inside a past story, use 'earlier' or 'previously' rather than 'before'.

annotations.span: The reason it's stayed with me isn't really the sailing.
annotations.label: Announces the last bullet and reframes
annotations.why: Saying what it isn't about buys you a whole sentence and sounds considered.

annotations.span: it took a power cut to fix that
annotations.label: 'It took X to Y' delivers the irony
annotations.why: The structure lets a small cause carry a large consequence.

annotations.label: Closes on a general claim
annotations.why: End above the story; it is the cheapest lift available in the last ten seconds.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The conversation I'd pick took place on a staircase during a power cut, three winters ago, and it went on for something like two hours.

The whole street lost power at six on a January evening and, since there was nothing to be done indoors, most of the building drifted out onto the landings with candles and phones. Among them was the man from the flat directly above mine, with whom, in four years, I had exchanged precisely nothing beyond a nod in the lift.

We sat on the stairs and talked until the lights came back. It emerged that he'd spent two decades at sea on cargo ships and had been to half the ports I've only ever read about, and that his wife had died five years earlier — which he mentioned in the same tone he'd been using for the shipping. He wasn't seeking sympathy. He was answering what I'd asked.

What has stayed with me isn't the biography. It's that I had lived twelve feet beneath a man for four years without discovering one thing about him, and that it took a failure of the electricity supply to correct that. We speak properly now, which is its own small indictment.

I've since come round to the view that most conversations which never happen aren't prevented by dislike, or even by shyness. They're prevented by there never being an occasion — and occasions turn out to be remarkably easy to arrange.

what_lifts_it.point: 'With whom' and 'it emerged that' compress background band 7 spread over three sentences.
'Drifted out', 'its own small indictment', 'come round to the view' choose register deliberately.
The close states a general position about conversation instead of summarising the evening.

annotations.span: with whom, in four years, I had exchanged precisely nothing beyond a nod in the lift
annotations.label: Relative clause with a fronted preposition
annotations.why: 'With whom' is worth having for exactly one sentence per turn.

annotations.span: It emerged that he'd spent two decades at sea on cargo ships
annotations.label: 'It emerged that' introduces reported facts
annotations.why: The structure lets you report several facts without saying 'he told me' repeatedly.

annotations.span: which he mentioned in the same tone he'd been using for the shipping
annotations.label: Describes the delivery, not the content
annotations.why: Noting how something was said is the most transferable observation here.

annotations.span: He wasn't seeking sympathy. He was answering what I'd asked.
annotations.label: Two short parallel sentences
annotations.why: Matching rhythm across two short sentences makes the contrast audible.

annotations.span: it took a failure of the electricity supply to correct that
annotations.label: Formal register used for dry effect
annotations.why: Deliberately over-formal wording is a joke a native speaker would make.

annotations.span: They're prevented by there never being an occasion
annotations.label: Names the real obstacle at the close
annotations.why: Explaining the cause rather than deploring the effect is the band-8 finish.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
Three winters ago the electricity went off across our whole street, and I spent the next two hours on a staircase talking to somebody I had never really spoken to.

It went at six on a January evening. Nothing could be done indoors, so the building emptied itself onto the landings with candles and phones held up like torches. Standing on the half-landing was the man from the flat immediately above mine — a man I had lived under for four years and greeted, in that time, with nothing more articulate than a nod in the lift.

We sat down on the stairs and stayed there until the lights came on. Twenty years at sea on cargo ships, it emerged, and half the ports I've only ever seen on a map. Somewhere in the middle he said that his wife had died five years before and the flat had been quiet since, delivered in precisely the voice he'd been using for the shipping. He wasn't fishing for anything. He was answering a question I'd put to him.

The part that won't leave me isn't his life. It's the four years. I lived twelve feet under a man and learned nothing whatever about him, and it took a substation failing to fix that. We hold actual conversations now, which is less flattering than it sounds.

I've concluded since then that the conversations that don't happen are almost never about dislike, and not usually about shyness either. They don't happen because nothing ever puts the two of you in the same place with nothing to do. Which, it turns out, is astonishingly easy to arrange — if it occurs to anybody to arrange it.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted participle with inversion and a verbless clause, both entirely conversational.
'Articulate', 'fishing for', 'a substation failing' — exact where band 8 was merely good.
The final clause withdraws the neatness the sentence before it supplied.

annotations.span: Standing on the half-landing was the man from the flat immediately above mine
annotations.label: Fronted participle forces inversion
annotations.why: Put the position first and the verb follows, so the new person lands last.

annotations.span: Twenty years at sea on cargo ships, it emerged, and half the ports
annotations.label: Verbless clause with an interruption inside
annotations.why: Drop the verb entirely and let the interruption carry the grammar.

annotations.span: greeted, in that time, with nothing more articulate than a nod
annotations.label: 'Articulate' applied to a gesture
annotations.why: Move a word off its usual noun and it does work it couldn't do before.

annotations.span: which is less flattering than it sounds
annotations.label: Undercuts a nice fact in six words
annotations.why: Deny yourself the credit and the observation becomes believable.

annotations.span: if it occurs to anybody to arrange it
annotations.label: A deflating clause after a tidy ending
annotations.why: Spoil your own conclusion slightly; it stops the turn sounding rehearsed.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Add what he actually said. Report two things in his words and the turn gains thirty seconds.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Every duration here needs a perfect tense — 'he'd been my neighbour for four years'. Fix those and the grammar mark moves.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Say how he said the difficult part, not only what he said. Tone is the detail this card wants.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Undercut your own conclusion in the last clause. A tidy ending sounds prepared; a slightly spoiled one does not.
