title: A friend you have known the longest

payload_json.topic: A friend you have known the longest

cue_card.topic: Describe a friend you have known longer than anyone else.
bullets: who this person is
how the two of you first met
what you usually do together now
and explain why you think the friendship has lasted.
rounding_off: Do the two of you live near each other now?
Is there anybody else you've known almost as long?

teaching.band_move: Characterise, don't narrate. For every fact about her life, add one sentence about what she's like.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Don't rank your friends. Take whoever you've known longest, even if you aren't close now — length is the card, not closeness.
prep_plan.trap: This card pulls candidates into a life story. The examiner needs a character, not a chronology.

time_plan.goal: Name her and fix how long you've known her.
Who she is, and the ordinary way you met.
What contact actually looks like now, concretely.
Why it lasted: one honest reason, not three vague ones.
One sentence about long friendships generally.

recovery_moves.prompt: Describe her — how she talks, what she wears, what she finds funny.
Say what she was like at fifteen, and how much of that survived.
Bring in a third person: who else knows both of you, and what they say.
Say plainly whether you'd choose her as a friend if you met today.

error_watchlist.wrong: I know her since twenty-two years.
error_watchlist.right: I've known her for twenty-two years.
error_watchlist.why: 'For' takes a length; 'since' takes a start point.

error_watchlist.wrong: We meet when we are six and then we go to the same school.
error_watchlist.right: We met when we were six and then we went to the same school.
error_watchlist.why: Anchor the meeting in the past and stay there.

error_watchlist.wrong: She is a very friend person.
error_watchlist.right: She's a very friendly person.
error_watchlist.why: 'Friend' is the noun; the adjective is 'friendly'.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Character adjectives are long words, and this card runs on very little else.

target_words.note: Four syllables, stress on the second.
Stress the second syllable, not the first.
The stress lands on the last part.
Three syllables, stress first, ending is weak.
Stress the second syllable; the fourth is swallowed.

chunking_drill.sentence: She grew up in the house next door, which is the whole reason we met.
chunks: She grew up in the house next door,
which is the whole reason
we met.

minimal_pairs.contrast: two syllables against one — a very common slip

teaching.examiner_note: Nothing you say here will be acknowledged. The examiner is writing, not listening for interest, and will cut in at two minutes without any warning.

swap_slots.span: more than twenty years now
swap_slots.prompt: Your own duration. Give a number of years, not 'a long time'.

swap_slots.span: She grew up in the house next door, which is the whole reason we met.
swap_slots.prompt: Your own person and the accident that put you together — one concrete circumstance, never 'we just met'.

swap_slots.span: long, rambling ones, usually recorded while one of us is walking somewhere
swap_slots.prompt: How you actually keep in contact now. One specific habit, described precisely enough to picture.

swap_slots.span: she knew me before I had any image to protect
swap_slots.prompt: Your own honest reason the friendship survived. It has to be specific to these two people.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now run the same three moves — who, how you met, why it lasted — about somebody you've known only a year. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my best friend. She is my oldest friend. We are friends since we are six years old.

She lived in the next house. So we play together every day when we are children. After, we go to different school, but we still meet.

Now she is not living here. She go to another city for her work. So we don't meet. We send messages, sometimes long messages. Last year we go to the sea for three days. It was very nice.

Why we are still friends, because she is very nice. And she know me long time. I don't must explain. And my mother like her also.

So this is my friend that I know the longest time. Yes. That's all.

what_caps_it.point: The turn dries up at about seventy seconds and hands the examiner back a full minute.
Present and past swap places in almost every sentence; no tense survives two clauses.
'Nice' does three separate jobs and nothing else is attempted anywhere.

annotations.span: She lived in the next house.
annotations.label: One clean, correct sentence
annotations.why: Keep this. A short accurate sentence is worth more than a long broken one.

annotations.span: We are friends since we are six years old.
annotations.label: Duration needs the present perfect
annotations.why: Say 'We've been friends since we were six.' 'Since' pulls a perfect tense.

annotations.span: She go to another city for her work.
annotations.label: Verb left completely unmarked
annotations.why: Say 'She moved to another city for work.' Pick a tense and mark the verb.

annotations.span: I don't must explain.
annotations.label: Two modals stacked together
annotations.why: Say 'I don't have to explain myself.' 'Must' has no 'don't' form.

annotations.span: It was very nice.
annotations.label: The only evaluation in the whole turn
annotations.why: Say what happened: 'we did almost nothing, which was the point.'

annotations.span: So this is my friend that I know the longest time. Yes. That's all.
annotations.label: Hands the turn back a minute early
annotations.why: Use rung one instead: describe one thing you did on that trip.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my oldest friend. She is a girl who was living next door to my family. We know each other since we are six years old, so it is a very long time.

When we were children we played together every day. We ride our bicycles in the street and we went to the same primary school. After that we go to different secondary schools, but we still met in the weekends, so we never stopped being friends.

Now she is living in another city because of her work. So we don't meet very often, maybe two times in a year. But we send voice messages and sometimes they are very long. And in the summer she comes back and we do something together. Last year we went to the coast for three days and it was very nice.

I think our friendship is lasting because she is a very nice person. She is also very easy, I don't need to explain myself with her. And she knows my family also, my mother likes her very much, so it is comfortable. So this is my oldest friend and why we are still friends until now.

what_caps_it.point: Five sentences begin with 'so'; the answer reads as a list of facts, not a portrait.
The tense slides between past and present four times inside one short story.
'Nice', 'easy', 'comfortable' — the whole characterisation runs on three flat adjectives.

annotations.span: I want to talk about my oldest friend.
annotations.label: Names the subject in six words
annotations.why: Keep this — it puts the examiner on-task before you've decided anything else.

annotations.span: We know each other since we are six years old
annotations.label: Duration needs the present perfect
annotations.why: Say 'We've known each other since we were six' — it started then and still holds.

annotations.span: We ride our bicycles in the street
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Fix the tense in your first sentence, then hold it for two minutes.

annotations.span: she is a very nice person
annotations.label: One flat adjective doing all the work
annotations.why: Replace 'nice' with what she actually does: 'she never keeps score'.

annotations.span: So this is my oldest friend and why we are still friends until now.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the card
annotations.why: Close on an idea about friendship, not on the wording of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The friend I want to talk about is somebody I've known longer than anyone outside my family — we've been friends since we were six, so that's more than twenty years now.

She grew up in the house next door, which is the whole reason we met. There was nothing chosen about it: our parents put us on the same street, we got on, and by the time we were about eight we were more or less inseparable. We went to different secondary schools, and I remember being genuinely worried that we'd drift apart, but somehow it never happened. We simply went back to the same street every afternoon, and that was that.

These days it's a lot more low-key. She moved away for work about six years ago, so we're down to voice notes — long, rambling ones, usually recorded while one of us is walking somewhere — plus one proper trip a year. It sounds thin written down, but it has turned out to be plenty. Last summer we spent three days on the coast and barely did anything, which was the point.

As for why it's lasted, I have actually thought about this. It isn't that we have a huge amount in common; honestly, we don't. It's that she knew me before I had any image to protect, so there's nothing to perform. And neither of us keeps score — if six months go by, nobody's counting. There's a version of this where the two of us would have let it fade quietly, and I'm well aware of that. What you can't manufacture is a shared history, and that's really all it comes down to.

what_lifts_it.point: 'We've been friends since' fixes the duration, and the narrative then stays reliably in the past.
'Drift apart', 'low-key', 'keeps score' — chunks and precise phrases replace 'nice' and 'easy'.
Three signposted moves, and a close that generalises instead of restating the card.

annotations.span: The friend I want to talk about is somebody I've known longer than anyone outside my family
annotations.label: Answers the card in one clause
annotations.why: Say who and how long before anything else; it buys you the rest of the turn.

annotations.span: we've been friends since we were six
annotations.label: Present perfect for a live duration
annotations.why: Use it whenever the situation began in the past and is still true today.

annotations.span: There was nothing chosen about it
annotations.label: Comments on the fact instead of listing it
annotations.why: One line of commentary after a fact turns description into characterisation.

annotations.span: by the time we were about eight we were more or less inseparable
annotations.label: Time clause anchors the jump forward
annotations.why: 'By the time…' lets you skip years without losing the listener.

annotations.span: we'd drift apart
annotations.label: 'Drift apart' is one item, not two words
annotations.why: Reuse it for any relationship that fades without an argument.

annotations.span: As for why it's lasted, I have actually thought about this.
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet out loud
annotations.why: Naming the move stops you skipping the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: neither of us keeps score
annotations.label: A chunk instead of 'she is easy'
annotations.why: Describe the behaviour and the flat adjective becomes unnecessary.

annotations.span: which was the point
annotations.label: Falls away after a short pause
annotations.why: A dropped final phrase carries dry humour that flat delivery loses.

annotations.span: What you can't manufacture is a shared history
annotations.label: Cleft sentence puts one idea in focus
annotations.why: Front the 'what' clause when you want a single idea to land hard.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd pick is the friend I've had longest — we've been in each other's lives since we were six, which is going on twenty-five years.

It was pure accident. She lived in the house next door, our parents were friendly, and we were simply handed to each other the way the children of neighbours are. What I find interesting, looking back, is that we've never had a great deal in common. Different subjects, different politics, different taste in almost everything. Had we met at twenty rather than at six, I doubt we'd have got past a polite conversation. The friendship predates every opinion either of us currently holds.

She moved away for work some years ago, so the shape of it has changed. It runs on voice notes now — the sort you record while walking, twelve minutes long and about nothing — plus one trip a year where we deliberately do as little as possible. The frequency has dropped and the weight of it hasn't, which I genuinely had not expected.

As to why it's survived, I think it comes down to her having known me before I'd built anything to defend. There's no version of me she hasn't already watched fail, which is oddly restful. Neither of us keeps a ledger, either; six months of silence isn't held against anybody. And that, I suspect, is what people actually mean by an old friend — not somebody you see often, but somebody in front of whom you don't have to be anyone in particular.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion — 'Had we met…' — replaces the standard conditional band 7 never reaches for.
'Handed to each other', 'keeps a ledger', 'oddly restful' — precise rather than decorative.
Closes on a definition of old friendship, not on this particular friendship.

annotations.span: Had we met at twenty rather than at six
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as a third conditional, higher register, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: we were simply handed to each other
annotations.label: One image replaces three sentences
annotations.why: Reach for the verb that does the work and you need fewer of them.

annotations.span: Neither of us keeps a ledger
annotations.label: A metaphor used where a native would
annotations.why: One well-placed image beats five ornamental idioms.

annotations.span: twelve minutes long and about nothing
annotations.label: The list runs on one falling contour
annotations.why: Group short items into a single run and fall on the last one.

annotations.span: not somebody you see often, but somebody in front of whom you don't have to be anyone in particular
annotations.label: Ends on a definition, not a summary
annotations.why: Abstracting in the final sentence lifts the whole turn out of anecdote.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
The friend I'd pick is the one I've had longest by some distance — we met at six and we're both now the wrong side of thirty, so it's most of a lifetime.

There was nothing chosen about it. She lived next door, our parents got on, and we were handed to each other the way the children of neighbours always are. What interests me, looking back, is how little we have in common: different subjects, different politics, different taste in more or less everything. Had we met at twenty we'd have managed one polite conversation and left it there. The friendship simply predates every opinion either of us now holds.

She moved away for work some years ago, so its shape has changed. It runs on voice notes — the sort you record while walking, twelve minutes long and about nothing in particular — plus one trip a year on which we make a point of doing as little as possible. The frequency has dropped through the floor and the weight of it hasn't shifted at all.

As to why it's held, I think it comes down to her having known me before I'd built anything worth defending. There's no version of me she hasn't already watched fall over, which is oddly restful. Nor does either of us keep a ledger — six months of silence goes unremarked and uncharged. And that is what people are reaching for when they say 'an old friend': not somebody you see a great deal of, but somebody in front of whom you're excused from being anyone in particular.

what_lifts_it.point: Inverted conditional and fronted 'Nor' arrive without a change of pace or pitch.
'Dropped through the floor', 'unremarked and uncharged' — figurative but exact, never decorative.
The shape is carried by rhythm rather than markers; nothing needs signposting.

annotations.span: Had we met at twenty we'd have managed one polite conversation
annotations.label: Inverted conditional at full speed
annotations.why: Drop 'if' and invert. It costs no extra words and reads as effortless.

annotations.span: Nor does either of us keep a ledger
annotations.label: Negative fronting with inversion
annotations.why: Start a clause with 'Nor' and invert the verb to link two negatives.

annotations.span: goes unremarked and uncharged
annotations.label: Two words doing two different jobs
annotations.why: Pair words that add, don't repeat; 'uncharged' carries the ledger image forward.

annotations.span: the wrong side of thirty
annotations.label: Idiom used because it fits
annotations.why: One natural idiom in the opening beats three assembled later on.

annotations.span: excused from being anyone in particular
annotations.label: Closes on a definition, not a summary
annotations.why: End by defining the thing itself; it lifts the turn out of anecdote.

annotations.span: different subjects, different politics, different taste in more or less everything
annotations.label: Three-part list on one breath
annotations.why: Level pitch on the first two, fall on the third. No pause between them.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Don't stop at seventy seconds. Add what you actually did on that trip — three details buy back the missing minute.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Every fact about her life needs a sentence about what she is like. Characterise, don't narrate.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Cut one explanation and put a judgement there instead. 'We've never had much in common' outperforms a paragraph of history.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Stop explaining your own good line. Deliver the observation and move straight on.

note_grid.cell: yr above me, barely knew her
never asked why. admin not drama

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a person who helped me when I had a difficult time. She was a student in the year above me at my college.

The problem was that my father was in the hospital for six weeks and I stopped going to my classes. So I was behind of all my work. I had three essays and I don't do any of them. I am very stressed at that time and I don't tell anybody about it, not even my friends.

Then one day she sends me a message. She is asking me why I am not coming to the Thursday class. I said I have some problems at home. And then she said we can go to the library on Sunday morning and do the work together. So we did that for six weeks. She made a list every week and we do one thing every time.

In the end I finished all the essays and I passed the year. I felt very grateful because she didn't have to do this, we were not even close friends before. She was very kind and very helpful. So this is the person who helped me when I was struggling.

what_caps_it.point: Past and present alternate all the way through, and reported speech never shifts back.
The turn is a chain of events with no evaluation until the last four words.
'Kind', 'helpful' and 'grateful' are the only evaluative words in the whole answer.

annotations.span: She was a student in the year above me at my college.
annotations.label: Places the person immediately
annotations.why: Locating somebody early stops you explaining who they are twice.

annotations.span: I had three essays and I don't do any of them.
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Choose past simple in sentence one and refuse to leave it.

annotations.span: She is asking me why I am not coming to the Thursday class.
annotations.label: Reported speech doesn't shift back
annotations.why: Say 'She asked me why I wasn't coming' — the whole clause moves back.

annotations.span: I was behind of all my work
annotations.label: Wrong preposition in a fixed phrase
annotations.why: It is 'behind with your work'. Learn the preposition inside the chunk.

annotations.span: She was very kind and very helpful.
annotations.label: Two flat adjectives, no behaviour
annotations.why: Say what she did instead: 'she never once asked what had happened'.

annotations.span: So this is the person who helped me when I was struggling.
annotations.label: Ends by reading the card back
annotations.why: Finish on what the episode taught you about accepting help.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd like to talk about is somebody I barely knew at the time, which is partly why it stuck with me. She was a year above me on the same course.

This was during my second year. My father was in hospital for about six weeks, and although it all resolved perfectly well in the end, I more or less stopped functioning while it was going on. I carried on turning up to my job and simply stopped going in to college, and by the time I looked up properly I had three essays outstanding and no idea where to start. I hadn't told a single person either, which made the whole thing considerably worse.

What she did was very small. She sent me a message out of the blue asking why I hadn't been at the Thursday seminar, and when I gave her a vague answer she suggested we meet in the library on Sunday morning. We ended up doing that for six weeks. She'd write a list at the start of each session, we'd get through one thing, and then she'd go off and do her own work.

The part I keep coming back to is that she never once asked me what had happened. She treated the whole thing as admin rather than as a crisis, and that was exactly what I needed, because at that point I couldn't have talked about it anyway. If she'd made a big deal of it, I think I'd have avoided her completely. The useful sort of help, it turns out, is rarely the dramatic sort.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect and a third conditional break up the flat run of past simples.
'Out of the blue', 'stopped functioning' and 'made a big deal of it' carry the evaluation.
Every paragraph opens with a signpost, so the listener always knows which bullet is running.

annotations.span: The person I'd like to talk about is somebody I barely knew at the time
annotations.label: Names the person and the angle at once
annotations.why: Saying why she is interesting stops the turn becoming a list of facts.

annotations.span: by the time I looked up properly I had three essays outstanding
annotations.label: Time clause layers two moments
annotations.why: 'By the time' lets you skip weeks without losing the listener.

annotations.span: What she did was very small.
annotations.label: Previews the next chunk in five words
annotations.why: A short framing sentence buys thinking time and sounds deliberate.

annotations.span: out of the blue
annotations.label: A chunk retrieved whole
annotations.why: Reuse it for anything unexpected: a message, an offer, a visit.

annotations.span: The part I keep coming back to is that
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluation bullet
annotations.why: Say it aloud and you cannot forget the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: she never once asked me what had happened
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'once'
annotations.why: Contrastive stress makes the point without adding a single word.

annotations.span: She treated the whole thing as admin rather than as a crisis
annotations.label: A precise contrast instead of an adjective
annotations.why: Naming what something was not is a cheap way to be exact.

annotations.span: If she'd made a big deal of it, I think I'd have avoided her completely.
annotations.label: Third conditional in its natural home
annotations.why: 'How did it feel' bullets almost always want an unreal past.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I want to describe was, at the time, not far off a stranger. She was a year ahead of me on the same course and we had probably exchanged four sentences in total.

The context is quickly told. My father spent six weeks in hospital during my second year, and although it resolved perfectly well, I quietly went to pieces. I kept turning up to my job and stopped turning up to anything else, and by the point I raised my head I was three essays down with no obvious route back. Nor had I told a soul, which is the part that compounds it.

Her intervention was almost aggressively undramatic. A message arrived asking where I'd got to on Thursday; I gave her a non-answer; she proposed the library, Sunday, nine o'clock. That ran for six weeks. She'd draw up a list, we'd knock off one item, and then she'd get on with her own work and leave me to it.

What has stayed with me is the thing she didn't do. Not once did she ask what had gone wrong. She dealt with it as a scheduling problem rather than an emotional one, which was the only version of help I was capable of accepting. Had she sat me down for a heart-to-heart, I'd have found reasons to be busy for the rest of term. I suspect that generalises: the help that works is rarely the help that looks like helping.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Nor had I' and 'Not once did she' put two inversions where band 7 used plain order.
'Went to pieces', 'knock off one item' and 'a heart-to-heart' sit naturally, not on display.
The close generalises the lesson instead of restating what the person did.

annotations.span: Nor had I told a soul
annotations.label: 'Nor' plus inversion joins two negatives
annotations.why: One of the cheapest ways to sound controlled inside a narrative.

annotations.span: Not once did she ask what had gone wrong.
annotations.label: Negative fronting for emphasis
annotations.why: Put the negative first and invert; it still sounds spoken, not written.

annotations.span: almost aggressively undramatic
annotations.label: An unexpected pairing that is exactly right
annotations.why: Precision at this level comes from the adverb, not from rare nouns.

annotations.span: I quietly went to pieces
annotations.label: Idiom placed where a native would
annotations.why: Two natural idioms in two minutes beat five decorative ones.

annotations.span: she proposed the library, Sunday, nine o'clock
annotations.label: Three items on one falling run
annotations.why: Keep the list level in pitch, then drop on the final item.

annotations.span: the help that works is rarely the help that looks like helping
annotations.label: Ends on a generalisation
annotations.why: Lifting out of the anecdote in the last clause raises the whole turn.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a person who makes me laugh. He is my uncle, he is the youngest brother of my mother, and he is around fifty years old.

He is coming to our house almost every month for lunch. He is a very funny person but he never tell jokes. He just describes normal things. For example one time he was talking about the post office in his town. He was waiting there for twenty minutes and he described everything, the old man in front of him, the woman with the small dog, the machine that was not working. He was talking maybe twenty minutes and everybody was laughing so much.

And the thing is, his face is always serious. He doesn't laugh himself. So this makes it more funny for us.

I like him because when he is there, nobody is arguing. In my family sometimes people argue at lunch about politics and other things. But when my uncle starts to talk, everybody just listen and laugh. Even my cousins who are very shy, they talk more. So he is a very good person to have in the family and this is why he makes me laugh.

what_caps_it.point: Third-person -s disappears repeatedly, and a continuous form is used for a monthly habit.
'Funny', 'good' and 'serious' carry every judgement in the whole turn.
'So' and 'and' link nearly every idea, and the close repeats the prompt.

annotations.span: For example one time he was talking about the post office in his town.
annotations.label: Moves to a concrete example
annotations.why: Keep this. One retold example is worth more than five adjectives.

annotations.span: He is coming to our house almost every month for lunch.
annotations.label: Continuous used for a habit
annotations.why: Repeated events take the present simple: 'He comes to our house every month.'

annotations.span: he never tell jokes
annotations.label: Third-person -s dropped
annotations.why: Habits with he or she always take -s: 'he never tells jokes'.

annotations.span: So this makes it more funny for us.
annotations.label: Wrong comparative form
annotations.why: Say 'funnier'. Two-syllable adjectives in -y take -er, not 'more'.

annotations.span: So he is a very good person to have in the family and this is why he makes me laugh.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: Close on what humour does to a room instead of on the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person who makes me laugh most is my mother's youngest brother, so my uncle. He's in his early fifties and he's been coming to our family lunches for as long as I can remember.

What's odd is that he doesn't tell jokes at all. I don't think I've ever heard him tell one. What he does instead is describe something completely ordinary in far too much detail. The one everybody in my family still quotes is his account of queuing in a post office. He'd been waiting about twenty minutes, and he took roughly the same amount of time to describe it: the man in front of him who kept counting his change, the woman with a dog in a bag, the ticket machine that had been broken since the previous winter. None of it was funny in itself. It was funny because he refused to let any of it go.

The other half of it is the delivery. He keeps a completely straight face throughout. He's never once laughed at his own story, which somehow makes everybody else laugh harder.

As for why I like it so much, it really isn't about the jokes. My family argues at the table, mostly about things nobody's going to resolve, and the moment he starts one of these accounts the whole argument simply stops. Even the cousins who barely speak end up joining in. That's the useful thing about somebody funny: they change the temperature of a room and nobody notices them doing it.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect and two relative clauses replace the band-6 chain of simple sentences.
'Keeps a straight face', 'refused to let it go', 'change the temperature of a room'.
The example is set up, delivered and then explained, so the humour has a visible shape.

annotations.span: What's odd is that he doesn't tell jokes at all.
annotations.label: Opens on the surprising thing
annotations.why: Leading with what is unexpected gives a listener a reason to keep listening.

annotations.span: the ticket machine that had been broken since the previous winter
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a relative clause
annotations.why: One layered clause shows range without lengthening the sentence.

annotations.span: He keeps a completely straight face throughout.
annotations.label: A collocation, not a description
annotations.why: 'Keep a straight face' is the phrase; assembling it word by word costs marks.

annotations.span: The other half of it is the delivery.
annotations.label: Announces the second part
annotations.why: Numbering your parts aloud makes a turn sound planned rather than remembered.

annotations.span: As for why I like it so much
annotations.label: Signposts the explain bullet
annotations.why: Name the move and you cannot skip the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: It was funny because he refused to let any of it go.
annotations.label: Explains the humour precisely
annotations.why: Say what the person does and 'funny' stops having to do all the work.

annotations.span: which somehow makes everybody else laugh harder
annotations.label: Non-defining relative adds a result
annotations.why: A comma plus 'which' adds a consequence without starting a new sentence.

annotations.span: None of it was funny in itself.
annotations.label: Falls hard on 'itself'
annotations.why: The contrast is carried by stress here, not by extra words.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The funniest person I know is my mother's youngest brother, and the peculiar thing about him is that he has never, to my knowledge, told a joke.

What he does is narrate. He takes some event of no consequence whatsoever and refuses to abbreviate it. The one my family has more or less canonised is his account of a post office queue. He had stood in it for twenty minutes; he then spent about the same again on the man ahead of him counting out coins, the dog being carried around in a shopping bag, the ticket machine which had been out of order since roughly the previous winter. Not one element of that is amusing. What made it unbearable was his absolute refusal to leave anything out.

Delivery is the other half. He does not crack. In thirty years I have never seen him laugh at his own material, and that flatness is precisely what does the damage. If anything it reads as a form of discipline.

Why I value it has surprisingly little to do with comedy. My relatives are enthusiastic arguers, largely about matters that will never be settled, and the instant he begins one of these monologues the argument evaporates. Even the shyer cousins find their way into it. That, I think, is what a genuinely funny person is for: not the laugh itself, but the fact that a room reorganises itself around them and nobody notices it happening.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted 'What made it unbearable was' does work band 7 spread over two clauses.
'Canonised', 'he does not crack', 'the argument evaporates' are each chosen for a shade.
It ends by defining what funny people are for, not by praising this particular one.

annotations.span: What made it unbearable was his absolute refusal to leave anything out.
annotations.label: Cleft puts the cause in focus
annotations.why: Front a 'what' clause when one idea has to land harder than the rest.

annotations.span: the argument evaporates
annotations.label: One verb replaces a whole clause
annotations.why: Choose the verb that carries the image and you need fewer words.

annotations.span: He does not crack.
annotations.label: Four words, entirely precise
annotations.why: Short sentences among long ones read as control, not as shortage.

annotations.span: the ticket machine which had been out of order since roughly the previous winter
annotations.label: Past perfect held inside a list
annotations.why: Keeping the tense accurate mid-list is what sustained control looks like.

annotations.span: not the laugh itself, but the fact that a room reorganises itself around them
annotations.label: Closes on a definition
annotations.why: End on a claim about the type, not the person, and the turn rises.

I want to describe my aunt. She is the sister of my father and she has a small bakery in our town.

She gave me a very useful advice when I was twenty years old. At that time I have a problem because I got a job offer and also I got a place in a course, and I don't know what to choose. So I asked everybody, my parents, my friends, my old teacher. Everybody said something different, so after that it was more confusing for me than before.

Then one day I was in her kitchen and I am telling her about this problem again. And she said, take a paper and write the answer that you already choose. Just write it. So I wrote it and it was the course. I wrote it very fast, without thinking.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one who comes to mind is my father's sister, who runs a small bakery in the town I grew up in. She's not somebody I'd have thought of as an adviser, which is probably why it worked.

This was when I was about twenty. I'd been offered a job and I'd also been given a place on a course, and the two of them started within a fortnight of each other. I asked everybody I could think of, and every single one of them had a different opinion, so by the end of that I was considerably less clear than when I started. That went on for the better part of three weeks.

I was sitting in her kitchen going over the whole thing yet again when she stopped me. She pushed a piece of paper across the table and said, write down the one you've already chosen. Not the one you should choose. The one you've already chosen. I wrote 'course' without thinking about it at all, which took roughly two seconds. She didn't even look up while I was writing.

And then she said the thing I still repeat to people: you're not undecided, you just want somebody to tell you it's all right. That was exactly what had been going on. I'd been collecting opinions rather than weighing anything up, because the choice had already been made and I hadn't admitted it. The useful part, in hindsight, wasn't the advice. It was being told what I was actually doing.

'Going over the whole thing', 'weighing anything up' and 'collecting opinions' do the evaluating.

annotations.why: One line of judgement up front tells the listener what to watch for.

annotations.why: Two things already true before the story starts belong in the past perfect.

annotations.span: I was sitting in her kitchen going over the whole thing yet again when she stopped me.
annotations.label: Continuous background, simple event
annotations.why: Set the scene in continuous, then interrupt it with a past simple verb.

annotations.span: She pushed a piece of paper across the table and said, write down the one you've already chosen.
annotations.label: Reports the gesture and the words
annotations.why: Give what they did as well as what they said; it doubles the detail for free.

annotations.why: Reuse it for any decision where two sides have to be compared.

annotations.span: And then she said the thing I still repeat to people
annotations.label: Signals the key line is coming
annotations.why: Flagging the important sentence makes a listener slow down for it.

annotations.span: I'd been collecting opinions
annotations.label: Names the behaviour in two words
annotations.why: A precise verb replaces a whole sentence of explanation.

annotations.span: Not the one you should choose. The one you've already chosen.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd point to is my father's sister. She runs a bakery, has never given a lecture in her life, and is the only person whose advice I have ever acted on immediately.

I was twenty and stuck between a job and a place on a course, both of them starting inside a fortnight. In the weeks before that, I had consulted, by my own count, nine separate people. All nine were confident, none of them agreed, and the net effect was that I understood the choice rather less well than before I began. It is a peculiar kind of paralysis, and I would not recommend it to anybody.

She listened to about four minutes of it in her kitchen and then slid a sheet of paper across the table. Write down the one you have already picked, she said. Not the sensible one. The one you have already picked. I wrote it in about two seconds, which was itself the answer.

Then came the line I have been quoting ever since: you are not undecided, you simply want permission. She was entirely right. What I had been doing was canvassing until somebody ratified a decision I had made weeks earlier and could not own. Rarely have I been read that accurately by anybody. And I think the lesson generalises: the most useful people are not the ones who tell you what to do, but the ones who describe what you are doing.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Rarely have I been' inverts, and the past perfect runs the entire background layer.
'Canvassing', 'ratified' and 'slid a sheet of paper' are chosen for exactness, not effect.
The close turns the anecdote into a claim about what useful people actually do.

annotations.why: Put the negative adverb first and invert; it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: What I had been doing was canvassing until somebody ratified a decision I had made weeks earlier
annotations.label: Cleft over a past perfect continuous
annotations.why: Two structures at once, both accurate: that is what band 8 sounds like.

annotations.span: the net effect was that I understood the choice rather less well than before I began
annotations.label: Precise rather than decorative
annotations.why: State the size of the effect and you never need the word 'confusing'.

annotations.span: you simply want permission
annotations.label: One noun replaces a paragraph
annotations.why: Find the abstract noun for a behaviour and the sentence shortens itself.

annotations.span: not the ones who tell you what to do, but the ones who describe what you are doing
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Abstract in the final clause and the turn stops being just an anecdote.

model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd point to is my father's sister. She runs a bakery, has never delivered a lecture in her life, and is the only person whose advice I've acted on the same afternoon I was given it.

I was twenty and caught between a job and a place on a course, the two of them starting inside a fortnight of each other. By the time I got to her I'd consulted, by my own count, nine people. All nine were confident, no two agreed, and the cumulative effect was that I understood the decision rather less well than before I began asking. It's a peculiar sort of paralysis, and I'd recommend it to nobody.

She gave it about four minutes in her kitchen and then slid a sheet of paper across the table. Write down the one you've already picked, she said. Not the sensible one. The one you've already picked. I had it down inside two seconds, and the two seconds were the answer.

Then came the line I've been repeating ever since: you're not undecided, you just want permission. She was entirely right. What I'd been doing was canvassing until somebody ratified a choice I'd made weeks earlier and couldn't yet own. Seldom have I been read that accurately by anyone, before or since.

And it generalises, I think. The people worth asking aren't the ones who tell you what to do — anybody will do that. They're the ones who describe, without any particular kindness, what you're already doing.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion after 'seldom' and a participle clause arrive with no shift in delivery speed.
'Canvassing', 'ratified', 'paralysis' — chosen for accuracy rather than for rarity.
The quoted advice comes in three short bursts, which is how people genuinely retell a line.

annotations.span: Seldom have I been read that accurately by anyone
annotations.label: Fronted adverb forces inversion
annotations.why: Put 'seldom' or 'rarely' first and invert. It lands as emphasis, not display.

annotations.span: the two of them starting inside a fortnight of each other
annotations.label: Participle clause replaces a relative
annotations.why: 'Which started' becomes 'starting'; the sentence keeps moving.

annotations.span: canvassing until somebody ratified a choice
annotations.label: Two exact verbs, neither decorative
annotations.why: 'Canvassing' and 'ratified' are the right words here, not the big ones.

annotations.span: It's a peculiar sort of paralysis
annotations.label: One noun replaces a description
annotations.why: Naming the state is faster and sharper than describing how it felt.

annotations.span: anybody will do that
annotations.label: Four-word aside carries the argument
annotations.why: Short interjected clauses are what stop a long turn sounding written.

annotations.span: Not the sensible one. The one you've already picked.
annotations.label: Contrastive stress on 'sensible' and 'already'
annotations.why: Two short sentences slowed down beat one long one for emphasis.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Answer the fourth bullet. Say what you did after she spoke — the decision, and how fast you made it.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Quote her in her own words. A paraphrase throws away the only memorable line the answer has.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Count the people you asked. A number where a vague plural was is the cheapest precision on offer.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Cut the sentence that explains your best line. Say 'you just want permission' and let it sit.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a woman in a bus. I met her one time only and I don't know her name.

It was maybe seven years ago. I go to another city for an interview. It was night. And then the bus is broken, so we stop in a petrol station and we wait four hours. It was very cold and everything is closed.

She sit near me. She is old, maybe sixty. She go to the hospital in the morning for an appointment. We start to talk and we talk very long, until the morning.

She asked me many questions. Difficult questions, not normal questions. Like what I want really from my job. Nobody ask me this before.

After, the new bus come and we sit in different place. And that's it. I still remember her.

Yes, that is all.

Verbs are unmarked — 'she sit', 'she go' — so the listener has to supply the tense.
'Difficult', 'normal', 'very long' carry the entire description of a five-hour conversation.

annotations.why: Say 'She was sitting across the aisle.' Mark it or the story has no time.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a woman who I met one time on a bus. It was a night bus and I never see her again after that.

It was about seven years ago. I was travelling to another city for a job interview and the bus was broken. So we stopped at a service station in the middle of the night and we waited there for four hours. It was very cold and there was nothing to do, all the shops are closed.

She was sitting next to me. She was around sixty years old, I think. She was going to a hospital in the same city because she had an appointment in the morning. We started to talk and then we talked until five o'clock. She asked me many questions about my life, my family, my job. Nobody asks me these questions normally, even my friends.

The strange thing is I don't know her name. I never ask her and she never ask me. When the new bus came we sat in different seats and that was all. But I still remember her and sometimes I use her questions with other people. So this is a person I met one time and I still remember.

what_caps_it.point: The present tense keeps intruding, and 'the bus was broken' should be a breakdown.
Everything is joined with 'and' or 'so', and the striking part arrives completely flat.
'Strange', 'cold' and 'many questions' are the only descriptive choices in the turn.

annotations.span: It was about seven years ago.
annotations.label: Fixes the time in five words
annotations.why: Keep this. One time phrase up front locks the whole answer into the past.

annotations.span: I never see her again after that
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Say 'I never saw her again'. Choose the tense once and hold it.

annotations.span: the bus was broken
annotations.label: Wrong verb for a breakdown
annotations.why: A vehicle 'breaks down'; 'was broken' describes a permanent state.

annotations.span: I never ask her and she never ask me.
annotations.label: Past tense missing twice over
annotations.why: Say 'I never asked her and she never asked me'.

annotations.span: So this is a person I met one time and I still remember.
annotations.label: Closes on the card's own words
annotations.why: End on why brief encounters stay with people at all.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd like to describe is somebody whose name I never actually found out, which is part of why she stuck.

This was about seven years ago. I was on an overnight coach to another city for an interview, and the coach broke down at around midnight. They pulled us into a service station and we sat there for something like four hours, in the cold, with nothing open. I'd been half asleep until then, so I was fairly annoyed about the whole thing.

She was in the seat across the aisle, a woman in her sixties, travelling to a hospital appointment first thing the next morning. I don't remember how we got chatting, but once we did we talked more or less until it got light. What I remember most clearly is that she asked far better questions than anybody I knew. Not the usual ones. She asked me what I'd been like at fourteen, and whether the job I was going for was one I actually wanted or one that would look sensible. Nobody had ever put it to me quite like that.

When the replacement coach turned up we ended up in different seats, and that was the end of it. I never asked her name, which I've regretted ever since. What I've kept is the questions. I've used two of them on other people since then, and they work every single time. It's an odd thing to take away from four hours in a car park, but there it is.

what_lifts_it.point: 'I'd been half asleep' and 'Nobody had ever put it' add a second layer of past time.
'Got chatting', 'until it got light' and 'there it is' are spoken rather than written.
One time frame holds for two minutes and the close names what actually survived.

annotations.label: Opens on the memorable detail
annotations.why: Put the strangest fact first; it gives the listener a reason to stay.

annotations.span: I'd been half asleep until then
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the earlier state
annotations.why: One backshifted verb shows two layers of time inside a story.

annotations.span: how we got chatting
annotations.label: Spoken chunk, not a formal phrase
annotations.why: 'Get chatting' is what people say; the formal version sounds written.

annotations.span: What I remember most clearly is that
annotations.label: Signposts the important part
annotations.why: Announcing the key detail makes a listener slow down for it.

annotations.span: Not the usual ones.
annotations.label: Short, falling, after a pause
annotations.why: A three-word sentence between long ones controls the rhythm of a turn.

annotations.span: whether the job I was going for was one I actually wanted or one that would look sensible
annotations.label: Embedded question with two options
annotations.why: Embedded questions keep statement order, and getting that right is very audible.

annotations.span: What I've kept is the questions.
annotations.label: Turns the story into a takeaway
annotations.why: Say what survived and the fourth bullet more or less answers itself.

annotations.span: It's an odd thing to take away from four hours in a car park
annotations.label: Understatement does the evaluating
annotations.why: Play a big point down and it lands harder than an intensifier would.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd choose is somebody I spent five hours with and cannot name, which is precisely why she has lasted.

Seven years ago I was on an overnight coach, travelling to an interview in another city, and somewhere around midnight the thing gave out. We were decanted into a service station forecourt and left there for the best part of four hours, in the cold, with everything shut. I had been asleep and was in no mood for any of it.

She was across the aisle. Sixties, on her way to a hospital appointment first thing, entirely unbothered by the delay. I have no memory of how the conversation started, only that it ran until the sky went grey. What struck me, and still does, is the quality of her questions. She asked what I had been like at fourteen. She asked whether the job I was travelling for was one I wanted, or one that would simply look defensible to other people. I had no answer to the second, which was itself informative.

The relief coach arrived, we were seated separately, and that was that. Not once did it occur to me to ask her name. What I took away was the questions themselves, two of which I have since used on other people to considerable effect. Some of the people who change how you think, it turns out, are people you meet for one night and never see again.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Not once did it occur' inverts, and 'two of which' replaces a whole extra sentence.
'Decanted', 'gave out' and 'look defensible' are each chosen for a shade of meaning.
The close states a general claim about brief encounters instead of summarising the night.

annotations.span: Not once did it occur to me to ask her name.
annotations.label: Negative fronting with inversion
annotations.why: Front the negative and invert; it reads as spoken emphasis, not as writing.

annotations.span: two of which I have since used on other people
annotations.label: Quantifier plus 'of which' relative
annotations.why: It joins two ideas without the extra 'and I have also' sentence.

annotations.span: We were decanted into a service station forecourt
annotations.label: One precise verb, faintly dry
annotations.why: The exact verb carries the tone as well as the meaning.

annotations.span: one that would simply look defensible to other people
annotations.label: Names the real motive precisely
annotations.why: Choosing 'defensible' over 'good' is the shade of meaning band 8 rewards.

annotations.span: Some of the people who change how you think, it turns out, are people you meet for one night
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Abstract in the last sentence and the whole turn stops being anecdote.

annotations.span: Sixties, on her way to a hospital appointment first thing, entirely unbothered by the delay.
annotations.label: Three groups, one falling contour
annotations.why: Keep a list level in pitch and drop only on the final group.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd choose is somebody I spent five hours beside and cannot name, which is precisely why she's lasted.

Seven years ago I was on an overnight coach to an interview in another city, and somewhere around midnight the thing gave out altogether. We were decanted onto a service station forecourt and left there the best part of four hours, in the cold, with every shutter down. I'd been asleep, and I was in no mood for any of it.

She was across the aisle. Sixties, on her way to a hospital appointment first thing, and entirely unbothered by the delay in a way I found faintly reproachful. I've no recollection of how we started talking, only that it ran until the sky went grey. What struck me then, and strikes me still, was the calibre of her questions. She asked what I'd been like at fourteen. She asked whether the job I was travelling for was one I wanted, or one that would simply look defensible to other people. I had nothing at all for the second, which was itself the answer.

The relief coach came, we were seated apart, and that was that. Not once did it occur to either of us to exchange names, and I've thought about that more than is probably healthy. What I took away were the questions. I've put two of them to other people since, to considerable effect.

Which is the odd thing about influence. Some of the people who genuinely alter how you think are people you spend one night with in a car park and never see again.

what_lifts_it.point: Fronted negative inversion and a split-tense cleft, neither interrupting the pace.
'Decanted', 'calibre', 'defensible' — three exact choices where band 8 used good general ones.
The close names the mechanism rather than the feeling, and does it in two sentences.

annotations.span: Not once did it occur to either of us to exchange names
annotations.label: Negative fronting with inversion
annotations.why: 'Not once did…' is one word longer than 'we never…' and lands far harder.

annotations.span: What struck me then, and strikes me still, was the calibre of her questions
annotations.label: Cleft holding two tenses at once
annotations.why: A single cleft can carry past and present together; use it for lasting effects.

annotations.span: We were decanted onto a service station forecourt
annotations.label: One verb chosen for its shade
annotations.why: 'Decanted' means moved without being consulted. No adjective needed after it.

annotations.span: faintly reproachful
annotations.label: A hedged adjective, not an intensified one
annotations.why: 'Faintly' is more precise than 'very' and costs exactly the same.

annotations.span: which was itself the answer
annotations.label: A gap in the story becomes the point
annotations.why: Say what your silence meant. It beats describing the silence.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Reproduce one of her actual questions. A card about a conversation needs somebody else's words in it.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Mark every verb for tense before you touch the vocabulary. 'She sat', 'she was going' alone moves this answer.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Give the delay a texture — cold, shut, in no mood for it — instead of the word 'boring'.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Let one detail carry its own meaning. 'I had nothing for the second' says more than explaining why.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a time I explained something difficult. It was to my grandmother and it was about her bank.

Last year her bank closed the branch in her town and they said everything is on the app now. She is eighty-one and she never used a smartphone before. My uncle explained her two times and the bank explained also, but she doesn't understand anything. She was very worried, she thought maybe her money is gone.

So I went to her house on a Sunday. First I show her the app, step by step, this button, then this button. But it was not working. She was more confused than before. Then I stopped and I asked her, what do you think happens with your money. And she said, it is in the building. She thought the money is physically inside the branch, like in a box.

So then I took a paper and I drew it. The bank, the computer, and the money is only a number. After that it was easy, in ten minutes she was fine.

I felt happy but also stupid, because I explained one hour the wrong thing. So this is the time I explained something difficult.

what_caps_it.point: The present tense keeps returning inside a past story, and reported speech never shifts.
'So' opens four sentences, and the key realisation arrives with no build-up at all.
'Difficult', 'confused', 'easy' and 'happy' do all of the evaluation between them.

annotations.span: Then I stopped and I asked her, what do you think happens with your money.
annotations.label: Reports the turning point directly
annotations.why: Keep this. Quoting the question you asked is the strongest moment in the turn.

annotations.span: they said everything is on the app now
annotations.label: Reported speech doesn't shift back
annotations.why: Say 'they said everything was on the app now'.

annotations.span: My uncle explained her two times
annotations.label: 'Explain' needs 'to'
annotations.why: Say 'explained it to her twice'. The preposition is part of the verb.

annotations.span: First I show her the app
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Decide on the past in your opening line and never drift out.

annotations.span: because I explained one hour the wrong thing
annotations.label: Word order, and 'for' is missing
annotations.why: Say 'because I spent an hour explaining the wrong thing'.

annotations.span: So this is the time I explained something difficult.
annotations.label: Ends by reading the card back
annotations.why: Close on what you learned about explaining, not on the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick is explaining online banking to my grandmother, which sounds trivial and absolutely was not.

Her local branch shut about a year ago and the bank moved more or less everything onto an app. She's eighty-one and had never owned a smartphone. By the time I got involved, my uncle had been through it with her twice and somebody at the bank had tried as well, and none of it had landed. What worried me was that she'd started saying she no longer knew where her money was, which is not a small thing to be thinking at eighty-one.

I went round on a Sunday and did exactly what everybody else had done. I opened the app and walked her through it, screen by screen. Twenty minutes in, it was clear this was going nowhere, so I stopped and asked her what she thought actually happened to her money when she paid it in. And she said it stayed in the building.

That was the whole problem. In fairness, it was an obvious thing to have checked. She wasn't confused about the app at all; she was confused about where money lives. So I drew it on the back of an envelope, the branch on one side and a number in a computer on the other. After that the app itself took about ten minutes.

What I took from it is that most failed explanations are answers to the wrong question. If I'd asked first instead of explaining first, I'd have saved us both an hour.

what_lifts_it.point: The past perfect runs the whole background, and a third conditional closes the reflection.
'None of it had landed', 'going nowhere' and 'where money lives' are precise and spoken.
The discovery is withheld until the right moment, so the explanation has a visible shape.

annotations.span: which sounds trivial and absolutely was not
annotations.label: Frames the story before telling it
annotations.why: Warning a listener that it gets harder buys their attention for nothing.

annotations.span: my uncle had been through it with her twice and somebody at the bank had tried as well
annotations.label: Past perfect for what came before
annotations.why: Everything that happened before your story starts belongs in past perfect.

annotations.span: none of it had landed
annotations.label: One verb for 'she didn't understand'
annotations.why: 'Land' is what people say about explanations that fail. Reuse it.

annotations.span: I went round on a Sunday and did exactly what everybody else had done.
annotations.label: Admits the wrong turn out loud
annotations.why: Naming your own mistake is what turns an anecdote into reasoning.

annotations.span: asked her what she thought actually happened to her money
annotations.label: Embedded question keeps statement order
annotations.why: Not 'what did she think happened'. This one is very visible to examiners.

annotations.span: That was the whole problem.
annotations.label: Marks the discovery in four words
annotations.why: A short sentence after a long one tells a listener something has changed.

annotations.span: she was confused about where money lives
annotations.label: An abstract idea in ordinary words
annotations.why: Saying the difficult thing simply demonstrates the very skill you're describing.

annotations.span: If I'd asked first instead of explaining first, I'd have saved us both an hour.
annotations.label: Third conditional carries the lesson
annotations.why: Any 'what would you change' bullet wants an unreal past somewhere in it.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The episode I'd choose is teaching my grandmother to bank on a phone, which I had assumed would take about twenty minutes.

Her branch closed last year and the bank shifted everything onto an app. She is eighty-one and had never held a smartphone. Two people had already attempted it before me, my uncle and somebody at the counter, and both attempts had sunk without trace. The detail that alarmed me was a remark she made about no longer knowing where her money was, which at eighty-one is not a small sentence.

I went round on the Sunday and proceeded to repeat everybody else's mistake. I opened the application and took her through it screen by screen, patiently and uselessly, for the better part of an hour. Only when I gave up did I think to ask what she believed happened to money once she had handed it over the counter. It stayed in the building, she said. She offered this without a trace of hesitation.

There was the entire problem. The obstacle was never the interface; it was a model of banking formed in about 1960 and never revised since. Two minutes with a pen and an envelope sorted it, and the app followed in ten.

What that taught me has outlasted the banking. Almost every explanation that fails is a well-constructed answer to a question nobody asked. Had I begun by finding out what she already believed, I would have saved us both the hour.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Only when I gave up did I think' and 'Had I begun' put two inversions into one turn.
'Sunk without trace', 'patiently and uselessly' and 'never revised' each carry a judgement.
It closes on a general principle about explanation rather than on the grandmother.

annotations.span: Only when I gave up did I think to ask
annotations.label: Fronted 'only when' forces inversion
annotations.why: It marks the turning point grammatically as well as in the content.

annotations.span: Had I begun by finding out what she already believed
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as a third conditional, one register higher, still spoken.

annotations.span: both attempts had sunk without trace
annotations.label: Idiom exactly where it belongs
annotations.why: Idiom counts when it is invisible; showy ones cost more than they earn.

annotations.span: a model of banking formed in about 1960 and never revised since
annotations.label: Names the real obstacle precisely
annotations.why: Diagnose in a noun phrase and you save yourself three whole sentences.

annotations.span: patiently and uselessly
annotations.label: The second adverb takes the stress
annotations.why: The contrast between the two words is the point; unstressed, it vanishes.

annotations.span: Almost every explanation that fails is a well-constructed answer to a question nobody asked.
annotations.label: Ends on a general principle
annotations.why: A closing generalisation is what separates a story from an argument.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a time when somebody was very kind to me. It happened about four years ago in November.

I was driving back from my cousin's house and my car stopped on a small road. It was nine o'clock in the night and it was very dark and cold. I try to call somebody but there was no signal on my phone. So I was waiting there for forty minutes and nobody stopped, maybe three cars passed but they don't stop.

Then a small van stopped. There was a woman inside, maybe fifty years old. She opened the window and she asked me what happened. I explained her about the car. And then she said, get in, I take you to the garage. The garage was twenty kilometres away in another town. She drove me there and she waited also, because it was closed and we must find the man with the key.

After that I want to give her some money but she refused. She said, somebody did this for me before, fifteen years ago. And then she went away. I was very surprised because she doesn't know me at all. So this is the time I was surprised by somebody's kindness.

what_caps_it.point: 'I try', 'they don't stop' and 'I want to give' all sit inside a past narrative.
'Kind', 'surprised' and 'very dark' carry the whole event between them.
A chain of events joined by 'and' and 'so', with the point never actually made.

annotations.why: Both verbs in one sentence must match: 'passed' and 'didn't stop'.

annotations.why: Say 'I explained the problem to her'. The preposition belongs to the verb.

annotations.why: End on what the evening made you think about strangers.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd choose happened about four years ago, in November, on a completely unremarkable stretch of road.

I'd been at my cousin's and I was driving home when the car simply died. This was somewhere around nine in the evening, in the middle of nowhere, and it turned out there was no signal at all where I'd stopped. I stood at the side of the road for the best part of forty minutes. Three or four cars went past without slowing down, which I honestly don't blame them for, and it was getting properly cold by then. I remember thinking I'd have to walk it.

Then a small van pulled up. The driver was a woman in her fifties, and she wound the window down and asked what had happened. Once I'd explained, she just said get in. She drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town, and when it turned out to be shut she waited with me until we'd tracked somebody down. That took another hour, easily.

The part that surprised me was the end of it. I tried to give her something for the petrol and she wouldn't hear of it. All she said was that somebody had done the same for her about fifteen years earlier, and then she drove off before I could ask her anything else at all. I've thought about that a great deal since. It wasn't really kindness towards me at all; it was more like a debt being passed along, and I'm the one holding it now.

'Simply died', 'wouldn't hear of it' and 'a debt being passed along' do the evaluating.

annotations.span: somebody had done the same for her about fifteen years earlier

annotations.why: Two steps back in time, and it has to be marked on the verb.

annotations.span: a debt being passed along
annotations.label: One image replaces an explanation
annotations.why: Find the metaphor and five words do the work of three sentences.

annotations.span: It wasn't really kindness towards me at all

annotations.why: Saying what something was not is the cheapest route to a precise point.

annotations.span: That took another hour, easily.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick took place about four years ago on a November evening, on a road with nothing on it in either direction.

I was driving back from my cousin's when the car gave up entirely. Nine o'clock, pitch dark, and of course no signal wherever it was that I had stopped. I stood on the verge for the best part of forty minutes. Several cars came past and not one of them slowed, which in fairness is probably what I would have done myself. It is a long forty minutes when nothing is coming.

Then a small van pulled in. A woman in her fifties, window down, asking what the trouble was. Having heard about thirty seconds of it she told me to get in, drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town, found it shut, and then waited with me for another hour while we located somebody with a key.

What has stayed with me is not the lift. It is what she said when I tried to press some money on her for the fuel. She would not take a penny, and remarked, almost in passing, that somebody had done exactly this for her fifteen years earlier. That reframed the whole evening. It had very little to do with me at all; I had simply been handed something that was already in circulation, and at some point I am expected to pass it on.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause opens a sentence, and past perfect handles the fifteen-year backshift.
'Gave up entirely', 'on the verge' and 'already in circulation' are exact, not decorative.
It ends by reframing what happened rather than by summing the evening up.

annotations.span: Having heard about thirty seconds of it she told me to get in
annotations.label: Participle clause compresses a sequence
annotations.why: 'Having done X, she did Y' packs two events into a single clause.

annotations.span: somebody had done exactly this for her fifteen years earlier
annotations.label: Past perfect for a second layer back
annotations.why: Two steps into the past must be marked, or a listener loses the order.

annotations.span: She would not take a penny
annotations.label: Idiomatic refusal, entirely natural
annotations.why: One idiom in the right slot outweighs a handful placed for display.

annotations.span: something that was already in circulation
annotations.label: The metaphor does the whole argument
annotations.why: One well-chosen image replaces a paragraph of explaining.

annotations.span: That reframed the whole evening.
annotations.label: Announces a change of reading
annotations.why: Tell a listener you are about to reinterpret and they follow the shift.

annotations.span: Nine o'clock, pitch dark, and of course no signal
annotations.label: Three groups, one falling run
annotations.why: Group short items at level pitch and fall only on the final one.

model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd describe is a walk to the market that the three of us do every Sunday morning. It's my father, my younger brother and me, and we've been doing it for about four years now.

It started when my father retired. Before that he worked most weekends, so Sunday morning was the first slot in the week that was genuinely free, and I think he wanted something in it. We leave at about seven, which is unreasonable, and walk for twenty minutes or so to the market on the far side of town. None of us has ever suggested going later.

The routine barely varies, which is half the point. We buy the vegetables for the week, my father insists on one particular stall because he maintains the tomatoes there are better, and my brother says every week that tomatoes are tomatoes. They've been having that argument for four years and neither of them has moved an inch. Then we sit in the same café for an hour, in the same three chairs, and nobody's in any hurry about any of it.

What I get out of it isn't really the market. During the week the three of us only ever talk about arrangements: who needs the car, who's collecting what. Sunday is the one stretch where nothing has to be decided. I'd say that's what a routine is actually for. It isn't the activity at all, it's the fact that the time is already booked and nobody has to propose it.

model_answers.transcript:
The routine I'd pick is a Sunday-morning walk to the market, done by three of us, and it has been running for roughly four years.

It began, as these things do, when my father retired. Until then he had worked most weekends, so Sunday was the first genuinely unclaimed morning he'd had in decades, and I suspect he wanted it occupied by something. We set off around seven, which nobody has ever formally agreed to, and walk twenty minutes across town in whatever weather happens to be available.

What makes it work is that nothing about it changes. We buy the week's vegetables; my father will not be moved from one particular stall on the grounds that its tomatoes are superior; my brother observes, weekly, that a tomato is a tomato. Four years of this and neither has conceded a millimetre. Neither of them ever will, either. Afterwards there is an hour in the same café, in the same three chairs, and nobody hurries anybody about anything.

The market, though, is not the point. Our weekday conversation consists almost entirely of logistics, who needs the car and who is collecting whom, and Sunday is the only stretch in which nothing at all has to be settled. That, I have come to think, is what a shared routine really provides. Not the activity, but a block of time that has already been agreed, so that nobody ever has to be the one who suggests it.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Will not be moved' as habitual refusal, and 'whom' used where it genuinely belongs.
'Unclaimed', 'conceded a millimetre' and 'observes, weekly' each carry judgement precisely.
The final sentence defines what routines are for rather than restating this one.

model_answers.transcript:
Three of us walk to the market every Sunday morning, and have done for about four years.

It started the way these arrangements usually start, which is that my father retired and had a Sunday for the first time in about thirty years. He'd worked most weekends until then. I think he wanted something in it, and never said so. We leave at seven, an hour nobody proposed and nobody has ever objected to, and walk the twenty minutes across town regardless of what the sky is doing.

The whole value of it is that nothing ever changes. Vegetables for the week; my father refusing to buy tomatoes anywhere but one particular stall, on the grounds that they are demonstrably better; my brother pointing out, as he has every Sunday for four years, that a tomato is a tomato. Neither of them has given an inch and neither of them intends to. Then an hour in the same café, the same three chairs, and no one hurrying anyone.

But the market has almost nothing to do with it. Monday to Friday the three of us talk exclusively about arrangements — the car, who's picking up whom, what time. Sunday is the only block of the week in which nothing has to be decided by anybody. And that, I've decided, is what a standing routine is for. Not the walk. The fact that the time is already agreed, so nobody ever has to propose it, and nobody is ever put in the position of turning it down.

what_lifts_it.point: A shared relative gap and a present perfect aside, both delivered without any construction.
'Given an inch', 'standing routine', 'demonstrably better' — precise in an ordinary register.
The close completes the thought in two halves where band 8 stopped at the first.

I want to describe a quiet place where I am going to think. It is near a water, a canal, behind an old factory. It is fifteen minutes walking from my house.

I find it by accident. There was a work in my street, so I go another way, and I see this small road next to the water. Before I don't know it. And I am living here six years already.

I want to describe the place where I go when I want to think. It is a canal, behind an old mill building, and it is about fifteen minutes from my house on foot.

So I found it by accident. There was road works on my normal street, so I go a different way, and I see this path next to the water. Before that I don't know it is there, even I live here six years.
