model_answers.label: The target — same place, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a stretch of canal towpath about fifteen minutes' walk from my flat, tucked away behind an old mill that hasn't been used for years.

I came across it completely by accident. There were roadworks on the route I normally take, so I ended up cutting through an industrial estate and coming out onto the water. I remember thinking it was odd that I'd lived here for six years and never known it was there. That was two summers ago, and I've been going most weeks ever since.

What I do is fairly unvarying. I walk for about twenty minutes, as far as a set of lock gates, and then I sit on the beam of the gate with my feet over the water. Sometimes I take a coffee, though half the time I forget. The important thing, I think, is that there's no phone signal down there at all, so the decision about whether to look at my phone gets taken away from me.

As for why it helps — it isn't really the quiet on its own, because it isn't silent. There's water moving through the gates the whole time and a low hum from the ring road. It's more that nothing there is waiting for me. At home there's always something in my line of sight that needs doing, whereas on the towpath the only thing in front of me is water. I find I do the actual thinking on the walk back rather than while I'm sitting there, which suggests it's the walking that does half the work. Either way, it's the only twenty minutes in my week when nobody can reach me.

The place is a stretch of canal towpath behind a derelict mill, about a quarter of an hour on foot from where I live, and I stumbled on it entirely by chance.

There were roadworks on my usual route, so I cut through an industrial estate and came out on the water, and I can remember standing there faintly annoyed with myself — six years in the same postcode and I'd never once gone two streets further. Not that it's picturesque, particularly. It's a working waterway with rubbish in the reeds.

What it is, is undemanding — nothing on that towpath is waiting for me to deal with it, whereas at home there's never a sightline without a job in it. And I've noticed the thinking tends to happen on the walk back rather than on the gate itself, which makes me suspect that what I actually go for isn't the place at all. title: A park or green space you use

note_grid.cell: rec ground, 10 min, past the church

/skt/ at the end; do not say 'ask'.

about ten minutes from my front door,
past the church and over a footbridge.

minimal_pairs.contrast: vowel plus the /r/ colouring in one of them

teaching.examiner_note: You may make notes for the whole minute, but the examiner will not look at them and nothing written down is assessed.

swap_slots.span: a recreation ground about ten minutes from my front door
swap_slots.prompt: Your own place and distance. Say what it is officially called, not just 'a park'.

swap_slots.prompt: Your own pattern, with a time attached. 'Sometimes' tells the examiner nothing.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to describe a park which I use. It is near my house, about ten minutes if I walk, and I pass a church to arrive there.

It is not a big park. There is a football field, and there is a path around it, and there is some trees on one side. Also there is a small playground for the children.

I go there three times in a week, in the morning, because I like to run. I run three or four times around the path and then I go home. On Sunday I go with my niece and she plays in the playground. She is five years old and she loves the swings very much.

If they build on it, it will be very bad for me. Because I don't have another place to run near my house. And also for my niece it is not good, she has nowhere to play. Many people use this park, old people, young people, everybody. So I think it is very important and I hope they don't build on it. This is the green space that I use.

what_caps_it.point: The conditional runs on 'will' throughout, so the imagined loss reads as a plan.
Three consecutive sentences begin 'there is', and the turn lists the contents.
'Big', 'small', 'very bad', 'very important' — the evaluation is all size and intensity.

annotations.span: I go there three times in a week, in the morning, because I like to run.
annotations.label: Frequency, time and reason together
annotations.why: Keep this shape — three pieces of information in one clean sentence.

annotations.span: there is some trees on one side
annotations.label: Singular verb with a plural subject
annotations.why: 'There are some trees'. Check the noun before you choose is or are.

annotations.span: If they build on it, it will be very bad for me.
annotations.label: Real conditional for an unreal case
annotations.why: Say 'if they built on it, I'd have nowhere to run'.

annotations.span: Many people use this park, old people, young people, everybody.
annotations.label: A list that says nothing specific
annotations.why: Name two actual users and what each of them does there.

annotations.span: she loves the swings very much
annotations.label: 'Very much' propping up a flat verb
annotations.why: 'The swings are the entire point for her' does the same job with more precision.

annotations.span: This is the green space that I use.
annotations.label: Signs off by repeating the task
annotations.why: End on a claim about places like it, not on the wording of the card.

model_answers.label: The target — same park, better language
model_answers.transcript:
It's a recreation ground about ten minutes from my front door, past the church and over a footbridge. Officially it has a name, but nobody uses it — everyone just calls it the rec.

It isn't much to look at. There's a football pitch that floods every winter, a tarmac path round the outside, and a line of lime trees along the road that take most of the traffic noise out. The far corner is completely overgrown, which I think is deliberate, because nobody has touched it in the four years I've been going.

I go three mornings a week, always before seven, and I do three laps of the path, which comes to about two miles. Then on Sundays I take my niece, and that's a different sort of visit altogether — my niece is at the age where the swings are the entire point of the outing, so we're there for an hour and I never make it round the path once.

As for what I'd miss if they built on it — it wouldn't really be the running, because I could run along the canal instead. It would be the fact that I see the same people every week without ever having arranged anything. There's a man with two greyhounds, a couple who always argue quietly by the gate, half a dozen people I only ever nod at. You can't get that indoors, and you certainly can't get it by planning it. That's what a scruffy field does that a nicer, further-away park couldn't.

what_lifts_it.point: A clean second conditional and two relative clauses where band 6 had 'there is' chains.
'The rec', 'scruffy', 'overgrown', 'floods every winter' — concrete instead of big and small.
The last bullet names what is lost and then argues why it can't be replaced.

annotations.span: Officially it has a name, but nobody uses it
annotations.label: One aside that buys credibility
annotations.why: A small local truth like this proves you are not reciting.

annotations.span: It isn't much to look at.
annotations.label: Undersells before describing
annotations.why: Say the modest thing first; whatever follows then sounds honest.

annotations.span: a football pitch that floods every winter
annotations.label: Relative clause instead of a list
annotations.why: Attach a 'that' clause to one noun and the flat listing disappears.

annotations.span: if they built on it
annotations.label: Second conditional, correctly formed
annotations.why: Past tense in the if-clause, 'would' in the other half.

annotations.span: As for what I'd miss
annotations.label: Signposts the explain bullet
annotations.why: Announce this move and the fourth bullet stops getting squeezed into ten seconds.

annotations.span: I see the same people every week without ever having arranged anything
annotations.label: Names an abstract benefit precisely
annotations.why: Say what a place gives you, not that it is important to you.

annotations.span: half a dozen people I only ever nod at
annotations.label: Exact detail beats a general claim
annotations.why: One image like this replaces a whole sentence of adjectives.

annotations.span: That's what a scruffy field does that a nicer, further-away park couldn't.
annotations.label: Falling stress on the contrast
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop on 'couldn't' so the comparison closes properly.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place I use is a recreation ground ten minutes' walk away, over a footbridge and past a church. It has an official name on the sign, which I have never once heard anybody say out loud.

It's a fairly unpromising piece of land — a pitch that turns to mud by November, a tarmac loop round the edge, and a row of limes doing a surprising amount of work against the traffic. One corner has been left to go wild, and rather to my surprise the council seem to have done that on purpose. Whether by design or by neglect, it's the only patch with any birds in it.

My own use of it is dull and regular: three laps before seven, three mornings a week. Sundays are a different proposition, because I have my niece with me, and at four years old the swings are non-negotiable, so the running never happens at all. I've stopped pretending otherwise and started taking a flask.

What I'd miss, though, isn't the exercise. I could run somewhere else easily enough. It's that the place produces a kind of company nobody has to organise — the man with the greyhounds, the couple who bicker by the gate, the handful of people I've nodded at for years without ever learning a name. Were it built on, that would simply stop, and it isn't the sort of thing you can reopen somewhere more convenient. Scruffy and close beats handsome and twenty minutes away, every time.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Were it built on' — inversion replaces the band 7's standard second conditional.
'Unpromising', 'non-negotiable', 'bicker' are picked for shade rather than for size.
The close is an aphorism about places, not a summary of this place.

annotations.span: Were it built on, that would simply stop
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same conditional, higher register, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: the swings are non-negotiable
annotations.label: A formal word used playfully
annotations.why: Borrowing a work word for family life is a very natural move.

annotations.span: the place produces a kind of company nobody has to organise
annotations.label: Abstracts the benefit in one phrase
annotations.why: Find the noun for what a place gives you and the answer lifts.

annotations.span: Scruffy and close beats handsome and twenty minutes away, every time.
annotations.label: Closes on a general principle
annotations.why: End one rung above the story and the whole turn sounds considered.

annotations.span: a row of limes doing a surprising amount of work against the traffic
annotations.label: Long noun phrase in one run
annotations.why: Do not pause inside the phrase; keep it as a single group.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about the kitchen in my flat. It is at the back and it is not a beautiful room, but I am there all the time.

The kitchen is long and it is not wide. There is the cupboards on one side and a table at the end near the window. The table is very big for this room, it was from the grandmother of my partner. So when somebody sits there, you must go sideways to pass. From the window you can see a small yard with the bins.

In the kitchen I do everything. I eat there, and also I work there in the morning with my laptop. I have a desk in my bedroom but I don't use it, I don't know why. When my friends come, we sit in the kitchen also.

Why I spend so much time there? Because it is sunny in the morning, and because it is comfortable. In the living room I feel I must relax, but in the kitchen I can do something and talk at the same time. It is more easy. So this is my favourite room and I spend there many hours every day.

what_caps_it.point: The turn is an inventory of the room, with no shape and a close that restates the card.
Articles, plural agreement, a comparative and word order all slip inside one minute.
'Beautiful', 'big', 'sunny', 'comfortable' — description with no physical consequence attached.

annotations.span: In the kitchen I do everything.
annotations.label: A clean topic sentence
annotations.why: Keep this — it tells the listener what the next thirty seconds will cover.

annotations.span: There is the cupboards on one side
annotations.label: Wrong verb, unnecessary article
annotations.why: 'There are cupboards down one side.' Plural verb, and no 'the'.

annotations.span: it was from the grandmother of my partner
annotations.label: Possession built the long way round
annotations.why: Say 'my partner's grandmother'. English puts the owner in front.

annotations.span: It is more easy.
annotations.label: Comparative with 'more'
annotations.why: 'Easier'. Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y take -ier.

annotations.label: Object and place the wrong way round
annotations.why: 'I spend hours in there.' Place goes after the object, not before.

model_answers.label: The target — same room, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The room I'd pick is the kitchen, which is at the back of the flat and is honestly the least impressive room we've got.

It's long and narrow, with units down one side and a table under the window at the far end. A galley kitchen, I think you'd call it. The table is far too big for the space — we inherited it from my partner's grandmother and nobody is willing to be the one who gets rid of it, so you have to turn sideways to get past. Out of the window there's a yard with three bins and a fig tree that has never produced a fig. It came with the flat and nobody has the heart to take it out.

I do more or less everything in there. I eat, obviously, but I also work at that table most mornings, even though there's a perfectly good desk in the bedroom that I've used about twice since we moved in. Friends end up in there too, because you can hand somebody a chair and carry on cooking at the same time.

Why it works is partly the light, since it faces east and it's the only room that gets any sun before midday. Mostly, though, it's that you can be doing something with your hands and talking at the same time, so nobody has to sit down opposite anybody. The living room always feels slightly formal, whereas nobody has ever been embarrassed to be standing in a kitchen. That's the real difference, I think.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect with 'since', a relative clause and a 'whereas' contrast replace flat statements.
'Galley', 'turn sideways to get past', 'slightly formal' — precision instead of size adjectives.
The fourth bullet tests the reason against another room instead of asserting it.

annotations.span: The room I'd pick is the kitchen
annotations.label: Commits to the choice at once
annotations.why: Decide before you start talking; hunting for a room on air always shows.

annotations.span: A galley kitchen, I think you'd call it.
annotations.label: Reaches for the technical word
annotations.why: Naming the type and flagging your uncertainty is a genuine band-7 move.

annotations.span: you have to turn sideways to get past
annotations.label: Shows the size, doesn't state it
annotations.why: One physical consequence is worth more than the word 'cramped'.

annotations.span: I do more or less everything in there.
annotations.label: Opens the bullet in one line
annotations.why: A short topic sentence hands you thirty seconds of obvious material.

annotations.span: there's a perfectly good desk in the bedroom that I've used about twice since we moved in
annotations.label: Present perfect with 'since'
annotations.why: Use 'since' plus the starting point whenever the situation still holds.

annotations.span: Why it works is partly the light
annotations.label: Names the explain bullet
annotations.why: Say 'why it works' aloud and the last bullet gets its full share of time.

annotations.span: whereas nobody has ever been embarrassed to be standing in a kitchen
annotations.label: Contrast plus present perfect
annotations.why: 'Whereas' joins two rooms and makes the comparison do real work.

annotations.span: it's the only room that gets any sun before midday
annotations.label: Stress falls on 'only'
annotations.why: The word carrying the contrast takes the beat; everything else stays level.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
It would have to be the kitchen, which is at the back of the flat and, objectively, the least attractive room in it. I've never once shown it to a visitor on purpose, and yet that is where they all end up.

It's a galley — units along one wall, a table at the far end under a window that looks onto a yard containing three bins and a fig tree which has stubbornly refused to fruit. The table itself is absurd for the space. It came down to us from my partner's grandmother, and since none of us is willing to be the one who disposes of it, we simply edge round it several times a day.

Practically everything happens in there. I eat, I work at that table most mornings, and I've barely touched the desk in the bedroom since the afternoon it was assembled. Even visitors drift in, which I've come to think is the point of the room: you can hand somebody a chair and carry on chopping, and nobody is required to perform. That was never planned; it simply turned out to be true.

What makes it work isn't really the light, though it does face east. It's that a kitchen gives you something to do with your hands while you talk. Sitting down opposite someone in a living room is a commitment; standing about in a kitchen isn't. Which is probably why the smartest room in most homes is also the emptiest one.

what_lifts_it.point: 'None of us is' and a fronted gerund subject go a step past band 7's relative clauses.
'Absurd', 'edge round', 'stubbornly refused' are chosen for shade, not for difficulty.
It closes on a claim about homes in general rather than about this kitchen.

annotations.span: since none of us is willing to be the one who disposes of it
annotations.label: Agreement after 'none of us'
annotations.why: 'None' takes a singular verb; the plural noun after it is a trap.

annotations.span: a fig tree which has stubbornly refused to fruit
annotations.label: A verb with a personality
annotations.why: Giving an object a human verb is precise and sounds completely natural.

annotations.span: we simply edge round it several times a day
annotations.label: The verb carries the size problem
annotations.why: Say what the space forces you to do and drop the adjective entirely.

annotations.span: Sitting down opposite someone in a living room is a commitment; standing about in a kitchen isn't.
annotations.label: Two balanced clauses, one idea
annotations.why: Parallel clauses land an abstract point without any linking words at all.

annotations.span: Which is probably why the smartest room in most homes is also the emptiest one.
annotations.label: Ends a rung above the story
annotations.why: Turn the last sentence into a claim about homes rather than yours.

It is crowded every Saturday, especially in the morning between ten and one o'clock. There is only one way to walk inside, so when the people stop to speak, nobody can pass. It is very difficult to move.

annotations.why: Say 'I don't feel comfortable' or 'I feel uncomfortable'.

annotations.span: So it depends.
annotations.label: Stops where the answer begins
annotations.why: Depends on what? Name the two situations and you have thirty more seconds.

model_answers.label: The target — same market, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd choose is the covered market in the middle of town, which is an iron and glass hall from the 1880s with about forty stalls in it.

It's busy most days, but Saturday between about ten and one is when it becomes genuinely unpleasant. There's only one main aisle running the length of the building, so the whole thing behaves like a bottleneck — if two people stop to talk in the middle, everything behind them comes to a standstill. And they do stop, constantly, because half the town is in there at once. Nobody plans for that.

The reason so many go is partly price, since the fruit and veg is a fraction of what the supermarket charges, and partly loyalty, because the stalls have been run by the same families for years. My mother still refuses to buy fish anywhere else. She's been buying from the same man since before I was born, and she isn't alone in that.

How I feel about it depends entirely on what I'm there for. If I need something specific, I find it genuinely stressful — you can't move, you can't hear what anybody is saying, and it takes forty minutes to do fifteen minutes of shopping. But if I've got no particular plan, it's the only place in town where I run into people I haven't seen for months, and that only happens because it's crowded. So I've more or less stopped resenting it. I just go early when I'm in a hurry.

what_lifts_it.point: A working conditional and a present perfect passive replace the band 6's flat statements.
'Behaves like a bottleneck', 'comes to a standstill', 'run into people' — chunks, not adjectives.
The feeling is split into two conditions instead of collapsing into 'it depends'.

annotations.why: Use conditionals to show how something works, not only to guess.

annotations.span: the whole thing behaves like a bottleneck

annotations.why: A precise image can replace three sentences of description.

annotations.span: The reason so many go is partly price
annotations.label: Counts the causes before giving them
annotations.why: Say 'partly... and partly' and the listener can hear the structure coming.

annotations.span: the stalls have been run by the same families for years
annotations.label: Present perfect passive
annotations.why: Use it for a state that started earlier and is still true today.

annotations.span: How I feel about it depends entirely on what I'm there for.
annotations.label: Splits the answer in two
annotations.why: Two conditions give you two chunks where one adjective gave you nothing.

annotations.span: you can't move, you can't hear what anybody is saying
annotations.label: Parallel clauses, matching rhythm
annotations.why: Keep the beat identical across the pair and let the second one fall.

annotations.span: it takes forty minutes to do fifteen minutes of shopping
annotations.label: Cost shown as a contrast
annotations.why: Put two numbers against each other and the irritation needs no adjective.

annotations.span: So I've more or less stopped resenting it.
annotations.label: States a settled view
annotations.why: Saying how your opinion moved sounds far more considered than stating it flat.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'd pick the covered market in town — a Victorian hall with an iron roof, forty-odd stalls, and a single aisle running the entire length of it. It has looked more or less the same since the 1880s.

That one aisle is the whole problem. On a Saturday morning, roughly ten till one, the place is heaving, and since there's nowhere to step aside, two people greeting each other in the middle will bring the building to a halt. Which they do, endlessly, because half the town is in there at the same time.

What draws everybody is partly cost, as the fruit and veg goes for a fraction of supermarket prices, and partly loyalty, because most of the stalls have been in the same families for two or three generations and buying elsewhere feels faintly disloyal. My mother has used the same fishmonger for thirty years and would not dream of changing.

As for how I feel about it, that depends on what I've come for. Needing something specific, I find it close to unbearable — you shuffle, you can't hear, and a fifteen-minute errand swallows an hour. Go in with nothing particular to buy, though, and it's the last place in town where you run into people by accident rather than by arrangement. That isn't a small thing, and it exists precisely because the place is too full. So I've made my peace with it, and I do the real shopping at half past eight.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause and an imperative conditional replace band 7's standard if-clauses.
'Heaving', 'swallows an hour', 'faintly disloyal' sit exactly where a native would put them.
It ends on a settled position and the behaviour that follows from it.

annotations.label: Participle clause instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Front an -ing clause and the sentence tightens without losing any meaning.

annotations.span: Go in with nothing particular to buy, though, and it's the last place in town
annotations.label: Imperative used as a conditional
annotations.why: 'Do X and Y happens' is a very natural spoken conditional.

annotations.span: a fifteen-minute errand swallows an hour
annotations.label: One verb does the complaining
annotations.why: 'Swallows' carries irritation that 'takes a long time' simply cannot.

annotations.span: buying elsewhere feels faintly disloyal
annotations.label: Hedging adverb plus exact adjective
annotations.why: 'Faintly' is the shade that stops the claim sounding melodramatic.

annotations.span: So I've made my peace with it, and I do the real shopping at half past eight.
annotations.label: Resolves instead of summarising
annotations.why: Close on what you now do about it rather than on the card's wording.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
I'd pick the covered market in town — a Victorian hall with an iron roof, forty-odd stalls, and one aisle running the entire length of it. It has looked much the same since the 1880s and it was plainly never designed for the number of people now in it.

That single aisle is the whole problem. Saturday, roughly ten till one, the place is heaving, and because there's nowhere to step aside, two people greeting each other in the middle will bring the building to a halt. Which they do, endlessly, since half the town is in there simultaneously.

What draws everyone is partly cost — the fruit and veg goes for a fraction of supermarket prices — and partly loyalty, because most of the stalls have been in the same families for two or three generations and shopping elsewhere feels faintly like defecting. My mother has used the same fishmonger for thirty years and wouldn't dream of it.

How I feel about it depends entirely on what I've come for. Needing something specific, I find it close to unbearable: you shuffle, you can't hear, and a fifteen-minute errand eats an hour. Go in with nothing particular to buy, though, and it's the last place in town where you meet people by accident rather than by arrangement — which is not a small thing, and which exists precisely because it's too full. So I've made my peace with it. I just do the real shopping at half past eight, when there's nobody in there but the traders.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle conditional and an imperative conditional in one turn, both delivered casually.
'Heaving', 'defecting', 'eats an hour' — colloquial precision rather than formal vocabulary.
The last clause supplies a fresh image — the empty hall at half eight — instead of a summary.

annotations.span: Needing something specific, I find it close to unbearable
annotations.label: Participle clause replaces an 'if' clause
annotations.why: 'If I need' becomes 'Needing'; the sentence starts moving a beat earlier.

annotations.span: Go in with nothing particular to buy, though, and it's the last place in town
annotations.label: Imperative plus 'and' as a conditional
annotations.why: 'Do X and Y happens' is a conditional that never uses the word 'if'.

annotations.span: shopping elsewhere feels faintly like defecting
annotations.label: One metaphor, sized by 'faintly'
annotations.why: Hedge a strong image and it becomes accurate instead of dramatic.

annotations.span: the place is heaving
annotations.label: The exact colloquial word for a crowd
annotations.why: 'Heaving' is what a speaker would actually say; 'very crowded' is what a book says.

annotations.span: which is not a small thing, and which exists precisely because it's too full
annotations.label: Turns the complaint into the argument
annotations.why: Show that the thing you dislike causes the thing you value.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Say when you personally go and what you buy. Two sentences of your own behaviour fills the missing minute.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Fix 'there is' with plurals and add one present perfect for the thirty years. Those two changes carry the grammar mark.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Split the feeling in two — needing something versus needing nothing — and give each half its own sentence.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a place where I was going when I was a child. It was an old railway near the house of my grandparents. The train was not there any more, so it is only trees and bushes, and there was a hole in the fence, so we can go inside.

I went there with my brother and two boys from our street. We go there every day in the summer holiday, when I was seven, eight, until maybe twelve years old.

We did many things there. We took some wood from a building place and we make a house, but always it is falling down and we build it again. In August we eat the blackberries. Also we put coins on the rail because we wanted to make them flat.

I remember it very well because it was our place, only for children. No adults came there. So we can do everything we want. Now it is a bicycle road with a bench, and my nephew goes there, but he doesn't know about our house. It is a little bit sad, but it is normal. This is the place from my childhood.

Every stage of the story arrives in the same flat two-clause sentence.
'Many things', 'very well', 'a little bit sad' — the wording never gets more exact.

model_answers.label: The target — same memory, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd talk about is an old railway embankment at the end of the street where my grandparents lived. The line had closed long before I was born, so by the time we found it, it was completely wild — brambles, birch trees, and a fence with a gap in it that everybody's parents pretended not to know about.

I went up there with my brother and two boys from the next street, more or less every day of the summer holidays, from when I was about seven until I was twelve or thirteen and it suddenly stopped being interesting.

What we did there was mostly build things. We dragged pallets up from behind the builders' yard and made a den against the bank, which collapsed regularly and got rebuilt slightly better each time. We picked blackberries in August, and we spent an unreasonable amount of time trying to flatten coins on the one length of rail that was still there. None of it was allowed, strictly speaking, and none of it was ever stopped.

As for why it's stayed with me so clearly — I think it's because it was the first place that was properly ours. Nobody had planned it for us and no adult ever came up there, so whatever happened was entirely our own doing. It's a cycle path now, tarmacked and signposted, with a bench roughly where the den was. My nephew rides along it and has no idea. I'm glad it's used, but there's nothing about it now that a child could claim.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a passive hold the timeline that band 6 kept losing.
'Pretended not to know about', 'an unreasonable amount of time' — chunks with attitude in them.
The turn ends in the present day, which closes the story instead of stopping it.

annotations.why: One backshift early on puts two layers of time into the story.

annotations.label: One clause carries the whole atmosphere

annotations.span: What we did there was mostly build things.
annotations.label: Heads the bullet before filling it
annotations.why: Give the heading first and the examples come out without hesitation.

annotations.label: Understatement doing the evaluating
annotations.why: This chunk transfers to anything you did too much of.

annotations.span: As for why it's stayed with me so clearly

annotations.why: Announce it and the last thirty-five seconds go where they belong.

annotations.span: Nobody had planned it for us and no adult ever came up there
annotations.label: Two negatives, both in past forms
annotations.why: Negative past clauses handled cleanly are strong grammar evidence.

annotations.span: It's a cycle path now, tarmacked and signposted
annotations.label: Brings the story into the present
annotations.why: A then-and-now switch adds a tense and ends the turn naturally.

annotations.label: Pitch falls on 'claim'
annotations.why: Drop the pitch on the final content word so the ending sounds finished.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place was a disused railway embankment at the end of my grandparents' road. The line had been lifted decades earlier, so what remained was a long green corridor running behind the houses, reached through a gap in the fence that every parent on that street knew about and none of them ever mentioned.

I was up there with my brother and a couple of boys from the next street on most days of the summer, from about seven until the year I turned thirteen and abruptly stopped going.

Chiefly, we built. Pallets were hauled up from the builders' yard behind the church, a den went against the bank, it fell down within a fortnight, and we rebuilt it marginally better each time. There were blackberries in August, and an absurd amount of effort spent flattening coins on the last surviving stretch of rail. None of that was permitted and none of it was ever prevented.

Why it has stayed with me is straightforward enough: it was the first territory that belonged to us. Nothing about it had been provided, which is precisely what made it valuable — no adult had ever set foot up there, so everything that happened was our own work and our own fault. It's a cycle path now, resurfaced and signposted, with a bench roughly where the den stood. My nephew uses it and hasn't the faintest idea. I'm pleased it's in use. I just doubt any child will ever call it theirs.

what_lifts_it.point: Two passives and a past perfect passive replace band 7's active past forms.
'Lifted', 'hauled', 'territory', 'resurfaced' are precise rather than decorative.
It concedes the modern use and then refuses it, in two short sentences.

annotations.span: Pallets were hauled up from the builders' yard behind the church

annotations.span: an absurd amount of effort spent flattening coins

annotations.why: Let one word carry the verdict so you never say 'we enjoyed it'.

teaching.examiner_note: The examiner reads the card aloud and then hands it to you. You keep it, so you can check the second bullet mid-talk.

swap_slots.span: a small town in the mountains, about three hours' drive from where my family live
swap_slots.prompt: Your own destination and its distance from somewhere real in your life.

swap_slots.span: for a long weekend in November
swap_slots.prompt: Your own season and length. The season is what makes the gap believable.

swap_slots.span: Two of the three cafés had shut for the winter
swap_slots.prompt: The specific disappointment. One closed thing, counted, not 'everything was closed'.

swap_slots.span: a woman in her eighties who had lived there her whole life

teaching.transfer_drill: Now do the same two-layer version of a place that matched its photographs exactly. Forty-five seconds, past perfect first.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a town in the mountain. I went there last year in November for three days. It is three hours by car from my parents.

Before, I think it will be very beautiful. I saw many photos in the internet with sun, and colourful houses, and people eating outside. So I expect this.

But when I arrive there is fog. Two days, fog. So I cannot see the mountain, and the mountain is the reason for go there. Also two cafés are closed and the museum also. I was very disappointed.

But after it was better. Because everything is closed, all the people go in the same café. And I talk with an old lady all the afternoon. She lived there all her life. It was very interesting.

So it was not like the photos, but it was okay in the end. This is my place.

what_caps_it.point: Bullet four never arrives; the turn ends about forty seconds early on a restatement.
The expectation and the reality sit in the same tense, so the contrast the card is built on disappears.
'Beautiful', 'disappointed', 'interesting' — one adjective per paragraph and nothing behind any of them.

annotations.span: But after it was better.
annotations.label: Turns the story instead of ending on disappointment
annotations.why: Keep this. A card about expectation needs a reversal somewhere in it.

annotations.span: Before, I think it will be very beautiful.
annotations.label: The expectation is left in the present
annotations.why: Say "I'd expected it to be beautiful." The expectation came first, so it takes 'had'.

annotations.span: But when I arrive there is fog.
annotations.label: The whole reversal is in the present
annotations.why: Say 'When I arrived there was fog.' This sentence sets the tense for the rest.

annotations.span: the mountain is the reason for go there
annotations.label: Preposition followed by a bare verb
annotations.why: Say 'the reason for going there.' After a preposition, verbs take -ing.

annotations.span: It was very interesting.
annotations.label: One word for a whole afternoon
annotations.why: Say what she told you, or how she said it. 'Interesting' hides the content.

annotations.span: This is my place.
annotations.label: Ends early on a phrase from the card
annotations.why: Bullet four asks how you felt about the difference. That answer is missing.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a town in the mountains where I went last year in November. It is about three hours by car from my parents house.

Before I go, I think it will be very beautiful. I saw many photos on internet, with sun and colourful houses and people sitting outside. So I expected the same thing.

But when I arrived, there was fog everywhere. For two days I cannot see the mountains, and the mountains are the reason to go there. Also two cafés were closed for the winter, and the museum was closed too. I was very disappointed and I thought it is a waste of money.

But after, it became better. Because everything was closed, all the people were in the same café, and I talked with an old lady for all the afternoon. She lived there all her life and she told me many things about the tourists in the town. It was very interesting, more interesting than the photos. So in the end I was happy, but also a little bit strange feeling, because I wanted a place like the photos. This is my experience.

what_caps_it.point: Nothing is backshifted: 'I think it will be' and 'I thought it is' inside one past story.
The reversal is flagged with 'but after' and then never developed into a point.
'Very beautiful', 'very disappointed', 'very interesting' stand in for any precision.

annotations.span: Because everything was closed, all the people were in the same café
annotations.label: Cause before result
annotations.why: Keep this — a 'because' clause at the front organises the whole sentence.

annotations.span: Before I go, I think it will be very beautiful.
annotations.label: The whole sentence is present
annotations.why: 'Before I went, I'd thought it would be beautiful.' Backshift every verb.

annotations.span: For two days I cannot see the mountains
annotations.label: Present modal in a past story
annotations.why: 'I couldn't see the mountains.' Past story, past modal.

annotations.span: I thought it is a waste of money
annotations.label: No backshift after 'thought'
annotations.why: 'I thought it was a waste of money.' The reported clause moves back too.

annotations.span: for all the afternoon
annotations.label: An article that shouldn't be there
annotations.why: 'All afternoon' or 'the whole afternoon' — you cannot have both.

annotations.span: a little bit strange feeling
annotations.label: The feeling is never named
annotations.why: 'It left me slightly uncomfortable' actually answers the fourth bullet.

model_answers.label: The target — same trip, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place was a small town in the mountains, about three hours' drive from where my family live, and I went there for a long weekend in November.

What I'd expected was essentially the photographs. Every image I'd seen of it was taken in September — clear light, painted houses, people eating outside — so I'd built up quite a specific picture of wandering around in the sun and taking a great many photographs of my own.

What I actually got was fog. The whole valley was under cloud for two days and you couldn't see the mountains at all, which are the only reason anyone goes. Two of the three cafés had shut for the winter, the museum was closed for repairs, and the one bus up to the ridge wasn't running either. By the second morning I'd more or less decided the trip was a write-off.

And then it wasn't, oddly. Because everything else was shut, everyone still in the town ended up in the same café, and I spent an entire afternoon talking to a woman in her eighties who had lived there her whole life and had a great deal to say about what the visitors had done to the place. I learned far more from that than I would have from a clear day, and she wasn't remotely sentimental about any of it. So what I came away with was a slightly uncomfortable feeling — that the version of the town I'd wanted was the version that had been produced for me.

what_lifts_it.point: Four past perfects hold the expectation apart from the reality throughout.
'A write-off', 'built up a picture', 'a great deal to say' — chunks instead of intensifiers.
Two clearly marked turns, and the answer ends on a judgement about itself.

annotations.span: What I'd expected was essentially the photographs.
annotations.label: Answers bullet two in one line
annotations.why: State the expectation as a thing, then spend your time on the evidence.

annotations.span: Every image I'd seen of it was taken in September
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a past clause
annotations.why: Backshift once and both layers of time stay obvious to the listener.

annotations.span: the trip was a write-off
annotations.label: One noun makes the judgement
annotations.why: Reuse 'a write-off' for any plan or day that came to nothing.

annotations.span: What I actually got was fog.
annotations.label: A short sentence marks the turn
annotations.why: Five words after a long sentence signal the reversal without a linker.

annotations.span: And then it wasn't, oddly.
annotations.label: A second, deliberate reversal
annotations.why: Two turns keep a listener with you far better than one does.

annotations.span: I learned far more from that than I would have from a clear day
annotations.label: Comparative against a hypothetical
annotations.why: Comparing what happened with what didn't earns real grammar credit.

annotations.span: had a great deal to say about what the visitors had done to the place
annotations.label: Reports an opinion without quoting
annotations.why: Summarising what somebody said avoids a long run of direct speech.

annotations.span: the version of the town I'd wanted was the version that had been produced for me
annotations.label: Contrastive stress on 'produced'
annotations.why: The entire point sits on one word, so give that word the beat.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This was a small mountain town three hours from my parents', and I went up for a long weekend at the end of November, which was my first mistake.

Everything I'd seen of the place had been photographed in September, mostly by people who had gone at the right time of year. Clear light, painted shutters, people eating outside — so that was the weekend I'd packed for and, in effect, paid for.

What I found was cloud. The valley stayed under it for two solid days, so the mountains, which are the entire point, might as well not have existed. Two of the three cafés had closed for the season, the museum was mid-refurbishment, and the bus up to the ridge had stopped running in October. By Saturday lunchtime I'd written the trip off completely.

Which is when it got interesting. With nothing else open, everybody still in the town converged on the one café that was, and I spent most of an afternoon with a woman in her eighties who'd been born in the next street and had a good deal to say — not much of it warm — about what tourism had done to the valley and to the people who had stayed in it. I came away having learned more than any amount of scenery would have taught me, and faintly uneasy with myself, because what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Might as well not have existed' and a cleft with a past perfect passive go past band 7.
'Converged', 'mid-refurbishment', 'not much of it warm' are dry and exact, never showy.
The self-criticism at the end is the point of the turn and it is made only once.

annotations.span: which was my first mistake
annotations.label: An aside that flags the structure
annotations.why: Signalling trouble early makes a listener wait for the payoff.

annotations.span: might as well not have existed
annotations.label: Modal perfect in a relative clause
annotations.why: A compact way of saying the whole thing failed, and it sounds spoken.

annotations.span: Which is when it got interesting.
annotations.label: Turns the story in five words
annotations.why: A short fragment after a long paragraph is the cleanest reversal available.

annotations.span: not much of it warm
annotations.label: Four words replace a sentence
annotations.why: An aside like this shows judgement without any adjective of your own.

annotations.span: what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect passive
annotations.why: Front the 'what' clause so the turn ends on the phrase that matters.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
This was a small mountain town three hours from my parents', and I went up for a long weekend at the end of November, which was the first of several mistakes.

Everything I'd seen of the place had been photographed in September, largely by people with the sense to go at the right time of year. Clear light, painted shutters, people eating outside — so that was the weekend I'd packed for and, in effect, paid for.

What I got was cloud. The valley stayed under it for two solid days, so the mountains, which are the entire point of the place, might as well not have been there. Two of the three cafés had shut for the season, the museum was mid-refurbishment, and the bus up to the ridge had stopped running in October. By Saturday lunchtime I'd written the whole thing off.

Which is when it became interesting. With nothing else open, everyone still in the town converged on the one café that was, and I spent the better part of an afternoon with a woman in her eighties who'd been born in the next street and had a great deal to say — very little of it warm — about what tourism had done to the valley and to the people who'd stayed in it.

I came away having learned more than any amount of scenery would have taught me, and slightly uncomfortable with myself, because what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me. The fog simply got in the way of the arrangement.

what_lifts_it.point: A modal perfect and a past perfect carrying two verbs, neither slowing the delivery.
The criticism is carried by understatement rather than by adjectives.
A short final sentence lands the point band 8 spent a whole clause explaining.

annotations.span: might as well not have been there
annotations.label: Modal perfect for a hypothetical past
annotations.why: 'Might as well not have' compresses a whole 'it made no difference that' clause.

annotations.span: so that was the weekend I'd packed for and, in effect, paid for
annotations.label: Past perfect across two stranded prepositions
annotations.why: Two verbs share one object and the prepositions stay at the end, as they do in speech.

annotations.span: largely by people with the sense to go at the right time of year
annotations.label: Dry understatement does the criticism
annotations.why: Aim the joke at yourself; it is more precise than 'unfortunately'.

annotations.span: converged on the one café that was
annotations.label: Exact verb plus ellipsis of 'open'
annotations.why: 'Converged' is precise, and dropping the repeated adjective sounds natural.

annotations.span: The fog simply got in the way of the arrangement.
annotations.label: A short final sentence reframes everything
annotations.why: One short sentence after a long one is the cleanest close there is.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Answer the fourth bullet. How you felt about the difference is where this card's marks are.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Put the expectation in past perfect and the reality in past simple. That split is the entire card.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Give the disappointment a date and a time — 'by Saturday lunchtime' — so the reversal has a hinge.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: End on a short sentence. After a long paragraph, six words land harder than another clause.

title: A change you would like to see in your town

payload_json.topic: A change you would like to see in your town

cue_card.topic: Describe a change you would like to see in the town or city where you live.
bullets: what the change would be
why the place needs it
who would have to make it happen
and explain what difference it would make to the people there.
rounding_off: Is anything like that being discussed at the moment?
Would everyone welcome it?

teaching.band_move: Size the change so it sounds possible, then name every party who would have to agree to it.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Pick something you could point at from a bus window. A small, specific change argues far better than a grand one.
prep_plan.trap: Candidates say what they want and never say who would have to do it or what it would cost them.

time_plan.goal: State the change in one sentence.
The proposal, then the problem it answers.
Name the parties and what each would give up.
The obvious gain, then the real one.
One line about towns that work.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe the street itself — width, shopfronts, what is parked on it.
Add time depth: say what that street looked like ten or twenty years ago.
Contrast it with a nearby town that has already made the same change.
Speculate: say what the objectors think would happen and whether they're right.

error_watchlist.wrong: If they will close the street, more people come.
error_watchlist.right: If they closed the street, more people would come.
error_watchlist.why: Past tense in one half, 'would' in the other.

error_watchlist.wrong: The council must to do this change.
error_watchlist.right: The council would have to do it.
error_watchlist.why: 'Must' takes no 'to'; imagined duty takes 'would have to'.

error_watchlist.wrong: It would make a good effect on the town.
error_watchlist.right: It would have a real effect on the town.
error_watchlist.why: You have an effect, but you make a difference.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: This card runs on 'would have to' and 'a lot of it', which reduce heavily in real speech.

target_words.note: Reduces to /wəd/, or just 'd after a pronoun.
In 'would have to' it becomes /əv/.
Unstressed /tə/ before a consonant.
Usually /ən/ — 'buses an' bikes'.
Weakens to /fə/ unless you are stressing it.

chunking_drill.sentence: The council, who own the road, the bus company, who would have to accept a longer route, and the traders themselves.
chunks: The council, who own the road,
the bus company, who would have to accept a longer route,
and the traders themselves.

minimal_pairs.contrast: identical when stressed, but only one ever reduces

teaching.examiner_note: An abstract card is answered the same way as any other: one instance, described concretely. The examiner is not testing your politics.

swap_slots.span: about two hundred metres of the main street
swap_slots.prompt: Your own change, sized with a number. Vague scale makes the whole proposal vague.

teaching.transfer_drill: Argue the opposite case in forty-five seconds: give the traders' side of the same change, with their reasons and their evidence.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a change in my town. I want that they close the main street for cars, near the market, maybe two hundred metres.

The reason is the market is dying. Everybody say it is because of the supermarkets. But I think it is the cars. There is always cars between the stalls and the shops. So it is dangerous and also very loud. Old people cannot cross, and people with a baby also cannot. And in front there is a big shop, it is closed since three years.

For make this change, the council must do it, because the street is from them. Also the buses. And the shop owners, but they don't want, they think if there is no cars nobody come.

If they close it, it will be better. More space for the market. That is my change.

Yes.

what_caps_it.point: The turn ends about fifty seconds early and the fourth bullet gets one four-word sentence.
'Want that', 'for make', 'there is cars', 'since three years' — four structural errors in a minute.
'Dangerous', 'loud', 'better' — an argument about a whole town made from three adjectives.

annotations.span: But I think it is the cars.
annotations.label: Argues a cause nobody supplied
annotations.why: Keep this. Disagreeing with the obvious explanation is worth real credit.

annotations.span: I want that they close the main street for cars
annotations.label: 'Want' followed by a that-clause
annotations.why: Say "I'd like them to close it." Wanting takes 'somebody to do'.

annotations.span: There is always cars between the stalls and the shops.
annotations.label: 'There is' with a plural noun
annotations.why: Say 'There are always cars between the stalls and the shopfronts.'

annotations.span: it is closed since three years
annotations.label: 'Since' with a length, and no perfect
annotations.why: Say "It's been closed for three years." 'For' takes a length of time.

annotations.span: For make this change
annotations.label: A preposition followed by a bare verb
annotations.why: Say 'To make this change' or 'For this to happen'.

annotations.span:
That is my change.

Yes.
annotations.label: Stops at seventy seconds with a bullet unanswered
annotations.why: The last bullet asks what difference it would make. It needs its own thirty seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about a change in my town. I want that they close the main street for the cars, near the market, maybe two hundred metres.

The reason is because the market is dying. Everybody says it is the supermarkets, but I think it is the traffic. There are always cars between the stalls and the shops, so it is dangerous and it is very loud. Old people cannot cross the road, and people with a baby cannot cross also. And in front there is a big shop which is closed since three years.

For do this, the council must do it, because the street is theirs. Also the bus company, because the buses go there. And the shop owners, but they don't want it, they think if there is no cars, nobody comes to their shops.

If they close the street, it will be much better. There is more space for the market. And people will stay more time, because now everybody walks fast and goes home. When people stay, they meet other people. So this is my change and I hope one day they do it.

what_caps_it.point: The whole answer is imagined, yet every conditional in it is built as though it were real.
Reasons arrive as short clauses stitched together with 'and' and 'also'.
'Better', 'dangerous', 'loud' — nothing here would survive into a Part 3 answer.

annotations.span: Everybody says it is the supermarkets, but I think it is the traffic.
annotations.label: Rejects the obvious cause
annotations.why: Keep this — disagreeing with the easy explanation is a genuine band-7 habit.

annotations.span: I want that they close the main street
annotations.label: 'Want' cannot take that
annotations.why: 'I'd like them to close the main street.' Want takes object plus 'to'.

annotations.span: The reason is because
annotations.label: Two connectors, one job
annotations.why: 'The reason is that…' or simply 'because…', but never both at once.

annotations.span: which is closed since three years
annotations.label: Wrong tense with 'since'
annotations.why: 'Which has been closed for three years.' Duration needs a perfect form.

annotations.span: For do this
annotations.label: Preposition before a bare verb
annotations.why: 'To do this.' Purpose takes an infinitive, never 'for' plus verb.

annotations.span: If they close the street, it will be much better.
annotations.label: Real conditional for an imagined change
annotations.why: 'If they closed it, it would be much better.' The card is hypothetical.

model_answers.label: The target — same proposal, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd like is fairly small in scale — I'd close about two hundred metres of the main street to cars, the stretch that runs past the market, and move the buses one street over.

The reason is that the market is slowly dying, and I don't think it's dying for the obvious reason. It isn't the supermarket, or not only. It's that there's a constant line of traffic between the stalls and the pavement, so you can't cross, you can't hear, and nobody with a pushchair or a walking frame will attempt it. The department store opposite has been boarded up for three years, and every time a shop shuts it takes a bit more footfall with it.

Making it happen would need three parties who don't currently agree on anything. The council, who own the road, the bus company, who would have to accept a longer route, and the traders themselves, who are convinced that taking the cars out would finish them off. I understand why they think that, and I'd probably think it too if my rent depended on it, but the evidence from the next town along suggests the opposite.

So what difference would it make? Practically, you'd more or less double the usable space in front of the stalls, which the traders could take over. But the real change would be that people would linger. Nobody stands still on that street at the moment, and a town where nobody stands still is a town where nothing accidental happens. You buy what you came for and you leave.

what_lifts_it.point: Second conditionals and 'would have to' are handled consistently across the whole turn.
'Footfall', 'finish them off', 'linger' — the words belong to the subject, not to a list.
Each bullet gets a signposted paragraph and the last one ranks two arguments.

annotations.span: The change I'd like is fairly small in scale
annotations.label: States the change and its size
annotations.why: Naming the scale early stops the proposal sounding like a daydream.

annotations.span: I don't think it's dying for the obvious reason
annotations.label: Refuses the easy explanation
annotations.why: Rejecting the obvious cause obliges you to supply a better one.

annotations.span: you can't cross, you can't hear, and nobody with a pushchair or a walking frame will attempt it
annotations.label: Three parallel clauses
annotations.why: Parallel structure is grammar you can plan for in advance.

annotations.span: it takes a bit more footfall with it
annotations.label: The trade word, used naturally
annotations.why: One precise term proves you know the subject, not just the vocabulary.

annotations.span: who would have to accept a longer route
annotations.label: 'Would have to' for imagined duty
annotations.why: This is the workhorse structure for any change you are proposing.

annotations.span: So what difference would it make?
annotations.label: Asks the bullet as a question
annotations.why: Turning the bullet into a question is the cleanest signpost there is.

annotations.span: the real change would be that people would linger
annotations.label: One verb carries the argument
annotations.why: 'Linger' means stop, stay and look, without three separate verbs.

annotations.span: You buy what you came for and you leave.
annotations.label: Deliberately flat ending
annotations.why: Let the last clause drop away; the flatness is itself the point.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd argue for is a modest one: closing a couple of hundred metres of the main street to traffic, the stretch alongside the market, and diverting the buses onto the road behind it.

The market is dying, and the usual explanation, which is the supermarket out on the bypass, strikes me as only half true. The other half is that there's a permanent queue of cars between the stalls and the shopfronts, so the street is impossible to cross, impossible to hear across, and quietly hostile to anybody slow. With the department store opposite boarded up since 2022, each closure drags a little more footfall out with it.

Getting it off the ground would need three parties who agree on very little: the council, who own the road; the bus company, who'd be asked to swallow a longer route; and the traders, who are convinced that removing the cars would ruin them. Their fear is perfectly rational, and I'd share it if my rent depended on that street. It just happens to be contradicted by every comparable town I know of.

The obvious gain is space, and quite a lot of it. The less obvious one, and I think the important one, is that people would stop moving. Nobody stands still on that street at present, and a town in which nobody stands still is a town where nothing unplanned ever happens. You buy what you came for and you go home.

what_lifts_it.point: A 'with' participle clause and a hedged passive replace band 7's plain relative clauses.
'Quietly hostile', 'swallow a longer route', 'drags footfall out' are exact and unshowy.
It grants the objectors' logic before rejecting their conclusion, which band 7 only implies.

annotations.span: quietly hostile to anybody slow
annotations.label: Four words instead of a sentence
annotations.why: Give the street an attitude and the argument largely makes itself.

annotations.span: With the department store opposite boarded up since 2022
annotations.label: 'With' plus a participle clause
annotations.why: A compact way to add background without building another sentence.

annotations.span: who'd be asked to swallow a longer route
annotations.label: 'Swallow' carries the reluctance
annotations.why: Choose a verb that shows how a party feels about what they're given.

annotations.span: It just happens to be contradicted by every comparable town I know of.
annotations.label: Hedged passive after a concession
annotations.why: Grant the reasoning, then disagree with the conclusion, in one clause.

annotations.span: The less obvious one, and I think the important one, is that people would stop moving.
annotations.label: Ranks two arguments aloud
annotations.why: Saying which of your points matters more is exactly what gets rewarded.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd push for is small and boring, which is probably why it might actually happen: take cars off roughly two hundred metres of the main street, the bit that runs past the market, and send the buses round the back.

The market is going under. Everyone blames the supermarket on the bypass and I'd say that accounts for about half of it. The rest is that there is a stationary line of traffic sitting between the stalls and the shopfronts all day, so you can't get across, you can't hear a word anybody says, and if you happen to be slow the street is effectively closed to you. The old department store facing it has been boarded up since 2022, and each shutter that comes down takes a little more passing trade with it.

Three parties would have to sign it off, and they agree on almost nothing. The council own the road. The bus company would be asked to accept a longer run for no benefit at all. And the traders themselves are certain it would finish them, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to be certain of when your rent depends on that pavement — it just isn't what happened in any comparable town I've looked at.

You'd gain the space, obviously, and a fair amount of it. What you'd really gain is people standing still. At the moment nobody does, and a place where nobody stands still is a place where nothing happens by accident. You get what you came for and you leave, and ten years of that leaves a street with no reason to walk down it.

what_lifts_it.point: A sentential 'which' with a stranded preposition, and a second conditional that drops its 'if'.
'Going under', 'stationary line', 'passing trade' — verbs and nouns doing the persuading.
The concession to the traders is folded into the same sentence that answers it.

annotations.span: which is a perfectly reasonable thing to be certain of when your rent depends on that pavement
annotations.label: Sentential 'which' with a stranded preposition
annotations.why: 'Which' refers to the whole clause, and 'of' stays at the end as it does in speech.

annotations.span: You'd gain the space, obviously, and a fair amount of it.
annotations.label: Second conditional with the 'if' left out
annotations.why: Once the hypothesis is established, 'would' carries it alone. No 'if' needed.

annotations.span: each shutter that comes down takes a little more passing trade with it
annotations.label: A concrete image argues the economics
annotations.why: Show the shutter, not the statistic. The listener supplies the rest.

annotations.span: the street is effectively closed to you
annotations.label: 'Effectively' hedges a claim into accuracy
annotations.why: One adverb makes an exaggeration true, and true is more persuasive.

annotations.span: ten years of that leaves a street with no reason to walk down it
annotations.label: Projects the consequence forward and stops
annotations.why: Give the harm a timescale; it turns a complaint into a forecast.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Answer the last bullet. What difference it makes to people is thirty seconds you're not using.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Size the change so it sounds possible — a number of metres, a named street — then say who has to agree.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Concede the traders' fear before you dismiss it. An argument that admits nothing convinces nobody.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Put a timescale on the consequence. 'Ten years of that' turns a complaint into a forecast.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Look round the room in your head and take the first thing that annoys you. Annoyance supplies detail; importance does not.

time_plan.goal: Name the object and where it sits.
What it is, and how it came to you.
Four faults, each one physical.

target_words.note: The ending is /z/ after a vowel.
