model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about our sofa. It is green and it has three places. We have it nine years.

I buy it from my colleague. She go to another country, so she sell it very cheap, eighty pounds only. It was a good price.

But now there is many problems. The left cushion is broken, so if you sit there you are more low than the others. And there is a spring inside, you can feel it in your back. Also the colour is not the same everywhere because of the sun. And my cat, he make the corner very bad.

Why I don't buy a new one? Because it is expensive. And also our door is very small. I think a new sofa cannot come inside. So I look and after I stop.

Maybe we keep it forever. That's all about my sofa.

what_caps_it.point: The turn runs about eighty seconds and the last bullet gets three short sentences.
No present perfect anywhere, so nine years of ownership reads as one past event.
'Broken', 'bad', 'expensive', 'small' — four flat adjectives cover an object the card wants described.

annotations.span: And there is a spring inside, you can feel it in your back.
annotations.label: Describes one fault at a time
annotations.why: Keep this. Faults described part by part beat the single word 'broken'.

annotations.span: We have it nine years.
annotations.label: Duration with no perfect tense
annotations.why: Say "We've had it for nine years." A stretch of time up to now takes 'have had'.

annotations.span: She go to another country, so she sell it very cheap
annotations.label: Two past verbs left unmarked
annotations.why: Say 'She was moving abroad, so she sold it cheap.' Both verbs, both past.

annotations.span: But now there is many problems.
annotations.label: 'There is' with a plural
annotations.why: Say 'there are several things wrong with it.'

annotations.span: you are more low than the others
annotations.label: Comparative built the wrong way
annotations.why: Say 'you sit lower than everyone else.' Short adjectives take -er, not 'more'.

annotations.span: That's all about my sofa.
annotations.label: Hands back with the last bullet barely started
annotations.why: Say what you measured, and when. That is the answer the card is asking for.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe something in my house that I must replace. It is our sofa, it is green and it has three places for sitting.

We have it since nine years. I bought it from my colleague, she was going to another country, and it was very cheap, only eighty pounds. So it was a good price for us.

Now there are many problems. The cushion in the left side is broken, so when you sit there you are lower than the other people. Also there is a spring inside and you can feel it in your back. The colour is not same in all the parts, because of the sun from the window. And our cat, he scratches the corner every day.

Why I don't buy a new one? First, because sofas are expensive. But also there is another problem: our door is very small, and I think a new sofa cannot pass. The old sofa came before we changed the door. So every time I look for a sofa, I remember this and I stop. Maybe we will keep it forever.

what_caps_it.point: Duration, question form, articles and a doubled subject all slip inside two minutes.
The reasons come in the right order, but each one lands as a bare statement.
'Very cheap', 'many problems', 'not same' — the object never becomes visible.

annotations.span: But also there is another problem: our door is very small
annotations.label: Introduces a second reason
annotations.why: Keep this — flagging that a better reason is coming holds the listener.

annotations.span: We have it since nine years.
annotations.label: Two errors in five words
annotations.why: 'We've had it for nine years.' Perfect form, and 'for' with a length.

annotations.span: The cushion in the left side is broken
annotations.label: Wrong preposition, extra noun
annotations.why: 'The cushion on the left has collapsed.' Drop 'side' altogether.

annotations.span: The colour is not same in all the parts
annotations.label: 'Same' without its article
annotations.why: 'The same' — it takes 'the' in every position, without exception.

annotations.span: our cat, he scratches the corner
annotations.label: The subject appears twice
annotations.why: Choose one of them: 'our cat scratches the corner'.

annotations.span: Why I don't buy a new one?
annotations.label: Statement order in a question
annotations.why: 'So why haven't I replaced it?' The auxiliary comes before the subject.

model_answers.label: The target — same sofa, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd talk about is our sofa, which is a three-seater, dark green, and quite obviously on its last legs.

We've had it about nine years. I bought it second-hand from a colleague who was moving abroad, for something like eighty pounds, which felt like a bargain at the time and has worked out at under a tenner a year. It's the only thing in that flat which has genuinely paid for itself.

What's wrong with it is fairly comprehensive. The cushion on the left has collapsed, so anybody sitting there sinks about six inches lower than everyone else. One of the springs has worked its way loose and you can feel it through the fabric if you lean back properly. The arms have faded by completely different amounts, depending on how close they are to the window. And the cat has done to one corner exactly what cats do. None of that is anybody's fault, mind you; it's nine years of ordinary use.

So why is it still there? Partly money, obviously — sofas cost more than I want to spend on somewhere to sit. But mostly it's that I measured the door frame about a year ago and discovered that almost nothing sold now would actually fit through it — this sofa came in before we had the front door replaced. So replacing it isn't really a sofa problem, it's a door problem, and every time I get as far as looking at sofas I remember that and give up. I suspect it'll outlast us both.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect for duration and 'one of the springs has' are both handled correctly.
'On its last legs', 'worked its way loose', 'under a tenner a year' — chunks with content.
The last bullet reframes the problem instead of restating the price.

annotations.span: quite obviously on its last legs
annotations.label: Idiom used at the right moment
annotations.why: 'On its last legs' fits any object, machine or plan that is failing.

annotations.span: We've had it about nine years.
annotations.label: Present perfect for duration
annotations.why: Possession that still holds takes 'have had', never the past simple.

annotations.span: has worked out at under a tenner a year
annotations.label: Arithmetic as evaluation
annotations.why: Working the cost out per year persuades far better than 'it was cheap'.

annotations.span: What's wrong with it is fairly comprehensive.
annotations.label: Heads the bullet, dryly
annotations.why: One summary sentence buys you four examples with no hesitation.

annotations.span: One of the springs has worked its way loose
annotations.label: Singular verb after 'one of the'
annotations.why: The verb belongs to 'one', never to the plural noun beside it.

annotations.span: So why is it still there?
annotations.label: Turns the bullet into a question
annotations.why: Ask the bullet aloud and you cannot then forget to answer it.

annotations.span: replacing it isn't really a sofa problem, it's a door problem
annotations.label: Reframes the whole answer
annotations.why: Naming the real obstacle is what lifts an ordinary object card.

annotations.span: I suspect it'll outlast us both.
annotations.label: Quiet drop on the last line
annotations.why: A soft ending sounds finished; a loud one sounds like you ran out.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The obvious candidate is our sofa: three seats, dark green, and visibly finished.

We've had it nine years. I bought it off a colleague who was emigrating, for eighty pounds, which struck me as a bargain then and has since worked out at rather less than a tenner a year — the only purchase in that flat I can honestly say that about. Whether that reflects well on the sofa or badly on everything else, I couldn't tell you.

Its faults are extensive. The left-hand cushion gave up years ago, so whoever sits there ends up several inches below the rest of the room. A spring has escaped somewhere behind the fabric and makes itself known if you lean back. The arms have faded at conspicuously different rates according to their distance from the window. And the cat has done to one corner precisely what cats do. None of it is anyone's fault; it is nine years of ordinary use.

The interesting question is why it's still in the room, and the answer isn't really money. About a year ago I measured the door frame and worked out that virtually nothing on sale now would come through it; the sofa predates the front door we had fitted. So this isn't a sofa problem at all, it's a door problem, which is a considerably more expensive thing to admit. Every time I get as far as browsing I remember that and stop. Realistically, the sofa will see me out.

what_lifts_it.point: A 'whoever' clause and a sentential 'which' go past band 7's ordinary relatives.
'Predates', 'conspicuously', 'see me out' are dry and exact rather than decorative.
The reframing arrives as the punchline of the turn instead of as an explanation.

annotations.span: whoever sits there ends up several inches below the rest of the room
annotations.label: 'Whoever' as a subject clause
annotations.why: A cleaner way to generalise than 'if a person sits there'.

annotations.span: faded at conspicuously different rates
annotations.label: Precision where band 6 said colour
annotations.why: Describe the process rather than the state and the picture sharpens.

annotations.span: the sofa predates the front door we had fitted
annotations.label: One verb replaces a clause
annotations.why: 'Predates' carries 'came before' in a single word and fits the register.

annotations.span: which is a considerably more expensive thing to admit
annotations.label: Relative clause on a whole idea
annotations.why: 'Which' can refer to your entire previous sentence, not just to a noun.

annotations.span: Realistically, the sofa will see me out.
annotations.label: A one-line landing
annotations.why: Finish on a short dry sentence and the whole turn sounds complete.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
The sofa, without any competition. Three seats, dark green, and it has clearly stopped trying.

It's been in the flat nine years. I bought it from a colleague who was leaving the country, for eighty pounds, which felt cheap then and has since amortised down to something under a tenner a year. No other object I own has behaved that well, and I'm not sure whether that's a compliment to the sofa.

The list of things wrong with it is long. Whoever takes the left-hand seat drops four or five inches below everybody else, because the cushion collapsed some time ago and never recovered. There's a spring loose behind the fabric that makes itself felt if you lean back properly. The two arms have bleached at completely different rates, purely according to how much window they get. And a cat has spent nine years doing to one corner what cats do to corners. None of that is neglect. It's what nine years of being sat on looks like.

The real question is why it's still there, and money isn't the honest answer. What happened is that I measured the door frame last spring and discovered that almost nothing currently on sale would fit through it — the sofa arrived before the front door was replaced. So it was never a furniture problem. It's a doorway problem, which costs considerably more to admit than to ignore, and every time I get as far as opening a website I remember and close it again. On present form, the sofa outlasts me.

what_lifts_it.point: A comparative across two infinitives and a passive gerund subject, both dropped in casually.
'Amortised', 'bleached', 'stopped trying' — one borrowed register and two exact verbs.
The opening is four words long, which sets a pace band 8 never reaches.

annotations.span: which costs considerably more to admit than to ignore
annotations.label: Comparative across two infinitives
annotations.why: 'More to admit than to ignore' compares two actions, not two things.

annotations.span: It's what nine years of being sat on looks like.
annotations.label: Passive gerund as the subject
annotations.why: 'Being sat on' turns an event into a subject; the sentence needs nothing else.

annotations.span: it has clearly stopped trying
annotations.label: The object is given a will it lost
annotations.why: Let the thing act. It beats any adjective you could put in that slot.

annotations.span: has since amortised down to something under a tenner a year
annotations.label: A financial verb used for a sofa
annotations.why: Borrow a word from another field and the joke arrives with the meaning.

annotations.span: So it was never a furniture problem. It's a doorway problem
annotations.label: Reclassifies the problem in two sentences
annotations.why: Renaming the problem is the sharpest answer to a 'why haven't you' bullet.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Add the price, the year and the room. Concrete numbers are the easiest forty seconds on this card.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: One present perfect for the nine years, past simple for how you got it. Two tenses, two jobs.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Give the faults a cause you don't blame anyone for. 'Nine years of ordinary use' is worth a paragraph.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Let the object do the verbs. 'It has clearly stopped trying' beats any adjective you could put in that slot.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe the market near my home. It is about five minutes walking from my flat, at the end of my street, next to the bus stop.

Before, it was a normal market for vegetables and fruit. My mother went there every Saturday when I was small. It was very old and the roof was broken in some places, and honestly it was not so nice. In the last years many sellers left, so it was half empty.

Then two years ago the council repaired it. Now there are food stalls and small shops, and also a coffee place. In the evening it is very busy and many young people go there.

I feel happy about this change because before it was dying. But also I feel a little bit sad, because the old sellers could not pay the new rent, so they went away. If they get help, they stay. So it is good and bad, but I think it is better than before. So this is the place near my home that has changed.

what_caps_it.point: The whole 'before' section sits in past simple with no present perfect anywhere.
'Nice', 'good', 'busy', 'sad' — four flat adjectives carry every judgement.
Sentences are chained with 'so' and 'but'; nothing signals a new bullet.

annotations.why: Keep this — it lets the listener picture the place before you describe it.

annotations.label: Distance phrase built wrongly
annotations.why: Say 'about a five-minute walk from my flat' — noun, not -ing form.

annotations.why: Say what was wrong: the roof leaked, the lighting was terrible.

annotations.span: In the last years many sellers left
annotations.label: Past simple where the change reaches now
annotations.why: Use 'Over the last few years a lot of the sellers have left.'

annotations.span: If they get help, they stay.

annotations.why: Regret about the past needs 'If they'd been given help, they'd have stayed.'

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'd like to talk about a place two streets from my flat: the old covered market, which sits right next to the main bus stop.

When I was growing up it was basically a fruit and vegetable market. My mother used to drag me round it every Saturday morning, and I remember it being cold and a bit run-down. The roof leaked in two or three places, and by the time I was a teenager half the units were shut. It had been going downhill for years before anybody did anything about it.

What's happened since is that the council took the building over and refurbished the whole thing. They kept the original iron frame, which I'm glad about, but the rest is new: food stalls now, a couple of small independent shops, and a coffee place that seems to be permanently full. In the evenings it's packed, mainly with people in their twenties, whereas before it was dead by four o'clock.

As for how I feel about it, I'm genuinely pleased on the whole, because the alternative was watching the roof come in. What I'm less comfortable with is that hardly any of the original traders are still there. The rents went up and they simply couldn't absorb it, so they drifted off to other markets. If the council had capped the rent for the existing stallholders, I think a few of them would have stayed. So it's a change I'm in favour of with one reservation, which is probably the honest position on most regeneration.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect for background and a third conditional replace the flat past simples.
'Going downhill', 'couldn't absorb it', 'drifted off' — chunks doing the work adjectives did.
Three audible signposts mark the three bullets instead of a chain of 'so'.

annotations.why: Fix the place before you describe it; the listener needs somewhere to put it.

annotations.span: It had been going downhill for years before anybody did anything about it.
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the background
annotations.why: One past perfect per story shows two layers of time and costs nothing.

annotations.span: cold and a bit run-down
annotations.label: Two precise adjectives, not 'not nice'
annotations.why: Pick adjectives that describe the fault, not your feeling about it.

annotations.span: What's happened since is that the council took the building over
annotations.label: Announces the change bullet aloud
annotations.why: Naming the move stops you sliding from bullet two into bullet three unnoticed.

annotations.span: whereas before it was dead by four o'clock
annotations.label: Contrast joined with 'whereas'
annotations.why: 'Whereas' wants a whole clause on each side; 'but' would flatten this.

annotations.span: As for how I feel about it
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: This is the bullet candidates forget. Say its name out loud.

annotations.span: they simply couldn't absorb it
annotations.label: A precise verb instead of 'pay'
annotations.why: 'Absorb a cost' is the natural partner; reuse it for any price rise.

annotations.span: If the council had capped the rent for the existing stallholders, I think a few of them would have stayed.
annotations.label: Third conditional for the regret
annotations.why: Any 'how do you feel' bullet will take one of these. Prepare it.

annotations.span: What I'm less comfortable with is
annotations.label: Cleft opening for the reservation
annotations.why: Fronting the reservation makes mixed feelings sound deliberate, not confused.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place I want to describe is the old covered market a couple of streets from my flat, which has been through a fairly dramatic transformation in the last five years.

For most of my childhood it was a fruit and vegetable market, and not a thriving one. My mother took me round on Saturday mornings, and what I mainly remember is the cold and the smell of wet cardboard. The roof leaked, the lighting was miserable, and by the time I was in my teens half the units had been boarded up. It had been quietly dying for a decade, and everybody had rather made their peace with that.

Then the council stepped in and gutted the building. They had the sense to keep the original ironwork, which is the only reason it still feels like the same place, but the rest is unrecognisable: food stalls, two or three independent shops, a coffee place that's rammed from morning to night. It used to be dead by four.

How do I feel about it? Broadly delighted, with one caveat I can't quite talk myself out of. Hardly any of the original traders survived the rent increase. They were priced out rather than pushed out, which is somehow worse, because nobody had to make a decision about it. Had the council staggered those rents over a few years, a handful of them would almost certainly still be trading. What strikes me is that regeneration nearly always works that way round: the building gets saved and the people inside it don't.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces the standard 'if' clause the band 7 used.
'Made their peace with', 'priced out rather than pushed out' — shades of meaning, not rare words.
The close generalises about regeneration instead of summarising the market.

annotations.span: Had the council staggered those rents over a few years
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Identical to the third conditional in meaning, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: everybody had rather made their peace with that
annotations.label: Idiom placed where a native would
annotations.why: Two idioms that fit beat five that are on display.

annotations.span: They were priced out rather than pushed out
annotations.label: One contrast carries the whole judgement
annotations.why: Choosing between two near-synonyms is what band 8 lexis actually looks like.

annotations.span: food stalls, two or three independent shops, a coffee place that's rammed from morning to night
annotations.label: A list delivered as one run
annotations.why: Hold the pitch level across the list, then fall on the final item.

annotations.span: the building gets saved and the people inside it don't
annotations.label: Abstracts the anecdote into an idea
annotations.why: End one rung above the story and the whole turn lifts.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The job I'd eventually like to do is physiotherapy, and specifically in a sports clinic rather than a hospital, because I'd rather follow the same person through a whole course of treatment than meet them once.

In terms of what it takes, it's a four-year degree here, and a fair chunk of that is anatomy, which I'd genuinely have to work at. But from what I've seen, the qualification is only half of it. The real skill is persuading somebody to keep doing a set of extremely boring exercises for six weeks when nothing seems to be improving. That's far more about communication than it is about the body.

As for preparing, I've made a start. Since last autumn I've been working two days a week on reception at a physio clinic, mainly to get my foot in the door, and it has been useful in ways I honestly hadn't expected. On top of that I'm doing an evening biology course, because my school science wasn't strong enough to get me onto the degree.

The reason it appeals to me is fairly personal. I tore a ligament playing football when I was nineteen, and I spent five months with a physiotherapist who changed how I thought about the injury. I'd assumed the knee would never be right again. She didn't reassure me, exactly. She gave me something to do every morning and let the evidence build up, and if I could do that for somebody else, I'd be content with that as a career.

annotations.why: Contrastive stress does the work of a whole extra sentence.

annotations.label: Second conditional closes the turn
annotations.why: An unreal plan is exactly what 'if I could… I'd…' is for.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The job I'd like to end up doing is physiotherapy, and I've got a fairly specific version of it in mind: a sports clinic rather than a hospital ward, because what appeals to me is following one person right through a course of treatment.

The formal requirement is a four-year degree, a good deal of which is anatomy, and that's the part I'd have to grind through rather than enjoy. What strikes me, though, having watched it up close, is how little of the job is technical. Most of it is getting somebody to keep doing dull exercises for six weeks while nothing visibly improves. Not many people are cut out for that, and it isn't examined anywhere on the degree.

On preparation, I've made a modest start. I've been on the reception desk at a clinic two days a week since last autumn, which has taught me more about how a practice really runs than a placement would have, and I'm working through an evening biology course to get my science up to entry standard.

As for why: I tore a ligament at nineteen and spent five months with a physiotherapist who quietly dismantled my assumption that the knee was finished. She never once told me it would be fine. She set me something to do each morning and let the evidence accumulate. Had she handled it differently, I suspect I'd have given up inside a fortnight, and that, far more than the anatomy, is the thing I'd like to be able to do.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion and a reduced participle clause replace the band-7 'if' and 'because'.
'Cut out for', 'grind through', 'dismantled my assumption' — precision rather than rare words.
The close names what the job is for instead of restating the ambition.

annotations.span: Had she handled it differently, I suspect I'd have given up inside a fortnight
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Identical in meaning to the third conditional, but it lifts the register.

annotations.span: What strikes me, though, having watched it up close, is
annotations.label: Reframes the job mid-answer
annotations.why: A reduced participle clause adds a source for your claim in four words.

annotations.span: Not many people are cut out for that
annotations.label: Idiom placed exactly right
annotations.why: Use it about suitability of character, never about ability or skill.

annotations.span: quietly dismantled my assumption that the knee was finished
annotations.label: A verb chosen for its shade
annotations.why: 'Dismantled' says slowly and piece by piece; 'changed' says nothing.

annotations.span: She never once told me it would be fine.
annotations.label: Weight falls on 'never once'
annotations.why: Stress the negative and the sentence stops sounding like a complaint.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my headphones. They are the big ones, over the ears, and they can block the noise. I bought them two years ago in a sale.

Before this I use my colleague's headphones one time on the train, because the train was late and there was a lot of noise. It was very good, so after two weeks I bought the same.

I use them every day. My train is forty-five minutes, so I put them and I read or I listen to music. Also in my office it is open plan and in the afternoon it is very noisy, so I use them there also. Sometimes I put them on and I don't listen anything, only for the silence.

Without them my life is more difficult. I can't read in the train, and in the office I can't concentrate. Maybe I ask to work from home more. Also I think I am more angry in the evening. So they are very useful for me and I am very happy that I bought them. This is my piece of technology.

what_caps_it.point: The fourth bullet is answered in the present, so the conditional never appears at all.
'Very good', 'very noisy', 'very useful', 'very happy' — four intensifiers, no content.
'Also' opens three sentences, and the final line hands the prompt straight back.

annotations.span: They are the big ones, over the ears, and they can block the noise.
annotations.label: Describes the object physically first
annotations.why: Keep this — one physical detail lets the listener see the thing before you explain it.

annotations.label: Past event told in the present
annotations.why: 'I'd borrowed a colleague's once on the train' — past event, past tense.

annotations.span: so I put them and I read or I listen to music
annotations.label: Phrasal verb missing its particle
annotations.why: 'Put them on'. Without the particle the verb means something else entirely.

annotations.span: Without them my life is more difficult.
annotations.label: The whole bullet, in the wrong tense
annotations.why: 'Without them my life would be a good deal harder.' This bullet is the conditional.

annotations.span: So they are very useful for me and I am very happy that I bought them.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The piece of technology I'd pick is a pair of over-ear noise-cancelling headphones, which I bought about two years ago in a sale and have used almost every day since.

I came to them slightly by accident. I'd been stuck on a delayed train with a colleague, she lent me hers for twenty minutes, and the difference was so obvious that I ordered a pair within a fortnight. That is not, on the whole, a decision I would normally make that quickly.

As for how I use them, there are three situations really. The commute is the main one: it's about forty-five minutes each way, and with the headphones on I can genuinely read, whereas before I just stared out of the window. Then there's the office, which is open plan and gets steadily louder through the afternoon; I put them on at about three and the room disappears. And now and again I wear them with nothing playing at all, purely for the silence, which sounds slightly odd but is probably the use I value most.

If I didn't have them, I don't think I'd manage the commute in the same way. I'd get almost no reading done, and I'd probably end up asking to work from home more often than I really want to, which isn't the arrangement I would choose. It's a fairly unglamorous object, but it's bought me back something like an hour and a half a day, and very little else I own can claim that.

what_lifts_it.point: A present perfect, a past perfect continuous and a second conditional do what simple tenses did.
'Came to them by accident', 'the room disappears', 'unglamorous' — content instead of intensifiers.
'There are three situations really' announces the shape before filling it.

annotations.span: and have used almost every day since
annotations.label: Present perfect for ownership up to now
annotations.why: Any object card hides this tense in bullet two. Prepare one sentence of it.

annotations.span: I came to them slightly by accident.
annotations.label: Opens bullet two with a hook
annotations.why: 'When did you start' is a story, not a date. Say how it happened.

annotations.span: I'd been stuck on a delayed train with a colleague
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the earlier layer
annotations.why: Use it once to show the event before the event; it costs four words.

annotations.span: As for how I use them, there are three situations really.
annotations.label: Counts the parts before listing them
annotations.why: Announcing the number of parts up front buys you thinking time.

annotations.span: whereas before I just stared out of the window
annotations.label: Contrast joined with 'whereas'
annotations.why: 'Whereas' takes a full clause on each side; 'but' flattens it into a list.

annotations.span: I put them on at about three and the room disappears
annotations.label: A metaphor instead of an adjective
annotations.why: One image replaces 'very quiet' and is far harder to forget.

annotations.span: If I didn't have them, I don't think I'd manage the commute in the same way.
annotations.label: Second conditional, stated plainly
annotations.why: The fourth bullet is grammar, not feeling. Get the form out early.

annotations.span: It's a fairly unglamorous object
annotations.label: Concedes before it claims
annotations.why: Talking the object down first makes the claim after it sound earned.

annotations.span: it's bought me back something like an hour and a half a day
annotations.label: Quantifies the value at the close
annotations.why: A number ends the turn far better than another adjective.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The object I'd choose is a pair of over-ear noise-cancelling headphones, which is hardly a glamorous answer, but nothing else I own has altered my day as much.

I bought them in a sale a couple of years back, and rather against my usual habits, on almost no research at all. I'd been stranded on a delayed train with a colleague who handed me hers for twenty minutes, and the silence was such a shock that I'd ordered my own inside a fortnight.

They get used in three ways. The commute is the obvious one: three quarters of an hour each way, and with them on I read, whereas without them I used to arrive having done nothing but resent the journey. Then the office, which is open plan and grows steadily louder as the afternoon wears on, so I put them on around three and the room simply recedes. And occasionally I wear them with nothing playing whatsoever, which sounds faintly absurd but is the use I would defend hardest.

Were they to break tomorrow, I'd replace them the same week. Not because the commute would become impossible, but because I'd slide back into working from home to get any concentration at all, and I know from experience where that ends. What strikes me about it, in the end, is that the good technology in my life isn't the clever kind. It's the kind that quietly hands me back ninety minutes a day and then gets out of the way.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces the band-7 'if' clause, and a participle clause replaces a 'because'.
'Stranded', 'recedes', 'wears on' — words picked for shade rather than rarity.
The close generalises about technology instead of summarising the object.

annotations.span: Were they to break tomorrow, I'd replace them the same week.
annotations.label: Inverted second conditional
annotations.why: Same meaning as 'if they broke', one register higher, still spoken.

annotations.span: I'd been stranded on a delayed train
annotations.label: One precise verb replaces three words
annotations.why: 'Stranded' carries stuck, stationary and unable to leave all at once.

annotations.span: the room simply recedes
annotations.label: Verb chosen for its shade
annotations.why: 'Recedes' says gradually and partly; 'disappears' says neither.

annotations.span: having done nothing but resent the journey
annotations.label: Participle clause instead of 'because'
annotations.why: Compress a whole clause into three words once per turn.

annotations.span: the good technology in my life isn't the clever kind
annotations.label: Lifts the object into an idea
annotations.why: Step off the anecdote in the last sentence; that step is the lift.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a skill I learned outside the school, it is cutting hair. I can cut men's hair with the machine and also with scissors.

I learned it from my aunt. She has a small salon two streets from our house, and when I was sixteen I go there on Saturday to clean the floor. I don't pay for lessons, I only watch her, and sometimes she explain me.

It took a long time. The first three months were very bad. My brother was my first customer and honestly his hair was terrible, and my mother was angry with me for one day. After maybe eight months people started to trust me.

This skill is very useful for me. First, I save money because I don't go to the barber. Also my brother and two neighbours come to my house, and last year my friend asked me before his wedding. It is a nice feeling when people ask you. And I learned that if you repeat something many times, you will become good at it. So this is my skill that I learned outside school.

what_caps_it.point: The narrative slides into the present three times and a third-person -s goes missing.
'Very bad', 'terrible', 'nice feeling', 'very useful' — four flat words carry the whole evaluation.
'Also' and 'And' open half the sentences, and the close repeats the card.

annotations.span: It took a long time. The first three months were very bad.
annotations.label: Answers the timeline bullet honestly
annotations.why: Keep this — admitting the bad early months is more convincing than claiming it was easy.

annotations.span: outside the school
annotations.label: Article where English uses none
annotations.why: 'Outside school' — the institution as a concept takes no article.

annotations.span: I go there on Saturday to clean the floor
annotations.label: Past narrative slips into the present
annotations.why: 'I went there on Saturdays' — set the tense once and hold it.

annotations.span: sometimes she explain me
annotations.label: Missing -s and missing preposition
annotations.why: 'She'd explain things to me.' Explain always takes 'to' before a person.

annotations.span: It is a nice feeling when people ask you.
annotations.label: The best idea in the answer, undersold
annotations.why: Say what it means: that the skill became something you do for people.

annotations.span: So this is my skill that I learned outside school.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The skill I'd choose is cutting hair — men's hair specifically, with clippers and scissors, which is not something I would ever have predicted about myself.

I picked it up from my aunt. She's had a small salon two streets from our house for as far back as I can remember, and when I was sixteen I started going in on Saturdays to sweep up and wash towels. There were never any lessons as such. I just watched, and every so often she'd stop and make me look at the angle she was holding the comb at.

It took far longer than I expected. The first three months were genuinely bad, and my brother, who was the only person willing to sit down, ended up with a haircut he had to wear a hat over for a fortnight. My mother didn't speak to me for a day. It was probably eight months before anybody trusted me without a certain amount of negotiation first.

As for why it's been useful, the obvious answer is money, and I haven't paid for a haircut since I was seventeen. But the thing I'd actually point to is that it turned into the way I do something for people. My brother still comes round, two of the neighbours do, and a friend asked me the week before his wedding, which I took as a real compliment. And it taught me something I've leaned on ever since: almost nothing is talent. It's repetition, plus somebody standing next to you telling you what your hands are doing wrong.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Would' for repeated past and a present perfect with 'since' replace the flat past simples.
'Picked it up', 'ended up with', 'as such' — chunks where the band 6 used bare verbs.
Each bullet is opened by name and the close moves off the anecdote.

annotations.span: I picked it up
annotations.label: The exact verb for informal learning
annotations.why: 'Pick up' means learned without lessons — which is what the card asks about.

annotations.span: There were never any lessons as such.
annotations.label: Heads off the obvious question
annotations.why: Answering what the examiner was about to ask sounds like control, not evasion.

annotations.span: every so often she'd stop and make me look at the angle she was holding the comb at
annotations.label: 'Would' for a repeated past action
annotations.why: Use 'would' for things that happened many times; keep past simple for single events.

annotations.span: It took far longer than I expected.
annotations.label: Opens the timeline bullet
annotations.why: Name the bullet you are answering and you cannot silently skip it.

annotations.span: ended up with a haircut he had to wear a hat over
annotations.label: One image instead of an adjective
annotations.why: Show the bad result; never tell the examiner it was 'terrible'.

annotations.span: As for why it's been useful
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: This is the bullet that carries the band. Announce it out loud.

annotations.span: I haven't paid for a haircut since I was seventeen
annotations.label: Present perfect with 'since'
annotations.why: A state running from a past point to now takes 'have' plus 'since'.

annotations.span: But the thing I'd actually point to is
annotations.label: Rejects its own first answer
annotations.why: Giving the obvious reason then overriding it reads as genuine thought.

annotations.span: almost nothing is talent
annotations.label: Stress falls hard on 'talent'
annotations.why: Slow down and stress the key word; the sentence does the rest.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The skill I'd pick is cutting hair, which is not something I ever set out to learn. Men's hair, clippers and scissors, nothing elaborate, but competent.

I got it from my aunt, who has run a small salon two streets from us for about thirty years. From the age of sixteen I spent Saturdays there sweeping up and washing towels, and there was never anything you could reasonably call a lesson. She'd simply stop mid-cut now and then and make me look at the angle of the comb, which in retrospect was a far better method than being told.

It came slowly. The first three months were dreadful, and my brother, the only volunteer available, spent a fortnight in a hat. It was the best part of a year before anyone sat down without first checking whether I had improved.

Why has it been useful? The money is the obvious answer, and I haven't paid for a cut since I was seventeen. But what I'd really say is that it turned into the thing I do for people. My brother still turns up, so do a couple of neighbours, and a friend asked me the week before his wedding, which I took rather more seriously than he probably intended. Had I been formally taught, I doubt any of that would have followed. What sticks with me is how little of it was aptitude. It was repetition, and somebody beside me naming what my hands were getting wrong.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion with a passive replaces the band-7 'if' clause entirely.
'Aptitude', 'the best part of a year', 'in retrospect' — precision rather than display.
The close names what the whole experience was evidence of, not what happened.

annotations.span: Had I been formally taught, I doubt any of that would have followed.
annotations.label: Inversion carrying a passive
annotations.why: Two structures stacked in one clause, and none of it sounds written.

annotations.span: spent a fortnight in a hat
annotations.label: Compression doing the joke's work
annotations.why: Five words replace two sentences of explanation. Aim for that once per turn.

annotations.span: It was the best part of a year
annotations.label: Idiomatic duration, not a bare number
annotations.why: 'The best part of' means nearly all of, and it sounds native.

annotations.span: which in retrospect was a far better method than being told
annotations.label: Aside delivered lower and faster
annotations.why: Drop the pitch on a parenthesis; it makes the main clause stand out.

annotations.span: What sticks with me is how little of it was aptitude.
annotations.label: Lifts the story into a claim
annotations.why: Finish above the story rather than inside it, and the answer lifts.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my healthy habit. My habit is that I get off the bus two stops before my home and I walk the last part. It is about twenty minutes.

I start this three years ago. That winter I was sitting all the day in the office and I feel very bad and tired, and I don't do any sport. So I decide something must change. I try the gym but I go only three times, and after that I try this.

It was easy to put in my routine because I take this bus every day anyway. I don't need special clothes and I don't need to pay. So there is no decision, I just don't press the button and I walk.

The difference is good. First, I sleep better, and this is the biggest thing. Also, when I arrive at home I am not thinking about the work any more. Before, I was arriving and I was still angry about the office. Now the walk finishes the day. So this is my healthy habit and I am very happy that I keep it.

what_caps_it.point: Past events are told in the present, and no present perfect appears anywhere.
'Very bad', 'good', 'biggest thing' — the evaluation runs entirely on flat words.
'So' opens five sentences and the final line repeats the prompt.

annotations.span: It was easy to put in my routine because I take this bus every day anyway.
annotations.label: Explains why the habit stuck
annotations.why: Keep this — the reason a habit survives is the most interesting thing about it.

annotations.span: I start this three years ago.
annotations.label: Past event in the present tense
annotations.why: 'I started it three years ago' — a finished point in the past takes past simple.

annotations.span: I was sitting all the day in the office and I feel very bad
annotations.label: Two tenses in one sentence, plus an article
annotations.why: 'I was sitting all day and I felt terrible.' Drop 'the' before 'day'.

annotations.span: I try the gym but I go only three times
annotations.label: Finished attempt told in the present
annotations.why: 'I tried the gym and went three times.' Set the tense once and keep it.

annotations.span: The difference is good.
annotations.label: The whole fourth bullet, in three words
annotations.why: Name two differences and put a timescale on one of them.

annotations.span: So this is my healthy habit and I am very happy that I keep it.
annotations.label: Ends by naming the card
annotations.why: Close on why some habits last and others don't.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The habit I'd talk about is a completely undramatic one: I get off the bus two stops before mine and walk the last twenty minutes home.

I started doing it about three years ago, after a winter in which I'd basically sat down for four months. I was sleeping badly, I felt sluggish from about two o'clock every afternoon, and I'd joined a gym in the January and been three times in total. So what I was really looking for was something with a much lower barrier to it.

The reason it fitted into my routine is that it isn't really an addition. It replaced part of a journey I was making anyway. There's no kit, no changing, nothing to book and nothing to pay for, and, this is the part I'd underline, there's no decision to make. I simply don't press the button, and by the time the thought even arrives I'm already walking. Anything that needs a decision at half past six in the evening was never going to survive.

As for what difference it's made, the honest answer is that there are two of them. My sleep improved within about a month, which I honestly hadn't been expecting at all. But the bigger one is that the walk has turned into the boundary between work and home. I used to come through the door still arguing with somebody from the office in my head, whereas now that argument runs out somewhere around the second junction. Twenty minutes has bought me an evening.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect, a 'used to' and a future-in-the-past replace the flat present forms.
'Sluggish', 'a lower barrier', 'runs out' — content words instead of 'bad' and 'good'.
Three named signposts, and the close quantifies the result instead of repeating it.

annotations.span: a completely undramatic one
annotations.label: Undersells before it explains
annotations.why: Lowering the claim first makes what follows sound honest rather than rehearsed.

annotations.span: after a winter in which I'd basically sat down for four months
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a relative clause
annotations.why: 'In which' plus a past perfect sets the background in one clause.

annotations.span: I felt sluggish from about two o'clock every afternoon
annotations.label: One precise adjective, plus a time
annotations.why: 'Sluggish' plus a clock time beats 'I felt very tired' every time.

annotations.span: The reason it fitted into my routine is that it isn't really an addition.
annotations.label: Opens bullet three by naming it
annotations.why: This is the bullet candidates skip. Say its name and you cannot.

annotations.span: something with a much lower barrier to it
annotations.label: Abstract noun doing real work
annotations.why: 'A lower barrier' explains why the gym failed without criticising yourself.

annotations.span: this is the part I'd underline
annotations.label: Flags the key point aloud
annotations.why: Telling the listener what matters is cohesion, and it costs five words.

annotations.span: Anything that needs a decision at half past six in the evening was never going to survive.
annotations.label: Future seen from the past
annotations.why: 'Was never going to' judges the past from inside it. Use it once.

annotations.span: As for what difference it's made
annotations.label: Signposts the final bullet
annotations.why: The fourth bullet carries the band. Never let it arrive unannounced.

annotations.span: I used to come through the door still arguing with somebody from the office in my head
annotations.label: 'Used to' for the lapsed habit
annotations.why: Any before-and-after card wants one 'used to'. This is where it goes.

annotations.span: Twenty minutes has bought me an evening.
annotations.label: Short closing line, dropped pitch
annotations.why: End on a short sentence and let the pitch fall; it sounds finished.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The habit I've managed to keep is an unremarkable one: I get off the bus two stops early and walk the final twenty minutes home.

It dates from about three years ago, after a winter I'd spent almost entirely seated. I was sleeping badly, flagging by mid-afternoon, and I'd joined a gym in January and been three times by March, which told me something fairly useful about the kind of scheme that works for me. What I needed wasn't more willpower. It was something that required none.

That is precisely why it stuck. It isn't an addition to the day, it's a substitution inside a journey I was making regardless: no kit, no booking, no cost, and, crucially, no moment at which I have to talk myself into it. I don't press the button. Anything requiring a decision at half past six in the evening was doomed from the outset.

The difference falls into two parts. My sleep improved inside a month, which I hadn't anticipated and still can't entirely explain. The larger effect, though, is that the walk has become the seam between work and home. I used to arrive still conducting an argument with somebody from the office; these days that argument tends to run out somewhere around the second junction. Which is the thing about habits, I suppose. The ones that last aren't the ambitious ones. They're the ones you've hidden inside something you were doing anyway.

what_lifts_it.point: A reduced relative and a fronted cleft replace the band-7 full clauses.
'Flagging', 'the seam', 'doomed from the outset' — shade of meaning, not rarity.
The close states a general rule about habits rather than summarising this one.

annotations.span: Anything requiring a decision at half past six in the evening was doomed from the outset.
annotations.label: Reduced relative clause
annotations.why: Cut 'that needs' to 'requiring' once per turn; it tightens everything.

annotations.span: flagging by mid-afternoon
annotations.label: One verb replaces a clause
annotations.why: 'Flagging' means losing energy gradually — exactly what you mean.

annotations.span: the seam between work and home
annotations.label: A metaphor chosen, not decorated
annotations.why: 'Seam' says join and division at once; 'boundary' says only one.

annotations.span: What I needed wasn't more willpower. It was something that required none.
annotations.label: Contrastive stress across two sentences
annotations.why: Stress 'willpower', then 'none'. The contrast does the arguing.

annotations.span: The ones that last aren't the ambitious ones.
annotations.label: States the rule the story proves
annotations.why: End on the general claim; the anecdote has already earned it.

model_answers.transcript:
I'd like to describe something I do for the environment. I make compost from the food waste in my kitchen. I do it on the balcony because I live in a flat and I have no garden.

I start two years ago in the spring. My friend told me about a box with worms inside, and I bought one from the internet.

Honestly it was very difficult in the beginning. In the first summer it was smelling very bad and there were many flies, and my flatmate was very angry, and she said she will throw it from the balcony. So I read a lot and I try again, and the second time it was better because I put more paper inside.

Why I decided. One week I was throwing the rubbish and I saw that almost half of the bag was food. And I thought it is stupid to pay for this. Now I give the compost to my neighbour, she has a small garden near the river. It is only a small thing, but if everybody does a small thing it will be better. So this is what I did for the environment.

what_caps_it.point: The narrative starts in the present, and reported speech is never backshifted.
'Very difficult', 'very bad', 'very angry', 'stupid' — four flat words in one paragraph.
Each bullet arrives as a bare heading, and the ending is the prompt again.

annotations.span: I do it on the balcony because I live in a flat and I have no garden.
annotations.label: Explains the setting in one clause
annotations.why: Keep this — a constraint makes an ordinary action interesting immediately.

annotations.span: I start two years ago in the spring.
annotations.label: Past event in the present tense
annotations.why: 'I started two years ago' — fix the tense here and the rest follows.

annotations.span: Honestly it was very difficult in the beginning.
annotations.label: The difficulty, asserted not shown
annotations.why: Say what went wrong: it smelled, there were flies, the balance was off.

annotations.span: she said she will throw it from the balcony
annotations.label: Reported speech with no backshift
annotations.why: 'She said she'd throw it off the balcony.' 'Said' pulls the verb back.

annotations.span: And I thought it is stupid to pay for this.
annotations.label: Reported thought in the present
annotations.why: 'It struck me as absurd to be paying for it.' Backshift after 'thought' too.

annotations.span: So this is what I did for the environment.
annotations.label: Ends by naming the prompt
annotations.why: Close on scale: what one household can and cannot do.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd talk about is composting, which sounds ordinary until you know I do it on a first-floor balcony with no garden anywhere near it.

I started about two years ago, in the spring. A friend had been going on about a wormery — essentially a stacked plastic box with worms in it — and I ordered one without thinking terribly hard about it.

It was much harder than I'd expected, and I'd say the first summer was a straightforward failure. It smelled, it attracted flies, and my flatmate announced that if it wasn't dealt with by the weekend it was going over the railing. What I'd got wrong was the balance: far too much wet food and almost no paper, so the whole thing had turned into a sort of soup. I read properly, started shredding envelopes into it, and by the second autumn it was behaving. Nobody warns you that composting is basically a ratio.

As for why I started, it was one specific moment. I was carrying the bin bag downstairs one evening and it split, and I could see that something like half of it was peelings and leftovers. It struck me as slightly absurd to be paying to send water and vegetable ends to a landfill site. I'm under no illusions about the scale of it, and one flat is a drop in the ocean, obviously. But the compost goes to a neighbour with an allotment, and I'd rather do a small thing properly than a large thing in my head.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect continuous, a cleft with past perfect and proper backshift replace flat past simples.
'A straightforward failure', 'a drop in the ocean', 'behaving' — content instead of 'very difficult'.
The difficulty bullet is given real material, and the close concedes before it claims.

annotations.span: which sounds ordinary until you know I do it on a first-floor balcony with no garden anywhere near it
annotations.label: Turns an ordinary answer into a hook
annotations.why: Name the constraint in sentence one and the examiner is listening for it.

annotations.span: A friend had been going on about
annotations.label: Past perfect continuous sets the background
annotations.why: Something ongoing before your story starts takes 'had been -ing'.

annotations.span: It was much harder than I'd expected
annotations.label: Opens the difficulty bullet by name
annotations.why: Say the bullet's name aloud and you cannot silently skip it.

annotations.span: a straightforward failure
annotations.label: A noun phrase instead of 'very bad'
annotations.why: Naming the outcome is stronger and shorter than grading an adjective.

annotations.span: What I'd got wrong was the balance
annotations.label: Cleft sentence carrying a past perfect
annotations.why: Fronting the mistake makes the explanation sound analysed, not confessed.

annotations.span: As for why I started, it was one specific moment.
annotations.label: Signposts the final bullet
annotations.why: Announcing the fourth bullet is the cheapest cohesion mark available.

annotations.span: one flat is a drop in the ocean
annotations.label: Idiom used exactly where a native would
annotations.why: Conceding the scale in an idiom sounds honest rather than defensive.

annotations.span: I'd rather do a small thing properly than a large thing in my head
annotations.label: Closes on a judgement, not a summary
annotations.why: End with the position the story earned you.

annotations.span: Nobody warns you that composting is basically a ratio.
annotations.label: Short sentence, falling on 'ratio'
annotations.why: Drop the pitch on the last word and the aside lands as a joke.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd describe is composting, which sounds unremarkable until I add that I do it on a first-floor balcony, with no garden within half a mile.

It began two years ago, in the spring. A friend had been evangelising about wormeries, which are essentially stacked trays with worms living in them, and I bought one on very little evidence.

It was considerably harder than I'd bargained for, and the first summer was, frankly, a failure. It smelled, it drew flies, and my flatmate gave me until Sunday before it went over the railing. The error was proportion: far too much wet waste and nothing dry to offset it, so it had turned into something closer to soup than to compost. Once I started shredding envelopes into it, the whole thing settled inside a fortnight. Nobody tells you that composting is essentially arithmetic.

As for what set it off, it was one evening in particular. The bin bag split on the stairs and I found myself looking at what was, at a rough guess, half a sack of peelings. Paying a company to carry water and vegetable ends to a landfill site struck me as faintly ridiculous. Not that I'm under any illusion about the scale of it; a single flat is neither here nor there. But the compost goes to a neighbour's allotment, and I've gradually come to think that a small thing done properly is worth rather more than a large thing intended.

what_lifts_it.point: A gerund subject and a 'not that' fragment replace the band-7 full clauses.
'Evangelising', 'neither here nor there', 'bargained for' — precision rather than display.
The close states a principle the anecdote has already paid for.

annotations.span: A friend had been evangelising about wormeries
annotations.label: One verb carries the whole tone
annotations.why: 'Evangelising' says enthusiastic, repetitive and slightly annoying at once.

annotations.span: Paying a company to carry water and vegetable ends to a landfill site struck me as faintly ridiculous.
annotations.label: Gerund phrase as the subject
annotations.why: Making an action the subject compresses a whole clause. Use it once.

annotations.span: a single flat is neither here nor there
annotations.label: Idiom conceding the scale
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever you want to admit something is too small to count.

annotations.span: Nobody tells you that composting is essentially arithmetic.
annotations.label: Aside delivered flat and fast
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level and let the last word do the work.

annotations.span: a small thing done properly is worth rather more than a large thing intended
annotations.label: Ends on a general principle
annotations.why: Get out of the anecdote in your last sentence; that is the lift.

title: Protecting the environment

payload_json.topic: Protecting the environment

part3_themes.title: individual action and the environment
questions: How much difference can the choices of individuals really make to the environment?
Should people be fined for failing to recycle?
Why are some environmental habits much easier to adopt than others?
part3_themes.counterpoint: asking individuals to recycle distracts from what industry ought to be doing
part3_themes.counter_probe: So is sorting your bins just a way of feeling better about doing nothing?
part3_themes.concession_frame: That's largely right, and even so ___

question_notes.answer_shape: Give the honest scale, then name what individual action does that carbon figures don't capture.
question_notes.watch_out: Don't overclaim. Conceding the small scale first makes everything after it credible.

question_notes.answer_shape: Take a side on fines, name who they would hit hardest, then offer the alternative.
question_notes.watch_out: Fines punish, they don't enable. Say what you'd build alongside them.

question_notes.answer_shape: Give one habit that's easy and one that isn't, then name the difference between them.
question_notes.watch_out: The answer is cost, time or visibility. Name which one, don't list all three.

part3_themes.title: cities and the natural world
questions: Why does green space matter in a crowded city?

part3_themes.counterpoint: land in a growing city is too valuable to be left as grass
part3_themes.counter_probe: Can a city really afford to leave prime land empty just for the view?
part3_themes.concession_frame: On the economics you're right, though ___

abstraction_ladder.concrete: How far is your nearest park, and do you actually use it?
abstraction_ladder.local_general: Is there enough green space where you live for the people there?
abstraction_ladder.societal_abstract: What does a city owe its residents beyond housing and transport?

question_notes.answer_shape: Name one measurable effect and one social effect, then say which would convince a planner.
question_notes.probe: Is that worth the land, though?
question_notes.watch_out: 'It's good for people' is not a reason. Name the mechanism behind it.

question_notes.answer_shape: Say required or merely encouraged, name who pays, then what happens if it's voluntary.

question_notes.watch_out: 'Should be required' is a passive worth using; the modal drumbeat gets dull.

teaching.band_move: Quantify or concede. Either name the scale of the effect, or admit you can't and say why it still matters.

error_watchlist.wrong: The individuals cannot change the climate.
error_watchlist.right: Individuals can't change the climate on their own.
error_watchlist.why: Plural generalisations take no article at all.

error_watchlist.wrong: Recycling is more easy as reducing.
error_watchlist.right: Recycling is easier than cutting down.

title: your work or studies and where you live

payload_json.topic: your work or studies and where you live
questions: Do you work, or are you still studying?
How often do you have to be there in person?
Has that changed at all in the last few years?

Would you rather live in a house or a flat?
Is it somewhere you'd recommend to a friend?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple, present perfect for recent change, comparatives at the end
teaching.band_move: Name one concrete detail in every answer — a street, a floor, a day of the week.

questions.answer_shape: Say which one, name the field, then say where the workplace is.
questions.extend_move: I work — I'm in the payroll team at a haulage firm just outside the city.

common_error.wrong: I work in a firm of haulage since I finish university.
common_error.right: I've worked for a haulage firm since I finished university.
common_error.why: 'Since' plus past simple; the main verb goes perfect.

questions.answer_shape: Give the number of days, then say what decides which days.
questions.extend_move: Three days a week — Tuesdays are fixed because that's when the whole team's in.

common_error.wrong: I go there in Tuesday.
common_error.right: I go in on Tuesdays.
common_error.why: 'On' with days of the week.

questions.answer_shape: Say what the pattern used to be, then name what replaced it.
questions.extend_move: Hugely — I used to be in every day, and now half the office is empty by Thursday.

common_error.wrong: Before, I was going every day to the office.
common_error.right: I used to go into the office every day.
common_error.why: Past habit takes 'used to', not past continuous.

questions.answer_shape: Name one feature, say what it lets you do, then add a detail.
questions.extend_move: The location, mainly — I can walk to the station in six minutes, which I never take for granted.

common_error.wrong: The best thing is that is very near the station.
common_error.right: The best thing is that it's very near the station.
common_error.why: The clause after 'that' still needs its subject.

questions.answer_shape: State the preference, give one reason each way, then commit.
questions.extend_move: A house, on balance — a flat's easier to heat, but I'd want somewhere to put a bike.

common_error.wrong: A house is more better than a flat.
common_error.right: A house is better than a flat.
common_error.why: 'Better' is already comparative — never 'more better'.

questions.answer_shape: Take a position, name who it would suit, then add one caveat.
questions.extend_move: To anyone commuting, yes — though I'd warn them the rents have gone up sharply.

common_error.wrong: I recommend it for my friends who work in city.
common_error.right: I'd recommend it to friends who work in the city.
common_error.why: Recommend to someone; 'the city' takes an article.

title: travelling

payload_json.topic: travelling
questions: Do you enjoy travelling long distances?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple for habits, past simple for the last trip, quantifiers for the country question
teaching.band_move: Give the reason with the answer. 'Yes, I enjoy it' is half a sentence and the examiner will just wait.

questions.answer_shape: Say how much, name what you like or dislike about it, then give one condition.
questions.extend_move: I do, as long as I'm not driving — I'd happily sit on a train for six hours.

common_error.wrong: I enjoy to travel long distances.
common_error.right: I enjoy travelling long distances.
common_error.why: 'Enjoy' always takes the -ing form.

questions.answer_shape: Use a quantifier, name the usual method, then say what decides it.
questions.extend_move: Most people drive, mainly because the train fares are unpredictable and the coach takes forever.

common_error.wrong: The people in my area travels by car.
common_error.right: Most people in my area travel by car.
common_error.why: 'People' is plural, and generalisations take a quantifier.

questions.answer_shape: Name one or two things, say which comes first, then admit what you never manage.
questions.extend_move: I always intend to read and I generally end up staring out of the window instead.

common_error.wrong: I like to hearing music in the journey.
common_error.right: I like listening to music on the journey.
common_error.why: 'Like' takes -ing, and it is 'on' a journey.

questions.answer_shape: Pick one, give the practical reason, then say when you'd do the other.
questions.extend_move: Overnight, if it saves a hotel — although I arrive in a fairly poor state.

common_error.wrong: I prefer travel in the night.
common_error.right: I prefer travelling at night.
common_error.why: It is 'at night', and 'prefer' takes -ing.

questions.probe: Is that common where you live?

questions.answer_shape: Name the place, say when and why, then one detail from it.
questions.extend_move: The coast, back in August — my sister moved there and we hadn't seen the flat.

common_error.wrong: Last month I have been to the coast.
common_error.right: Last month I went to the coast.
common_error.why: A finished time phrase takes past simple, not present perfect.

teaching.tense_focus: present simple with frequency adverbs, plus 'would' on the final question

questions.answer_shape: Name the usual shape of a holiday, then one thing you always do.
questions.extend_move: Fairly quietly — we tend to rent somewhere near water and barely move for a week.

common_error.wrong: I usually go to holiday with my family.
common_error.right: I usually go on holiday with my family.
common_error.why: You go 'on' holiday; 'to' takes a place.

questions.probe: How long do you normally go for?

questions.answer_shape: Choose one, say what you want from a holiday, then name when you'd swap.

common_error.wrong: I prefer quiet holidays than busy holidays.
common_error.right: I prefer quiet holidays to busy ones.

common_error.right: I go on holiday with my friends.

common_error.why: 'Detail' is uncountable in this phrase: 'in detail'.

title: A journey you remember well

payload_json.topic: A journey you remember well

cue_card.topic: Describe a journey that you remember well.
bullets: where you went
how you travelled
who you were with
and explain why you remember this journey so well.
rounding_off: Would you make the same journey again?
Do you often travel that way?

teaching.band_move: Anchor the story with one time phrase in sentence one, then never leave the past.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Pick the journey where something went wrong. A smooth trip gives you nothing for the fourth bullet, and that is where the marks are.
prep_plan.trap: 'Why you remember it' is not 'because it was beautiful'. Name the thing that happened, and it is rarely the destination.

time_plan.goal: Name the destination and roughly how far.
Where you went, and how you travelled there.
Who was with you, and why them.
What happened, and why it stayed with you.
One line on what journeys do to people.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe one thing you could see or hear at that exact moment.
Add time depth: say what you'd expected the journey to be like.
Bring in the others: say what the rest of the passengers were doing.
Speculate: say what would have happened if nothing had gone wrong.

error_watchlist.wrong: At three o'clock the coach stops and everybody goes outside.
error_watchlist.right: At three the coach stopped and everybody got out.
error_watchlist.why: Set the past once and hold it to the end.

error_watchlist.wrong: If the coach doesn't break, he never tells me.
error_watchlist.right: If the coach hadn't broken down, he'd never have told me.
error_watchlist.why: An unreal past needs 'had' plus 'would have'.

error_watchlist.wrong: We did a journey by coach in the night.
error_watchlist.right: We travelled overnight by coach.
error_watchlist.why: You make or take a journey; you never do one.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: A story works only if the new information is the loudest word; this one turns on one moment.

target_words.note: Stress the particle; that is where the news lives.
Stress the negative and the whole clause changes weight.
Last syllable as an adverb, first as an adjective.
Stress the middle; both ends reduce to a schwa.
First syllable takes it; '-ful' becomes /fəl/.

chunking_drill.sentence: The driver got everybody off, so about forty of us ended up standing on the hard shoulder in the dark, in October, waiting for a replacement that took an hour and a half to appear.
chunks: The driver got everybody off,
so about forty of us ended up standing on the hard shoulder
in the dark, in October,
waiting for a replacement that took an hour and a half to appear.

minimal_pairs.contrast: /əʊ/ against /aʊ/ — one is a bus, one is a sofa

teaching.examiner_note: You are stopped at exactly two minutes, mid-sentence if necessary. Being cut off is the intended ending, so put the reason before the two-minute mark.

swap_slots.span: my cousin's wedding, in a city about four hundred kilometres north of where we live
swap_slots.prompt: Your own destination with a distance or a duration attached to it.

swap_slots.span: it left at eleven at night, which meant arriving at around eight the next morning
