model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a journey I remember very well. It was to my cousin's wedding, in a city in the north, about four hundred kilometres from my town.

We went by night coach because the train was too expensive. I was with my father. We start at eleven o'clock in the night.

At three o'clock in the morning the coach was broken. The driver said we must go out, so all the people were standing on the side of the road and it was very cold. We waited maybe one hour and a half for another coach.

I remember this journey because of my father. He is not a person who talks a lot, but that night he talks about his father, my grandfather, who died before I was born. He told me many things I never heard before, and I was very surprised. If the coach doesn't break, maybe he never tells me this. So it was a bad journey but also a good one. This is the journey that I remember.

what_caps_it.point: Tense slips into the present twice and the counterfactual collapses into a present conditional.
'Very well', 'very cold', 'very surprised', 'bad', 'good' — five flat words carry everything.
'So' links half the sentences and the turn ends by repeating the card.

annotations.span: It was to my cousin's wedding, in a city in the north, about four hundred kilometres from my town.
annotations.label: Fixes destination and distance at once
annotations.why: Keep this — a distance is worth more than any adjective about the place.

annotations.span: We start at eleven o'clock in the night.
annotations.label: Present tense, and the wrong preposition
annotations.why: 'We set off at eleven at night.' It is 'at night', never 'in the night'.

annotations.span: the coach was broken
annotations.label: Passive where English uses a phrasal verb
annotations.why: 'The coach broke down.' Vehicles break down; they are not broken.

annotations.span: but that night he talks about his father
annotations.label: Story slips into the present
annotations.why: 'That night he talked about his father.' One tense, all the way through.

annotations.span: If the coach doesn't break, maybe he never tells me this.
annotations.label: The counterfactual, in the wrong tense
annotations.why: 'If the coach hadn't broken down, he'd never have told me.'

annotations.span: This is the journey that I remember.
annotations.label: Ends by naming the prompt
annotations.why: Close on what the breakdown gave you, not on the card.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The journey I'd talk about was an overnight coach trip to my cousin's wedding, in a city about four hundred kilometres north of where we live.

We went by coach rather than by train because everything that weekend was either full or absurdly priced, and it left at eleven at night, which meant arriving at around eight the next morning. My father came with me. He isn't somebody who travels much these days, and I think he'd agreed to it mainly because he hadn't seen his brother in about six years.

We'd made good time until roughly three in the morning, when the engine simply gave out somewhere between two of the service stations. The driver got everybody off, so about forty of us ended up standing on the hard shoulder in the dark, in October, waiting for a replacement that took an hour and a half to appear. Nobody had a coat on.

And that's the part I actually remember, though not for the reason you'd expect. My father is not a talker. I'd have said we'd had perhaps three real conversations in my adult life. But standing on that verge he started telling me about his own father, who died before I was born, and he didn't stop until the second coach arrived. I heard things that night I'd never heard before and haven't heard since. If the coach hadn't broken down, I don't think that conversation would ever have happened, which is a strange thing to be grateful for.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a third conditional replace the band-6 flat past simples.
'Made good time', 'gave out', 'not a talker' — chunks doing the work of adjectives.
The fourth bullet is announced and then deliberately misdirected, which holds attention.

annotations.span: The journey I'd talk about was an overnight coach trip
annotations.label: Names the journey and the mode at once
annotations.why: Two bullets answered in six words leaves you time for the fourth.

annotations.span: he'd agreed to it mainly because he hadn't seen his brother in about six years
annotations.label: Two past perfects in one sentence
annotations.why: Use them for anything that happened before your story's main events.

annotations.span: made good time
annotations.label: The natural chunk for travelling fast
annotations.why: Reuse it for any journey that was going well until it wasn't.

annotations.span: And that's the part I actually remember, though not for the reason you'd expect.
annotations.label: Signposts and misdirects at once
annotations.why: Naming the bullet and delaying the reason keeps the examiner listening.

annotations.span: My father is not a talker.
annotations.label: A noun, not a sentence of explanation
annotations.why: 'Not a talker' does what 'he doesn't like to speak much' does, in three words.

annotations.span: I'd have said we'd had perhaps three real conversations in my adult life.
annotations.label: Conditional plus past perfect
annotations.why: 'I'd have said' softens a big claim without weakening it.

annotations.span: I heard things that night I'd never heard before and haven't heard since.
annotations.label: Stress on 'before' and 'since'
annotations.why: The contrast lives in those two words; slow down and let them land.

annotations.span: If the coach hadn't broken down, I don't think that conversation would ever have happened
annotations.label: Third conditional, exactly where it belongs
annotations.why: Every 'why do you remember it' bullet will take one of these.

annotations.span: which is a strange thing to be grateful for
annotations.label: Closes on an unresolved judgement
annotations.why: Ending on something you haven't settled sounds like thinking, not reciting.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The journey that stays with me is an overnight coach to my cousin's wedding, four hundred kilometres or so north of where we live.

We took the coach because the trains that weekend were either sold out or priced like short-haul flights, so we left at eleven at night on the understanding that we would be there by eight. My father came too, largely, I suspect, because he hadn't seen his brother in six years and wasn't going to say so.

We'd been making decent time until about three, when the engine failed somewhere between two service stations. The driver turned everyone out, and forty-odd of us stood on the hard shoulder in the October dark for the best part of ninety minutes, waiting for a replacement. Not one of us had thought to bring a coat.

Which is what I remember, though not for the obvious reason. My father is not, by any measure, a talker. Up to that night I'd have put our total number of real conversations somewhere in single figures. Yet standing on that verge he began telling me about his own father, who died before I was born, and he carried on until the second coach pulled in. I learned more in that hour and a half than in the previous decade. Had the engine held, I don't imagine any of it would ever have been said, which is an uncomfortable thing to be thankful for and I've never entirely resolved it.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion carrying a passive replaces the band-7 'if' clause.
'Priced like short-haul flights', 'turned everyone out', 'forty-odd' — precision, not display.
The close refuses to resolve the feeling instead of tidying it away.

annotations.span: Had the engine held, I don't imagine any of it would ever have been said

title: A meal you enjoyed with other people

payload_json.topic: A meal you enjoyed with other people

cue_card.topic: Describe a meal you enjoyed with other people.
bullets: where you ate
who you were with
what you ate
and explain why the meal was so enjoyable.
rounding_off: Do you often eat with those people?
Would you like to eat there again?

teaching.band_move: The fourth bullet is not about the food. Name the thing that was different about the people or the occasion.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Choose the meal you can still see, not the best one you've eaten. Bullet four wants a reason, and 'the food was delicious' is not one.

note_grid.cell: friend's new flat, 3rd floor, no lift
5 of us, moved him all Saturday

prep_plan.trap: Candidates spend ninety seconds on the food and ten on the people, when the reason it was enjoyable is almost never the cooking.

time_plan.goal: Name the place and the occasion in one line.
Where you ate, and who was there.
What was actually on the floor or table.
Why it worked: a reason, not an adjective.
One line on what makes a meal good.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe one dish, or describe what you were sitting on.
Bring in a person: say what one of them said or did.
Contrast: describe a formal meal that was far less enjoyable.
Speculate: say what it would have been like if somebody had planned it.

error_watchlist.wrong: We sit on the boxes and everybody is talking.
error_watchlist.right: We sat on the boxes and everybody talked.
error_watchlist.why: One past marker, then hold it to the end.

error_watchlist.wrong: If we plan it, maybe it is not the same.
error_watchlist.right: If we'd planned it, it wouldn't have been the same.
error_watchlist.why: An unreal past takes 'had' plus 'would have'.

error_watchlist.wrong: We ate some breads and many rices.
error_watchlist.right: We ate some bread and a pan of rice.
error_watchlist.why: 'Bread' and 'rice' are uncountable; count the container.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: This is a warm story, and a flat pitch makes affection sound like a police report.

target_words.note: Let the pitch jump on the stress, not just the volume.
Start high and fall away; it marks an aside.
A rise here signals you are correcting an assumption.
Fall sharply on 'no' and the negative lands properly.
Rising means doubt; falling means agreement.

chunking_drill.sentence: A pan of rice, a bag of tomatoes, half a jar of olives that had rolled around in a box all day, and a loaf from the shop downstairs.
chunks: A pan of rice,
a bag of tomatoes,
half a jar of olives that had rolled around in a box all day,
and a loaf from the shop downstairs.

minimal_pairs.contrast: rising pitch questions it, falling pitch accepts it

teaching.examiner_note: Event cards look like description cards and are not. The examiner is listening for a reason in bullet four, and a list of food will not supply one.

swap_slots.span: at a friend's flat
swap_slots.prompt: Your own place, named in three words. Explain the occasion after it, not inside it.

swap_slots.span: A pan of rice, a bag of tomatoes, half a jar of olives that had rolled around in a box all day, and a loaf from the shop downstairs.
swap_slots.prompt: Your own food, in containers and quantities. Never a category like 'traditional dishes'.

swap_slots.span: His mother had sent a cake up with him
swap_slots.prompt: The one thing that was planned, or the one thing that surprised you.

swap_slots.span: until about one in the morning
swap_slots.prompt: Your own proof that nobody wanted to leave: a time, or a thing that ran out.

teaching.transfer_drill: Take the same four moves through a meal you didn't enjoy. Forty-five seconds, past tense consistent throughout.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a meal with other people. It was at my friend's new flat, last summer. He moved to a flat on the third floor and there is no lift.

Five of us helped him all the Saturday. We were carrying the boxes and the sofa up the stairs, and after that everybody was very tired.

We ate in the living room because there was no table. We sit on the boxes. The food was not special: rice, tomatoes, some olives and bread from the shop downstairs. Also his mother sent a cake, so we ate the cake too. There were only two plates, so some people ate from the pan.

It was the best meal I remember. I think because nobody prepared anything and nobody was trying to make a good impression. Everybody was too tired for this. We talked until one o'clock in the night and nobody wanted to go home. If we plan it, maybe it is not the same. So this is the meal I enjoyed with other people.

what_caps_it.point: The story drops into the present twice, and the counterfactual has no past form.
'Very tired', 'not special', 'good impression' — the food and the mood both described in defaults.
'So' and 'Also' carry the joins, and the last line repeats the card.

annotations.span: We ate in the living room because there was no table.
annotations.label: Locates the meal and explains it
annotations.why: Keep this — a reason attached to a fact is always worth the four extra words.

annotations.span: and there is no lift
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past sentence
annotations.why: 'There was no lift.' The whole story is one tense.

annotations.span: We sit on the boxes.
annotations.label: Past narrative told in the present
annotations.why: 'We sat on the boxes.' Fix it here and the rest follows.

annotations.span: The food was not special
annotations.label: Says nothing about the food
annotations.why: Name it instead: a pan of rice, a bag of tomatoes, half a jar of olives.

annotations.span: If we plan it, maybe it is not the same.
annotations.label: Counterfactual with no past form
annotations.why: 'If we'd planned it, it wouldn't have been the same.'

annotations.span: So this is the meal I enjoyed with other people.
annotations.label: Ends by naming the prompt
annotations.why: Close on what actually makes a meal good, not on the card.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The meal I'd describe was at a friend's flat, the evening after five of us had spent an entire Saturday moving him into it. Third floor, no lift, in July.

By about seven we'd got everything up the stairs, and nobody had the energy to go anywhere, so we ate where we were. There was no table yet — it was still in pieces against the wall — so in the end we sat on packing boxes in the living room with all of the food in the middle of the floor.

What we actually ate was whatever had survived the move. A pan of rice, a bag of tomatoes, half a jar of olives that had rolled around in a box all day, and a loaf from the shop downstairs. His mother had sent a cake up with him, which was the only thing anybody had planned. There were two plates between five of us, so three of us ate straight out of the pan.

And I'd say it's the best meal I can remember, which is odd, because objectively it was the worst food. I think the reason is that nobody was performing. Normally when people eat together somebody has cooked, and there's a small anxiety running underneath it about whether it has gone well. That was completely absent on this occasion, because everybody was simply too tired to bother. We sat on those boxes until about one in the morning. If it had been planned, I doubt it would have worked at all.

what_lifts_it.point: Three past perfects plus a third conditional do what band 6 did with present tenses.
'Nobody was performing', 'a small anxiety running underneath it' — abstraction instead of adjectives.
The evaluation contradicts itself deliberately, which is a shape the listener follows.

annotations.span: Third floor, no lift, in July.
annotations.label: Verbless fragment sets the scene fast
annotations.why: One fragment per turn is spoken English, not an error. Use it early.

annotations.span: the evening after five of us had spent an entire Saturday moving him into it
annotations.label: Past perfect fixes the earlier day
annotations.why: Two layers of time in one clause, and it costs you nothing.

annotations.span: so we ate where we were
annotations.label: Answers the 'where' bullet in five words
annotations.why: Short answers to easy bullets buy you time for the hard one.

annotations.span: What we actually ate was whatever had survived the move.
annotations.label: Cleft sentence opens bullet three
annotations.why: Fronting 'what we ate' announces the bullet without listing anything yet.

annotations.span: There were two plates between five of us
annotations.label: Stress the two numbers
annotations.why: Let 'two' and 'five' carry the weight; the contrast is the joke.

annotations.span: which is odd, because objectively it was the worst food
annotations.label: Contradicts its own judgement on purpose
annotations.why: Setting up a puzzle makes the examiner wait for your reason.

annotations.span: nobody was performing
annotations.label: One verb explains the whole evening
annotations.why: 'Performing' names the thing most social meals are doing.

annotations.span: there's a small anxiety running underneath it
annotations.label: Abstract noun with a physical verb
annotations.why: Pairing an abstract noun with a concrete verb is a band-7 habit.

annotations.span: If it had been planned, I doubt it would have worked at all.
annotations.label: Third conditional carrying a passive
annotations.why: The counterfactual is the natural close on any 'why was it good' bullet.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The meal that comes to mind was at a friend's flat, on the evening of the day five of us had carried his entire life up three flights of stairs. July, no lift, and none of us in any state to go anywhere.

We had finished at around seven, and the idea of going out anywhere was unthinkable, so we ate more or less where we had collapsed. The table was still in pieces against the wall, so the boxes became furniture and the floor became the table.

What we ate was, strictly speaking, salvage. Rice, a bag of tomatoes, half a jar of olives that had spent the day rolling round a crate, a loaf from the shop downstairs. The single element anybody had intended was a cake his mother had pressed on him that morning. Between five of us there were two plates, so most of us ate out of the pan.

And it remains the best meal I can remember, which is faintly absurd, given that it was easily the worst food. What was missing, I think, was the performance. Ordinarily somebody has cooked, and underneath the evening there runs a faint anxiety about whether it has landed. Exhaustion had stripped all of that out before anybody sat down. We stayed on those boxes until something like one in the morning. Had anybody organised it, I'm fairly sure it would have been a perfectly pleasant, entirely forgettable dinner.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion and an inverted existential replace the band-7 'if' and 'there is'.
'Salvage', 'pressed on him', 'landed' — words chosen for shade, not for size.
The close reframes the evening instead of summarising it.

annotations.span: What we ate was, strictly speaking, salvage.
annotations.label: One noun carries the whole list
annotations.why: 'Salvage' says rescued, accidental and unglamorous in a single word.

annotations.span: the boxes became furniture and the floor became the table
annotations.label: Parallel clauses replace description
annotations.why: Two matched clauses are faster and more memorable than four adjectives.

annotations.span: underneath the evening there runs a faint anxiety about whether it has landed
annotations.label: Inverted existential with a precise verb
annotations.why: 'Landed' is what a native says about a meal or a joke.

annotations.span: Had anybody organised it, I'm fairly sure it would have been a perfectly pleasant, entirely forgettable dinner.
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as the third conditional, one register up, still spoken.

annotations.span: July, no lift, and none of us in any state to go anywhere.
annotations.label: Three chunks, falling at the end
annotations.why: Group the fragment into three and let the pitch drop on the last.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a news which interested me. It was about the bank in my town. The bank said they will close the last branch, and after that there is no bank in our town.

I read it on the local news website. Actually my mother told me first, and after that I looked it on the internet.

I discussed it with my mother and also with my colleague, because his father lives in the same town, and he is seventy-eight and he doesn't use the internet.

Why it interested me. First, because it is my town, and I know this bank since I am a child. But the more interesting thing came after. In the library they started a class on Wednesday, and two people who worked in the bank before, now they are retired, they come and help the old people with the phone banking. Nobody paid them. So the bank closed but something else opened. I think this is interesting. This is the news that interested me.

what_caps_it.point: Reported speech is never backshifted, and 'since I am a child' has no present perfect.
'Interesting' appears four times, and 'a news' is not English at all.
The turn is a list of headings, and it ends on the prompt itself.

annotations.span: because his father lives in the same town, and he is seventy-eight and he doesn't use the internet
annotations.label: Grounds the story in one real person
annotations.why: Keep this — one named person makes an abstract story concrete instantly.

annotations.span: a news which interested me
annotations.label: 'News' with an article
annotations.why: Say 'a story' or 'a piece of news'. 'News' never takes 'a'.

annotations.span: The bank said they will close the last branch
annotations.label: Reported speech with no backshift
annotations.why: 'The bank said it would be closing the branch.' 'Said' pulls the verb back.

annotations.span: I know this bank since I am a child
annotations.label: Present tense across a duration
annotations.why: 'I've known that bank since I was a child.' 'Since' needs the perfect.

annotations.span: I think this is interesting.
annotations.label: The whole reason, in four words
annotations.why: Say what surprised you: a service closed and something unofficial replaced it.

annotations.span: This is the news that interested me.
annotations.label: Ends by naming the prompt
annotations.why: Close on what local reporting is actually for.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The story I'd pick was a local one: the last bank branch in my town announced it was closing, which meant there'd be no bank at all within about fifteen miles.

I heard about it from my mother first, actually, and then went and found the piece for myself on the local news site. The piece itself was only three paragraphs long and it never made headlines anywhere else, which is more or less the point of it. Three paragraphs is what a town gets when a service disappears.

I talked about it with her, obviously, and then at some length with a colleague, because his father is seventy-eight, lives in the same town and has never used a computer in his life. For him it wasn't an inconvenience, it was the removal of the only place he could hand somebody a piece of paper and be told what it meant. He'd been going in there since the seventies and knew half the staff by name.

What actually made it interesting, though, was what happened afterwards. About a month later the library started running a session on Wednesday mornings, and two of the people who'd worked in that branch, both retired by then, turned up and started helping people with online banking. Nobody's paying them. Nobody organised it centrally. It simply started happening. A service was withdrawn and something considerably less official grew back in the gap, which I'd never have predicted, and I've been slightly less pessimistic about the town ever since.

what_lifts_it.point: Backshifted reporting, a past perfect relative clause and a conditional perfect all appear.
'Made headlines', 'the removal of', 'grew back in the gap' — content instead of 'interesting'.
A cleft sentence opens the fourth bullet, and the close names what changed in you.

annotations.span: The story I'd pick was a local one
annotations.label: Narrows the story in six words
annotations.why: Saying what kind of story it is orients the listener before any detail.

annotations.span: announced it was closing, which meant there'd be no bank at all
annotations.label: Two backshifts in one clause
annotations.why: After a past reporting verb, everything downstream moves back one tense.

annotations.span: it never made headlines anywhere else
annotations.label: The natural collocation for coverage
annotations.why: 'Make headlines' beats 'was on the news in a big way' every time.

annotations.span: For him it wasn't an inconvenience, it was
annotations.label: Rejects the small version of the point
annotations.why: Correcting your own first description shows judgement, not indecision.

annotations.span: What actually made it interesting, though, was what happened afterwards.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Fronting the reason tells the examiner the bullet has arrived.

annotations.span: two of the people who'd worked in that branch, both retired by then, turned up
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a relative clause
annotations.why: Use it for anything that had already finished before your main event.

annotations.span: Nobody's paying them. Nobody organised it centrally.
annotations.label: Two short sentences, matched stress
annotations.why: Repeat the opening word and stress it both times; the pattern does the emphasis.

annotations.span: something considerably less official grew back in the gap
annotations.label: A metaphor doing the analysis
annotations.why: 'Grew back' says slow, unplanned and organic in two words.

annotations.span: which I'd never have predicted
annotations.label: Conditional perfect as an aside
annotations.why: Four words that add a whole extra structure without slowing you down.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The item I'd choose was purely local: the last remaining bank branch in my town gave notice that it was shutting, leaving nowhere to bank inside about fifteen miles.

My mother told me before I read it, which is usually how news reaches me, and I then dug out the piece on the local site. Three paragraphs, no follow-up, and it certainly never troubled a national front page. The whole scale of it was local.

I discussed it with her, and at rather more length with a colleague whose father is seventy-eight, still lives there, and has never once been near a computer. What was being taken away from him wasn't convenience. It was the last counter at which he could put a piece of paper in front of somebody and be told, in words, what it said. He had banked there since the seventies and knew every one of them by name.

The part that genuinely held my attention came later. A month or so on, the library quietly began opening on Wednesday mornings, staffed by two women who had worked in that branch and had since retired, walking people through their banking on a phone. Nobody pays them. No organisation stands behind it. A service was withdrawn and something markedly less formal filled the space, which I would not have predicted for a moment. I've been fractionally less gloomy about the place ever since, though I'm aware that isn't a system anybody could rely on.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause chained onto a past perfect replaces the band-7 finite clauses.
'Troubled a national front page', 'markedly', 'gave notice' — shade, not size.
The close undercuts its own optimism instead of ending on a neat note.

annotations.span: it certainly never troubled a national front page
annotations.label: Understatement instead of a negative
annotations.why: 'Never troubled' is drier and more precise than 'wasn't reported'.

annotations.span: staffed by two women who had worked in that branch and had since retired, walking people through their banking on a phone
annotations.label: Participle clause onto a past perfect
annotations.why: Chain a participle after a finite clause once; it compresses two sentences.

annotations.span: something markedly less formal filled the space
annotations.label: One adverb carries the judgement
annotations.why: 'Markedly' grades the claim precisely where 'very' would blur it.

annotations.span: Nobody pays them. No organisation stands behind it.
annotations.label: Parallel negatives, falling twice
annotations.why: Two matched short sentences land harder than one long one.

annotations.span: though I'm aware that isn't a system anybody could rely on
annotations.label: Qualifies its own conclusion
annotations.why: Undercutting your close reads as thought, not as a memorised ending.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about an older person who I admire. She is a woman who worked with my mother in the hospital. Now she is seventy-eight and she is retired.

I know her since I am a small child, because she came to our house many times, and also she came to all the birthdays.

What is she like. She is not a soft person, she says directly what she thinks, and when I was young I was a little bit afraid of her. She is very organised and she remembers everything about everybody. Also she is very funny, but you must wait for it.

Why I admire her. First, because she brought up four children alone and she never talks about this. But the main thing is different. She is the only person I know who can say 'I was wrong'. Other people, when you show them they are wrong, they get angry or they change the subject. She just says okay, and after that she thinks differently. I think this is very rare and very difficult. This is the person I admire.

what_caps_it.point: There is no present perfect after 'since', and two clauses carry a doubled subject.
'Very' appears four times and does the work three precise adjectives should.
The four bullets are recited as labels, and the close restates the prompt.

annotations.label: Names one specific, unusual quality
annotations.why: Keep this — one quality nobody else has beats five that everybody has.

annotations.why: 'I've known her since I was a child.' 'Since' always needs the perfect.

annotations.why: 'Other people get angry when you show them they're wrong.'

annotations.label: The key judgement, graded not described
annotations.why: Say what it costs a person to do it, instead of grading it twice.

annotations.span: This is the person I admire.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd talk about is a woman who worked with my mother, a nurse who spent about forty years training new staff on the same ward. She's seventy-eight now and officially retired, although she still goes in twice a month for reasons that nobody in the family has ever fully explained.

I've known her since I was about five, because she was at every birthday we ever had, and for a very long time, well into my twenties, I was slightly frightened of her.

As for what she's like, she isn't warm in the obvious way. She's direct to the point of bluntness, she remembers every detail about everybody she has ever worked with, and she has a sense of humour you have to wait for. If you ask her opinion she'll give you the real one, which is precisely why people ask.

But the thing I actually admire isn't any of that. She's the only person I know who can say, out loud, in front of other people, that she was wrong. Most of us simply can't do it. We get defensive, or we quietly change the subject and adjust our position later where nobody can see us doing it. She'll listen, think about it for a second, say 'yes, that's fair', and then genuinely argue the other side the following week. I have spent years trying to do that, without any real success at all, and I am nowhere near it, which is probably why I notice it in her.

what_lifts_it.point: A present perfect with 'since' and characteristic 'will' replace the flat present forms.
'Direct to the point of bluntness', 'a sense of humour you have to wait for' — description, not grading.
A cleft opens the fourth bullet and the close turns the judgement back on the speaker.

annotations.why: One clause tells the examiner who she is without a separate sentence.

annotations.label: Present perfect for a lasting relationship
annotations.why: Anything that started in the past and still holds takes 'have'.

annotations.span: As for what she's like
annotations.label: Signposts the third bullet
annotations.why: Announce the bullet and the shape of the answer becomes audible.

annotations.span: She's direct to the point of bluntness
annotations.label: One quality, graded precisely
annotations.why: 'To the point of' sets the exact strength of an adjective.

annotations.span: a sense of humour you have to wait for
annotations.label: Describes the humour instead of rating it
annotations.why: Say how a quality behaves, never how much of it there is.

annotations.span: But the thing I actually admire isn't any of that.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the final bullet
annotations.why: Rejecting your own description makes what follows sound chosen.

annotations.span: out loud, in front of other people
annotations.label: Two chunks, both stressed
annotations.why: Slow right down on the two phrases that carry the whole point.

annotations.span: She'll listen, think about it for a second, say 'yes, that's fair'
annotations.label: 'Will' for characteristic behaviour
annotations.why: Use 'will' for what somebody typically does, not for the future.

annotations.span: which is probably why I notice it in her
annotations.label: Turns the judgement back on yourself

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd choose is a woman who worked alongside my mother: a nurse who spent the best part of forty years training new staff onto the same ward. She's seventy-eight, nominally retired, and still turns up on the ward twice a month for reasons that she has never once bothered to justify to anybody.

I've known her since I was about five, since she was present at every birthday we ever had, and for most of my childhood, and a fair portion of my twenties, I found her mildly terrifying.

She isn't warm in any conventional sense. She's blunt, she retains every detail about everyone she has ever met, and her humour arrives about four seconds after you expect it. Ask her opinion and you get the real one, which is precisely why people ask.

What I admire, though, is none of that. She is the only adult I know who can say aloud, in company, that she was wrong. The rest of us simply cannot do it. We become defensive, or we drop the subject and quietly revise our position later, somewhere nobody is watching. She listens, pauses, says 'yes, that's fair', and by the following week is arguing the opposite case as though it had always been hers. It looks like humility and it isn't, quite. It's something closer to a lack of vanity about being right, which strikes me as a good deal harder and considerably rarer.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative used as a conditional replaces the band-7 'if you ask her'.
'Nominally', 'retains', 'a lack of vanity' — precision chosen over warmth.
The close redefines the quality rather than repeating the admiration.

annotations.span: Ask her opinion and you get the real one
annotations.label: Imperative doing a conditional's work
annotations.why: 'Do X and you get Y' is a spoken conditional worth one use per turn.

annotations.span: her humour arrives about four seconds after you expect it
annotations.label: A number makes the quality concrete
annotations.why: Specificity where an adjective was expected is a band-8 habit.

annotations.span: She listens, pauses, says 'yes, that's fair'
annotations.label: Three short beats, level pitch
annotations.why: Match the rhythm to the behaviour and the sentence performs it.

annotations.span: It looks like humility and it isn't, quite.
annotations.label: Refuses the obvious word
annotations.why: Naming and then rejecting the expected word shows real control.

annotations.span: It's something closer to a lack of vanity about being right
annotations.label: Redefines the quality at the close
annotations.why: Ending on a better definition lifts the whole turn out of description.

I want to talk about something cheap that I bought and it is very useful. It is a flask, a metal one, for hot drinks. It is very light, so I don't notice it in my bag.

I bought it in a hardware shop near my office. It was in the sale, and the price was more or less the same like two coffees from the coffee shop.

I use it every day. In the morning I make coffee at home and I put it in the flask and I take it in the train. Also in the winter I take soup for the lunch, and on Sunday I take it when I go to watch my nephew's football.

Why it is good value. Because I have it four years now, and every day I don't buy a coffee outside. So it is maybe one thousand coffees. Also it is still working perfectly and nothing is broken. Some people spend a lot of money for a special one, but I don't think it is necessary. Mine was very cheap and it does the same. So this is the cheap thing that was very useful for me.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd choose is a stainless steel vacuum flask, which is not an exciting object, but I'd defend it as the best money I've ever spent.

I bought it in a hardware shop near my office, in a January sale, for roughly what two takeaway coffees cost. I hadn't gone in for a flask at all. I'd gone in for a light bulb, and I bought it more or less because it happened to be sitting by the till.

I use it in three ways. The main one is the commute: I make coffee at home, fill it before I leave, and drink it on the train at about half past eight. In winter I take soup in it instead, which has saved me from the sandwich shop next to the office more times than I'd like to admit. And on Sundays it comes with me to watch my nephew play football, where it does considerably more for me than the football does.

As for why it's good value, the arithmetic is fairly brutal. I've had it four years, and on the days I use it I buy nothing, so it has quietly replaced something in the region of a thousand cups of coffee. It cost the price of two. Nothing has broken, nothing has worn out, and it still keeps things hot for about seven hours. People do spend a great deal on the branded ones, and as far as I can tell they're buying the label rather than the vacuum.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a present perfect for possession replace the flat present forms.
'The arithmetic is fairly brutal', 'more times than I'd like to admit' — content instead of 'very'.
The uses are counted before they are listed, and the close is a judgement.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd describe is a stainless steel vacuum flask: hardly a thrilling object, and yet I'd argue it's the most efficient money I have ever parted with.

I bought it in a hardware shop near the office, in a January sale, for approximately the price of two takeaway coffees. I hadn't gone in looking for one. I had gone in for a light bulb, it happened to be sitting on the shelf by the till, and I bought it very largely out of proximity.

There are three uses. The commute is the principal one: coffee made at home, filled before I leave, drunk on the train somewhere around half eight. In winter it carries soup instead, which has rescued me from the sandwich shop beside the office more often than is entirely dignified. And on Sundays it comes to my nephew's football, where it delivers a good deal more satisfaction than the football manages.

The value case, when you set it out, is almost embarrassingly simple. Four years in, and on every day I use it I buy nothing, so it has displaced something in the order of a thousand cups. It cost two. Nothing has broken, nothing has worn out, and it still holds its heat for the better part of a working day. People spend extraordinary sums on the branded versions, and what they are buying, as far as I can see, is the badge rather than the vacuum inside it.

what_lifts_it.point: A chain of reduced past participles replaces the band-7 finite verbs.
'Parted with', 'displaced', 'entirely dignified' — shade of meaning rather than size.
The close is a cleft judgement about buyers, not a summary of the object.

annotations.span: coffee made at home, filled before I leave, drunk on the train somewhere around half eight
annotations.label: Three reduced participles in a row
annotations.why: Cutting the subject and auxiliary compresses three clauses into one breath.

annotations.span: more often than is entirely dignified
annotations.label: Dry understatement, exactly placed
annotations.why: Humour at your own expense reads as fluency, not as filler.

annotations.span: It cost two.
annotations.label: Three words, full stop, falling
annotations.why: The shortest sentence in the turn should carry the biggest point.

annotations.span: what they are buying, as far as I can see, is the badge rather than the vacuum inside it
annotations.label: Cleft judgement closes the turn
annotations.why: Fronting 'what they are buying' turns an opinion into a conclusion.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about an activity that I enjoy. It is badminton. I play doubles, so we are four people.

We play every Tuesday in the evening, from eight until half past nine. It is in a sports hall of a school near my house, because the council rents it in the evening for the people.

I play with three friends. One of them I know from the school, and the other two I met in the club. We play together six years now.

Why I enjoy it. First, because when I am playing I cannot think about the work. If somebody asks me a question about my job in this time, I am not able to answer. This is very good for me. Also, nobody in our group is good. We don't count the points seriously, and if somebody wins, nobody remembers next week. So there is no pressure. Some people go to the gym alone but for me this is boring. I need other people. So this is the activity that I enjoy.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The activity I'd talk about is badminton, which I've been playing for about six years and am still not remotely good at.

We play doubles on Tuesday evenings, from eight until half past nine, in the sports hall of a secondary school about ten minutes from my flat. The council rents it out in the evenings, which I assume is how the school pays for something, and it costs each of us very little. It isn't a glamorous room. There are lines on the floor for four other sports and the lighting is unforgiving.

There are four of us. I've known one of them since school, and I met the other two through the club, in the sense that they were already there when I turned up and nobody ever formally introduced anybody to anybody. We've never once arranged it by message; it simply happens.

As for why I enjoy it, there are two reasons and the second one is the real one. The first is straightforward: for ninety minutes I can't think about work. If somebody asked me anything about my job at half past eight on a Tuesday I genuinely couldn't answer them. It's the only ninety minutes in the week that's properly sealed off. But the more important thing is that none of us is any good. We keep score in a loose sort of way, and by the following week nobody can remember who won. That takes all the pressure out of it, and I've come to think that's why it has lasted six years when everything else I've tried lasted three months.

what_lifts_it.point: A present perfect continuous and a second conditional replace the flat present forms.
'Unforgiving', 'in a loose sort of way', 'takes the pressure out of it' — description, not grading.
The two reasons are announced and ranked before either one arrives.

annotations.span: which I've been playing for about six years and am still not remotely good at
annotations.label: Present perfect continuous plus a wry admission
annotations.why: Duration and self-deprecation in one relative clause; use it on any hobby card.

annotations.span: We play doubles on Tuesday evenings, from eight until half past nine
annotations.label: Answers 'when' with actual times
annotations.why: Two clock times are worth more than any adverb of frequency.

annotations.span: the lighting is unforgiving
annotations.label: One adjective describes the whole room
annotations.why: 'Unforgiving' about light means harsh and revealing at once.

annotations.span: As for why I enjoy it, there are two reasons and the second one is the real one.
annotations.label: Announces and ranks before explaining
annotations.why: Telling the listener which reason matters buys you their attention.

annotations.span: If somebody asked me anything about my job at half past eight on a Tuesday I genuinely couldn't answer them.
annotations.label: Second conditional as evidence
annotations.why: A hypothetical is a way of proving a claim without exaggerating it.

annotations.span: But the more important thing is that none of us is any good.
annotations.label: Delivers the promised second reason
annotations.why: Announce two, then deliver two. Unclosed structures sound disorganised.

annotations.span: We keep score in a loose sort of way
annotations.label: Hedged manner phrase
annotations.why: 'In a loose sort of way' softens any claim about how carefully something is done.

annotations.span: That takes all the pressure out of it
annotations.label: Stress falls on 'pressure'
annotations.why: One stressed word tells the listener this is the point of the paragraph.

annotations.span: when everything else I've tried lasted three months
annotations.label: Closes on a contrast, not a summary
annotations.why: Ending on what didn't last explains what did, and costs six words.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The activity I'd choose is badminton, which I have been playing for six years and remain conspicuously bad at.

We play doubles on Tuesday evenings, eight until half nine, in the sports hall of a secondary school ten minutes from the flat. The council hires it out after hours, which presumably pays for something the school otherwise couldn't afford, and it costs each of us almost nothing. It is not a beautiful room. The floor carries the markings of four other sports and the lighting is entirely without mercy.

There are four of us. One I've known since school; the other two I acquired through the club, in the sense that they were already on the court when I first turned up and no introduction was ever made. Nothing about the arrangement has ever been put in writing.

As to why I enjoy it, there are two reasons and the second is the honest one. The first is simple enough: for ninety minutes work is unreachable. It is the one hour and a half in the week that is genuinely sealed. Were anybody to ask me about my job at half past eight on a Tuesday, I could not have answered them. The larger reason is that none of us is any good. Scores are kept in a spirit of approximation, and by the following Tuesday nobody recalls who took the last game. That removes the pressure entirely, and I've come round to thinking it is precisely why the thing has survived six years when everything else I took up collapsed inside three months.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion and an agentless passive replace the band-7 'if' and 'we keep'.
'Conspicuously', 'without mercy', 'a spirit of approximation' — shade rather than size.
The close explains why the habit survived instead of restating the enjoyment.

annotations.span: Were anybody to ask me about my job at half past eight on a Tuesday, I could not have answered them.
annotations.label: Inverted conditional without 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning, one register higher, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: the lighting is entirely without mercy
annotations.label: Prepositional phrase doing an adjective's job
annotations.why: 'Without mercy' is funnier and more precise than 'very harsh'.

annotations.span: Scores are kept in a spirit of approximation
annotations.label: Formal register used for comic effect
annotations.why: Deliberate over-formality about something trivial reads as control.

annotations.span: It is not a beautiful room.
annotations.label: Short flat sentence between two long ones
annotations.why: Level pitch and a full stop; the contrast in length does the work.

annotations.span: it is precisely why the thing has survived six years when everything else I took up collapsed inside three months
annotations.label: Explains the survival, not the enjoyment
annotations.why: Answering a question the card didn't ask is what lifts a close.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a decision I make when I was twenty-three years old. At that time I had two job offers in the same month. One was a big company in the centre, and one was a very small workshop near my house.

So I choose the small one. And the reason was very simple, it was the bus. From my home to the centre it is one hour and a half, and to the workshop it is fifteen minutes walking. So I think, okay, I take the small one. My family said the big company is better for my future, but I don't listen to them.

At that time I think it is only about the bus. But actually it was not only that. In the small workshop we are three people, so I must do everything, the drawings, the prices, talking with the clients. In a big company I only do one job.

And then after some years I understand it. Now I work for myself, and I can do all these things because of that job. If I go to the big company, maybe I don't have this now. So it was a good decision, but I didn't know it in that time. I only understand it later.

what_caps_it.point: The narrative slips into the present eight times; the past frame never holds.
Almost every sentence opens with 'so' or 'and', so nothing is subordinated.
'Very small', 'very simple', 'good' — the whole judgement rests on flat adjectives.

annotations.span: At that time I had two job offers in the same month.
annotations.label: Sets the situation in one sentence
annotations.why: Keep this — two options named early gives the whole turn something to hang on.

annotations.span: I want to tell about a decision I make when I was twenty-three years old.
annotations.label: Opens in the wrong tense
annotations.why: Say 'a decision I made'. The first verb sets the tense for two minutes.

annotations.span: So I choose the small one.
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: 'Chose'. Fix it here and the rest of the turn follows.

annotations.span: If I go to the big company, maybe I don't have this now.
annotations.label: Conditional collapses
annotations.why: Past cause, present result: 'If I'd gone there, I wouldn't have this now.'

annotations.span: but I didn't know it in that time
annotations.label: Wrong preposition in a fixed chunk
annotations.why: 'At the time'. Learn the whole chunk, not the preposition rule.

annotations.span: So it was a good decision
annotations.label: Flat evaluation on the key bullet
annotations.why: Swap for 'it turned out to be the making of me' or similar.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The decision I'd like to talk about is one I made about eleven years ago, when I was twenty-three, and at the time I genuinely thought it was a minor one.

I'd been offered two jobs inside the same fortnight. One was with a big logistics firm in the centre of the city, and the other was with a two-person workshop about fifteen minutes from where I lived. The bigger firm paid noticeably better, and everyone in my family assumed I'd take it.

I took the small one, and the reason I gave — the only reason I actually thought about — was the journey. The commute into town would have been an hour and a half each way, whereas the workshop I could walk to if the buses stopped running. That was it. That was the whole of my thinking.

What I couldn't see at the time was what that choice was really deciding. Because there were only three of us, I ended up doing every part of the job: pricing, drawing, going out to sites, arguing with suppliers. In the bigger firm I'd have spent five years doing one narrow thing extremely well.

It was probably six or seven years before that clicked. I'm self-employed now, and the only reason that's possible is that I can handle a job from start to finish on my own. So the strange part is that I made the most important decision of my working life on the strength of a bus timetable. I'd like to claim I saw it coming, but I'd be making that up.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect for the background and a clean third conditional replace the flat past run.
The turn is built in two layers — then and later — and the pivot is signposted.
'Ended up doing', 'that clicked', 'on the strength of' are chunks, not decoration.

annotations.span: one I made about eleven years ago, when I was twenty-three
annotations.label: Fixes the time frame at once
annotations.why: One date in sentence one locks every verb that follows into the past.

annotations.span: I'd been offered two jobs inside the same fortnight
annotations.label: Past perfect passive as background
annotations.why: Use it once per story to show two layers of time.

annotations.span: everyone in my family assumed I'd take it
annotations.label: Reported thought with backshift
annotations.why: 'I'd take it' inside a past clause — cheap grammar credit, natural to say.

annotations.span: whereas the workshop I could walk to if the buses stopped running
annotations.label: Contrast carried by 'whereas'
annotations.why: 'Whereas' joins two full clauses; 'but' would flatten the comparison.

annotations.span: That was it. That was the whole of my thinking.
annotations.label: Two short sentences for emphasis
annotations.why: Drop the pace and the pitch here; the pause does the work.

annotations.span: What I couldn't see at the time was what that choice was really deciding.
annotations.label: Cleft announces the pivot
annotations.why: Naming the turn stops you forgetting the fourth bullet entirely.

annotations.span: I ended up doing every part of the job
annotations.label: 'Ended up' for unplanned outcomes
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever the result wasn't the intention.

annotations.span: In the bigger firm I'd have spent five years doing one narrow thing extremely well.
annotations.label: Third conditional without the 'if'
annotations.why: The 'if' clause is understood; this sounds far more spoken.

annotations.span: before that clicked
annotations.label: One chunk for a whole idea
annotations.why: Say 'it clicked' instead of 'I finally understood'. Shorter, more natural.

annotations.span: I'd be making that up
annotations.label: Honest close, not a summary
annotations.why: Refusing the tidy ending sounds like a person, not a script.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about a choice I made at twenty-three, which I'd have described at the time as barely a choice at all.

Two offers landed in the same fortnight: one from a large logistics firm in the middle of town, the other from a workshop that employed a grand total of two people, ten minutes from my front door. The firm paid appreciably better, and my family took it as read that I'd go there.

I went to the workshop, and the reason I gave myself was the journey — ninety minutes each way against a walk. Nothing more considered than that.

What I had no way of seeing was that I wasn't choosing a commute; I was choosing the shape of a career. With three of us in the building, nobody could afford to specialise. I priced jobs, drew them, went out to sites and fell out with suppliers, often in the same week. Had I taken the other offer, I'd have spent those years becoming very good indeed at one narrow thing, and I'd have been unemployable the moment that thing went out of fashion.

It took the best part of a decade for the penny to drop. I work for myself now, and that's only viable because I can carry a job from the first phone call to the final invoice. What I take from it isn't that I was shrewd — I wasn't, I was thinking about buses. It's that the decisions which turn out to matter almost never announce themselves, which makes me considerably more careful about the ones I'm currently filing under minor.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces 'if', and the conditional runs on into a second consequence.
'Took it as read', 'the penny to drop', 'fell out with' sit where a native would put them.
The close abstracts into a rule about decisions rather than restating the story.

annotations.span: Had I taken the other offer
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as the third conditional, higher register, still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: my family took it as read that I'd go there
annotations.label: Idiom in exactly the right slot
annotations.why: Two well-placed idioms beat six decorative ones every time.

annotations.span: I wasn't choosing a commute; I was choosing the shape of a career
annotations.label: Reframes the whole story
annotations.why: Say what the thing actually was, not just what happened.

annotations.span: I priced jobs, drew them, went out to sites and fell out with suppliers
annotations.label: A four-part list as one run
annotations.why: Level pitch across the list, then fall on the final item.

annotations.span: for the penny to drop
annotations.label: Idiom for delayed understanding
annotations.why: Exactly the phrase this card was written for; use it once.

annotations.span: the decisions which turn out to matter almost never announce themselves
annotations.label: Closes on a generalisation
annotations.why: Lift the last ten seconds out of the anecdote and into a claim.

Has anything you were sure about turned out to be wrong?
Who is most likely to persuade you of something?
Do people around you admit it when they get something wrong?
Is being willing to change your mind a strength or a weakness?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple for habits, present perfect for the second one, opinion present for the last
teaching.band_move: Say the honest answer first, then qualify it. Qualifying before answering sounds evasive.

questions.answer_shape: Answer straight, then split it by topic — easy about what, hard about what.
questions.extend_move: About facts, easily. About people, almost never, which probably isn't a good thing.

common_error.wrong: I change easily my mind.
common_error.right: I change my mind easily.
common_error.why: Don't split a verb from its object with an adverb.

questions.answer_shape: Name the belief, say when it broke, then what replaced it.
questions.extend_move: Plenty of things — I was certain until about twenty that ambition and talent were the same.

common_error.wrong: I have changed my mind two years ago.
common_error.right: I changed my mind two years ago.
common_error.why: A finished time phrase blocks the present perfect.

questions.answer_shape: Name who it is, then describe the method that actually works on you.
questions.extend_move: My sister, mostly, because she never argues — she just keeps asking me questions.

common_error.wrong: She persuades me to change.
common_error.right: She talks me into changing my mind.
common_error.why: 'Talk into' takes the -ing form after it.

questions.answer_shape: Generalise with a quantifier, then name the one setting where it's different.
questions.extend_move: Not many, honestly — although at work people admit mistakes far more readily than at home.

common_error.wrong: The people don't like to admit the mistakes.
common_error.right: People don't much like admitting mistakes.
common_error.why: General plurals take no article at all.

questions.answer_shape: Pick a side, name the risk on that side, then hold your position.
questions.extend_move: A strength, though it can tip into having no position at all, which isn't the same thing.

common_error.wrong: I am agree it is a strength.
common_error.right: I'd say it's a strength.
common_error.why: 'Agree' is a verb and never follows 'am'.

title: Something you believed as a child and no longer believe

payload_json.topic: Something you believed as a child and no longer believe

cue_card.topic: Describe something you believed when you were a child that you no longer believe.
bullets: what the belief was
where you think the idea came from
how long you held on to it
and explain what made you stop believing it.
rounding_off: Do the children in your family believe that too?
Was it a comfortable thing to believe?

teaching.band_move: Name the belief in one flat sentence, then spend the rest of the turn on evidence and the break.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Skip anything about magic or holidays. Pick a belief about how the adult world works — those give you evidence to describe.
prep_plan.trap: Candidates spend ninety seconds on the belief and ten on what broke it. Invert that.

time_plan.goal: State the belief in one plain sentence.
Where the idea came from, with a scene.
How long it lasted and why it was comfortable.
The event that broke it, in detail.
What you think about the belief now.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe the exact scene that seemed to prove the belief — where, what time.
Bring somebody in: say what a friend or sibling believed instead, and why.
Contrast: say what you'd have to see now to believe it again.
Evaluate: say whether you'd let a child of your own keep believing it.

error_watchlist.wrong: I believe that all adults know what they are doing.
error_watchlist.right: I believed that all adults knew what they were doing.
error_watchlist.why: A dead belief goes fully into the past, both clauses.

error_watchlist.wrong: It was a big surprised for me.
error_watchlist.right: It came as a real surprise.
error_watchlist.why: Noun after 'a', adjective before one.

error_watchlist.wrong: I keep this idea for long time.
error_watchlist.right: I held on to that idea for a long time.
error_watchlist.why: 'A long time' is fixed; the article is not optional.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: The whole card turns on a contrast between then and now, and contrast lives in stress.

target_words.note: Stress the second syllable and lean on it.
Four syllables in speech, not five.
First syllable carries it; the rest reduce.
Stress falls early, then everything flattens.

chunking_drill.sentence: You can't take proper responsibility for your own decisions while some part of you still believes there's a plan waiting upstairs.
chunks: You can't take proper responsibility
for your own decisions
while some part of you still believes
there's a plan waiting upstairs.

teaching.examiner_note: If you finish before two minutes the examiner will simply wait, then ask a rounding-off question. Silence there is not a hint that you failed.

swap_slots.span: my father, who left the house at seven twenty every single morning for about eleven years
swap_slots.prompt: Your own evidence: one person, one repeated action, one number. Never a general description.

swap_slots.span: well into my late teens
swap_slots.prompt: How long you actually held it. Give an age, not the word 'later'.

swap_slots.span: my uncle lose his job at forty-eight
swap_slots.prompt: The event that broke your belief. It must be something you watched, not something you read.

swap_slots.span: a nineteen-year-old
swap_slots.prompt: How old you were when it broke. One number does more work than a sentence.

teaching.transfer_drill: Take a belief you still hold and describe the evidence behind it, honestly. Forty-five seconds, no hedging.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about one thing I believe when I am a child. I believe that all adults know exactly what they are doing.

I think this idea come from my father. Every morning he go out from the house at seven twenty, every day, for many years, and he never look confused about anything. So for me, an adult means a person who has a plan for his life.

I keep this idea for long time, maybe until nineteen years old. It was a nice idea, because I think when I am twenty-five, everything will be clear automatic.

And then my uncle lost his job. He is forty-eight and he work in the same company from school time. After that, for six months, he don't know what to do with himself. And one day he ask me, what should I do now? And I am only nineteen years old. So I was very shocked in that moment.

After this I understand that nobody knows. All the adults are just guessing, but they are guessing with more confidence. It was a strange feeling for me. But I think it is good, because now I don't wait for somebody to give me the plan.

what_caps_it.point: The past narrative keeps sliding into the present; almost no verb is marked.
'Nice', 'strange', 'good' carry every judgement in the answer.
'And then', 'after this', 'so' are the only links between four minutes of ideas.

annotations.span: I think this idea come from my father.
annotations.label: Answers the second bullet directly
annotations.why: Keep this — naming the source in one sentence gives the turn its spine.

annotations.span: one thing I believe when I am a child
annotations.label: Dead belief left in the present
annotations.why: 'Believed when I was a child'. Both verbs move back together.

annotations.span: he go out from the house at seven twenty
annotations.label: No past marking on a habit
annotations.why: 'He used to leave the house at seven twenty' — the natural form here.

annotations.span: everything will be clear automatic
annotations.label: Adjective used as an adverb
annotations.why: 'Automatically'. Adverbs modify verbs; adjectives modify nouns.

annotations.span: I was very shocked in that moment
annotations.label: Wrong preposition in a fixed phrase
annotations.why: 'At that moment'. Learn the whole phrase as one unit.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The belief I want to talk about is one I had right through childhood: I was completely convinced that adults knew what they were doing.

And not in a small way, either. I assumed that every grown-up had at some point sat down, worked out a plan for their life, and was now quietly following it. I think it came from watching my father, who left the house at seven twenty every single morning for about eleven years and never once appeared to be improvising.

I held on to that far longer than I should have — well into my late teens. It was a comforting thing to believe, because it meant that whatever was confusing about being fifteen would sort itself out on its own by the time I got to twenty-five.

What broke it was watching my uncle lose his job at forty-eight. He'd been at the same firm since the day he left school, and for about half a year afterwards he genuinely didn't know what to do with himself. I remember him asking me — a nineteen-year-old with no qualifications — what I thought he ought to do next. That was the moment it dawned on me that nobody was in charge, and that the adults I'd been looking up to had simply been improvising with more confidence than I could manage.

I'd say I lost something when that went, but I gained rather more. You can't take proper responsibility for your own decisions while some part of you still believes there's a plan waiting upstairs.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect for the uncle's history, and reported thought held in backshift throughout.
Four bullets become four paragraphs, each opened by an audible signpost.
'Held on to', 'it dawned on me', 'looking up to' replace flat single verbs.

annotations.span: I was completely convinced that adults knew what they were doing
annotations.label: Belief and content both backshifted
annotations.why: If the belief is dead, every verb inside it moves back too.

annotations.span: And not in a small way, either.
annotations.label: Short sentence buys emphasis
annotations.why: One very short sentence after a long one resets the listener's attention.

annotations.span: never once appeared to be improvising
annotations.label: Precise verb instead of 'confused'
annotations.why: Choose the verb that names the behaviour, not the feeling.

annotations.span: I held on to that far longer than I should have
annotations.label: Answers bullet three and judges it
annotations.why: Cover the bullet and evaluate it in the same sentence — it saves you time.

annotations.span: He'd been at the same firm since the day he left school
annotations.label: Past perfect for prior history
annotations.why: Use it once, for the layer of time behind your main story.

annotations.span: it dawned on me
annotations.label: A chunk for gradual realisation
annotations.why: Far better than 'I understood'; it carries the slowness for free.

annotations.span: the adults I'd been looking up to had simply been improvising with more confidence than I could manage
annotations.label: States the new belief explicitly
annotations.why: Say what replaced the belief, or the fourth bullet is only half done.

annotations.span: I lost something when that went, but I gained rather more
annotations.label: Balanced close, not a summary
annotations.why: Weigh two things against each other instead of restating the card.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The belief I'd pick is one I carried well past the point where it made any sense: that adults, as a category, knew what they were doing.

It wasn't a vague impression either. I took it as an article of faith that every grown person had at some stage sat down, drawn up a plan, and was now executing it. My evidence, such as it was, came down to my father, who left the house at twenty past seven every morning for the better part of eleven years without ever appearing to improvise.

I clung to it into my late teens, largely because it was consoling. If the adults were working to a plan, then whatever was baffling about being fifteen would presumably resolve itself somewhere around twenty-five, without my having to do anything about it.

It came apart when my uncle was made redundant at forty-eight, having been at the same firm since the week he left school. For half a year he was visibly adrift, and at one point he asked me — nineteen, and qualified in precisely nothing — what I thought he ought to do. Never has a single conversation rearranged my head so quickly.

What I'd say now is that losing it was worth the discomfort, though it took a while to feel that way. You cannot take full responsibility for a decision while some part of you still assumes there's an adult upstairs holding the plan — and that assumption turns out to be remarkably difficult to shake off.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion and a participle clause do work the band-7 version did with 'and'.
'An article of faith', 'visibly adrift', 'came apart' are placed, not displayed.
The last line generalises the belief into a claim about responsibility.

annotations.span: Never has a single conversation rearranged my head so quickly.
annotations.label: Negative inversion for emphasis
annotations.why: Front the negative adverb and invert; keep it to once per turn.

annotations.span: having been at the same firm since the week he left school
annotations.label: Participle clause replaces a whole sentence
annotations.why: Compresses background without another 'and he had'.

annotations.span: I took it as an article of faith
annotations.label: Exact phrase for unexamined belief
annotations.why: One well-chosen collocation outweighs three unusual adjectives.

annotations.span: For half a year he was visibly adrift
annotations.label: One adjective does the whole scene
annotations.why: 'Adrift' carries the six months; the alternative is three sentences.

annotations.span: nineteen, and qualified in precisely nothing
annotations.label: Aside delivered lower and faster
annotations.why: Drop pitch inside the dashes, then come back up. It sounds spoken.

annotations.span: that assumption turns out to be remarkably difficult to shake off
annotations.label: Ends on the general case
annotations.why: Close on what the story shows about people, not about you.

teaching.tense_focus: present simple with frequency adverbs, present perfect for the final question
teaching.band_move: Put the frequency adverb before the main verb. It is the highest-density slip in this frame.

questions.answer_shape: Say which, name it, then one line about the size of the place.

common_error.right: I've got a job in a garden centre.

questions.extend_move: I cycle, mostly — it's twenty minutes and about half of it is along the canal.

common_error.wrong: I go there by walk.
common_error.right: I walk there.
common_error.why: 'On foot' or just 'walk'; 'by walk' does not exist.

questions.extend_move: Pretty much, apart from Saturdays, when we're open late and it's completely different.

common_error.wrong: I go always at the same time.
common_error.right: I always go at the same time.
common_error.why: Frequency adverbs sit before the main verb.

questions.extend_move: It's quiet, actually — a lot of older residents and one very loud primary school.

common_error.wrong: My area is very quiet place.
common_error.right: My area's a very quiet place.
common_error.why: Singular countable nouns need an article.

common_error.right: I only know a few people.
