model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about a tradition from the town of my grandparents. It is in the north, about two hours from my city.

The tradition is on the first day of the new year. In the morning, all the people walk in the street and they knock every door. And in every house they give you food. You must eat something in every house, it is not polite to say no.

My grandmother is preparing the food from very early. When I was child, the people are coming from eight o'clock until three o'clock. It was a very nice day.

But now, only the old people are doing all the houses. My parents also go but only to some houses, maybe four. And the young people don't do it. My cousins live in the city, in flat, and they must work on the second of January.

So I think this tradition will disappear. Because the people don't live in the same street now, and they have no time. Maybe in twenty years nobody will do it. It is sad, because it is the only day when you go inside the house of your neighbour. So this is my tradition which will disappear.

what_caps_it.point: The custom is narrated in the continuous, so it reads as one particular morning.
The final sentence simply repeats the cue card back to the examiner.
'Very nice', 'sad' and 'no time' carry the whole argument for disappearance.

annotations.span: You must eat something in every house, it is not polite to say no.
annotations.label: Names the social rule
annotations.why: Keep this — stating the obligation is exactly what makes a custom vivid.

annotations.span: My grandmother is preparing the food from very early.
annotations.label: Continuous used for a yearly habit
annotations.why: 'My grandmother starts cooking early' — habits take present simple.

annotations.span: When I was child
annotations.label: Missing article
annotations.why: 'When I was a child.' Singular countable nouns need a determiner.

annotations.span: the people are coming from eight o'clock until three o'clock
annotations.label: Article plus wrong tense together
annotations.why: 'People came from eight until three' — drop 'the', use past simple.

annotations.span: they have no time
annotations.label: The reason is left unexplained
annotations.why: Say what fills the time: work, distance, children. Reasons need content.

annotations.span: So this is my tradition which will disappear.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: End on a judgement about the custom, not on the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The tradition I'd pick is one from where my grandparents live, in a small town about two hours north of here. On the first morning of the new year, everybody walks round the whole street, knocks on every door unannounced, and gets fed at every single house.

It sounds exhausting, and it is. You're expected to eat something at every house, even if it's one spoonful, and refusing is genuinely rude. My grandmother would have four or five dishes out by eight in the morning, and the last visitors wouldn't leave until three in the afternoon.

The people who still do the full round are almost all over sixty. My parents' generation turns up, but they drive in, do the four or five houses that matter and go home again. Nobody in their twenties does the whole street any more, and to be fair, half of them don't live there.

The reason I don't think it'll survive is quite a practical one. It only works if people live within walking distance of each other and are actually at home. My cousins live in flats in three different cities, with entry phones instead of doors, and they're expected back at work on the second of January.

If it did go, I'd mind more than I'd have expected to. It's the one day of the year when you end up sitting in the kitchens of people you would otherwise never talk to, and you find out what they have been doing. Nothing at all has replaced that, and a group message on the day certainly hasn't.

what_lifts_it.point: Present simple holds the custom while 'would' handles the older version cleanly.
'Unannounced', 'the full round', 'entry phones instead of doors' are precise, not decorative.
Three generations are contrasted in one paragraph, so the prediction is earned.

annotations.span: everybody walks round the whole street, knocks on every door unannounced, and gets fed at every single house
annotations.label: Three present-simple verbs in a row
annotations.why: Habitual customs live in the present simple; hold it for the whole description.

annotations.span: It sounds exhausting, and it is.
annotations.label: Pre-empts the listener's reaction
annotations.why: Saying what someone is thinking buys attention and sounds unrehearsed.

annotations.span: My grandmother would have four or five dishes out by eight in the morning
annotations.label: 'Would' for repeated past
annotations.why: Use 'would' rather than 'used to' when the habit is already established.

annotations.span: to be fair, half of them don't live there
annotations.label: Concedes against your own point
annotations.why: Undercutting yourself once makes the rest of the argument credible.

annotations.span: The reason I don't think it'll survive is quite a practical one.
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Announce the explanation and you cannot forget to give it.

annotations.span: with entry phones instead of doors
annotations.label: One detail carries the argument
annotations.why: A concrete obstacle beats the phrase 'modern life' every time.

annotations.span: I'd mind more than I'd have expected to
annotations.label: Two conditionals in one clause
annotations.why: Hypothetical present plus hypothetical past, done in seven words.

annotations.span: a group message on the day certainly hasn't
annotations.label: Ellipsis lands the joke
annotations.why: Leaving the verb out at the end sounds natural and confident.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The custom I'd choose belongs to my grandparents' town, a couple of hours north of where I am now, and it happens once a year on the first morning of January.

What happens is that the entire street visits the entire street. You knock, unannounced, you are fed, and you move on. Refusal isn't really available to you: turning down what's put in front of you is read as a slight, so people pace themselves across a dozen kitchens with a great deal of care. My grandmother would have a spread laid out by eight, and the last of them would drift off some time after three.

The full round is now done almost exclusively by the over-sixties. My parents' generation drives in, calls at the four houses that would notice if they didn't, and leaves. Among my cousins it has already petered out, though in fairness most of them moved away years ago.

What makes me think it's finished is nothing to do with attitudes. It's simply that the custom presupposes a street where people are within walking distance and are at home on a Tuesday morning — and that street barely exists any more. Take away the proximity and the whole thing has nothing to stand on.

What we'd lose isn't the food, obviously. It's the one morning a year on which you find yourself sitting in a kitchen you'd otherwise never see the inside of, listening to somebody you have known by sight for thirty years.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative-style conditional and a fronted 'what' clause replace plain sentences.
'Read as a slight', 'petered out', 'presupposes' are chosen for shade, not size.
The argument names its own premise, then removes it — a genuinely analytic close.

annotations.span: Take away the proximity and the whole thing has nothing to stand on.
annotations.label: Imperative as a conditional
annotations.why: 'Take away X and Y' is a compact spoken conditional. Use it once.

annotations.span: turning down what's put in front of you is read as a slight
annotations.label: Passive plus precise noun
annotations.why: 'A slight' says in one word what 'not polite' takes five to say.

annotations.span: it has already petered out
annotations.label: The exact verb for slow fading
annotations.why: 'Petered out' beats 'disappeared' because it carries the gradualness.

annotations.span: the entire street visits the entire street
annotations.label: Repetition with equal stress
annotations.why: Say both halves at the same weight; the symmetry is the point.

annotations.span: the custom presupposes a street where people are within walking distance
annotations.label: Names the hidden condition
annotations.why: Identifying what a practice depends on is the highest-value analytic move.

annotations.span: a kitchen you'd otherwise never see the inside of
annotations.label: Closes on the human loss
annotations.why: End on the specific thing that goes, never on the word 'culture'.

I want to describe a situation with my friend. She is my friend from school time, and two years ago she wants to open a small coffee business in the market.

She asked me to check her prices, because I am good with numbers. So I check everything, and I see a big problem. Her price for one coffee is lower than the cost of the coffee and the cup. So she will lose money every time she sells one coffee.

It was very difficult for me to tell her this. Because she already told all her family and friends, and she left her job, and she spent all her money for the cart. So if I say the truth, maybe she cannot open.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
This was about two years ago, and it involved a friend of mine — someone I've known since school — who was two weeks away from opening a coffee cart in the market.

She'd asked me to look over her costings, mostly, I think, because she wanted somebody to tell her they were fine. They weren't. When I actually worked through them, she was charging less for a cup of coffee than the coffee, the cup and the lid were costing her. Not by a small margin either. She'd have lost money on every single sale, and she'd already spent most of her savings on the cart itself.

What made it hard wasn't the arithmetic. It was that she'd told everybody. Her family had finally come round to the idea, she'd handed in her notice, and there was a date. Saying the numbers didn't work effectively meant saying the thing she'd announced to everyone might not happen.

I did say it in the end, sitting in her car outside the unit. I remember trying to soften it, then giving up and putting it bluntly, because the gentle version wasn't landing at all. She went very quiet, and then she was angry with me for a fortnight.

She did put the prices up in the end, though, and the cart is still going three years later. I'd say we're still friends because I said it rather than in spite of it — but I want to be clear that I didn't know that at the time, and I very nearly said nothing.

what_lifts_it.point: Backshifted reporting plus three past perfects keep two time layers apart.
'Come round to the idea', 'handed in her notice', 'wasn't landing' are natural chunks.
A cleft names the real difficulty, and the close refuses the tidy moral.

annotations.label: Cleft isolates the real difficulty

annotations.label: 'Landing' used precisely
annotations.why: Reuse 'that didn't land' for anything said and not received.

annotations.why: Two reactions in sequence read as a real person, not a summary.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This goes back a couple of years, to a friend I've known since we were eleven, who at that point was a fortnight from opening a coffee cart in the covered market.

She'd sent me her costings to look over. In theory that was a request for a second opinion; in practice, I suspect, it was a request for reassurance. And the figures were unsalvageable. She had priced a cup below what the coffee, the cup and the lid were costing her — so every sale would have taken money off her, and she'd already sunk her savings into the cart.

The arithmetic was the easy part. What made it difficult was that the thing had already been announced. She'd resigned, her family had come round, there was a launch date on a poster. Telling her the numbers were wrong amounted to telling her the version of her life she'd been describing to everyone might not arrive.

I told her in her car outside the unit. I did try to break it to her gently, gave that up about a minute in, and said it flatly instead, because nothing softer was getting through. She said almost nothing, and didn't speak to me for a fortnight.

She raised the prices. The cart is still there. And while I'd like to say I knew it would end that way, the honest position is that I said it not knowing, which is the only part of it I'd call difficult.

'Unsalvageable', 'sunk her savings', 'amounted to' are chosen for exactness.
The close redefines what 'difficult' meant instead of restating the story.

annotations.why: The verb carries the fact that the money can't come back.

annotations.span: amounted to telling her the version of her life she'd been describing to everyone might not arrive
annotations.label: Restates the stake at a higher level
annotations.why: Say what the sentence really meant to the other person.

annotations.span: She said almost nothing, and didn't speak to me for a fortnight.
annotations.label: Two flat clauses, no rise
annotations.why: Deliberately unemotional delivery here does more than an adjective would.

annotations.span: the honest position is that I said it not knowing
annotations.label: Redefines the key word
annotations.why: Ending by redefining the card's own word lifts the turn out of anecdote.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about the traffic problem in the area where my parents are living. It is on a hill and there is only one road for going up and down.

The road is very narrow, only one car can pass. And now there are maybe three hundred houses up there. So in the morning, from eight to nine, nothing is moving. It is blocked.

This is a problem for everybody but especially for the old people. Two years ago an ambulance needed twenty-two minutes for coming to our neighbour, and the distance is very short. So it is not only about the time, it can be dangerous.

The council tried some things. They made one way, but then all the cars go past the school, so they stopped it. They want to make the road bigger, but for this they must take a part of the gardens, and the people don't accept. Also there was a small bus but after one year there was no money.

So I think there is no good solution for this problem. Every solution is bad for someone. If you help one group, you make problem for another group. So nobody can decide and nothing is changing.

what_caps_it.point: Continuous forms are used for states, and the conditional in the close is broken.
'Very narrow', 'bigger', 'bad for someone' — no cost-benefit vocabulary at all.
Each attempted solution is listed, but never joined to the argument it supports.

annotations.span: Two years ago an ambulance needed twenty-two minutes
annotations.label: One hard fact, with a number
annotations.why: Keep this — a single measured fact is worth a paragraph of description.

annotations.span: the area where my parents are living
annotations.label: Continuous used for a permanent state
annotations.why: 'Where my parents live.' Long-term situations take present simple.

annotations.span: for coming to our neighbour
annotations.label: Wrong form after 'for'
annotations.why: 'To reach our neighbour' — purpose takes 'to' plus the base verb.

annotations.span: they must take a part of the gardens, and the people don't accept
annotations.label: 'Accept' used without an object
annotations.why: 'Residents won't agree to it.' Give 'accept' something to accept.

annotations.span: If you help one group, you make problem for another group.
annotations.label: Missing article in the key sentence
annotations.why: 'You create a problem for another group.' Singular nouns need determiners.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The problem I'd describe is in the part of town where my parents still live. It sits up a hill, and there is exactly one road in and out of it.

The road was built for carts, essentially. It's wide enough for a single car, with passing places every hundred metres or so, and about three hundred houses now sit behind it. Between eight and nine the whole hill grinds to a halt. That's an inconvenience. What isn't an inconvenience is that an ambulance took twenty-two minutes to get to a neighbour of ours two winters ago, over a distance of under a mile.

It affects the older residents most, and they are exactly who lives up there — people who bought in the seventies and never moved.

Things have been tried. They made it one-way, which sent everything past the primary school and lasted about four months. They proposed widening it, which means taking the front six feet off the houses on the left-hand side, and those happen to be the oldest houses on the street. There was a shuttle bus for a year, until the funding ran out.

And that's why I don't think there's an answer. Every option takes something real off somebody. Widening it costs the people who have lived there longest their gardens; leaving it costs everybody else an ambulance. You can move the cost around, but you cannot make it disappear — and because a different group pays each time, nothing ever gets a majority behind it.

what_lifts_it.point: Non-defining relative clauses attach each solution to its own failure in one sentence.
'Grinds to a halt', 'ran out', 'takes something off somebody' carry the argument.
Three options are raised and dismissed in parallel, then one principle explains all three.

annotations.span: there is exactly one road in and out of it
annotations.label: The whole problem in nine words
annotations.why: State the structural fact first; everything else is consequence.

annotations.span: The road was built for carts, essentially.
annotations.label: Historical detail does the describing
annotations.why: One fact about origin beats three adjectives about size.

annotations.span: the whole hill grinds to a halt
annotations.label: Idiom used where it belongs
annotations.why: Save it for traffic and processes; it sounds forced anywhere else.

annotations.span: That's an inconvenience. What isn't an inconvenience is that
annotations.label: Escalates from minor to serious
annotations.why: Name the small version of the problem, then reject it for the real one.

annotations.span: which sent everything past the primary school and lasted about four months
annotations.label: Relative clause carries the failure
annotations.why: Attach the outcome to the plan with 'which' instead of a new sentence.

annotations.span: those happen to be the oldest houses on the street
annotations.label: The detail that makes it impossible
annotations.why: Find the fact that turns a cost into an obstacle, and say it last.

annotations.span: Widening it costs the people who have lived there longest their gardens; leaving it costs everybody else an ambulance.
annotations.label: Parallel structure across a semicolon
annotations.why: Two clauses in identical shape make a trade-off audible instantly.

annotations.span: nothing ever gets a majority behind it
annotations.label: Explains the deadlock, not the traffic
annotations.why: Close on the mechanism, which is the part that generalises.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd choose is the access road to the hill where my parents live. There is a single way up and a single way down, and they are the same road.

It was laid out for carts, and it has never been widened. One car's width, passing places at intervals, and something in the region of three hundred houses now sitting behind it. For an hour each morning the hill is effectively sealed. That much is merely irritating. Less irritating is the twenty-two minutes an ambulance took to reach a neighbour of ours two winters ago, for a journey of under a mile.

And the people it hits hardest are precisely the people who live there — a street bought in the seventies and never sold on.

Everything reasonable has been attempted. A one-way system simply relocated the queue to the school gates and was abandoned within the term. Widening would require six feet from the front of every house on one side, and those are the oldest properties on the hill. A shuttle bus survived exactly as long as its funding did.

What I've come round to is that the problem isn't technical at all. Each solution works; each one simply presents the bill to a different set of people, and no set of people has ever volunteered to pay. Where a problem's cost can be shifted but never cancelled, my experience is that nothing whatsoever gets decided.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted 'where' clause and two verbless noun phrases replace ordinary sentences.
'Effectively sealed', 'relocated the queue', 'presents the bill' are precise and unshowy.
The close states a general principle that would apply to any problem of this shape.

annotations.span: Where a problem's cost can be shifted but never cancelled, my experience is that nothing whatsoever gets decided.
annotations.label: Fronted 'where' clause as a rule
annotations.why: 'Where X, Y' states a general law without sounding like an essay.

annotations.span: One car's width, passing places at intervals, and something in the region of three hundred houses
annotations.label: Verbless list, spoken as one unit
annotations.why: Group it into three even beats and drop the pitch on the last.

annotations.span: the hill is effectively sealed
annotations.label: One verb replaces a description
annotations.why: 'Sealed' does more than 'completely blocked with a lot of cars'.

annotations.span: each one simply presents the bill to a different set of people
annotations.label: Metaphor doing analytic work
annotations.why: A metaphor is worth using when it makes the logic clearer, not prettier.

annotations.span: A shuttle bus survived exactly as long as its funding did.
annotations.label: Dismissal delivered as one line
annotations.why: Compressing a whole failed scheme into a sentence sounds controlled.

annotations.span: the problem isn't technical at all
annotations.label: Reclassifies the problem
annotations.why: Saying what kind of problem it is lifts the answer above description.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I want to change is about my grandfather. He came to live in our house when I have fourteen years old, because my grandmother died. And he stayed with us until I was seventeen.

So he was living in the room next to me for three years. Every day I saw him. But I never asked him nothing about his life. I just say hello, and sometimes we watched the football together. That is all.

And the thing is, he was working in ships when he was young. He travelled to many countries. He saw many things. But I don't know nothing about this, because I never asked, and he was a quiet man, he don't tell you if you don't ask.

If I can go back, I will ask him. Maybe one time in a week, with a recorder, and I record his stories. Only thirty minutes, it is not so much.

Now it is too late because he died in 2016. My father knows a little bit but not the details. So this is the thing I want to do different. And now I ask my parents more questions, because I don't want the same problem again.

what_caps_it.point: The counterfactual is built with 'if I can' and 'I will', so no regret is expressed.
'Many countries', 'many things', 'a little bit' — the detail never becomes specific.
The turn restates the card at the end instead of landing on a thought.

annotations.label: Explains why it didn't happen
annotations.why: Keep this — giving the reason stops the regret sounding like carelessness.

annotations.span: when I have fourteen years old
annotations.label: Age built with the wrong verb
annotations.why: 'When I was fourteen.' English uses 'be' plus the number alone.

annotations.span: I never asked him nothing about his life
annotations.label: Double negative
annotations.why: 'I never asked him anything.' One negative per clause in English.

annotations.span: If I can go back, I will ask him.
annotations.label: Real conditional for an impossible past
annotations.why: 'If I could go back, I'd ask him' — the past cannot be a real condition.

annotations.span: So this is the thing I want to do different.
annotations.label: Adjective where an adverb belongs
annotations.why: 'Differently'. And close on an idea rather than the card.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd do differently isn't really a decision — it's the way I spent about three years.

My grandfather lived with us from when I was fourteen, after my grandmother died, and he was in the room next to mine until he went into hospital the year I turned seventeen. So I saw him more or less every day for the best part of three years.

And in all that time I don't think I asked him a single serious question. I'd say hello, I'd complain about school, occasionally we'd watch the football. That was it. He'd been in the merchant navy from sixteen to about thirty-five, and he'd been to places I still haven't been, and none of that ever came up — because I never asked, and he wasn't a man who volunteered anything.

What I'd do instead is embarrassingly simple. I'd sit down with him once a week with a recorder and ask him about the ships. Not a formal interview, nothing organised — just half an hour, regularly, while he was well enough to enjoy being asked about it.

The reason it matters is that there's nobody left to ask. My father knows the outline and none of the detail. What I've taken from it, honestly, is that I now ask my parents things that feel slightly intrusive, and I ask them earlier than I want to, on the grounds that the alternative is a whole set of questions that can never be answered by anybody at all.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect, habitual 'would' and a sustained hypothetical all sit in the same turn.
'Volunteered anything', 'the outline and none of the detail' are precise and unforced.
The alternative gets its own paragraph, so the fourth bullet is genuinely answered.

annotations.span: isn't really a decision — it's the way I spent about three years
annotations.label: Reframes the card in one line
annotations.why: Saying what your answer is not is a fast way to sound precise.

annotations.span: I'd say hello, I'd complain about school, occasionally we'd watch the football
annotations.label: 'Would' for repeated past
annotations.why: Three habitual 'would' forms in a row build a routine cheaply.

annotations.span: He'd been in the merchant navy from sixteen to about thirty-five
annotations.label: Past perfect for the earlier layer
annotations.why: His life came before your story, so it takes the perfect form.

annotations.span: he wasn't a man who volunteered anything
annotations.label: Character in one relative clause
annotations.why: Define a person by what they don't do; it's sharper than adjectives.

annotations.span: What I'd do instead is embarrassingly simple.
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Announcing the alternative makes it impossible to skip.

annotations.span: while he was well enough to enjoy being asked about it
annotations.label: Passive gerund after a preposition
annotations.why: 'Enjoy being asked' — a small structure that reads as very controlled.

annotations.span: My father knows the outline and none of the detail.
annotations.label: Contrast in six words
annotations.why: Pairing two nouns against each other beats a whole explanation.

annotations.span: I now ask my parents things that feel slightly intrusive
annotations.label: Shows the regret changed behaviour
annotations.why: End on what you do now; it proves the regret is real.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd change isn't a choice I made. It's a stretch of about three years that I simply wasted.

My grandfather moved in with us after my grandmother died — I was fourteen — and he was in the next room until he went into hospital when I was seventeen. I saw the man daily for three years and I don't believe I ever asked him one question worth answering. Hello, a complaint about school, the occasional football match. That was the sum of it.

And he had been at sea from sixteen until his mid-thirties, in places I have still never got to. None of that ever surfaced, partly because I never asked, and partly because he belonged to a generation that didn't offer things up unprompted.

What I'd do instead is almost humiliating in its simplicity. Half an hour a week, a recorder on the table, and a few questions about the ships — while he was still well enough to be flattered by the asking rather than tired by it.

And the reason I'd want it back isn't sentiment. It's that the information is gone. My father has the outline; nobody has the detail; and no amount of caring about it now produces a single fact. What it has left me with is a slightly indecent habit of asking my parents things I have no business asking, on the grounds that unasked questions have a way of becoming unanswerable ones.

what_lifts_it.point: A nominalised subject and a three-part semicolon list replace the plainer band-7 clauses.
'Never surfaced', 'offer things up unprompted', 'slightly indecent habit' are exact.
The close turns one regret into a general observation about questions.

annotations.span: My father has the outline; nobody has the detail; and no amount of caring about it now produces a single fact.
annotations.label: Three-part list across semicolons
annotations.why: Parallel clauses build to a point without any linking word at all.

annotations.span: he belonged to a generation that didn't offer things up unprompted
annotations.label: Explains a person by their era
annotations.why: Attributing a habit to a generation is more interesting than to a mood.

annotations.span: flattered by the asking rather than tired by it
annotations.label: Two passives in exact contrast
annotations.why: One precise pair of verbs does the work of a whole explanation.

annotations.span: almost humiliating in its simplicity
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'simplicity'
annotations.why: Put the weight on the final word and let the pitch fall away after it.

annotations.span: unasked questions have a way of becoming unanswerable ones
annotations.label: Generalises out of the anecdote
annotations.why: Close with a sentence that would be true for somebody else's story too.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about the skill of translation, especially in the hospitals. My aunt is doing this job since fifteen years in a hospital in the north.

Her job is to help when the doctor and the patient don't speak the same language. But it is not only about the words. She told me that many times the patient says yes but actually he doesn't understand. And she can see this, and she stops and she explains again.

For this job she studied two years and she got a certificate. But she says the real learning was in the hospital, with the real patients. Maybe one thousand appointments.

And I think in the future the machines will do this job. Not because they are better, because they are not better. But they are free and they are very fast and they can speak forty languages. And the hospital has no money. So they will choose the machine.

So what we lose is the person who can say to the doctor, please speak more slowly. This is not written in her contract but it is very important. So this is my opinion about the skill which machines will replace.

what_caps_it.point: 'Is doing since fifteen years' gets both the tense and the preposition wrong.
Five sentences in a row begin with 'and' or 'but', and the close restates the card.
'Very fast', 'very important', 'better' — nothing names the trade-off precisely.

annotations.why: Keep this — dismissing the expected answer makes the real one land.

annotations.why: 'My aunt has done this job for fifteen years.' Perfect plus 'for'.

annotations.label: Article on a generalisation
annotations.why: 'In hospitals' — plural generalisations take no article.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The skill I'd pick is medical interpreting — standing between a doctor and a patient who don't share a language.

My aunt has done it for about fifteen years, in a hospital in the north. It isn't translation in the way people imagine. Half of what she does is noticing: she'll hear a patient say yes and know from the way they said it that they haven't understood a word, and she'll stop the consultation and say so, which is not something anybody asked her to do.

Nobody really teaches that part. She took a qualification, which took two years and was mostly vocabulary, and then she learned the rest on the job, across something like a thousand awkward appointments.

And I do think it'll go, within a decade or so. Not because a machine will do it better — I don't believe it will, not the noticing. It'll go because a machine will do it well enough, instantly, in forty languages, at no cost, and a hospital that is short of money will take that trade every time. That does seem to be the pattern with all of these: the skill isn't replaced by something better at all, it's replaced by something merely adequate that happens to scale.

What we'd lose is the one person in the room who can tell a consultant to slow down. That was never anywhere in her job description, and it is exactly the sort of thing that nobody notices has gone until it has already gone.

what_lifts_it.point: Hedged futures and a non-defining relative clause replace the flat 'will' chain.
'Well enough', 'take that trade', 'something adequate that scales' are exact and plain.
The argument names the wrong explanation, rejects it, then gives the real mechanism.

annotations.why: Describe what the person physically does; it beats a job title.

annotations.span: Half of what she does is noticing
annotations.label: One gerund names the whole skill
annotations.why: Turning a verb into the subject makes an abstract point concrete.

annotations.span: which is not something anybody asked her to do
annotations.label: Relative clause adds the judgement
annotations.why: Attach your evaluation with 'which' instead of a separate sentence.

annotations.span: across something like a thousand awkward appointments
annotations.label: A number does the arguing
annotations.why: An estimated figure is more persuasive than the words 'a lot of'.

annotations.span: Not because a machine will do it better
annotations.label: Rules out the expected reason
annotations.why: Say what your explanation is not, then give the one you mean.

annotations.span: a hospital that is short of money will take that trade every time
annotations.label: Names who actually decides
annotations.why: Predictions get sharper the moment you say whose choice it is.

annotations.span: it's replaced by something merely adequate that happens to scale
annotations.label: The whole argument in six words
annotations.why: Compress your thesis into one clause and it becomes quotable.

annotations.span: nobody notices has gone until it has
annotations.label: Ellipsis at the end of the clause
annotations.why: Dropping the repeated verb sounds natural and confident.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The skill I'd nominate is hospital interpreting — sitting between a clinician and a patient with no language in common.

My aunt has been doing it for the best part of fifteen years. What she does is only partly linguistic. A good deal of it is reading the room: she picks up on the fractional pause before a patient agrees to something, works out that nothing has landed, and stops the consultation to say so. Nobody instructed her to do that, and no version of her job description mentions it.

The formal training took two years and consisted largely of terminology. The rest she acquired the slow way, over what must be several thousand difficult appointments.

I'd give it ten years, perhaps fifteen. And not, I should say, because the software will match her — I doubt it will come close on the reading-the-room element. It will win because it is instantaneous, available in forty languages, and free, and a hospital running a deficit will take adequate-and-free over excellent-and-scarce every single time. That, as far as I can tell, is how these things actually go: not replacement by something better, but displacement by something sufficient.

And what disappears with her is the only person in that room whose job allows them to interrupt a consultant. It was never anybody's official duty in the first place, which is precisely the reason why nobody will ever be able to say when exactly it stopped.

what_lifts_it.point: A parenthetical 'I should say' and paired hyphenated compounds compress two band-7 clauses.
'Reading the room', 'running a deficit', 'displacement by something sufficient' are exact.
The close identifies a structural reason the loss will go unrecorded.

annotations.why: Dropping a short aside mid-sentence sounds spoken, not written.

annotations.span: she picks up on the fractional pause before a patient agrees to something
annotations.label: Precision instead of length
annotations.why: 'Fractional pause' does what a whole sentence of explanation would.

annotations.span: adequate-and-free over excellent-and-scarce
annotations.label: Invented compound pair
annotations.why: Building a compound to fit the point is a band-8 lexical move.

annotations.span: not replacement by something better, but displacement by something sufficient
annotations.label: Parallel phrases, stress on the nouns
annotations.why: Match the rhythm of both halves and stress the contrasting words.

annotations.span: which is precisely the reason why nobody will ever be able to say when exactly it stopped
annotations.label: Explains why the loss is invisible
annotations.why: A final sentence that explains rather than summarises lifts the turn.

I want to talk about a change in my town. Four years ago the council decided to close our main street for the cars, only people can walk there now.

At that time I am completely against this. My father has a hardware shop in this street from the eighties. And in a hardware shop the people buy heavy things, paint, wood, tools. They come with the car and they put it in the car. So I thought, if there is no car, there is no customer.

But they closed the street anyway, for a test, eighteen months. And after this, the money in the shop is more than before. Not so much more, but more. And it stayed like this.

The change I'd describe happened about four years ago, when the council closed our high street to traffic.

I was completely against it. My father has run a hardware shop on that street since the eighties, and the argument I made — at a public meeting, in front of about sixty people — was that his customers arrive by car precisely because they've got something heavy to carry, and that if you take the cars away you take the shop away with them.

And I didn't say it once and leave it. I signed the petition, I helped collect signatures outside the shop, and I fell out fairly badly with a neighbour who has since become a friend again.

They closed it anyway, as an eighteen-month trial. And the honest answer is that the takings went up. Not dramatically, but they went up, and they have stayed up ever since. People stop now. They simply didn't stop before, because there was nowhere at all to stand that wasn't a road.

So I have come round to it entirely, and I would happily sign the opposite petition tomorrow morning if anybody seriously tried to reverse it. What I'd say in my defence is that I wasn't wrong about everything: the elderly customers who used to park outside really have lost something, and four years on nobody has done anything whatsoever about that. I just happened to think that was the whole of the argument, when in fact it turned out to be a detail.

'The takings', 'fell out with', 'come round to it' are the exact words for the situation.

annotations.label: Old position in its strongest form
annotations.why: Argue your former view properly; it makes the reversal worth hearing.

annotations.label: Shows commitment without adverbs

annotations.why: The event is finished; the state is not. Two tenses, one sentence.

annotations.span: I would happily sign the opposite petition tomorrow morning if anybody seriously tried to reverse it
annotations.label: Second conditional, result first
annotations.why: Putting the result clause first sounds far more spoken.

annotations.span: I wasn't wrong about everything

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd pick is the pedestrianisation of our high street, roughly four years back.

I opposed it, and not quietly. My father has had a hardware shop on that street since the eighties, and my case — put to a public meeting and about sixty of my neighbours — was that people come to a hardware shop precisely because they have something heavy to get home, and that removing the cars would, in effect, remove the customers.

Nor did I leave it at that. I signed the petition, stood outside the shop collecting names for a fortnight, and fell out with a neighbour badly enough that it took a year to repair.

They went ahead regardless of all of it, as an eighteen-month trial. And then the takings rose. Not spectacularly, but they rose, and they have held. What I had entirely failed to anticipate was that people would linger. Nobody had ever lingered there, for the straightforward reason that the only place to stand was a carriageway.

So I have eaten my words, publicly, and on more than one occasion since then. Where I'd still defend myself is on a narrower point: the older customers who used to park at the door genuinely have been left worse off, and four years on not one thing has been done for them. My mistake wasn't being wrong about that. It was in mistaking what was a perfectly real objection for a decisive one.

'Linger', 'carriageway', 'held' are chosen for exactness rather than for effect.

annotations.why: 'Nor' at the start forces the auxiliary in front of the subject.

annotations.span: What I had entirely failed to anticipate was that people would linger.
annotations.label: Cleft with past perfect inside
annotations.why: A 'what' clause front-loads the surprise and buys you a beat.

annotations.span: the only place to stand was a carriageway
annotations.label: One noun explains the behaviour
annotations.why: The precise word for the surface does the whole explanation.

annotations.span: I have eaten my words, publicly, and on more than one occasion
annotations.label: Idiom sharpened by two adverbials
annotations.why: An idiom plus a specific qualifier stops it sounding like filler.

annotations.span: Not spectacularly, but they rose, and they have held.
annotations.label: Three short units, falling tone
annotations.why: Cut the sentence into three beats and drop the pitch on each.

annotations.span: It was in mistaking what was a perfectly real objection for a decisive one.
annotations.label: Distinguishes two kinds of error
annotations.why: Ending on a distinction rather than a conclusion is a band-8 close.

title: A time you arrived later than you meant to

payload_json.topic: A time you arrived later than you meant to

bullets: where you were going and why
what made you late
what happened when you got there
and explain how you felt about it afterwards.
rounding_off: Did anyone else end up affected by it?
Is that a journey you'd done before?

teaching.band_move: Fix the time and the outcome in your first sentence, then hold past simple to the end.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Take the first lateness that comes to mind, even a small one. Marks come from the reason and the fallout, never from how dramatic the delay was.

note_grid.cell: line shut - eng work, didn't check

prep_plan.trap: Almost everyone spends the whole turn on the delay and never says how they felt or what they changed afterwards.

time_plan.goal: Name what you were late for and by how much.
Where you were going and what went wrong.
What actually happened when you got there.
How you felt, and where the mistake really was.
One general line about why people run late.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in on the notice at the station: what it said, who else was standing there reading it.
Go back a night: say what you checked before bed and what you didn't bother checking.
Bring her in: say what she'd been doing for that hour and what she said first.

error_watchlist.wrong: So I go to the station and there is a notice on the door.
error_watchlist.right: So I got to the station and there was a notice on the door.
error_watchlist.why: Anchor the tense in sentence one and stay in it.

error_watchlist.wrong: If I checked the night before, I took a taxi.
error_watchlist.right: If I'd checked the night before, I'd have taken a taxi.
error_watchlist.why: Regret about the past needs two perfect forms.

error_watchlist.wrong: I must take a bus instead.
error_watchlist.right: I had to take a bus instead.
error_watchlist.why: 'Must' has no past form; past obligation is 'had to'.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: The point sits in a contrast — the morning against the night before — and stress carries it.

target_words.note: Stress the middle; the first syllable is barely there.
Four syllables, main stress on the third.
Stress the middle; '-ment' stays weak.
Stress first, then two light syllables.
Never stress the first syllable of this one.

chunking_drill.sentence: It wasn't the morning at all; it was the ten seconds the night before when I didn't look at the line status.
chunks: It wasn't the morning at all;
it was the ten seconds the night before
when I didn't look at the line status.

minimal_pairs.contrast: 'checked' ends in a /kt/ cluster — two consonants, not one

teaching.examiner_note: The examiner will not react while you speak, not even to a story about a disaster. The silence is procedure, not disapproval, and it stops you dead at two minutes.

swap_slots.span: a morning two years ago
swap_slots.prompt: Your own time reference. One is enough — a season, a year, 'a couple of years back'.

swap_slots.span: my cousin, who was flying in from abroad
swap_slots.prompt: Your own person: one relationship plus the single fact that made being late matter.

swap_slots.span: the line was shut for engineering work
swap_slots.prompt: Whatever actually went wrong, named concretely in about five words.

swap_slots.span: the ten seconds the night before when I didn't look at the line status
swap_slots.prompt: The exact moment your version of the mistake happened. Give it a duration and an action.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now run the same three moves — what went wrong, what it cost, where the real mistake was — about a time you forgot something. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a time when I was late for my cousin. It was two years ago, in the summer.

So my cousin was coming from abroad and her flight is landing at seven o'clock in the morning. I said I will pick her up at the airport, because it is her first time here. I put two alarms in my phone, so I woke up fine, no problem.

But then I go to the station and there is a paper on the door. The trains are not running because of the works. So I must take a bus instead, and this bus is very slow, it stops everywhere. I was very stressed in the bus and I can do nothing.

I came to the airport at five to eight. She is waiting near the barrier with two big suitcases and her phone has no internet. I felt very bad. I said sorry many times and she said it's okay, no problem.

Actually the problem was not the morning. The problem was the night before, because I didn't check the trains. If I check the night before, I take a taxi. So it was my mistake and now I always check. So this is my story about being late.

what_caps_it.point: Nearly every sentence opens with 'so' or 'and'; it lands as a list of steps.
The narrative slips into the present four times and the regret has no conditional at all.
'Very stressed', 'very bad', 'very slow' — one intensifier is doing all the evaluating.

annotations.span: It was two years ago, in the summer.
annotations.label: Puts a time marker in early
annotations.why: Keep this — one date near the start is what a past narrative hangs on.

annotations.span: her flight is landing at seven o'clock in the morning
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Say 'was landing'. Decide the tense in sentence one and hold it.

annotations.span: I said I will pick her up at the airport
annotations.label: Reported speech not backshifted
annotations.why: After a past reporting verb, 'will' becomes 'would': 'I said I'd pick her up'.

annotations.span: So I must take a bus instead
annotations.label: 'Must' cannot carry past obligation
annotations.why: Use 'I had to take a bus'. 'Must' has no past form.

annotations.span: If I check the night before, I take a taxi.
annotations.label: Regret with no conditional in it
annotations.why: Say 'If I'd checked the night before, I'd have taken a taxi.'

annotations.span: So this is my story about being late.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the prompt
annotations.why: Close on a thought about lateness, not on the wording of the card.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a morning two years ago when I turned up almost an hour late to meet my cousin, who was flying in from abroad.

Her flight was due to land at seven, and I'd said I'd be at arrivals to meet her, because it was her first time in the country and she wouldn't have a working phone. I set two alarms the night before and I was up in plenty of time, so I honestly thought I had it covered.

What I hadn't done was check the trains. When I got to the station there was a printed notice taped to the doors — the line was shut for engineering work, as it apparently is most weekends — and we were being put on a replacement bus instead. The bus stopped everywhere, and it took about fifty minutes longer than the train would have. I spent the whole journey watching the clock and knowing there was nothing I could do about it.

I got there at five to eight. She'd been standing by the barrier for nearly an hour with two suitcases and no way of contacting anybody.

As for how I felt about it — mortified, obviously, although she was completely relaxed about the whole thing, which somehow made it worse. The bit that has stayed with me, though, is where the mistake actually happened. It wasn't the morning at all; it was the ten seconds the night before when I didn't look at the line status. If I'd checked then, I'd have booked a taxi and none of it would have happened.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft, a past perfect and a full third conditional replace the flat run of past simples.
'Had it covered', 'mortified', 'in plenty of time' — chunks rather than 'very' plus an adjective.
It names where the mistake really was, so the turn ends on an idea, not the prompt.

annotations.span: I'll talk about a morning two years ago when I turned up almost an hour late
annotations.label: Time and outcome in one sentence
annotations.why: Say how late you were up front; the listener then hears everything as explanation.

annotations.span: I had it covered
annotations.label: A chunk instead of 'I was prepared'
annotations.why: Reuse it any time you want to say you thought you were ready.

annotations.span: What I hadn't done was check the trains.
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect in one line
annotations.why: This is the sentence that turns a list of events into a story with a cause.

annotations.span: we were being put on a replacement bus instead
annotations.label: Passive for something done to you
annotations.why: Use the passive when the doer is an institution and doesn't matter.

annotations.span: watching the clock and knowing there was nothing I could do about it
annotations.label: Says how it felt while it was happening
annotations.why: One line of interior detail buys ten seconds and adds no new facts.

annotations.span: mortified, obviously, although she was completely relaxed about the whole thing
annotations.label: One precise adjective beats three vague ones
annotations.why: Pick the exact feeling word, then contrast it with the other person's.

annotations.span: As for how I felt about it
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet aloud
annotations.why: Naming the move is the cheapest way to stop yourself forgetting it.

annotations.span: If I'd checked then, I'd have booked a taxi
annotations.label: Third conditional for regret
annotations.why: On any 'how did you feel' bullet this is the natural structure to reach for.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about a morning a couple of summers back when I left my cousin standing at arrivals for the best part of an hour.

She was flying in for the first time, with no working phone and nobody else here she could ring, so I'd made rather a performance of promising I'd be there when she came through. Two alarms, clothes out the night before, the lot. And I was up bang on time.

What I'd completely failed to do was look at the trains. There was a notice taped to the station doors: the line was closed for repairs, which it turns out it is most weekends, and everyone was being funnelled onto a replacement bus that seemed to stop at every lamp-post between there and the airport. Fifty minutes gone, and not a thing to be done about it except sit and watch the minutes go.

She'd been by the barrier with two suitcases since half past seven. She could not have been nicer about it, which, if anything, made it worse.

Looking back, what interests me isn't the lateness itself; it's how far upstream the mistake sat. Had I spent ten seconds on the line status the night before, I'd have ordered a taxi and the whole thing would have evaporated. The morning was never the problem — the morning was only where the problem finally surfaced. I suspect that's true of most lateness: the failure is a decision taken hours earlier, comfortably, by somebody who assumed things would run.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces 'if', and 'could not have been nicer' does emphasis without an intensifier.
'Made a performance of', 'how far upstream', 'the lot' — idiom sits where a native would put it.
The close generalises about lateness itself instead of summarising the anecdote.

annotations.span: Had I spent ten seconds on the line status the night before
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as the third conditional, higher register, still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: I'd made rather a performance of promising
annotations.label: Idiom that also judges the speaker
annotations.why: Choose a phrase that carries an attitude, not just a fact.

annotations.span: Two alarms, clothes out the night before, the lot.
annotations.label: A list run at level pitch
annotations.why: Group short items into one rhythmic run and drop the pitch on the last.

annotations.span: She could not have been nicer about it
annotations.label: Emphasis without an intensifier
annotations.why: Negative plus comparative outperforms 'very nice' every single time.

annotations.span: it's how far upstream the mistake sat
annotations.label: One precise metaphor carries the point
annotations.why: 'Upstream' does the work six words of explanation would have done.

annotations.span: the morning was only where the problem finally surfaced
annotations.label: Abstracts the story into an idea
annotations.why: Ending on a generalisation lifts the whole turn out of anecdote.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
Okay, so, a disagreement at my work. It was last year in the spring, and I am disagree with my manager about a survey.

So our team is planning to send a survey to the customers, about the service, if they are happy or not. But my manager said we send it in the same week when the new prices are starting. And I think this is a very bad idea, because the people will only think about the money, they don't think about the service.

So in the meeting I said this. Maybe I said it too strong, because everybody became quiet and my manager didn't like it. After that I felt bad. So I wrote one page for her, with my reasons, and I put two questions again in a different way.

In the end we sent the survey two weeks later, and more people answered it. So I was right.

But also I was not right, because I said it in front of four persons. If I say it after the meeting, it is better for everybody. So the lesson is, the idea was good but the way was bad. This is my experience about disagreeing with someone.

what_caps_it.point: The whole turn is joined with 'so' and 'but'; nothing marks which part is the point.
The story slides into the present five times and the regret has no conditional.
'Bad idea', 'felt bad', 'the way was bad' — one adjective covering three different meanings.

annotations.span: So I wrote one page for her, with my reasons
annotations.label: One concrete action, precisely sized
annotations.why: Keep this — a specific thing you did beats three sentences about feelings.

annotations.span: I am disagree with my manager
annotations.label: 'Disagree' is already a verb
annotations.why: Say 'I disagreed with my manager'. Never put 'am' in front of it.

annotations.span: our team is planning to send a survey
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: 'Was planning'. Pick the tense before you start and never let go of it.

annotations.span: in front of four persons
annotations.label: 'Persons' is not the spoken plural
annotations.why: Say 'four people'. 'Persons' belongs on legal notices, not in conversation.

annotations.span: If I say it after the meeting, it is better for everybody.
annotations.label: Regret told in the present
annotations.why: Say 'If I'd said it afterwards, it would have been better for everybody.'

annotations.span: This is my experience about disagreeing with someone.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: End on what you now think, not on the wording of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a disagreement I had at work last spring, with my line manager, over something fairly small that turned out to matter.

We were putting together a customer survey — twelve questions about how people rated the service — and she wanted it to go out in the same week our new prices took effect. I thought that was a mistake. My argument was that whatever we asked, we'd get answers about the price rise, and the whole thing would tell us nothing about the service at all.

The problem was how I said it. I put my case in the meeting itself, in front of four other people, and I was fairly blunt about it. Nobody said very much afterwards, which is usually a bad sign. So that evening I wrote her a one-page note instead — the reasoning laid out properly, plus two of the questions rewritten so she could see what I actually meant. She came round to it within about a week, and we pushed the survey back a fortnight. The response rate was noticeably better than the last one.

As for how I feel about it now, it's mixed. I'd defend the position — I still think I was right about the timing, and I'd have regretted saying nothing. What I got wrong was the setting. Disagreeing with somebody in front of their team turns a question about a survey into a question about who's in charge, and that's a much harder thing for anyone to back down from.

what_lifts_it.point: A third conditional and a 'would have' regret replace the band-6 present-tense apology.
'Put my case', 'came round to it', 'blunt' — precise chunks in place of 'bad'.
It separates being right on substance from being wrong on delivery, and says so.

annotations.span: over something fairly small that turned out to matter
annotations.label: Sets the stakes in sentence one
annotations.why: Tell the listener why a small story is worth two minutes before you tell it.

annotations.span: My argument was that
annotations.label: Labels the position before defending it
annotations.why: Naming your claim first stops the reasons arriving in a heap.

annotations.span: I put my case in the meeting itself
annotations.label: 'Put my case' is a single chunk
annotations.why: Reuse it any time you argued something properly rather than just objecting.

annotations.span: which is usually a bad sign
annotations.label: Reads the silence instead of reporting it
annotations.why: Interpreting a reaction is worth more than describing it, and costs five words.

annotations.span: She came round to it within about a week
annotations.label: Phrasal verb for a slow change of mind
annotations.why: 'Came round to it' says gradually and reluctantly in four words.

annotations.span: I'd have regretted saying nothing
annotations.label: Counterfactual about the road not taken
annotations.why: Use 'would have' to defend a decision, not only to regret one.

annotations.span: Disagreeing with somebody in front of their team turns a question about a survey into a question about who's in charge
annotations.label: Turns the mistake into a rule
annotations.why: One general sentence about your own error lifts the whole ending.

annotations.span: and that's a much harder thing for anyone to back down from
annotations.label: Comparative plus a stranded preposition
annotations.why: Ending a clause on the preposition is how spoken English actually does this.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is a disagreement I had with my line manager a couple of springs ago, over a customer survey — which sounds trivial, and in a sense was, except that it wasn't.

The plan was to send out twelve questions about how people rated our service, in the same week the new prices landed. My objection was simple enough: ask anybody anything that week and you'd get an answer about money. We'd have spent a fortnight collecting data on a subject we hadn't asked about.

Where I went wrong was the venue. I said all of it in the meeting, with four colleagues in the room, and rather more bluntly than the point required. What followed was that particular silence people fall into when somebody has been contradicted in public. So I went away and wrote it out instead — a page, the reasoning set out step by step, two questions redrafted so she could see the difference. She never conceded the argument in so many words, but the survey went out a fortnight later and the response rate was the best we'd had.

Looking back, I'd separate the two halves of it. On the substance I'd do the same again; saying nothing would have cost us the data. On the delivery I was tactless, and not in a trivial way. Contradict someone in front of their own team and you quietly change the subject: it stops being about a survey and starts being about authority. Had I said precisely those sentences to her in the corridor afterwards, I doubt any of the rest would have happened.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces 'if', and 'what followed was' fronts the result as a cleft.
'In so many words', 'not in a trivial way' — understatement instead of an intensifier.
Substance and delivery are judged separately, in that order, and both are named.

annotations.span: which sounds trivial, and in a sense was, except that it wasn't
annotations.label: Undercuts its own framing at once
annotations.why: Anticipating the listener's objection buys you their attention for the rest.

annotations.span: that particular silence people fall into when somebody has been contradicted in public
annotations.label: Describes a reaction with no adjective
annotations.why: A precise description outscores 'the atmosphere was very awkward' every time.

annotations.span: She never conceded the argument in so many words
annotations.label: Idiom placed exactly where it belongs
annotations.why: 'In so many words' marks something admitted without ever being said.

annotations.span: it stops being about a survey and starts being about authority
annotations.label: Names what the argument became
annotations.why: Say what a conflict turned into; that is the abstraction band 8 rewards.

annotations.span: Had I said precisely those sentences to her in the corridor afterwards
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as a third conditional, one register higher, still spoken.

I want to describe an occasion when I dressed up. It was three years ago, the wedding of my friend from school.

Normally I am wearing very simple clothes, jeans and a shirt, because my work is not formal. But for this wedding I must wear a suit, because also I have to read something in the ceremony, in front of maybe eighty people.

The problem is I don't have a suit. So I borrow one from my sister's husband. He is more big than me, so the jacket is very large in the shoulders. Then my mother said go to the tailor near the station. And this lady, she took it in, it took half an hour and it was very cheap.

On the day I felt very strange, like a costume. I was thinking everybody is looking at me. But after I read the poem, I forgot about the clothes completely, and after that I enjoyed the day.

So this is my experience. I think the clothes are not so important for the party, but they are important for before, when you are nervous. So this is my occasion of dressing up.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll describe a wedding I went to about three years ago — an old school friend of mine — where I ended up far more dressed up than I have ever been before or since.

The reason it mattered was that I'd been asked to read something during the ceremony, so I'd be standing at the front for two or three minutes with roughly eighty people watching. I wear jeans and a shirt to work, and at that point I didn't own a suit at all — I had genuinely never needed one. What I did in the end was borrow one from my sister's husband, who is a good deal broader across the shoulders than I am, so it hung on me like a tent.

My mother sent me to a tailor a couple of streets from the station, a place I'd walked past for years without ever noticing it. She took the jacket in at the shoulders in about half an hour and charged me almost nothing, and the difference was startling — from something borrowed to something that fitted.

As for how I felt about it, it wasn't what I expected. For the first hour I was horribly self-conscious, convinced everybody could tell it wasn't mine. Then I did the reading, sat down, and never thought about the suit again for the rest of the day. Which has stayed with me: the clothes did almost nothing during the wedding itself, but they did an enormous amount in the hour beforehand, when I was nervous and needed something to feel confident about.

'Hung on me like a tent', 'took the jacket in', 'self-conscious' — chosen words, not 'very'.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is a wedding about three years ago — a friend I'd known since we were eleven — and the one occasion in my adult life when I have genuinely dressed up.

What made it a problem was the reading. I'd been asked to stand at the front for a couple of minutes with eighty-odd people in front of me, and I owned precisely one jacket, bought for an interview and never worn since. Hiring one felt absurd for a two-minute reading. So the suit came from my sister's husband, who is broader through the shoulders by some margin, with the result that it sat on me like something hired for a school play.

My mother, who has no patience with any of this, marched me to a tailor near the station. Half an hour, a handful of pins and almost no money later, it fitted. I hadn't understood until then how much of a suit is simply the shoulders; everything below them is more or less decoration.

What surprises me, looking back, is where the clothes actually did their work. During the ceremony I forgot them entirely; I was thinking about not stumbling over the second verse. It was the hour beforehand that they earned their keep, when I was pacing a corridor with nothing else to feel confident about. Not one person mentioned the suit all day, and I suspect that was rather the point. Dressing up isn't performed for anybody else, whatever we tell ourselves.

'Earned their keep', 'by some margin', 'no patience with any of this' — idiom not on display.

annotations.label: Idiom placed where a native would

annotations.span: Dressing up isn't performed for anybody else, whatever we tell ourselves.

I want to talk about a time when the technology is not working. It was two winters ago, and I am working in a shop at the weekend.

It was Saturday before a holiday, so the shop is very full, maybe thirty people. And at eleven o'clock the card machine stopped. We tried many times but nothing is going. We called the company and they said wait, it will come back, but it didn't come back.

The problem is that almost nobody has cash now. And we also don't have much change in the till. So the people are standing with the full baskets and they cannot pay, and some of them left everything and go away.

Then my manager said okay, we take a paper. So we write the name and the phone number of every person, and they take the things and pay on Monday. It was very slow but it worked.

Almost everybody came back and paid. Only two people never came. So I felt surprised, because I think people are honest more than we expect. And this is my story about a technology problem.

model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a Saturday two winters ago, when I was working weekends in a garden and hardware shop, and the card terminal died on us.

It was the Saturday before a public holiday, which is easily the busiest day of the year in a shop like that — thirty-odd people inside, most of them with full baskets. At about eleven the terminal lost its connection. Nothing would go through: not tap, not chip, nothing. We rang the provider, who told us it would come back by itself, and it never did.

The awkward part was that almost nobody carries cash any more, and we had perhaps forty pounds of change in the till. So within ten minutes the whole shop had ground to a halt. People were standing there holding things they couldn't buy, and a few of them simply put everything down and walked out.

What we ended up doing was going back forty years. My manager fetched a notebook, and we wrote out each order by hand — name, phone number, what they were taking — and let people carry the goods away and settle up on the Monday. It was slow and slightly ridiculous, and it worked.

Nine out of ten came back and paid. Two never did, which I'd say is a remarkably good return. What struck me afterwards wasn't really the failure itself. It was how much of a normal trading day turned out to be resting on one small plastic box that none of us had ever thought about.

model_answers.transcript:
This is a Saturday a couple of winters ago. I was doing weekends in a garden and hardware shop, and the card terminal chose the busiest morning of the year to give up.

It was the Saturday before a bank holiday — a shop like that takes a fifth of its December money in a single day — and at around eleven the machine simply lost the line. No tap, no chip, no explanation. The provider's advice, delivered with great calm, was to wait. We waited. It was still dead at six.

The trouble is that hardly anybody carries notes now, and there was perhaps forty pounds of change in the till. Inside ten minutes the place had stalled completely: thirty people holding things they were no longer able to buy, a handful of whom put their baskets down and left without a word.

So we reverted to 1975. My manager produced a notebook, and for the rest of the day we took down every order by hand, with a name and a number, and let people walk off with their goods on the understanding that they would pay on Monday. Absurd, laborious, and entirely effective.

Nine in ten came back. What has stayed with me isn't the outage. It's that a whole trading day, and a fair amount of trust between strangers, turned out to be balanced on one unremarkable plastic box nobody had ever given a moment's thought to.

what_lifts_it.point: A reduced participle clause and a verbless sentence do work band 7 needed full clauses for.
'Give up', 'reverted', 'without a word' — the register lifts with no rare vocabulary.
It names what was actually at risk — trust between strangers — not just the machine.

I will describe a time when I must be patient. It was two years ago, in the winter, with my aunt.

My aunt is seventy-eight and her grandson moved to another country. So she wanted to see him on the video call. She has a phone but she doesn't use it for this, only for calling.

So every Tuesday and Sunday I go to her house and I show her. But it was very difficult. Every time she is forgetting the same button, the green one. And sometimes she is pressing the wrong thing and the call is finishing. We did this maybe six weeks.

Then I changed. I don't touch the phone, I only say the steps with my voice. And after two weeks she can do it alone.

model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the winter before last, when I spent about six weeks teaching my aunt to make video calls. She's seventy-eight, and her grandson had moved abroad that autumn, so this was the only way she was going to see him.

The situation was that she'd had a smartphone for years but only ever used it for ordinary calls. So twice a week, Tuesdays and Sunday evenings, I'd go round and we'd go over the same three steps. None of it was complicated, and that was rather the difficulty — I couldn't see what there was to find hard. And every single time she'd lose the same green button. Nine times out of ten she'd hang up by accident halfway through, and we'd start again.

I'd like to say I handled it well, and for the first fortnight I did. After that my patience wore thin. There was one evening when I simply took the phone out of her hand and did it for her, which was easily the worst thing I could have done — it told her she'd been right to think she couldn't manage.

What actually worked was the opposite. I stopped touching the phone altogether and just said the steps out loud while she pressed them, however long it took. She had it within a fortnight.

As for what I learned, it's slightly uncomfortable. My impatience was never really with her. It was with my own idea of how long this ought to take, which I'd invented and she'd never agreed to. Going slower turned out to be the quicker route.

what_lifts_it.point: A modal perfect and two past perfects layer the events instead of listing them.
'Wore thin', 'nine times out of ten', 'however long it took' — chunks doing the evaluating.
It admits the failure before the fix, so the ending is earned rather than announced.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is the winter before last. My aunt is seventy-eight; her grandson had moved abroad in the September, and video calls were going to be the only way she saw him. I said I'd teach her. Six weeks, twice a week, Tuesdays and Sunday evenings.

She'd owned a smartphone for years and used perhaps two per cent of it. So we worked through the same three steps, over and over, and every time the same green button would vanish from her field of vision entirely. More often than not she'd hang up mid-sentence and we would begin again.

For a fortnight I was exemplary. Then, one Sunday, I took the phone out of her hand and did it myself — which, of all the available options, was the one that did most damage. It confirmed for her precisely what she already suspected about her own competence.

The thing that eventually worked was doing less. I put my hands in my lap and narrated the steps while she pressed them, at whatever speed she pressed them, and inside two weeks she was ringing him unaided.

What I took from it isn't especially flattering. My impatience had nothing to do with her; it was with a timetable I'd made up and never mentioned to anyone. It hadn't occurred to me that the fastest route through something is often the one that looks slowest from outside. I still don't find that easy to remember.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted qualifier and 'it hadn't occurred to me that' put the judgement inside the grammar.
'Exemplary', 'two per cent of it', 'unaided' — precision, with the irony left unstated.
It ends by admitting the lesson still hasn't stuck, which reads truer than a resolution.

annotations.why: State the general principle once and let it stand without explaining it.

title: An occasion when you unexpectedly met somebody you knew

payload_json.topic: An occasion when you unexpectedly met somebody you knew

cue_card.topic: Describe an occasion when you unexpectedly met somebody you knew.
