when you had last seen them
what the two of you talked about
and explain how the meeting left you feeling.
rounding_off: Have you seen them since?
Was it a good place for a conversation?

teaching.band_move: Say how long the gap was in your first sentence. The gap is the story.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Take the first chance meeting you can picture, however ordinary it was. The card is really about the gap in time, not about the person.
prep_plan.trap: Almost everybody spends ninety seconds on the meeting itself and never says what the gap in time felt like.

time_plan.goal: Name who it was and how long the gap was.
Where you met and when you'd last seen them.
What the two of you actually talked about.
How it left you feeling, and why that surprised you.
One line about people you've lost touch with.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in on the twenty silent minutes: what you were doing, where you were looking.
Add time depth: say what you'd always assumed had happened to him.
Bring the son in: say what you were told about him and what you thought.
Speculate: say whether you'd have recognised him if he hadn't laughed.

error_watchlist.wrong: So I am sitting there and then he laughs and I know him.
error_watchlist.right: So I was sitting there, and then he laughed and I knew him.
error_watchlist.why: Anchor with a time phrase, then let every verb follow it.

error_watchlist.wrong: I don't see him since nineteen years.
error_watchlist.right: I hadn't seen him for nineteen years.
error_watchlist.why: 'For' plus a length; a gap before a past event takes 'had'.

error_watchlist.wrong: His son is the same like us before.
error_watchlist.right: His son is the same age as we were.
error_watchlist.why: It is 'the same as', never 'the same like'.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: The words this story needs are long and easily mis-stressed, and a mis-stressed long word stops the listener.

target_words.note: Five syllables, main stress on the third.
Stress the second syllable, never the first.
Stress the second and keep it short.
Stress the first; the middle is very weak.
Middle syllable only; both ends stay weak.

was that I'd been carrying an eleven-year-old around in my head
for nineteen years,
and that the actual person had been getting on with his life
the entire time.

teaching.examiner_note: The examiner writes nothing down while you speak and gives you no encouragement. That is the same for every candidate and tells you nothing about how it is going.

swap_slots.span: last October
swap_slots.prompt: Your own month or season, and nothing more precise than that.

swap_slots.span: It was Marek. He'd sat next to me in class from when we were eleven until we were about fourteen
swap_slots.prompt: Your own person: how you knew them, and for exactly how long.

swap_slots.prompt: The moment of recognition. Name the small thing that gave them away.

swap_slots.span: his son, who is eleven now
swap_slots.prompt: One fact about their life now — ideally one that measures the gap for you.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now run the same shape — the gap, the trigger, the feeling — about somebody you have deliberately not stayed in touch with. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
This is a story about meeting somebody I didn't expect. It was last year in October, on the train.

The train was late, so I am sitting there maybe one hour and a half. In front of me there is a man, about my age. We don't speak, we are just sitting. And after twenty minutes he laughed because the conductor said something funny, and immediately I know this laugh.

It was Marek. He was sitting next to me in the school when we are eleven, twelve, thirteen years old. After that his family moved and I never saw him again. So it is nineteen years.

We talked all the journey. About the school, about who is still living in the town. He has a son now who is eleven, the same like us before.

I felt strange. Not bad, but strange. Because in my head he is a boy, and now he is a man with a son. It was difficult to put the two together. So this was my unexpected meeting.

what_caps_it.point: Past and present alternate inside single sentences, so the listener has to guess the timeline.
'Strange', 'difficult', 'funny' — the vocabulary never reaches the actual feeling.
There is a genuinely good idea in the last four lines and no signposting towards it.

annotations.span: I felt strange. Not bad, but strange.
annotations.label: Corrects itself to be more precise
annotations.why: Keep this — refining a word out loud is a fluency move, not a mistake.

annotations.span: so I am sitting there maybe one hour and a half
annotations.label: Present continuous in a past story
annotations.why: Say 'I was sitting there for about an hour and a half'.

annotations.span: immediately I know this laugh
annotations.label: Present tense for a past realisation
annotations.why: 'I knew that laugh straight away' — realisations belong in past simple.

annotations.span: when we are eleven, twelve, thirteen years old
annotations.label: Two tenses inside one sentence
annotations.why: 'When we were eleven'. Both halves have to sit in the past.

annotations.span: the same like us before
annotations.label: 'The same like' is not English
annotations.why: Say 'the same age as we were'. It is always 'the same as'.

annotations.span: So this was my unexpected meeting.
annotations.label: Closes by naming the card
annotations.why: The line before it was the ending. Stop on that instead.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about last October, when I ran into somebody on a train that I hadn't seen for nineteen years.

The train was delayed, so what should have been forty minutes turned into an hour and a half, and for most of it I was sitting opposite a man of roughly my own age, reading nothing and looking out of the window. Neither of us said anything for the first twenty minutes. Then the conductor made some dry remark about the timetable, and this man laughed — and I recognised the laugh before I recognised anything else about him.

It was Marek. He'd sat next to me in class from when we were eleven until we were about fourteen, and then his family moved to the other side of the country and that was that. No falling out, nothing dramatic; we simply drifted apart, in the way people did before everybody was reachable.

We talked for the rest of the journey — mostly about who had stayed in the town and who hadn't, and about his son, who is eleven now, which is exactly the age we were when we met.

As for how it left me feeling, it was more disorienting than pleasant. He was perfectly good company, and I still couldn't make him line up with the boy I remembered. What I hadn't realised until that afternoon was that I'd been carrying an eleven-year-old around in my head for nineteen years, and that the actual person had been getting on with his life the entire time.

what_lifts_it.point: A modal perfect, a cleft and a past perfect continuous do the joining that 'so' was doing.
'Drifted apart', 'dry remark', 'disorienting' — one exact word instead of two approximate ones.
It ends on what the meeting revealed about the speaker, not on the meeting itself.

annotations.span: what should have been forty minutes turned into an hour and a half
annotations.label: Modal perfect for a plan that failed
annotations.why: 'What should have been X turned into Y' fits any delay you ever describe.

annotations.span: I recognised the laugh before I recognised anything else about him
annotations.label: Names the exact trigger
annotations.why: One precise detail of recognition is worth a paragraph of description.

annotations.span: No falling out, nothing dramatic
annotations.label: Rules things out instead of explaining
annotations.why: Saying what did not happen is quick and it sounds entirely natural.

annotations.span: we simply drifted apart
annotations.label: The precise verb for a slow ending
annotations.why: 'Drifted apart' says gradual and blameless in three words.

annotations.span: in the way people did before everybody was reachable
annotations.label: One clause dates the whole story
annotations.why: Locating a habit in a period shows range without any rare vocabulary.

annotations.span: which is exactly the age we were when we met
annotations.label: Relative clause closing a time loop
annotations.why: Tie the present detail back to the past one and the story feels finished.

annotations.span: it was more disorienting than pleasant
annotations.label: Chooses the honest word over the expected one
annotations.why: Rejecting the obvious feeling is the fastest way to sound unrehearsed.

annotations.span: What I hadn't realised until that afternoon was that I'd been carrying an eleven-year-old around in my head
annotations.label: Cleft with a past perfect continuous
annotations.why: Use this shape whenever the point is something you only saw afterwards.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
Last October, on a train that was going nowhere in particular for an hour and a half, I found myself sitting opposite somebody I had last seen in 2006.

Neither of us spoke for the first twenty minutes. Then the conductor said something faintly sardonic about the timetable, the man opposite laughed, and the laugh arrived in my head roughly a decade before his name did.

Marek. He'd sat beside me in class from eleven to fourteen, at which point his family moved four hundred miles away and the whole thing simply stopped. There was no falling-out to report. We drifted, as people did in the years before everybody was permanently contactable, and nineteen years went past without either of us doing anything about it.

We talked the rest of the way: who had stayed, who hadn't, what had become of two or three teachers, and whether the school still put eleven-year-olds in alphabetical order. His son is eleven, which is precisely the age we were when we were first put next to each other.

What surprised me was how unsettling I found it, rather than how pleasant. He was good company, and I would happily have spent another hour on that train. The difficulty was that I couldn't get the two versions of him to sit together in one head. Not until that afternoon had it occurred to me that I'd been keeping a boy of eleven in storage for nineteen years, while the real one went quietly on being forty.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion after 'not until' replaces band 7's cleft, and the rest stays spoken.
'Faintly sardonic', 'in storage', 'permanently contactable' — precision rather than volume.
The last line leaves the point implied instead of stating it, which is harder and better.

annotations.span: the laugh arrived in my head roughly a decade before his name did
annotations.label: One image carries the whole recognition
annotations.why: Let a metaphor do the explaining and you save fifteen seconds.

annotations.span: faintly sardonic
annotations.label: A precise adjective, used exactly once
annotations.why: One well-placed low-frequency word beats five scattered ones.

annotations.span: There was no falling-out to report.
annotations.label: Dismisses the obvious question
annotations.why: Answering the question the listener was about to ask sounds effortless.

annotations.span: Not until that afternoon had it occurred to me
annotations.label: Negative inversion after 'not until'
annotations.why: Front the time, invert the verb; it is the highest-value structure here.

annotations.span: while the real one went quietly on being forty
annotations.label: Closes on a contrast, not a lesson
annotations.why: Leave the conclusion unsaid and the listener draws it for you.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
My topic is a time when I changed my mind. It is about the road in front of my street.

Three years ago the council said they will close this road for the cars, only for walking and bicycles. And I was completely against it. Because I use my car every day for the work, and now I must park two streets away and walk. So I signed a paper against it, and I go to two meetings and I speak there.

But they made it anyway, for six months, like a test.

And in these six months something is changing. I take my daughter to the school every morning by walking. Before, at the corner, I am holding her hand very strong because the cars are coming fast. After some months I realise I don't hold her hand anymore. She walks alone and it is safe.

So I changed my mind. But honestly I feel a little bit strange, because nobody convinced me with arguments. So maybe my first opinion was also not from arguments. This is my experience of changing my mind.

what_caps_it.point: Reported speech, past obligation and past narration all default into the present tense.
The best idea in the answer arrives in the last ten seconds with no preparation at all.
'Against', 'strange', 'safe' — the evaluation runs on whichever adjective arrives first.

annotations.span: But honestly I feel a little bit strange, because nobody convinced me with arguments.
annotations.label: Says something genuinely uncomfortable
annotations.why: Keep this — an honest reservation is worth far more than a tidy conclusion.

annotations.span: the council said they will close this road
annotations.label: Reported speech not backshifted
annotations.why: 'They said they'd close it'. After a past verb, 'will' becomes 'would'.

annotations.span: now I must park two streets away
annotations.label: 'Must' inside a past narrative
annotations.why: Say 'I'd have to park'. 'Must' cannot carry a past obligation.

annotations.span: I go to two meetings and I speak there
annotations.label: Present tense in a past story
annotations.why: 'I went to two meetings and spoke at both.' One tense, held.

annotations.span: I am holding her hand very strong
annotations.label: Adjective where an adverb belongs
annotations.why: 'Very tightly'. Manner always needs an adverb, not the bare adjective.

annotations.span: This is my experience of changing my mind.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the card
annotations.why: The sentence before it was the real ending. Stop on that one.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about something I was wrong about, which is the road at the end of my street.

About three years ago the council proposed closing it to cars — buses, bikes and people on foot only. I was dead set against it. My reasoning was practical: I drive to work, and the plan meant parking two streets away and walking the rest with whatever I happened to be carrying. I signed the petition, and I spoke against it at two public meetings, which for me is quite unusual.

They went ahead anyway, as a six-month trial, on the basis that if it was a disaster they could simply take the bollards out again.

What changed my mind wasn't anything anybody said. I walk my daughter to school every morning, and there's a junction halfway along that I'd always hated — cars came round it far too fast, and I'd hold her hand there without even thinking about it. Some time in the fourth month I noticed that I'd stopped. She was walking that stretch on her own, and I hadn't registered when it started, or noticed that the traffic on it had more or less disappeared.

As for how I feel about having changed my mind, it's less comfortable than you'd expect. Nobody argued me out of my position; the circumstances simply moved and my opinion quietly followed them. Which raises an awkward question about where the original opinion came from, because I'd defended it in public, with reasons, and it turns out the reasons weren't what was holding it up.

what_lifts_it.point: A negative cleft, a 'would' habit and two past perfects replace the band-6 present drift.
'Dead set against', 'went ahead', 'holding it up' — chunks doing the argument's work.
It refuses the tidy ending and names what the change actually exposed.

annotations.span: something I was wrong about
annotations.label: Announces the outcome immediately
annotations.why: Give away the ending in the first line and everything after it reads as explanation.

annotations.span: I was dead set against it
annotations.label: Idiom measuring how strong the view was
annotations.why: 'Dead set against' rates the opinion; 'I didn't like it' doesn't.

annotations.span: My reasoning was practical
annotations.label: Labels the argument before giving it
annotations.why: Naming what kind of reason is coming stops the reasons arriving in a heap.

annotations.span: which for me is quite unusual
annotations.label: A small aside that characterises you
annotations.why: One clause of self-description makes a story about a road into a story about a person.

annotations.span: What changed my mind wasn't anything anybody said.
annotations.label: Cleft built round a negative
annotations.why: Say what didn't cause it first; the real cause then lands harder.

annotations.span: I'd hold her hand there without even thinking about it
annotations.label: 'Would' for a repeated past habit
annotations.why: Use 'I'd' rather than 'I used to' when the habit sits inside a scene.

annotations.span: I hadn't registered when it started
annotations.label: Past perfect for what you missed
annotations.why: The backshift is what makes a slow realisation sound slow.

annotations.span: the reasons weren't what was holding it up
annotations.label: A metaphor delivering the final judgement
annotations.why: One structural image beats three sentences of self-analysis.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about the road at the end of my street, and about being wrong in public.

Three years ago the council proposed closing it to through traffic — buses, bicycles and pedestrians only. I objected, loudly. My case was entirely practical: I drive to work, and the scheme meant parking two streets away and carrying everything the rest of the way. I signed the petition and spoke against the plan twice at meetings, which is not something I make a habit of.

They ran it as a six-month trial regardless, which in retrospect was the clever part: nobody had to concede anything, and the bollards could always come out again.

Nothing anybody said shifted me. What shifted me was a junction. I walk my daughter to school, and there is a corner halfway along that I had always disliked, because cars used to take it far too quickly; I would reach for her hand there automatically, every day, without deciding to. Somewhere in the fourth month it dawned on me that I had stopped doing it, and that I could not say when.

What I feel about it now is less comfortable than you might expect. I was not persuaded of anything by anybody. My circumstances changed and my opinion followed on behind, several weeks late. Which rather suggests the original position was never resting on the reasons I gave for it — and I gave them in public, at some length, to a room full of neighbours.

what_lifts_it.point: A negative subject followed by a cleft sharpens the contrast band 7 made with one cleft.
'Dawned on me', 'followed on behind', 'at some length' — register lifted with no rare words.
The close returns to the public meetings, so the ending answers the opening.

annotations.span: which is not something I make a habit of
annotations.label: Understated self-description
annotations.why: Say less than you mean and the listener supplies the rest.

annotations.span: which in retrospect was the clever part
annotations.label: Credits the other side's tactics
annotations.why: Praising your opponents mid-story is a quick way to sound fair-minded.

annotations.span: Nothing anybody said shifted me. What shifted me was a junction.
annotations.label: Negative subject, then a cleft
annotations.why: Two short sentences in this shape do the work of a paragraph.

annotations.span: it dawned on me that I had stopped doing it
annotations.label: The exact verb for a slow realisation
annotations.why: 'Dawned on me' carries the slowness that 'I realised' throws away.

annotations.span: my opinion followed on behind, several weeks late
annotations.label: Gives an abstraction a timetable
annotations.why: Putting a number on something abstract makes it concrete for free.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a difficult choice. It was about two flats, three years ago.

The first flat is in the centre, very small, only one room, but everything is near — the work, the shops, my friends. The second flat is forty minutes outside, it is bigger, two rooms and a small garden, and also cheaper.

So both are good, this is the problem. If one is bad it is easy. I had two weeks for decide.

Every night I am making a list, advantages and disadvantages. But the lists are the same, more or less equal. I asked my sister and she said take the big one, my friend said take the small one. So this doesn't help me at all.

In the end I take the small one in the centre. Because I imagine a normal Wednesday, and in the big flat I am spending two hours in the bus.

Do I choose well? I think yes, for that time. But after two years I want the garden. So maybe not. Anyway, this is my difficult choice.

'Good', 'bad', 'big', 'small' — four adjectives carrying a two-minute comparison.

annotations.label: Wrong form after the preposition

annotations.label: Continuous for a repeated past action

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a choice I had to make about three years ago, between two flats, both of which I actually wanted.

The first was right in the middle of town — one room, not much bigger than this, but five minutes from work and from everybody I knew, and I could have carried everything I owned there in two trips. The second was forty minutes out: two bedrooms, a small garden, and about fifty pounds a month cheaper. So there wasn't a bad option, which is precisely what made it hard. If one of them had been obviously worse, I'd have decided in an afternoon.

I had a fortnight, and I spent most of it weighing them up in a fairly useless way — lists of advantages and disadvantages that came out more or less level every single time. I asked people, and everybody I asked told me the opposite of the last person, with total conviction, which I've since decided is what advice usually does.

What tipped the balance in the end wasn't on either list. I stopped comparing the flats and imagined an ordinary Wednesday in each of them, and in the second one I spent two hours of that Wednesday on a bus.

As for whether I chose well — I did, for the person I was then. Two years later I badly wanted that garden, and I still don't think that means I got it wrong. You can only choose for the person doing the choosing.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Both of which', a third conditional and a reduced relative replace the band-6 present tense.
'Weighing them up', 'tipped the balance', 'more or less level' — chunks, not adjectives.
It answers the last bullet twice, yes then no, and explains why both answers stand.

annotations.span: So there wasn't a bad option, which is precisely what made it hard.
annotations.label: Names the difficulty out loud
annotations.why: Say why the choice was hard or the listener assumes it wasn't.

annotations.span: If one of them had been obviously worse, I'd have decided in an afternoon.
annotations.label: Third conditional making a point
annotations.why: The counterfactual argues here; it isn't there to express regret.

annotations.span: weighing them up in a fairly useless way

annotations.why: Attach an evaluation to the action and you get two marks for one phrase.

annotations.span: which I've since decided is what advice usually does
annotations.label: Turns one detail into an observation
annotations.why: A short general remark mid-story keeps a narrative from becoming a list.

annotations.span: What tipped the balance in the end wasn't on either list.
annotations.label: Cleft plus idiom announces the turn
annotations.why: Signal that the real reason is coming and the listener leans in.

annotations.span: I spent two hours of that Wednesday on a bus
annotations.label: One concrete detail settles it
annotations.why: End the comparison with a fact, not with another adjective.

annotations.span: You can only choose for the person doing the choosing.
annotations.label: Reduced relative closes the answer
annotations.why: 'The person doing the choosing' is shorter and stronger than a full clause.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
About three years ago I had a fortnight to choose between two flats, and the difficulty was that I wanted both of them.

One was in the middle of town: a single room, no bigger than it needed to be, five minutes from work, the shops and everyone I knew, and cheap enough that I never once looked at the rent. The other was forty minutes out — two bedrooms, a garden the size of a tablecloth, and fifty pounds a month cheaper. Neither was the wrong answer, which is exactly what made it unbearable. Had one of them had a serious flaw, the whole thing would have taken an afternoon.

I spent most of the fortnight producing lists, which came out level every time, and consulting people, who contradicted each other with great confidence. Advice, I've concluded, mostly tells you about the person giving it.

In the end what decided it wasn't on any list. I stopped comparing the flats as objects and imagined an ordinary Wednesday inside each one — and in the second version of that Wednesday, two of my waking hours were spent on a bus.

Did I choose well? For the person making the choice, yes, without much doubt. Two years on I'd have given a great deal for that garden, and I still don't count that as a mistake. You cannot choose on behalf of somebody who doesn't exist yet, and that is exactly who you are deciding for.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces the third conditional, and 'I've concluded' sits parenthetically inside the clause.
'The size of a tablecloth', 'with great confidence', 'given a great deal' — precision, lightly worn.
The verdict is split cleanly in two, and neither half is withdrawn.

annotations.why: Drop the 'if', invert the auxiliary; the register lifts and stays spoken.

annotations.label: One clause of dry characterisation
annotations.why: Describe people by what they did, never by an adjective about them.

annotations.span: Advice, I've concluded, mostly tells you about the person giving it.
annotations.label: A general claim dropped in mid-story
annotations.why: One aphorism, placed early, buys the ending its authority.

annotations.span: You cannot choose on behalf of somebody who doesn't exist yet
annotations.label: Abstracts the choice into a principle
annotations.why: Close on the rule your story demonstrates, and then stop talking.

model_answers.transcript:
I'm going to talk about a tape measure that I have in my kitchen drawer. It is not expensive, maybe it costs two or three pounds when it was new, but I don't want to give it away.

It was my grandfather's. He was a carpenter, he worked with wood for forty years. When he died, my mother give me a box of his tools, and this one was inside. So I have it since that time. Inside the cover he wrote some numbers with a pencil, I think they are the sizes of a door.

I keep it in the drawer in the kitchen, with the scissors and all this things. It is not in a special place, because I use it. When I moved to my flat I use it for measuring the windows and the shelf and everything.

Why I don't want to give it away? Because it makes me remember him. When I hold it, I feel he is close, and it is a very good feeling. Also it still works good, so it is useful too. So this is the thing I will never throw away.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about something that's worth almost nothing — a metal tape measure that lives in a drawer in my kitchen. You could pick one up for a couple of pounds, but I wouldn't part with this one.

It belonged to my grandfather. He'd been a joiner for the best part of forty years, and when he died my mother handed me a box of his tools with this sitting at the bottom of it. So I've had it for about nine years now. The case is dented on one corner, the yellow has worn off the first few inches, and inside the lid he'd pencilled a set of measurements — a door frame, I think, though nobody has ever been able to tell me for certain.

It doesn't live anywhere special, and that's deliberate, because the moment you put something in a box on top of a wardrobe you've stopped using it and started storing it. So it stays in the kitchen drawer with the scissors and the string.

As for why I'd never part with it, there's the obvious reason, which is that it reminds me of him. But if I'm honest, what I value more is that it still does its job. I measured every window in my first flat with it. A photograph of him would sit on a shelf gathering dust, whereas this comes out two or three times a year and works perfectly. I suppose what I like is that it's a keepsake nobody has retired yet.

'Part with', 'gathering dust', 'worn off' — chunks doing the work single adjectives did before.
Three signposts and a 'whereas' contrast give the turn a shape you can hear coming.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd pick is worth practically nothing — a steel tape measure, the sort you could replace for two pounds — and it sits in a drawer in my kitchen.

It was my grandfather's. He spent the best part of four decades as a joiner, and when he died my mother passed on a box of his tools with this at the bottom. I've had it for nine years or so. The case is dented at one corner, the first few inches have worn back to bare metal, and inside the lid there's a column of figures in pencil — a door frame, at a guess, though that's family theory rather than fact.

Where it lives is the point, in a way. Not in a box, not on a shelf: in the kitchen drawer with the scissors and the string. Put a thing like that somewhere safe and you've quietly demoted it from a tool to a relic.

As for why I wouldn't part with it, the sentimental answer is the obvious one, and it's true as far as it goes. What I'd actually say is that it's the only thing of his I own that still has a job to do. Photographs of him gather dust on a shelf; this comes out whenever a shelf needs putting up, and it's every bit as accurate as the day he bought it. I've come round to thinking that the things we keep longest aren't the ones we protect. They're the ones we're still willing to use.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative used as a conditional replaces the standard 'if' clause band 7 used.
'Demoted', 'relic', 'as far as it goes' — precision rather than display.
The close abstracts into a general claim instead of summarising the object.

annotations.label: Concedes a point in five words
annotations.why: Use it whenever you want to accept something and then improve on it.

annotations.span: Where it lives is the point, in a way.
annotations.label: Fronts the idea before the detail
annotations.why: Announcing why a detail matters stops it sounding like a list item.

annotations.span: Not in a box, not on a shelf: in the kitchen drawer with the scissors and the string.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a chair that I bought for my desk. It is a office chair, second-hand, and it costs me about seventy pounds.

Before, I was sitting on a chair from the kitchen. I work at home three days in a week, so I am sitting there many hours. After some months my back was hurting every evening and I sleep bad also. So I decided I must buy a proper chair.

New chairs are very expensive, so I looked online, and I find one from a company that was closing their office. The man deliver it in his van. It is not beautiful, it is grey and there is a mark on one arm, but everything is working.

I have it since four months. I use it every day, maybe six or seven hours, so I think I use it more than anything else in the flat. And my back is much better now, I don't feel pain in the evening.

So it was good money. Seventy pounds is a lot for me, but I use it every day, so it is worth it. I think it was a very good decision and I am happy with it.

what_caps_it.point: Four verbs drop back into the present, and the duration is built without a perfect form.
'Good money', 'very good decision', 'happy' — the argument for the price is three flat words.
The final paragraph repeats the third paragraph instead of adding the reason.

annotations.span: Before, I was sitting on a chair from the kitchen.
annotations.label: Sets up a before and after
annotations.why: Keep this — the contrast is what makes the purchase make sense.

annotations.span: it costs me about seventy pounds
annotations.label: Present tense for a past purchase
annotations.why: 'It cost me seventy pounds'. Check every verb once the story starts.

annotations.span: three days in a week
annotations.label: Wrong preposition in a rate
annotations.why: 'Three days a week'. Rates always take 'a', never 'in a'.

annotations.span: The man deliver it in his van.
annotations.label: Unmarked past tense verb
annotations.why: 'Delivered'. An unmarked verb reads as a tense error even when it isn't.

annotations.span: I have it since four months.
annotations.label: Duration without the perfect
annotations.why: 'I've had it for four months' — 'for' with a length, and a perfect form.

annotations.span: So it was good money.
annotations.label: The judgement is one flat word
annotations.why: Say what it replaced or what it saved you instead of 'good'.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a second-hand office chair I bought about four months ago, which is easily the least glamorous thing I've ever been pleased with.

Up until then I'd been working at the kitchen table on a wooden dining chair. I'm at home three days a week, so that's twenty-odd hours of sitting, and by about November my lower back was aching every evening and I wasn't sleeping properly either. I'd been putting off doing anything about it, mainly because a decent new chair sets you back three or four hundred pounds and I couldn't justify that.

What I ended up doing was looking at second-hand listings instead, and I found a company that was clearing out an office and selling everything off. The chair had been used for about two years. It's grey, there's a scuff on one arm, and the height lever is stiff, but it adjusts properly and the back holds you up where it should. It cost me seventy pounds and a man brought it round in a van the same week.

As for whether it was worth it — I've had it four months and it's been used every single working day, which must be somewhere over three hundred hours. The back pain went within a fortnight, which I honestly wasn't expecting to happen that fast. What convinced me wasn't really the money side, though. It was realising I'd spent the best part of a year putting up with something I could have fixed in an afternoon.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect continuous and a passive past perfect give the story two layers of time.
'Sets you back', 'putting up with', 'clearing out' — chunks carrying the argument.
A cleft and two signposts mark each bullet, so the shape is audible without being announced.

annotations.span: the least glamorous thing I've ever been pleased with
annotations.label: Opens on a hook, not a label
annotations.why: One interesting clause at the start buys the examiner's attention for free.

annotations.span: I'd been working at the kitchen table on a wooden dining chair
annotations.label: Past perfect continuous for the build-up
annotations.why: Use it for the situation that existed before the event you're telling.

annotations.span: sets you back three or four hundred pounds
annotations.label: An idiom for cost, used naturally
annotations.why: Reuse it for any price you think is high — rent, courses, repairs.

annotations.span: What I ended up doing was
annotations.label: Cleft opening announces the action
annotations.why: It buys half a second of thinking time and sounds organised, not stalled.

annotations.span: The chair had been used for about two years.
annotations.label: Passive plus past perfect in one clause
annotations.why: Perfect for describing second-hand things without naming who used them.

annotations.span: there's a scuff on one arm, and the height lever is stiff
annotations.label: Named faults instead of 'not perfect'
annotations.why: Two precise defects sound more honest, and score higher, than one vague hedge.

annotations.span: As for whether it was worth it
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Naming the move out loud stops you skipping the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: which I honestly wasn't expecting to happen that fast
annotations.label: Non-defining relative clause
annotations.why: Hang a comment on a whole clause with 'which' rather than starting a new sentence.

annotations.span: putting up with something I could have fixed in an afternoon
annotations.label: Phrasal verb plus a past modal
annotations.why: This pairing is the natural way to express mild regret about a delay.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The purchase I'd pick is spectacularly unromantic: a second-hand office chair, bought roughly four months ago for seventy pounds.

Until then I'd been working at the kitchen table on a wooden dining chair, three days a week, which comes to something over twenty hours of sitting. By November my lower back ached most evenings and my sleep had gone with it. I'd been putting it off on the grounds that a decent new chair will set you back the better part of four hundred, and that felt indulgent.

What shifted things was looking at the sum from the other end — not what a chair costs, but what a chair costs per hour. Once I'd framed it that way, a company clearing out an office and selling the contents off looked less like a compromise and more like an obvious answer. The one I bought had done two years' service. Grey, a scuff on one arm, a lever that sticks. Structurally, though, faultless.

Four months on, it has been used every working day, which is somewhere north of three hundred hours, and the back pain disappeared inside a fortnight. Had I bought it the previous spring, I'd have spared myself an entire winter of bad evenings. That's really what I took from it, and it isn't about chairs at all. The things that quietly cost us the most are rarely the expensive ones; they're the small daily irritations we've decided are not worth the bother of fixing.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces the third conditional, and a fronted 'once' clause carries the pivot.
'Spectacularly unromantic', 'north of', 'indulgent' — precision rather than decoration.
The close leaves the object behind and states a general principle instead.

annotations.span: Had I bought it the previous spring
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Identical meaning to the third conditional, higher register, still natural aloud.

annotations.span: spectacularly unromantic
annotations.label: An adverb doing real work
annotations.why: One well-chosen intensifier says more than three ordinary adjectives.

annotations.span: not what a chair costs, but what a chair costs per hour
annotations.label: Reframes the question mid-answer
annotations.why: Changing the measure, out loud, is the clearest way to show reasoning.

annotations.span: Grey, a scuff on one arm, a lever that sticks.
annotations.label: Three short items as one run
annotations.why: Level pitch across the first two, then fall on the third.

annotations.span: somewhere north of three hundred hours
annotations.label: Idiomatic way to approximate a number
annotations.why: Better than 'about', and it signals you are estimating deliberately.

annotations.span: The things that quietly cost us the most are rarely the expensive ones
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Lift out of the anecdote in the last two sentences, every time.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will describe a present that I gave to my friend. She was going to live in another country for her work, so we want to give her something before she leave.

The present was a small book with a hard cover, for addresses. It is not expensive, maybe eight pounds. But inside, I asked all our friends to write something. Everybody write one line and their phone number, with their own hand.

How I choose it? First I think about a book, but she has many books already. Then I think about a voucher, but a voucher is boring. Then I remember she is not sad about the city, she is sad about the people. So I decided this one.

When she opened it she was crying, and after she was laughing. She said it is the best present she got. She take it with her in her hand luggage, not in the big bag.

I think it goes well because it is personal. If I give her a voucher, she forget it in one week. So for me, money is not important for a present, the important thing is that you think about the person.

what_caps_it.point: Verbs lose their past forms across the whole talk and the conditional never forms.
'Boring', 'best', 'personal', 'important' carry every judgement in the answer.
Three paragraphs open with 'Then I think', so the reasoning sounds like a list.

annotations.span: Then I remember she is not sad about the city, she is sad about the people.
annotations.label: The insight that justifies the choice
annotations.why: Keep this sentence — it is the strongest thing in the answer.

annotations.span: we want to give her something before she leave
annotations.label: Two verbs left in the present
annotations.why: 'We wanted to give her something before she left.' Fix tense at sentence one.

annotations.span: Everybody write one line
annotations.label: Past tense unmarked after 'everybody'
annotations.why: 'Everybody wrote'. Singular subjects still need the past form.

annotations.span: She take it with her in her hand luggage
annotations.label: Third verb in the present
annotations.why: 'She took it with her'. The whole story sits in one time.

annotations.span: If I give her a voucher, she forget it in one week.
annotations.label: Past alternative built in the present
annotations.why: 'If I'd given her a voucher, she'd have forgotten it in a week.'

annotations.span: but a voucher is boring
annotations.label: One flat adjective ends the reasoning
annotations.why: Say what a voucher admits about you instead of calling it boring.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The present I'll talk about was for a friend of mine called Anna, who was moving abroad for work about two years ago.

What I gave her was a small hardback address book — the sort of thing you'd pick up for eight or nine pounds. On its own that would have been a fairly thin present. What made it work was that I'd spent a fortnight quietly getting fourteen people to write in it: one line each, in their own handwriting, with a phone number underneath.

Choosing it took a great deal longer than buying it did. My first thought was a book, but she reads more than anyone I know and I'd only have been duplicating something. Then I considered a voucher, which is really an admission that you haven't thought about it at all. What settled it was realising that she wasn't upset about leaving the city at all — she was upset about leaving people. Once I'd worked that out, the present more or less chose itself.

As for why it went down so well, I'd say it answered the thing she was genuinely worried about rather than the occasion itself. She opened it, cried for about a minute, and then spent twenty minutes reading other people's handwriting out loud and laughing at it. She carried it in her hand luggage rather than putting it in a case. I suppose the lesson is that a good present isn't the one you would want yourself; it's the one that fits the week somebody is having.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect and a past modal carry the reasoning that band 6 flattened into present tense.
'Settled it', 'chose itself', 'an admission that' — chunks replacing 'boring' and 'best'.
Rejected options are sequenced and then closed off, so the choice sounds argued.

annotations.span: Choosing it took a great deal longer than buying it did.
annotations.label: Announces that reasoning is coming
annotations.why: One sentence like this tells the examiner the next thirty seconds have structure.

annotations.span: I'd only have been duplicating something
annotations.label: Past modal for a rejected option
annotations.why: 'Would only have been' is the natural form for a choice you didn't make.

annotations.span: which is really an admission that you haven't thought about it at all
annotations.label: Judges the option instead of labelling it
annotations.why: Say what an option reveals rather than calling it good or bad.

annotations.span: What settled it was realising that
annotations.label: Cleft marks the deciding moment
annotations.why: It separates the decision from the description so both get heard.

annotations.span: Once I'd worked that out
annotations.label: Past perfect after 'once'
annotations.why: Use it to show one thing had to happen before the next could.

annotations.span: the present more or less chose itself
annotations.label: An idiomatic way to end a decision
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever a choice became obvious once you saw something.

annotations.span: As for why it went down so well
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluative bullet
annotations.why: Say the bullet out loud and you will not forget to answer it.

annotations.span: cried for about a minute, and then spent twenty minutes reading other people's handwriting out loud
annotations.label: Reaction shown, not named
annotations.why: Two actions beat 'she was very happy' every single time.

annotations.span: it's the one that fits the week somebody is having
annotations.label: Closes one level above the story
annotations.why: A general claim at the end lifts the whole turn out of anecdote.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The present in question went to a friend of mine, Anna, who was leaving the country for a job a couple of years ago.

In itself it was unremarkable: a small hardback address book, eight or nine pounds at most. The part that took the effort was invisible. Over about a fortnight I got fourteen people to write a line in it, each in their own handwriting with a phone number underneath, and not one of them gave it away.

The choosing was the hard part, not the buying. A book was the obvious answer, and I ruled it out precisely because it was obvious — she reads more than anybody I know, and I'd have been competing with her own taste. A voucher I dismissed as what you give when you have run out of time. Only when I noticed that she wasn't grieving for the city did the answer become clear. She was grieving for a set of people, most of whom she would now see once a year at best.

It landed well because it addressed what she was anxious about rather than the occasion that caused it. She cried, briefly, and then spent the rest of the evening reading handwriting aloud and mocking it. She carried it onto the plane in her hand luggage. If there is a general point in any of this, it is that presents fail when they are aimed at a person in the abstract, and they work when they are aimed at the particular fortnight that person is living through.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion after 'only when', a fronted object and a 'most of whom' clause do the linking.
'Ruled it out', 'landed well', 'grieving for' — chosen for shade, not for size.
The close states a principle about presents rather than summarising this one.

annotations.span: Only when I noticed that she wasn't grieving for the city did the answer become clear
annotations.label: Inversion after 'only when'
annotations.why: Front the condition and invert the verb; it marks the turning point without extra words.

annotations.span: most of whom she would now see once a year at best
annotations.label: Quantifier plus 'whom' in one clause
annotations.why: 'Most of whom', 'several of which' — one of these per talk is plenty.

annotations.span: A voucher I dismissed as what you give when you have run out of time.
annotations.label: Object fronted for emphasis
annotations.why: Putting the object first signals that you are dealing with it and moving on.

annotations.span: The part that took the effort was invisible.
annotations.label: Separates cost from effort
annotations.why: A short sentence between two long ones controls the pace of the whole turn.

annotations.span: It landed well
annotations.label: Two words instead of a sentence
annotations.why: 'Landed' says received and worked at once; keep it for reactions.

annotations.span: presents fail when they are aimed at a person in the abstract
annotations.label: States the principle, then stops
annotations.why: End on the rule you have just demonstrated, and resist explaining it.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about my sewing machine. It is not a new one, it is from about 1980, it is heavy and it is green.

I use it for many things. Mostly I make shorter the trousers, because I am not tall, so every trousers I buy is too long. Also I fix the zips, and last year I make curtains for my bedroom.

I get it from my aunt. She stopped to sew because of her eyes, and she asked me if I want it. I said yes, but I don't know how to use it. So she showed me for two afternoons, and after that I practise alone.

If I don't have it, it will be a problem. In my city, a shop takes ten pounds for one trousers, and I buy maybe six trousers in a year, so it is sixty pounds. And also I must wait one week.

So this machine is very useful for me. It is old, but it is working very good, and I think it will work more years than me.

what_caps_it.point: The final bullet is a conditional and it never forms; three past verbs stay in the present.
'Many things', 'useful', 'good' — every judgement is a first-choice word.
Uses run as a list of 'also' clauses with nothing marking which matters most.

annotations.label: Costs the alternative in numbers
annotations.why: Keep this — pricing the alternative is exactly what the bullet wants.

annotations.span: I want to tell about my sewing machine.

annotations.why: 'I'll tell you about' or simply 'I'd like to talk about'.

annotations.span: I make shorter the trousers

annotations.why: 'I take the trousers up' — the phrasal verb is the natural choice.

annotations.span: She stopped to sew because of her eyes
annotations.label: 'Stop' plus infinitive reverses the meaning
annotations.why: 'Stopped sewing' ends the activity; 'stopped to sew' means she paused to do it.

annotations.span: If I don't have it, it will be a problem.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd pick is a sewing machine — an old one, made some time in the early eighties, cast iron, painted green, and it weighs an absolute ton.

I use it for fairly unglamorous jobs. Mostly taking up trousers, because I'm short and everything I buy is three or four inches too long, but also replacing zips, patching things, and on one ambitious weekend, running up a pair of curtains for the bedroom.

It came from my aunt, so I paid nothing for it. She'd been sewing on it since she was in her twenties, making everything from school uniforms to a wedding dress, and she gave it up a few years ago because her eyesight had got too poor for the needle. She asked whether I wanted it and I said yes before it occurred to me that I had no idea how to use it. She spent two afternoons showing me the basics, and I've picked up the rest by getting it wrong.

As for what I'd do without it, I'd simply have to pay somebody, and that's where it stops being sentimental. A shop near me charges about ten pounds a pair, and I get through five or six pairs a year, so the machine has paid for itself several times over despite having been free. It's the waiting I'd mind more than the money, though. There's a week between handing something over and getting it back, and in that week you simply do without. Being able to deal with a thing the evening it breaks changes how you feel about owning it at all.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect continuous, a clean second conditional and a fronted cleft all appear once each.
'Running up', 'picked up', 'paid for itself' — chunks replacing 'many things' and 'useful'.
Uses are ranked with 'mostly' and 'also' rather than simply listed in a row.

annotations.span: it weighs an absolute ton
annotations.label: Everyday exaggeration used naturally
annotations.why: Native-sounding overstatement is cheap and it makes description memorable.

annotations.span: on one ambitious weekend, running up a pair of curtains
annotations.label: One vivid exception to the routine
annotations.why: Follow a routine list with one odd example and the answer stops sounding generic.

annotations.span: She'd been sewing on it since she was in her twenties
annotations.label: Past perfect continuous for the backstory
annotations.why: Use it for the long activity that was happening before your part begins.

annotations.span: I said yes before it occurred to me that I had no idea how to use it
annotations.label: A self-deprecating detail carries the story
annotations.why: Admitting a small failure buys credibility and gives you a clause for free.

annotations.span: I've picked up the rest by getting it wrong
annotations.label: Learning described in a phrasal verb
annotations.why: 'Picked up' says learned informally in two words. Reuse it for any skill.

annotations.span: As for what I'd do without it
annotations.label: Signposts the conditional bullet
annotations.why: Naming the bullet aloud is the single cheapest way to avoid missing it.

annotations.span: the machine has paid for itself several times over despite having been free
annotations.label: A value claim in one phrase
annotations.why: 'Paid for itself several times over' works for any object you use often.

annotations.span: It's the waiting I'd mind more than the money, though.
annotations.label: Cleft puts the real point first
annotations.why: 'It's X I'd mind, not Y' — use it to correct an expectation you just raised.

annotations.span: changes how you feel about owning it at all
annotations.label: Ends above the object
annotations.why: Move from your machine to owning things in the last sentence.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The piece of equipment I'd choose is a sewing machine — cast iron, painted a rather municipal green, made at some point in the early eighties, and heavy enough that it has never once been moved for cleaning.

What it does for me is mundane. Trousers taken up, because nothing off the peg is cut for somebody my height; zips replaced; the occasional patch; and once, over a weekend I'd rather not revisit, a pair of curtains.

It reached me by inheritance of a sort. My aunt had sewn on it since her twenties and finally admitted defeat when her eyes could no longer manage the needle. She offered it to me and I accepted on the spot, which was generous of me given that I couldn't thread it. Two afternoons of instruction later I was competent enough to be dangerous, and everything since has been learned by unpicking my own mistakes.

Were it to disappear tomorrow, the cost would at least be measurable — around ten pounds a pair at the shop on the corner, five or six pairs a year — so on money alone it has repaid itself many times over, and it arrived free. What I'd actually miss is harder to price. There's a particular calm in knowing that a broken thing can be dealt with on a Tuesday evening rather than joining a queue, and I don't think I appreciated that until I had it.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Were it to' replaces the ordinary conditional, and a participle clause carries the aside.
'Municipal green', 'off the peg', 'unpicking' — precise rather than decorative.
The close names a feeling the story earned rather than restating the object.

annotations.span: Were it to disappear tomorrow
annotations.label: Inverted conditional without 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as 'if it disappeared', and it marks a shift into the hypothetical.

annotations.span: painted a rather municipal green
annotations.label: One unexpected modifier does the describing
annotations.why: An adjective that carries an attitude beats three that only carry colour.

annotations.span: which was generous of me given that I couldn't thread it
annotations.label: Dry understatement instead of a joke
annotations.why: Understatement adds personality without costing you accuracy anywhere.

annotations.span: Trousers taken up, because nothing off the peg is cut for somebody my height; zips replaced; the occasional patch
annotations.label: A list delivered in three beats
annotations.why: Keep each item as one thought group, with a clear break between them.

annotations.span: everything since has been learned by unpicking my own mistakes
annotations.label: A precise verb from the topic itself
annotations.why: Borrowing a technical verb from your own subject reads as fluency, not display.

annotations.span: There's a particular calm in knowing that a broken thing can be dealt with on a Tuesday evening
annotations.label: Names the real benefit last
annotations.why: Save the least obvious reason for the end; it is what the listener remembers.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about an application for the buses. It shows you where is the bus now, in real time, and how many minutes you must wait at the stop.

I will recommend it to my father. He is seventy-one years, he is retired, and he goes two times in a week to my sister, for the grandchildren. He must take two buses.

I find it when I moved to this city, because I don't know the buses here. My friend showed me on his phone and after that I use it every day.

I think it is good for him because he always looks the paper timetable in his kitchen. But the paper timetable is not true, because sometimes the bus doesn't come. With the app he can see the real situation, so he don't go out in the rain for nothing.

annotations.why: 'Looks at'. The preposition is part of the verb, not an extra.

annotations.span: so he don't go out in the rain
annotations.label: Third person auxiliary wrong
annotations.why: 'He doesn't go out'. Check every 'he' and 'she' in the present tense.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd recommend is a bus app — nothing clever about it, it simply shows you where the buses on your route actually are and how many minutes the next one is away.

The person I'd give it to is my father. He's seventy-one, he's been retired for six years, and twice a week he goes across town to pick my sister's children up from school, which means two buses and a fifteen-minute gap in the middle.

I came across it when I first moved here and had no idea how the routes worked. A friend produced it on a platform one evening while the pair of us were standing there wondering whether anything was coming at all, and I've used it more or less every day since, including on routes I could walk.

The reason I think it would suit him is quite specific. He isn't nervous about technology in general — he does his banking online perfectly happily — but he still trusts the printed timetable pinned up in his kitchen, and that timetable tells you when a bus is supposed to come, which isn't the same thing at all. What he'd get from the app is the difference between the plan and what is actually happening. And crucially, it doesn't ask you to sign up for anything, which is what puts him off most apps within about four seconds. I wouldn't try to teach him the whole thing either. I'd sit down and talk him through one route he already knows, and I suspect that would be enough.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect duration, a passive 'supposed to' and two relative clauses replace flat statements.
'Came across', 'puts him off', 'talk him through' — three phrasal verbs used exactly.
The fourth bullet argues from his habits, and concedes what he is already good at.

annotations.span: nothing clever about it, it simply shows you
annotations.label: Defines by function, not by category
annotations.why: Say what a thing does in the first sentence and you never need to describe a screen.

annotations.span: he's been retired for six years
annotations.label: Present perfect for a continuing state
annotations.why: Use 'has been' plus 'for' whenever a situation started in the past and holds.

annotations.span: I came across it when I first moved here
annotations.label: Finding something by accident, in two words
annotations.why: 'Came across' is the natural verb for anything you didn't go looking for.

annotations.span: The reason I think it would suit him is quite specific.
annotations.label: Promises a reason before giving it
annotations.why: It tells the examiner the next thirty seconds are an argument, not more description.

annotations.span: he does his banking online perfectly happily
annotations.label: Concedes the obvious objection first
annotations.why: Refusing the lazy explanation makes the real one sound earned.

annotations.span: tells you when a bus is supposed to come, which isn't the same thing at all
annotations.label: 'Supposed to' plus a comment clause
annotations.why: 'Supposed to' marks an intention that reality may not match.

annotations.span: the difference between the plan and what is actually happening
annotations.label: One abstract phrase carries the point
annotations.why: Naming an abstraction precisely is worth more than three concrete examples.

annotations.span: which is what puts him off most apps within about four seconds
annotations.label: Objection named in a phrasal verb
annotations.why: 'Puts him off' works for food, jobs, places and people as well.

annotations.span: I'd sit down and talk him through one route he already knows
annotations.label: Ends on a concrete plan
annotations.why: Finishing with an action rather than a feeling gives the turn somewhere to stop.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The recommendation I'd make is deliberately unambitious: a bus app that does exactly one thing, which is to show you where the buses on your route currently are and how long the next one will take to reach you.

I'd give it to my father. He's seventy-one, six years into retirement, and twice a week he crosses town to collect my sister's children from school — two buses, with a quarter of an hour of standing about in between.

I stumbled on it myself when I moved here and couldn't make head or tail of the network. A friend produced it on a platform one evening while the pair of us stared hopefully down an empty road, and I've barely travelled without it since.

What makes it right for him is narrower than the usual line about older people needing help with technology, which isn't true of him anyway; he runs his bank account online without a murmur. His problem is that he still puts his faith in the timetable on the kitchen wall, and a timetable describes intentions, not events. The app closes precisely that gap, and closes nothing else, which is why I think it would stick. It also asks nothing of him — no account, no password, no email address — and it is that request, rather than the technology behind it, that loses him every time. I wouldn't attempt to teach him the whole thing. Show him one route he already knows and the rest tends to look after itself.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft isolates the real obstacle where band 7 used an ordinary relative clause.
'Make head or tail of', 'without a murmur', 'puts his faith in' — idiom placed where it belongs.
The answer refuses the stereotype out loud before offering its own explanation.

annotations.span: it is that request, rather than the technology behind it, that loses him every time
annotations.label: Cleft isolates the real cause
annotations.why: 'It is X, rather than Y, that…' is the cleanest way to correct an assumption.

annotations.span: a timetable describes intentions, not events
annotations.label: The whole argument in six words
annotations.why: When you can name the distinction abstractly, do it once and move on.

annotations.span: couldn't make head or tail of the network
annotations.label: Idiom used where a native would
annotations.why: Two natural idioms across a talk beat six decorative ones every time.

annotations.span: narrower than the usual line about older people needing help with technology
annotations.label: Rejects the easy generalisation
annotations.why: Naming the cliché and refusing it is a fast way to sound like you're thinking.

annotations.span: stared hopefully down an empty road
annotations.label: One image, delivered as one group
annotations.why: Keep a picture in a single breath group so it lands as a picture.

annotations.span: the rest tends to look after itself
annotations.label: Closes on a small general rule
annotations.why: A modest general claim ends a turn better than a summary does.

title: Technology, age and being left behind

payload_json.topic: Technology, age and being left behind

part3_themes.title: learning something new later in life
questions: Why do some people find new technology so much harder once they are older?
Whose job is it to help people who are struggling — families, companies or the state?
Will the next generation of older people run into the same difficulty?
part3_themes.counterpoint: if a service can only be reached through an app, the people who cannot use one have been excluded quite deliberately
part3_themes.counter_probe: But isn't it simpler for everybody if there's one system and everyone uses it?

abstraction_ladder.local_general: Do the older people you know feel confident dealing with services online?
abstraction_ladder.societal_abstract: What does a society owe the people its systems are not designed for?

question_notes.answer_shape: Give one cause in the design and one in the person, then rank them.
question_notes.watch_out: Don't answer 'because they are old'. The interesting cause sits in the design.

question_notes.answer_shape: Split the job across two of the three, then justify where the line falls.
question_notes.watch_out: Answering 'everybody' is a way of answering nobody. Choose and defend it.

question_notes.answer_shape: Predict, hedge it, then name the thing that will still catch people out.
question_notes.watch_out: The lazy answer is no. Say what changes and what stubbornly doesn't.

part3_themes.title: designing things for everybody
questions: What actually makes a piece of software easy to use?
Do younger and older people want different things from the same service?
Is it worth keeping paper and telephone options open for a shrinking number of people?
part3_themes.counterpoint: keeping counters, paper forms and phone lines open for a small minority is a cost that everybody else quietly carries
part3_themes.counter_probe: Should the majority pay more so that a small group can carry on using paper?
part3_themes.concession_frame: There is a real cost, I'll grant you, but ___

abstraction_ladder.concrete: Is there an app you gave up on because it was badly made?
abstraction_ladder.local_general: Do people you know complain about the same kinds of design problems?
abstraction_ladder.societal_abstract: Should ease of use be a legal requirement for anything that replaces a public service?

question_notes.answer_shape: Define it by what the user doesn't have to do, then give one test.
question_notes.watch_out: 'Simple' is not a definition. Say what the design removes from the user.

question_notes.answer_shape: Name one real difference, explain the cause, then concede the overlap.
question_notes.watch_out: Don't turn this into two stereotypes facing each other. Find the shared want.

question_notes.answer_shape: Weigh the cost against the harm, then say what tips it either way.
question_notes.probe: Where would you draw that line?
question_notes.watch_out: Use 'on balance' once, at the end, after you've actually balanced something.

teaching.band_move: Replace 'old people' with a quantified group in every answer. Stereotypes invite a counter-probe you can't win.

error_watchlist.wrong: The old people are afraid of the technology.
error_watchlist.right: Older people are often wary of new technology.
error_watchlist.why: General groups take no article, and so do abstract nouns.

error_watchlist.wrong: Young people learn more fast than older ones.
error_watchlist.right: Young people learn faster than older ones.

teaching.tense_focus: present simple for now, present perfect with 'for' and 'since' for the home
teaching.band_move: Answer with a number wherever a number is possible. Numbers are the cheapest detail in Part 1.

questions.answer_shape: Say which, name the work or course, then one detail about it.
questions.extend_move: Working — I'm in the office of a haulage firm, which is less exciting than it sounds.

common_error.wrong: I am still in the college.
common_error.right: I'm still at college.
common_error.why: Institutions take 'at' and drop the article.

questions.answer_shape: Rate the week, then say what fills it and what doesn't fit.
questions.extend_move: Fairly relentless from Monday to Thursday, then Friday is almost civilised.

common_error.wrong: My week is very busy of work.
common_error.right: My week is packed with work.
common_error.why: 'Busy with', not 'busy of'.

questions.answer_shape: Give the duration, then say where you were before.

common_error.right: People in my city move house fairly often.

common_error.wrong: I pass the most time in the kitchen.
common_error.right: I spend most of my time in the kitchen.

common_error.right: I don't like being in photos.
common_error.why: 'Like' plus -ing for general dislikes, and no article.

common_error.wrong: I write with the hand only the lists.
common_error.right: I only write lists by hand.
common_error.why: 'By hand' is fixed, and 'only' goes before the verb phrase.

questions.answer_shape: Give an honest quantity, then say when it goes up.

common_error.wrong: It is about one page in the week.
common_error.right: It's about a page a week.

title: A photograph you would hate to lose

payload_json.topic: A photograph you would hate to lose

cue_card.topic: Describe a photograph you own that you would hate to lose.
bullets: what the photograph shows
when and where it was taken
how it came to be yours
and explain why losing it would matter to you.
rounding_off: Is it on display, or put away somewhere?
Have you ever had a copy made?

teaching.band_move: Describe the image in the present tense and its history in the past. Keep the two apart.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Choose a photograph you can see in your head with your eyes shut. If you can't picture the corners, choose a different one.
prep_plan.trap: The picture gets described twice and the fourth bullet arrives with fifteen seconds left on the clock.

time_plan.goal: Say who is in it and roughly when.
The image itself, then the date and place.
How it reached you, as a short story.
What the picture holds that nothing else does.
One line about photographs in general.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe one corner of it — the shop window, the pavement, the writing on the back.
Add time depth: say what that street looks like now, if it still exists.
Bring in another person: say who took it, or who else has seen it.
Speculate: say what she must have been thinking about that week.

error_watchlist.wrong: Nobody see this photo before.
error_watchlist.right: None of us had ever seen it before.
error_watchlist.why: An experience before another past event takes past perfect.

error_watchlist.wrong: She is nineteen years in this photo.
error_watchlist.right: She's nineteen in this photo.
error_watchlist.why: The number stands alone, or add 'years old'.

error_watchlist.wrong: Everybody say I have her face.
error_watchlist.right: Everybody says I've got her face.
error_watchlist.why: 'Everybody' is singular and takes -s.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Describing an image needs long sentences, and stressing every small word destroys their rhythm.

target_words.note: Unstressed inside a sentence; save the full form for contrast.
Reduces to a single weak syllable between two nouns.
Almost disappears before a place word.
The vowel is weak unless you are correcting somebody.
In a list it is barely more than a hum.

chunking_drill.sentence: She's standing on a pavement outside a shop, wearing a coat that's clearly two sizes too big for her, and she's laughing at whoever is holding the camera.
chunks: She's standing on a pavement outside a shop,
wearing a coat that's clearly two sizes too big for her,
and she's laughing at whoever is holding the camera.

minimal_pairs.contrast: the weak form of 'can' is what makes the second sound natural

teaching.examiner_note: There is no follow-up during the long turn, so an image you leave unexplained simply stays unexplained until the rounding-off questions.

swap_slots.prompt: Your own subject: name the relationship, and say how far back the picture sits.

swap_slots.span: not much bigger than a bank card
swap_slots.prompt: The physical size of yours, given by comparison with something the examiner knows.
