model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a photograph of my grandmother. It is a black and white photo, and it is small, maybe like a card. It is very old, from 1961 I think.

In the photo she is standing in the street, in front of a shop. She is wearing a coat which is too big for her, and she is laughing. She is nineteen years in this photo, and she is working in this shop at that time.

I don't take this photo, of course. When she died, we cleaned her house, and my mother found a box of biscuits with many photos inside it. Nobody see this photo before. My mother gave it to me because everybody say I have her face.

Why I don't want to lose it? Because in this photo she is not my grandmother. She is a young girl, she doesn't know anything about her life yet, she doesn't know she will have four children. When I look at it I feel strange, but also good. So it is very important for me and I keep it inside a book.

what_caps_it.point: The history of the photograph slips out of the past three separate times.
'Very old', 'strange', 'good', 'important' — four flat adjectives carry the whole point.
A rhetorical question opens the last section and the close restates the card.

annotations.span: Because in this photo she is not my grandmother. She is a young girl
annotations.label: The idea that justifies keeping it
annotations.why: Keep this — it is the one sentence nobody else would have said.

annotations.span: She is nineteen years in this photo
annotations.label: Age given with a stray noun
annotations.why: 'She's nineteen in this photo' — the number needs nothing after it.

annotations.span: I don't take this photo, of course.
annotations.label: Past fact told in the present
annotations.why: 'I didn't take it, obviously.' Your own history goes into the past.

annotations.span: a box of biscuits with many photos inside it
annotations.label: The wrong compound noun
annotations.why: A biscuit tin. 'A box of biscuits' means the biscuits are still in it.

annotations.span: Nobody see this photo before.
annotations.label: No perfect form for an earlier event
annotations.why: 'None of us had ever seen it before.' Past perfect for what came first.

annotations.span: everybody say I have her face
annotations.label: 'Everybody' treated as plural
annotations.why: 'Everybody says'. It looks plural and behaves singular.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The photograph I'd talk about is of my grandmother, and it was taken about ten years before my mother was born.

It's a small black-and-white print, not much bigger than a bank card, and the corners have gone soft. She's standing on a pavement outside a shop, wearing a coat that's clearly two sizes too big for her, and she's laughing at whoever is holding the camera. On the back somebody has written a date in pencil — 1961 — and nothing else at all — no name, no place, no explanation.

I obviously had nothing to do with taking it. It only came to light when she died and we were clearing out her flat. My mother found a biscuit tin at the back of a wardrobe with about forty photographs in it, and not one of us had ever seen this particular one. She handed it to me rather than to either of my brothers, because there's a family theory that I take after her, and in that picture you can see why.

The reason I'd hate to lose it is that in it she isn't anybody's grandmother yet. She's nineteen, she's working in that shop, and she has no idea what's coming — the marriage, the four children, the illness at the end of it. Every other photograph I have of her was taken after all that had already happened. This is the only one where she is still a person with the whole thing in front of her, and I don't think there's another copy anywhere.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect, a 'whoever' clause and a clean present-tense description of the image.
'Came to light', 'take after her', 'gone soft' — chunks where band 6 had adjectives.
The image, its history and its meaning are three separate blocks with audible joins.

annotations.span: about ten years before my mother was born
annotations.label: Dates it by another event
annotations.why: Fixing time against a family event is more vivid than a bare year.

annotations.span: the corners have gone soft
annotations.label: What age has done, not 'old'
annotations.why: Describe the damage and the age comes free with it.

annotations.span: she's laughing at whoever is holding the camera
annotations.label: 'Whoever' clause instead of a guess
annotations.why: Use 'whoever', 'whatever' when you genuinely don't know the detail.

annotations.span: It only came to light when she died
annotations.label: An idiom for something surfacing
annotations.why: Works for documents, facts and objects; keep it for anything discovered late.

annotations.span: not one of us had ever seen this particular one
annotations.label: Past perfect for the earlier absence
annotations.why: Two past layers in one sentence is what band 7 is listening for.

annotations.span: there's a family theory that I take after her
annotations.label: Hedges a claim about resemblance
annotations.why: 'A family theory' lets you report something without asserting it.

annotations.span: The reason I'd hate to lose it is that
annotations.label: Signposts the final bullet
annotations.why: Say the bullet aloud and you cannot arrive at 1:55 without answering it.

annotations.span: she isn't anybody's grandmother yet
annotations.label: Reframes the whole description
annotations.why: One reframe near the end lifts a description into an argument.

annotations.span: the marriage, the four children, the illness at the end of it
annotations.label: Three items in one run
annotations.why: Hold the pitch steady across the first two items and fall on the third.

annotations.span: I don't think there's another copy anywhere
annotations.label: Ends on what is at stake
annotations.why: Closing on the risk, not a summary, gives the turn a natural stop.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The photograph I'd choose is of my grandmother, taken roughly a decade before my mother existed.

It's small — black and white, about the size of a bank card, and the corners have gone furry with handling. She is on a pavement outside a shop, in a coat plainly two sizes too big, laughing at whoever was behind the camera. On the reverse, in pencil, there is a date and nothing else: 1961.

It came to me by accident. When she died and we were emptying her flat, my mother turned up a biscuit tin at the back of a wardrobe with perhaps forty prints in it, not one of which any of us had seen. She gave me this one on the strength of a long-standing family theory that I take after her, and in that particular image the resemblance is difficult to argue with.

What I'd hate to lose is not the object. It's that in this photograph she is not yet anybody's grandmother. She is nineteen, she works in that shop, and none of it has happened to her — the marriage, the four children, the long illness at the end. Every other picture I own was taken on the far side of all that. This is the only one in which she is still a stranger with a life in front of her, and there is, as far as anyone knows, no second copy of it anywhere.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Not one of which' embeds the quantifier where band 7 needed a separate clause.
'Gone furry with handling', 'on the far side of all that' — precise, not ornamental.
A cleft refuses the obvious answer before the real one is given.

annotations.span: not one of which any of us had seen
annotations.label: Quantifier plus 'which' plus past perfect
annotations.why: One clause like this per talk is enough; two starts to sound written.

annotations.span: the corners have gone furry with handling
annotations.label: An unexpected but exact adjective
annotations.why: Choose the word for how the thing feels, not for how impressive it sounds.

annotations.span: What I'd hate to lose is not the object.
annotations.label: Refuses the obvious answer first
annotations.why: Rule out the easy reading, then give yours; it makes the point land.

annotations.span: on the far side of all that
annotations.label: Space used to talk about time
annotations.why: Spatial metaphors for time sound native and cost nothing to build.

annotations.span: there is, as far as anyone knows, no second copy of it anywhere
annotations.label: A parenthesis dropped in pitch
annotations.why: Say the middle phrase lower and faster, then come back up for the end.

annotations.span: she is still a stranger with a life in front of her
annotations.label: The idea the whole talk was for
annotations.why: Save your single best phrase for the last ten seconds.

title: Images, memory and what gets kept

payload_json.topic: Images, memory and what gets kept

part3_themes.title: photographs and remembering
questions: Has the way families record their lives changed since your grandparents' day?
Does having thousands of photographs make people remember more, or less?
If every family photograph in a country vanished, what would actually be lost?
part3_themes.counterpoint: photographs replace memory rather than preserving it; people end up remembering the picture and forgetting the afternoon

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a programme that I listen every week. It is a podcast, and in every episode one person is interviewed for one hour about their job. Not famous jobs — normal jobs that nobody knows about.

I listen it when I walk to the station in the morning, and also in the evening when I am cooking. One episode is about forty-five minutes, so for me it is two walks.

I start with it two years ago. My colleague sent me one episode about a man who tunes the pianos. I don't care about pianos, but I listened all of it, and after that I listened another one, and after that another.

Why I like it? Because it is slow. The person asks a question and then he is quiet, and the other person must talk. In other programmes everybody speaks fast and everybody wants to be funny. Here, sometimes nobody speaks for five seconds, and for me this is very interesting.

So this is my favourite programme. I think I listened maybe eighty episodes, and I will continue.

what_caps_it.point: 'Listen' loses its preposition three times and the running total misses the perfect.
'Slow', 'interesting', 'favourite' — the judgement rests on three ordinary words.
A rhetorical question opens the argument and the close simply announces the answer is over.

annotations.span: The person asks a question and then he is quiet, and the other person must talk.
annotations.label: Names the mechanism, not the mood
annotations.why: Keep this — describing how something works is the answer to the fourth bullet.

annotations.span: a programme that I listen every week
annotations.label: Verb missing its preposition
annotations.why: 'That I listen to every week'. The 'to' survives even at the end.

annotations.span: I listen it when I walk to the station
annotations.label: The same preposition dropped again
annotations.why: 'I listen to it'. A repeated error costs more than a one-off.

annotations.span: I start with it two years ago
annotations.label: Past event told in the present
annotations.why: 'I started listening to it two years ago' — a finished time needs past simple.

annotations.span: a man who tunes the pianos
annotations.label: Article on a general plural
annotations.why: 'Tunes pianos'. Generalisations about a category drop 'the'.

annotations.span: I think I listened maybe eighty episodes
annotations.label: Running total in the past simple
annotations.why: 'I've listened to about eighty by now' — a total up to today is perfect.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is a podcast I've been following for a couple of years now. The format is very simple: each week one person is interviewed for an hour about their job, and the jobs are deliberately ordinary — a piano tuner, a night-shift baker, somebody who reads water meters. Nobody on it is famous, and that is clearly the whole idea.

I take it in two halves, because an episode runs to about fifty minutes and my walk to the station only takes twenty-five. So it's Monday morning on the way in, and then whatever's left over while I'm cooking that evening, which means I never quite finish one in a day.

I got into it more or less by accident. A colleague sent me a single episode about a piano tuner, which I opened out of politeness and fully expected to abandon after five minutes. I listened to the whole thing standing in my kitchen with the shopping still in the bags.

What holds my attention, I think, is that it isn't in any hurry. The interviewer asks something and then simply stops talking, and quite often nobody says anything for four or five seconds, which almost nothing else on the radio permits. Most programmes are terrified of a gap and fill it with jokes. This one lets the person work out what they actually think, and you can hear them doing it, hesitations included. That turns out to be rarer than it sounds, and it's why I've stuck with it long after I've drifted away from most things.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect continuous for the habit and two contrasting perfects in the final sentence.
'Got into it', 'terrified of a gap', 'drifted away' — chunks instead of 'interesting'.
The last bullet is answered by contrast: what others do, then what this one refuses to do.

annotations.span: I've been following for a couple of years now
annotations.label: Present perfect continuous for a habit
annotations.why: Use it for anything you started in the past and are still doing.

annotations.span: the jobs are deliberately ordinary
annotations.label: States the principle, then illustrates
annotations.why: One abstract sentence before your examples makes a list sound argued.

annotations.span: I got into it more or less by accident
annotations.label: Two phrasal chunks in one clause
annotations.why: 'Got into' and 'more or less' are both worth stealing outright.

annotations.span: which I opened out of politeness and fully expected to abandon after five minutes
annotations.label: Admits a low expectation first
annotations.why: Setting up a low expectation makes what follows worth hearing.

annotations.span: with the shopping still in the bags
annotations.label: One detail proves the claim
annotations.why: A physical detail is better evidence than the word 'gripping' ever is.

annotations.span: What holds my attention, I think, is that it isn't in any hurry.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the final bullet
annotations.why: 'What holds me is…' forces you into a reason rather than a summary.

annotations.span: Most programmes are terrified of a gap and fill it with jokes.
annotations.label: Personifies the rivals in one line
annotations.why: Describing what everything else does is how you explain what this one is.

annotations.span: you can hear them doing it, hesitations included
annotations.label: Names the evidence for the claim
annotations.why: Follow an abstract claim immediately with the thing you actually hear.

annotations.span: it's why I've stuck with it long after I've drifted away from most things
annotations.label: Two perfects contrasted in one clause
annotations.why: Setting one perfect against another is a cheap way to show range.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The programme I'd choose is a weekly interview podcast, and its premise is almost aggressively unglamorous: one person, one hour, one job, and never a job anybody would envy. A piano tuner. A baker on nights. A man who reads water meters in the six streets he grew up in.

I take it in two sittings, since an episode runs close to fifty minutes and the walk to my station is twenty-five. Monday morning gets the first half; whatever survives is played over the chopping board that evening.

I came to it by accident and against my own expectations. A colleague forwarded the piano tuner episode, which I began out of politeness fully intending to give up inside five minutes, and finished standing in the kitchen with the shopping still in its bags.

As for why it holds me when so little else does, I think it comes down to a willingness to be silent. The interviewer asks, and then does nothing. Four or five seconds of nothing, which on the radio feels like a minute and a half. Most programmes treat a pause as a fault to be corrected and paper over it with a joke; this one treats the pause as the point. What you end up hearing is somebody working out what they think while you listen, rather than performing a view they arrived with. That, it turns out, is a great deal harder to switch off than cleverness is.

what_lifts_it.point: A free relative as subject and a semicolon contrast replace two separate sentences.
'Aggressively unglamorous', 'paper over it', 'performing a view' — chosen for shade.
Three fragments do the exemplifying, and the close abstracts into a claim about attention.

annotations.span: whatever survives is played over the chopping board that evening
annotations.label: Free relative used as the subject
annotations.why: 'Whatever survives' packs a whole clause into a subject; use it once.

annotations.span: almost aggressively unglamorous
annotations.label: An adverb sharpening an adjective
annotations.why: One unexpected pairing does more than a rare word on its own.

annotations.span: A piano tuner. A baker on nights. A man who reads water meters in the six streets he grew up in.
annotations.label: Three fragments instead of a list
annotations.why: Short fragments after a long sentence change the pace and hold attention.

annotations.span: paper over it with a joke; this one treats the pause as the point
annotations.label: An idiom placed inside a contrast
annotations.why: 'Paper over' is exactly right here, which is why it sounds unforced.

annotations.span: somebody working out what they think while you listen, rather than performing a view they arrived with
annotations.label: The distinction the whole talk was for
annotations.why: Name the difference precisely once, and then stop explaining it.

annotations.span: That, it turns out, is a great deal harder to switch off than cleverness is.
annotations.label: Parenthesis dropped, then a fall
annotations.why: Say the middle two words lower, then land firmly on the last word.

title: An advertisement that stayed in your mind

payload_json.topic: An advertisement that stayed in your mind

cue_card.topic: Describe an advertisement you saw that has stayed in your mind.
bullets: what it was advertising
where and when you saw it
what actually happened in it
and explain why you think it stayed with you when others didn't.
rounding_off: Did it make you buy anything?
Have you ever tried to find it again?

teaching.band_move: Tell your own viewing in the past and the advert in the present. Never let the two mix.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Take the first advert you can actually picture, even a bad one. Being able to see it beats having an opinion about it.

note_grid.cell: bakery, one shop, not a chain
made you wait; others start loud

prep_plan.trap: The third bullet needs a sequence of images, and most candidates give a summary of the mood instead.

time_plan.goal: Say what it was for and roughly when.
The product and the evening you saw it.
The film itself, shot by shot.
What others did, then what this withheld.
One line proving it stuck.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: describe one frame — the light, the pavement, what the dog is doing.
Add time depth: say what you thought it was for while you were still watching.
Contrast: describe the advert that came immediately after it.
Evaluate aloud: say whether it would still work if it ran tomorrow.

error_watchlist.wrong: At first I don't look at it because I was on my phone.
error_watchlist.right: At first I didn't look up, because I was on my phone.
error_watchlist.why: Your own viewing is finished; keep it in the past.

error_watchlist.wrong: It came in the break of the match.
error_watchlist.right: It came on during the break.
error_watchlist.why: 'During' for a period, and adverts 'come on'.

error_watchlist.wrong: All other advertisements are loud.
error_watchlist.right: Almost everything else in that break was loud.
error_watchlist.why: Narrow the claim to what you actually saw.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Counting shots, seconds and adverts fills this card with plurals that get swallowed.

target_words.note: Ends /ts/; both sounds, or the plural vanishes.
The ending is /z/ after the /n/.
Cluster at each end; slow the word down.
Voiced /vz/, and the vowel changes from 'loaf'.
Three consonants after the vowel, all pronounced.

chunking_drill.sentence: It just follows him for what must be fifty seconds, which is an extraordinary amount of time to do nothing on television.
chunks: It just follows him
for what must be fifty seconds,
which is an extraordinary amount of time
to do nothing on television.

minimal_pairs.contrast: the cluster is the only sign that you mean several

teaching.examiner_note: You may be stopped mid-sentence at two minutes. That is the timer, not a judgement, and it means you filled the turn.

swap_slots.span: about ten years ago
swap_slots.prompt: Your own time reference, given once. 'A long time ago' is not a time reference.

swap_slots.span: a bakery
swap_slots.prompt: What yours was advertising. Name the product, and say whether it was local or national.

swap_slots.span: at a friend's flat
swap_slots.prompt: Where you were sitting when you saw it, and who else was in the room.

swap_slots.span: inside a woman is shaping loaves

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about an advertisement that I saw maybe ten years ago on the television. It was for a bakery, a small one, not a big company.

I saw it in my friend's flat. We were watching a football match and it came in the break. In the beginning I don't look at it, because I was on my phone.

In the advertisement there is a man with a dog. He is walking in the street, it is very early, maybe five o'clock, it is winter and it is dark. There is no music and nobody speaks. It is only one camera and it doesn't cut. He walks and walks. And in the end he passes a window with a light, and there is a woman inside making the bread. Then one line comes on the screen with the name of the bakery.

I remember it because it was different. All other advertisements are loud, they have music, people are smiling and they say the name many times. This one says nothing until the last second. So it stayed in my head.

what_caps_it.point: The candidate's own viewing slips into the present, and one preposition is wrong.
'Different', 'loud', 'stayed in my head' — the judgement runs on the smallest available words.
The claim about other adverts is stated absolutely, with nothing narrowing it.

annotations.span: This one says nothing until the last second.
annotations.label: The contrast that explains everything
annotations.why: Keep this — it is the sentence the whole answer was building towards.

annotations.span: In the beginning I don't look at it, because I was on my phone.
annotations.label: Your own past told in the present
annotations.why: 'At first I didn't look up.' The advert stays present; you stay past.

annotations.span: it came in the break
annotations.label: Wrong preposition for a period
annotations.why: 'It came on during the break.' Use 'during' for a stretch of time.

annotations.span: there is a woman inside making the bread
annotations.label: Article on a general substance
annotations.why: 'Making bread'. Uncountable substances take no article here.

annotations.span: All other advertisements are loud
annotations.label: A claim far wider than the evidence
annotations.why: 'Almost everything else in that break was loud' — narrow it to what you saw.

annotations.span: So it stayed in my head.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the card
annotations.why: End with proof that it stuck, not with the claim that it did.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The advert I'd talk about was on television about ten years ago, and it was for a bakery — a small local one with two shops, not a chain anybody would have heard of.

I saw it at a friend's flat. We were half-watching a football match and it came on during the break, and to be honest I only looked up because the room went quiet.

The advert itself is a single shot. A man is walking a dog through an empty town, very early — five in the morning, midwinter, still dark. There's no music, nobody says anything, and the camera never cuts away. It just follows him for what must be fifty seconds, which is an extraordinary amount of time to do nothing on television. Then he passes a lit window, and inside a woman is shaping loaves, and a line of text comes up with the name of the bakery underneath. No voice, no slogan, no product held up to the camera. That's the whole thing.

The reason it stayed with me, I think, is that it made you wait for it. Everything else in that break was doing the opposite — music from the first frame, a voice telling you what to feel, the name repeated four times in thirty seconds. This one gambled that you'd stay even though it gave you nothing, and the ending only works because of the wait. I couldn't tell you what any of the others were advertising. I could still draw you that street.

what_lifts_it.point: Past continuous for the viewing and a clean present tense for the film, kept apart throughout.
'Half-watching', 'came on', 'gambled that' — precise verbs instead of 'different'.
The final bullet is answered by contrast and then proved with two short sentences.

annotations.span: We were half-watching a football match
annotations.label: Past continuous sets the scene
annotations.why: Use it for what was already going on when the thing you're telling happened.

annotations.span: I only looked up because the room went quiet
annotations.label: Proves attention with a detail
annotations.why: Show the moment you noticed rather than saying it caught your attention.

annotations.span: The advert itself is a single shot.
annotations.label: Present simple for the content
annotations.why: Films, books and adverts are always described in the present, whenever you saw them.

annotations.span: which is an extraordinary amount of time to do nothing on television
annotations.label: Evaluates inside the description
annotations.why: One judgement dropped into a description stops it being a list.

annotations.span: inside a woman is shaping loaves
annotations.label: A precise verb for the action
annotations.why: 'Shaping' does what 'making' cannot — the reader sees the hands.

annotations.span: The reason it stayed with me, I think, is that it made you wait for it.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the last bullet
annotations.why: Naming the reason as a reason forces you off description and into argument.

annotations.span: music from the first frame, a voice telling you what to feel, the name repeated four times in thirty seconds
annotations.label: Three items in one rhythm
annotations.why: Hold the pitch flat over the first two items, then drop and stop.

annotations.span: This one gambled that you'd stay even though it gave you nothing
annotations.label: A verb that carries the whole argument
annotations.why: 'Gambled' says risk and intention at once; one word doing two jobs.

annotations.span: I couldn't tell you what any of the others were advertising. I could still draw you that street.
annotations.label: Proves the claim instead of repeating it
annotations.why: Two short parallel sentences are the strongest way to finish a long turn.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The advertisement I'd choose ran on television roughly ten years ago, and it was for a bakery — a single shop rather than a chain.

I saw it at a friend's flat, during the interval of a football match, and what made me look up was not the advert itself but the silence: the room had been noisy and abruptly wasn't.

The film is one unbroken shot. A man walks a dog through a town at about five in the morning in midwinter, in the dark. No music, no voice, no cut. He simply walks, for what must be the better part of a minute, which on television is close to reckless. Eventually he passes a lit window; inside, a woman is shaping loaves; a single line of type appears with the name of the shop. That is the entire advertisement.

What made it stick, I suspect, is that it was prepared to be dull for fifty seconds in order to earn two. Everything else in that break did the reverse — a jingle from the opening frame, a voice explaining the emotion to you, the name pushed at you four times in half a minute. Those adverts spent their whole budget on the first second and had nothing left over. This one withheld, and the ending was worth having precisely because of it. I couldn't name a single other product from that evening. I could still walk you down that street.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft with 'not X but Y' carries the opening where band 7 used two clauses.
'Close to reckless', 'withheld', 'pushed at you' — economical and exact.
The budget metaphor explains the mechanism rather than restating the contrast.

annotations.span: what made me look up was not the advert itself but the silence
annotations.label: Cleft with 'not X but Y'
annotations.why: It corrects an expectation and introduces the real cause in one clause.

annotations.span: which on television is close to reckless
annotations.label: A judgement in three words
annotations.why: Choosing 'reckless' over 'unusual' is the shade of meaning band 8 rewards.

annotations.span: No music, no voice, no cut.
annotations.label: Three negatives, three beats
annotations.why: Equal stress on each, with real pauses between; do not run them together.

annotations.span: Those adverts spent their whole budget on the first second and had nothing left over.
annotations.label: A metaphor explains the mechanism
annotations.why: One worked metaphor beats another round of description every time.

annotations.span: it was prepared to be dull for fifty seconds in order to earn two
annotations.label: States the trade exactly
annotations.why: Put the cost and the payoff in the same sentence and the argument closes itself.

annotations.span: I could still walk you down that street
annotations.label: Ends on evidence, not a summary
annotations.why: Finish by demonstrating the claim; the examiner does the concluding for you.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about the man who had the bike shop on our road. He taught me how to fix a puncture when I was fourteen.

So my bike had a flat tyre and I took it to him, because I don't know how to do this. And he said okay, but you do it, I only watch. First I am a bit annoyed, because I want him to fix it fast and I want to go home.

So I take off the wheel, and then I take out the tube, and then I find the hole. It take a long time, maybe forty minutes. He is only speaking, he never touch the tools. And every time I go too fast he stops me and he asks me the name of the thing in my hand.

And I felt very good after, because I did it by myself. If he fixes it for me, I don't learn anything. It was a nice way to teach, I think. And now I always fix my own punctures, so it is very useful for me. So this is the person who taught me a practical thing.

The narrative drops into the present six times and the conditional at the end collapses.
'Nice', 'good', 'useful', 'a practical thing' — the whole evaluation runs on flat adjectives.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'd like to talk about a man who ran the bike shop at the end of our road, and about the summer he taught me to mend a puncture. I was about fourteen at the time.

I'd ridden over some glass and the back tyre had gone completely flat, so I wheeled the bike down to him fully expecting him to deal with it in five minutes. He didn't. He pulled a chair over, sat down on it, and told me that he'd talk me through it but he wasn't going to touch it. I remember being fairly annoyed, because I'd assumed I was dropping the bike off, not being taught something.

What he actually did was make me name things before I was allowed to touch them: the valve, the levers, the rim tape. Every time I rushed, he stopped me and made me say out loud what I was about to do next. The whole job took the best part of forty minutes, which is roughly four times longer than he'd have needed.

As for why it stuck, I think it's because he refused to help at exactly the point where helping would have been easiest. If he'd taken the wheel off me when I got stuck, I'd have gone home with a working bike and nothing else. Instead I was slow and irritated and I got it wrong twice, whereas now I can do the whole thing in ten minutes without really thinking. That is the difference between being taught something and watching somebody do it for you.

what_lifts_it.point: One past perfect and one third conditional replace the flat run of past simples.
'The best part of forty minutes', 'wheeled the bike down' — chunks doing the work.
Three audible signposts give the two minutes a shape the listener can follow.

annotations.why: Reuse it for any duration you are estimating out loud.

annotations.span: As for why it stuck

annotations.why: Say the bullet out loud and you cannot forget to answer it.

annotations.span: If he'd taken the wheel off me when I got stuck, I'd have gone home with a working bike and nothing else.
annotations.label: Third conditional, used where it belongs
annotations.why: This is the natural structure on any 'why did it matter' bullet.

annotations.span: whereas now I can do the whole thing in ten minutes

annotations.why: 'Whereas' links two clauses; 'but' would flatten the comparison.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about the man who kept the bike shop at the end of our road, and one afternoon the summer I turned fourteen, when he taught me to mend a puncture.

I'd gone over some glass, the back tyre was flat, and I wheeled the bike down there assuming he'd have it done before I'd finished explaining. He had other ideas. He dragged a chair out, sat himself down and announced that he would talk, and I would do the touching. Not unkindly, but there was clearly no negotiating.

His method, if you can call it that, was to make me name every part before my hands were allowed near it: valve, levers, rim tape. The moment I started rushing he'd stop me and make me say what was coming next. Forty minutes it took, four times what it would have cost him, and at no point did his hands leave the arms of that chair.

Looking back, what makes it worth remembering is that he withheld help at precisely the moment it would have been most welcome. Had he simply taken the wheel from me, I'd have ridden off with a mended bike and learned absolutely nothing. As it was I was slow, faintly humiliated and wrong twice over, and it is now something I do without thinking at all. I've come to suspect that is the whole distinction between being taught and being helped: one of them leaves something behind.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces the 'if' clause and a passive contrast closes the turn.
'He had other ideas', 'faintly humiliated' — precision rather than rare vocabulary.
The close generalises about teaching instead of summing the anecdote up.

annotations.why: Same meaning as the third conditional, higher register, still spoken.

annotations.span: He had other ideas.
annotations.label: Three words carry the whole refusal
annotations.why: Short idiomatic sentences between long ones control your rhythm.

annotations.span: faintly humiliated
annotations.label: One precise pair instead of 'a bit bad'
annotations.why: Choose the adverb as carefully as the adjective.

annotations.span: the whole distinction between being taught and being helped
annotations.label: Abstracts the story into an idea
annotations.why: Ending on a distinction lifts the turn out of anecdote.

annotations.span: valve, levers, rim tape
annotations.label: A list run as one rhythmic group
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across the list, then fall on the last item.

I want to describe the lady who works in the reception of our health centre. She is doing this job for many years, I think.

Her job is to take the people when they come in, and also she answer the phone, and she gives the appointments to everybody. It is a very busy job, because in the morning there is always many people waiting there.

One day in the winter I was there for a form. There was maybe eight people in the queue, and the phone is ringing all the time, and one man was very angry because he waited too long. model_answers.label: The target — same person, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'd like to talk about the woman who runs the front desk at our local health centre, because I've never seen anybody handle a room the way she does.

Her job is basically everything at once. She books people in, she takes the phone calls, she chases prescriptions that haven't turned up, and she's the first face you see when you come through the door — which means she gets the complaints as well.

The morning I'm thinking of was in February. I'd gone in to drop a form off, there were seven or eight people ahead of me, the phone was going constantly, and a man near the front had clearly been waiting far longer than he'd expected to. What struck me was that she never once told anybody what she couldn't do. She told each person exactly how long they'd have to wait, in minutes, and then she stuck to it. The man who was annoyed had stopped being annoyed within about ninety seconds, and I honestly couldn't tell you what she said to him.

What makes her good at it, I think, is that she treats the queue as one situation rather than as a run of interruptions. Anybody can be pleasant with one person in front of them, whereas doing it with eight and a ringing phone is a completely different skill. She never looks as though she's in a hurry, which is presumably an act, but it's an act that keeps the rest of us calm too. Places like that run on one person, and nobody notices until that person is off sick.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about the woman who keeps the front desk at our health centre running, and one particular February morning when I stood and watched her do it.

Her job, in theory, is reception. In practice it is triage: booking people in, fielding the phone, chasing prescriptions that have not arrived, and absorbing whatever mood people carry in through the door with them.

That morning there were seven or eight of us waiting, the phone had not stopped since I arrived, and a man at the front had plainly been there a good deal longer than he had been led to expect. Not once did she tell anybody what she was unable to do. Everyone was given a number of minutes, the number turned out to be accurate, and the man who had been on the edge of losing his temper was somehow no longer losing it a minute and a half later. I still could not tell you how.

What she has, I think, is an ability to treat a roomful of people as one situation rather than as a queue of interruptions. Being pleasant to a single person is nothing; being pleasant to eight of them while a phone rings is a different order of difficulty altogether. She is never visibly rushed, which must be deliberate, and the calm travels. The odd thing about that sort of competence is that it is invisible by design — you only discover it was holding the place up in the week somebody covers for her.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion and a fronted 'in theory / in practice' pair replace the band-7 clefts.
'Triage', 'absorbing whatever mood people carry in' — one exact word, then an exact phrase.
The close names a general property of competence instead of praising her again.

I will describe an old lady who has the garden plot next to my father. She is maybe eighty years old, and she is there every day, also in the winter.

I know her since about six years, because I go with my father on Saturday and we drink tea in her shed. In the beginning I don't talk with her so much, but after some time we are talking a lot about everything.

Now I ask her about many things, not only about the garden. For example, when I have a problem in my work, or when I don't know what to do about my studies, I ask her opinion. She is very direct person. She says exactly what she thinks, and sometimes it is not nice to hear.

model_answers.label: The target — same person, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person I want to talk about is a woman in her late seventies who has the allotment next to my father's. She's been growing things on that patch for longer than I've been alive, and she's down there most days, even in February.

I've known her for about six years, really by accident. I'd started going along on Saturday mornings to help my father, and we ended up drinking tea at her shed at eleven o'clock, which somehow turned into a fixed arrangement. It started with vegetables and it stopped being about vegetables fairly quickly.

These days I ask her about all sorts of things — whether to take a job, how to handle somebody at work I find difficult, whether I'm being unreasonable about something. She's blunt, and I've learned not to ask her unless I actually want the answer. She once told me I'd already decided and was only after permission, which was annoying mainly because it was true.

The reason I take her seriously, though, isn't the age and it isn't the experience exactly. It's that she's the only person I know who says 'I've no idea' without the slightest embarrassment. Everybody else fills the gap with something. She'll tell you what she's seen happen herself, she'll tell you what she's only heard about, and she keeps the two firmly apart. Once you've noticed somebody doing that, you start trusting the rest of what they say, whereas most advice arrives with no label on it at all.

annotations.why: Ruling out the obvious answer makes the real one land harder.

annotations.label: Two matching clauses, one rhythm
annotations.why: Parallel structures are easy to say and easy to follow.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about a woman in her late seventies who keeps the allotment next to my father's, and who has been growing things on that ground since long before I was born.

I got to know her by accident. I had started going along on Saturdays to help my father, and at some point the eleven o'clock tea at her shed turned from an occasional thing into an appointment nobody had actually made. What began as talk about soil stopped being about soil rather quickly.

Now I ask her about matters that have nothing to do with gardening — whether to take a job, whether I am being unreasonable about a colleague, that sort of thing. She is not gentle about any of it. Having once been told that I had already made my decision and merely wanted permission, I have learned not to ask unless I am ready to hear the answer.

What earns her the authority, though, is neither her age nor her experience. It is that she is the only person I know who will say 'I have no idea' and feel absolutely nothing about saying it. Everybody else patches the hole. She distinguishes, every single time, between what she has watched happen and what she has merely been told, and she tells you which is which. Once you have seen somebody do that consistently, their opinion acquires a weight no amount of confidence could buy — which is, I suspect, the exact opposite of how most of us try to be believed.

what_lifts_it.point: A perfect participle clause and a 'neither … nor' pair replace band 7's plain clefts.
'Patches the hole', 'acquires a weight' — figurative, but still ordinary spoken English.
The close states a general claim about credibility instead of restating the reason.

annotations.span: Everybody else patches the hole.

annotations.why: Short figurative sentences beat long formal ones.

annotations.span: What earns her the authority, though, is neither her age nor her experience.
annotations.label: Rules out two answers in one clause
annotations.why: 'Neither … nor' is compact and sounds deliberate.

annotations.span: an appointment nobody had actually made
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'nobody'
annotations.why: Put the stress on the surprising word and the joke works.

annotations.label: Turns the story into a claim
annotations.why: End on something arguable; it invites the Part 3 you want.

target_words.note: One syllable: /skt/ at the end, never 'ask-ed'.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to speak about a woman who is organising the volunteers in a community kitchen near my house. There is maybe thirty people in this group, and they are cooking food two evenings in a week for people who need it.

She is the person who makes the rota, so she decides who is working on which day. It is not an easy job, because many people say yes in the beginning and after that they don't come any more.

One time I saw her when a delivery didn't arrive. All the vegetables are not there, and everybody is standing in the kitchen and looking at her. And she just says okay, we make soup with the bread and the tomatoes, and she explains why. After four minutes everybody is working again. Nobody is panicking, because she is not panicking.

People follow her because she is very calm and also she is fair. She never shouts at somebody in front of the other people. And she is doing the worst job herself. So she is very good leader for this group of volunteers.

what_caps_it.point: 'There is' with a plural, and the whole incident drifts into the present tense.
'Very calm', 'fair', 'not easy', 'very good' — four flat adjectives carry the judgement.
The group and the incident never connect; each paragraph starts again from nothing.

annotations.span: One time I saw her when a delivery didn't arrive.
annotations.label: Backs the claim with one incident
annotations.why: Keep this — a leadership claim without a scene is unrateable.

annotations.span: There is maybe thirty people in this group
annotations.label: Singular 'there is' with a plural
annotations.why: 'There are about thirty people.' The verb follows the noun.

annotations.span: All the vegetables are not there, and everybody is standing in the kitchen
annotations.label: The scene slips into the present
annotations.why: Choose past simple in sentence one and stay in it.

annotations.span: she is very calm and also she is fair
annotations.label: Two flat adjectives instead of behaviour
annotations.why: Say what she does: 'she never corrects anybody in public'.

annotations.span: And she is doing the worst job herself.
annotations.label: Continuous used for a habit
annotations.why: 'She does the worst job herself.' Habits take present simple.

annotations.span: So she is very good leader for this group of volunteers.
annotations.label: Article missing, and the card repeated
annotations.why: 'A very good leader' — and close on an idea, not the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'd like to describe the woman who runs the volunteer rota at a community kitchen near where I live. There are about thirty of us on that rota, cooking two evenings a week for people who'd otherwise go without, and she's the one who holds the whole thing together.

Her actual job, if you can call it a job, is deciding who works which shift. That sounds administrative and it really isn't: roughly a third of the people who sign up in September have quietly disappeared by November, so the list is never the list.

The evening I always think about is the one where a delivery simply didn't arrive. We had bread, tinned tomatoes and almost nothing else, forty people were expected, and everybody in the kitchen turned round and looked at her. She took about four minutes. She said what we were making instead, who was doing what, and — this is the part I noticed — why she'd picked that rather than something else. Nobody panicked, largely because she visibly didn't. I've thought about those four minutes a great deal since.

What makes people follow her, I think, is that she has never corrected anybody in front of the group. If you can't do your shift, she asks you to find your own replacement, which sounds strict but means nobody is ever quietly resented. She also does the worst job herself most weeks. You'd follow somebody like that even if you disagreed with them, whereas plenty of people in charge are obeyed and nothing more.

what_lifts_it.point: A present perfect, a past continuous scene and one second conditional do the structural work.
'Holds the whole thing together', 'the list is never the list' — plain words, exact meaning.
The incident is announced, told and then used as evidence for the judgement.

annotations.span: The evening I always think about
annotations.label: Announces the incident before telling it
annotations.why: Naming the scene first tells the listener what to hold onto.

annotations.span: roughly a third of the people who sign up in September have quietly disappeared by November
annotations.label: Present perfect for a result that stands
annotations.why: Use it when the effect, not the event, is the point.

annotations.span: holds the whole thing together
annotations.label: Four ordinary words, exactly right
annotations.why: Reuse it for anyone a group would collapse without.

annotations.span: this is the part I noticed
annotations.label: Flags the detail that matters
annotations.why: Telling the listener where to look is free coherence.

annotations.span: the list is never the list
annotations.label: A short line that does real work
annotations.why: One compressed phrase beats a sentence of explanation.

annotations.span: What makes people follow her, I think, is that she has never corrected anybody in front of the group.
annotations.label: A cleft opens the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Say the judgement in one clause before you justify it.

annotations.span: You'd follow somebody like that even if you disagreed with them
annotations.label: Second conditional tests the claim
annotations.why: Naming the case that would break it makes the claim stronger.

annotations.span: bread, tinned tomatoes and almost nothing else
annotations.label: A three-part list in one breath
annotations.why: Level pitch across the list, then drop on the last item.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about the woman who runs the volunteer rota at a community kitchen five minutes from my flat — thirty-odd of us, two evenings a week, cooking for people who would otherwise go without.

Her role, on paper, is clerical: she decides who works which shift. In practice, about a third of the people who sign up in September have melted away by November, so what she is really managing is the gap between the list and the room.

The evening that stays with me was the one when a delivery never turned up. Bread, tinned tomatoes, not a great deal else, forty people expected, and every face in that kitchen swung round towards her. She took four minutes. What we were cooking instead, who was on what, and — the detail I have never forgotten — why that dish and not another one. Nobody panicked, for the straightforward reason that she conspicuously didn't. I have wondered since how much of it was rehearsed.

Why people follow her comes down to something quite small: she has never once corrected anybody within earshot of the group. Miss a shift and you find your own replacement, which sounds unforgiving and in fact means no grudge ever gets stored up. She takes the worst job herself more often than not. Authority of that sort survives disagreement, which is more than can be said for most of it — a great many people in charge are obeyed and never followed at all.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative-plus-'and' conditional replaces the band-7 'if' clause.
'Melted away', 'within earshot', 'the gap between the list and the room' — precise, not showy.
The close separates being obeyed from being followed, which the story never states outright.

annotations.span: Miss a shift and you find your own replacement
annotations.label: An imperative doing conditional work
annotations.why: Compact, spoken, and it varies your conditional forms.

annotations.span: have melted away by November
annotations.label: One verb carries the whole attrition
annotations.why: Choose a verb that contains the idea instead of explaining it.

annotations.span: the gap between the list and the room
annotations.label: Names the real job in eight words
annotations.why: Abstract the job before you describe it; it sounds considered.

annotations.span: Bread, tinned tomatoes, not a great deal else, forty people expected
annotations.label: Four fragments, one falling run
annotations.why: Fragments in a list are natural speech, not an error.

annotations.span: Authority of that sort survives disagreement
annotations.label: Turns the anecdote into a principle
annotations.why: Close on the general claim your story has just earned.

model_answers.transcript:
The rule I want to talk about is one at the city library, and it's about desks. If you leave your seat for more than twenty minutes, a member of staff is entitled to clear your things into a plastic box behind the counter and give the desk to whoever is next. Your bag no longer holds your place.

It applies to the main reading room on the first floor, which is the only part of the building with decent light and enough plug sockets, so it's the part everybody wants. In exam season there are perhaps sixty desks for what feels like three hundred people.

It has made my own life noticeably worse. I used to work in long stretches with a proper break in the middle, and now I don't dare go anywhere for lunch, so I eat a sandwich on the stairs in about six minutes and go straight back up. I've lost the habit of stopping properly, and I don't think that does the work any good.

Even so, I'd defend it. Before they brought it in, people were putting a coat over a chair at half past nine and reappearing at four, which meant the room was full and half empty at the same time. The rule costs me an hour of comfort a day and it gives somebody else a desk they'd otherwise never get. That strikes me as the right trade — a rule is fair when it takes the same thing from everybody, and this one does.

The rule I have in mind belongs to the city library and concerns its desks. Leave your seat for more than twenty minutes and a member of staff may lift your things into a plastic box behind the counter and hand the desk to whoever is waiting. A bag, in other words, no longer reserves anything.

It governs the main reading room on the first floor, which happens to be the only part of the building with decent light and enough sockets, and is therefore the part everybody is after. Come exam season, there are something like sixty desks for what feels like three hundred of us.

It has made my own days measurably worse. I used to work in long stretches with a real break in the middle; now I daren't leave the floor, so lunch is a sandwich on the stairs in six minutes flat. I have lost the habit of stopping properly, and I doubt the work is better for it.

I would still defend it, though. Before it came in, a coat went over a chair at half past nine and its owner reappeared at four, so the room managed to be full and half empty simultaneously. The change I'd like to see isn't a big one, and that's rather the point: I'd have public offices open one evening a week instead of only between nine and four.

At the moment anything official — renewing a document, registering a birth, sorting out a council problem — has to be done inside working hours, on a weekday, and almost none of it can be finished on a phone. Which is fine if you've got an understanding employer. It isn't fine if you're paid by the hour, or you're on a fixed shift, or you've got children to collect at half past three.

The thing that irritates me is that it could be done without spending anything. Nobody would have to work longer; the same hours would simply sit in a different place, so Thursday could run until eight and Friday could close at lunchtime. It's a rota, not a budget. Two of the counters sit empty after three o'clock as it is.

The reason I care is that I lost half a day's pay last spring renewing an identity card, and I could afford to. The man behind me in the queue had come in from a building site and clearly couldn't. That's the difference it would make — not convenience exactly, but the fact that a public service would stop costing more the less you earn. Changes that small never get made, I think, because it's nobody's job to notice them, whereas expensive ones at least have somebody arguing for them.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The change I would like is a small one, and that is rather the point of it: public offices open one evening a week, instead of only between nine and four.

As things stand, anything official — a document renewed, a birth registered, a dispute with the council — has to happen on a weekday, inside working hours, and very little of it can be finished over a phone. Which is perfectly manageable if your employer is relaxed about it, and not manageable at all if you are paid by the hour, tied to a shift, or standing at a school gate at half past three.

What makes it worth arguing about is that it need cost nothing whatsoever. Not one person would work an hour longer; the same hours would simply be arranged differently, with Thursday running to eight and Friday shutting at lunch. It is a question of rotas, not of spending. Two of the counters stand idle after three as things are.

I mind about it because I lost half a day's wages last spring renewing an identity card and could absorb it, whereas the man behind me had come straight off a building site and plainly could not. That is what the change would actually buy: not convenience, but an end to a public service quietly charging more to the people who earn least. Cheap improvements go unmade, I suspect, precisely because nobody's promotion depends on making them.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Need cost nothing' and a fronted fragment replace band 7's straight conditionals.
'Absorb it', 'quietly charging more' — precise verbs rather than impressive nouns.
The close explains why cheap improvements stall, which the story only implied.

annotations.span: it need cost nothing whatsoever
annotations.label: 'Need' used as a bare modal
annotations.why: Rare, correct and unshowy — exactly the band-8 register.

annotations.span: Which is perfectly manageable if your employer is relaxed about it
annotations.label: A fragment used on purpose
annotations.why: Spoken English starts sentences with 'which'; written English doesn't.

annotations.span: a document renewed, a birth registered, a dispute with the council
annotations.label: Three noun phrases in one rhythm
annotations.why: Keep the beat even, then drop the pitch on the last.

annotations.span: an end to a public service quietly charging more to the people who earn least
annotations.label: Names the injustice without raising the voice
annotations.why: Understated phrasing is more persuasive than strong adjectives.

annotations.span: precisely because nobody's promotion depends on making them
annotations.label: Explains the stalling in one clause
annotations.why: End on the mechanism, not on the wish.

teaching.band_move: Give the real reason in the last bullet, not the polite one. 'No time' is the answer that scores nothing.

target_words.note: Say it as one word; the 'v' becomes /f/.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my ambition to speak the language of my father. He is coming from another country, and all his family are speaking this language, but with me he speaks only English.

I have this ambition since I am maybe seventeen, so it is more than ten years now. Every time we are visiting his family, I sit at the table and I don't understand nothing, and my father must translate for me. It is not a nice feeling for me.

I did some steps for it. I downloaded two applications on my phone and I used them every day for two months. Also I started an evening class, but after five weeks I stopped to go, because the class is at seven o'clock and I finish my work at half past six.

Why I didn't achieve it? I think because there is no date for it. Nobody is waiting for me. If I have an exam, maybe I finish it. So this is my ambition which I don't achieve until now.

what_caps_it.point: The wanting never reaches the present perfect, and two verb patterns break outright.
'Some steps', 'not a nice feeling', 'no date' — the vocabulary never rises above the plainest option.
The last bullet is asked as a question and then answered in seven words.

annotations.span: I downloaded two applications on my phone and I used them every day for two months.
annotations.label: One step with real numbers in it
annotations.why: Keep this — durations are what make the third bullet credible.

annotations.span: I have this ambition since I am maybe seventeen
annotations.label: Duration built in the present
annotations.why: 'I've wanted this since I was seventeen.' Perfect plus past.

annotations.span: all his family are speaking this language
annotations.label: Continuous for a permanent state
annotations.why: 'His whole family speaks it.' States take the simple form.

annotations.span: I don't understand nothing
annotations.label: Two negatives cancelling out
annotations.why: 'I don't understand anything.' One negative per clause.

annotations.span: I stopped to go
annotations.label: Wrong pattern after 'stop'
annotations.why: 'I stopped going.' 'Stop to' means you paused to do it.

annotations.span: So this is my ambition which I don't achieve until now.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: Close on why ambitions without deadlines stall.

model_answers.label: The target — same ambition, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The ambition I'd like to talk about is learning to speak my father's first language properly — properly meaning well enough to sit at a family table and not need him.

I've wanted that since I was about seventeen, so we're talking eleven or twelve years, which sounds worse out loud than it does in my head. He came here in his twenties and uses it with everybody except me, and every visit to his side of the family finds me smiling at jokes I haven't followed while he translates the ones he thinks I'll like.

I have taken steps, in fits and starts. There were two apps, which I used religiously for about two months each. There was an evening class I signed up for and gave up on after five weeks, because it started at seven and I'm rarely out of work before half past six. And there's a phrasebook in the kitchen that I open roughly twice a year. None of it added up to anything you could call a method.

The honest reason I haven't managed it is that nothing has ever depended on it. There's no exam, no date, nobody waiting for me to be able to do it — and a thing with no deadline loses to everything that has one. If I'd booked a trip out there on my own, without him, I'd have been forced into it years ago. That's the part I keep not doing, and I'm fairly sure it's the only part that counts.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect holds the wanting and a third conditional names the route not taken.
'In fits and starts', 'religiously', 'roughly twice a year' — precision about effort, not adjectives.
Definition, duration, three attempts, one honest reason — each move signalled before it starts.

annotations.why: The wanting is still true, so it cannot go in the past simple.

annotations.label: An idiom that admits the truth
annotations.why: One honest idiom is worth five impressive ones.

annotations.span: The honest reason I haven't managed it is that nothing has ever depended on it.
annotations.label: Announces the real answer
annotations.why: Signal the last bullet, then give the reason you would rather not.

annotations.span: There's no exam, no date, nobody waiting for me to be able to do it
annotations.label: Three negatives in one falling run
annotations.why: Keep the rhythm even and let the pitch drop on the third.

annotations.span: a thing with no deadline loses to everything that has one
annotations.label: A rule of thumb, compressed
annotations.why: Turning your excuse into a general law sounds considered.

annotations.span: If I'd booked a trip out there on my own, without him, I'd have been forced into it years ago.
annotations.label: Third conditional for the road not taken
annotations.why: This is the natural structure for any 'why didn't I' bullet.

annotations.span: That's the part I keep not doing, and I'm fairly sure it's the only part that counts.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The ambition is to speak my father's first language properly — by which I mean well enough to sit at his family's table and manage without him.

I have wanted that since I was seventeen or so, which makes it a good twelve years, and it sounds a great deal worse said aloud than it does in my head. He arrived here in his twenties and uses that language with everybody on earth apart from me, so every visit to his side of the family finds me smiling at jokes I have not followed while he translates the ones he thinks I will enjoy.

Steps have been taken, in fits and starts. Two apps, used devotedly for about two months apiece. One evening class, signed up for and abandoned inside five weeks, because it began at seven and I am rarely out of work before half past six. A phrasebook that gets opened, generously, twice a year. None of it ever amounted to anything that could reasonably be called a method.

What I have never managed to arrange is a reason. There is no exam, no date, nobody waiting — and anything without a deadline loses, quietly, to everything that has one. Had I ever booked a trip out there on my own, I would have been forced into it years ago. That is the part I keep not doing, and I have come to suspect it was always the only part that counted.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion and an agentless passive replace band 7's 'if' clause and its plain past.
'Devotedly', 'generously', 'apiece' — irony carried by single, exactly chosen words.
Noun-phrase fragments compress the middle bullet so the last one gets its time.

annotations.span: Steps have been taken, in fits and starts.
annotations.label: Passive with the agent left out
annotations.why: It sounds wry, and it lets you skip 'I' for a sentence.

annotations.span: Two apps, used devotedly for about two months apiece.
annotations.label: A fragment delivered as one unit
annotations.why: Fragments are natural in speech; keep them short and even.

annotations.span: A phrasebook that gets opened, generously, twice a year. None of it ever amounted to anything that could reasonably be called a method.
annotations.label: One adverb doing all the irony
annotations.why: Place the adverb between commas and it carries the joke.

annotations.span: What I have never managed to arrange is a reason.
annotations.label: A cleft that reframes the whole failure
annotations.why: Recast the excuse as a missing thing, not a missing effort.

annotations.span: Had I ever booked a trip out there on my own
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning, higher register, still perfectly speakable.
