title: A piece of advice you decided not to take

payload_json.topic: A piece of advice you decided not to take

cue_card.topic: Describe a piece of advice you were given that you decided not to take.
bullets: who gave you the advice
what they told you to do
what you did instead
and explain how you feel about that decision now.
rounding_off: Have you told them what you did?
Would you give the same advice to somebody else?

teaching.band_move: Report the advice, don't act it out. 'What she said was' plus backshifted modals is the whole trick.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Pick advice you rejected and can still quote. If you cannot remember their actual words, the second bullet has nothing in it.

note_grid.cell: aunt, tried it herself 15 yrs ago
'wait a yr, don't do it part-time'
right re cost, wrong re outcome

prep_plan.trap: The fourth bullet wants a mixed verdict, and most candidates deliver a triumphant one, which is both less true and less interesting.

time_plan.goal: Name who gave the advice and why they had standing.
Who they were and what they actually told you.
What you did instead, with real durations.
The verdict now — mixed, and reasoned out loud.
One line about advice and hindsight.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in on the conversation: where you were, and the sentence you still remember.
Say what had happened to her when she tried it, and how long she lasted.
Contrast the person you were then with what you would decide now.
Say plainly whether you would give that advice to somebody younger.

error_watchlist.wrong: She told me that I must not do it because it will be too hard.
error_watchlist.right: She told me I shouldn't do it because it would be too hard.
error_watchlist.why: Reporting a past conversation pushes the modals back.

error_watchlist.wrong: If I listened to her, I was less tired in those two years.
error_watchlist.right: If I'd listened to her, I'd have been less tired.
error_watchlist.why: 'Had' plus 'would have' is what carries regret.

error_watchlist.wrong: I didn't take her advices and I did on my own way.
error_watchlist.right: I didn't take her advice and I went my own way.
error_watchlist.why: 'Advice' is uncountable, and you take or follow it.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: The whole card is past tense, and a swallowed -ed is heard as a tense error as well.

target_words.note: The -ed is /d/, joined onto the /z/.
One syllable; the -ed is /d/.
The -ed is /t/ here, never a syllable.
This -ed really is /ɪd/, an extra beat.
Stress the second syllable; the -ed is /d/.

chunking_drill.sentence: But she wasn't wrong about the cost — she was wrong about the outcome, and those aren't the same thing.
chunks: But she wasn't wrong about the cost
— she was wrong about the outcome,
and those aren't the same thing.

minimal_pairs.contrast: the tense lives entirely in the final /d/

teaching.examiner_note: If you finish early the examiner may ask one rounding-off question and move on. A short finish costs you turn time you cannot get back.

swap_slots.span: my aunt, who'd done the same thing fifteen years earlier
swap_slots.prompt: Your own person plus what gave them standing. The standing is why the advice mattered.

swap_slots.span: I started in the September
swap_slots.prompt: Your own starting point — name the month or the year, once, and early.

swap_slots.span: don't do the course part-time while you're working full-time
swap_slots.prompt: The advice itself, as close to their wording as you can manage. Not a paraphrase.

swap_slots.span: going to lectures until nine and doing coursework until midnight
swap_slots.prompt: What you did instead, with times or durations in it. This is where the cost becomes real.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now run the same four moves for advice you did take and were glad of. Forty-five seconds, mixed verdict included.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about an advice from my aunt. She told me not to study in the evening and work in the day at the same time, because she did this before and it was too hard for her.

She said to me: wait one year, save some money, and after that study normally. My mother is also agree with her. But I didn't listen to them.

I started the course in September and I was working full time also. Every evening I go to the class until nine, and after that I am doing the homework until midnight. For two years I don't see my friends and I was tired all the time. Twice I nearly stopped.

But I finished it. Now I have the qualification and I have a better job also. So I think I was right. But she was also right, because it was very hard, more hard than I think before. If I listened to her, maybe I am less tired now. So this is the advice which I didn't take.

what_caps_it.point: 'An advice', 'is agree', a broken comparative and a collapsed conditional in four minutes of speech.
'Very hard', 'tired', 'better job' — the verdict is delivered in the plainest words available.
The two-year period is told twice and the feeling is asserted rather than explained.

annotations.span: Twice I nearly stopped.
annotations.label: One honest detail, correctly in the past
annotations.why: Keep this — a small admission is worth more than a summary.

annotations.span: an advice from my aunt
annotations.label: 'Advice' is uncountable
annotations.why: 'Some advice' or 'a piece of advice' — never 'an advice'.

annotations.span: My mother is also agree with her.
annotations.label: 'Agree' does not take 'is'
annotations.why: 'My mother agreed with her too.' It is a verb on its own.

annotations.span: Every evening I go to the class until nine, and after that I am doing the homework until midnight.
annotations.label: Two past years told in the present
annotations.why: 'I went to class until nine and did coursework until midnight.'

annotations.span: more hard than I think before
annotations.label: Comparative and tense both slip
annotations.why: 'Harder than I'd expected.' One-syllable adjectives take -er.

annotations.span: If I listened to her, maybe I am less tired now.
annotations.label: Regret without the perfect forms
annotations.why: 'If I'd listened to her, I'd have been less tired.'

model_answers.label: The target — same decision, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The advice came from my aunt, who'd done the same thing fifteen years earlier and had every right to an opinion about it.

What she said, more or less, was: don't do the course part-time while you're working full-time. Wait a year, save up, and do it properly. She wasn't being discouraging — she'd tried exactly that combination herself, dropped out in the second year, and clearly didn't want to watch somebody repeat it. My mother agreed with her, which normally settles things.

I did it anyway. I started in the September, kept the job, and spent two years going to lectures until nine and doing coursework until midnight. I saw almost nobody, and nobody at work knew about it for the first six months, which made the timetable worse. There were two points, both in the second winter, when I came very close to giving up, and I still don't quite know why I didn't.

How I feel about it now is complicated, which I think is the honest answer. I finished, I've got the qualification, and it did change what I could apply for, so on the face of it I was right. But she wasn't wrong about the cost — she was wrong about the outcome, and those aren't the same thing. If I'd waited the year she suggested, I'd have arrived at the same place two years later and considerably less exhausted. What I actually do now is give her advice to other people, word for word, which tells you something.

what_lifts_it.point: Reported speech with backshift, one past perfect and one third conditional carry the whole card.
'On the face of it', 'word for word', 'settles things' — chunks instead of adjectives.
The verdict is announced as complicated and then actually made complicated.

annotations.span: What she said, more or less, was:
annotations.label: Reports the advice instead of performing it
annotations.why: Reporting is safer than acting, and it shows the grammar off.

annotations.span: she'd tried exactly that combination herself, dropped out in the second year
annotations.label: Past perfect gives her the standing
annotations.why: One backshift explains why the advice was worth hearing.

annotations.span: which normally settles things
annotations.label: Four words of dry understatement
annotations.why: Understatement sounds native far more than emphasis does.

annotations.span: I did it anyway.
annotations.label: A three-word pivot into bullet three
annotations.why: Short sentences between long ones control your pace.

annotations.span: How I feel about it now is complicated, which I think is the honest answer.
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet honestly
annotations.why: Announcing a mixed verdict buys you thirty seconds of reasoning.

annotations.span: on the face of it
annotations.label: Marks a verdict as provisional
annotations.why: Use it whenever the obvious conclusion is about to be complicated.

annotations.span: she was wrong about the outcome, and those aren't the same thing
annotations.label: Splits one judgement into two
annotations.why: Separating cost from outcome is the reasoning band 7 rewards.

annotations.span: If I'd waited the year she suggested, I'd have arrived at the same place two years later
annotations.label: Third conditional for the road not taken
annotations.why: The natural structure on any 'how do you feel now' bullet.

annotations.span: word for word, which tells you something
annotations.label: Falling tone on the last three words
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop and the implication does the work.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The advice came from my aunt, who had attempted the same thing fifteen years before me and had earned the right to an opinion on it.

Her position, in short, was this: do not take the course part-time while holding down a full-time job. Wait a year, put some money aside, then do it properly. There was nothing discouraging in it — she had tried precisely that combination, come off it in her second year, and had no wish to watch it happen twice. My mother agreed, which as a rule ends the discussion.

I went ahead regardless. Started that September, kept the job, and spent two years in lectures until nine and coursework until midnight, seeing virtually nobody. Nobody at work knew about it for the first six months. Twice, both times in the second winter, I came within a week of abandoning the whole thing, and I still could not tell you what stopped me.

What I feel about it now is genuinely mixed, which strikes me as the only honest answer available. I finished; the qualification opened doors; on the face of it, then, she was wrong. Except that she was not wrong about the cost — only about the outcome, and those are not the same error. Had I waited the year she proposed, I would have reached the same place two years later and a good deal less worn out. What I now do, naturally, is hand her advice on to other people, almost word for word.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion and a colon-led reported position replace band 7's 'if' clause and its framing.
'Come off it', 'as a rule', 'worn out' — ordinary phrases placed exactly.
The close treats the two errors as different in kind, which the story only implied.

annotations.span: Had I waited the year she proposed
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Identical meaning, higher register, and still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: come off it in her second year
annotations.label: A plain phrasal verb, exactly right
annotations.why: Everyday phrasal verbs read as fluent; formal synonyms do not.

annotations.span: which as a rule ends the discussion
annotations.label: Dry aside about a family habit
annotations.why: One wry clause makes the whole turn sound unrehearsed.

annotations.span: Started that September, kept the job
annotations.label: Subjectless fragments in one rhythm
annotations.why: Dropping 'I' twice is natural speech, not an error.

annotations.span: only about the outcome, and those are not the same error
annotations.label: Distinguishes two kinds of being wrong
annotations.why: Ending on a distinction lifts the answer above the anecdote.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a place where I go when I must decide something. It is car park near the market, on the top floor, and it is about ten minutes from my flat.

I go there in the evening, because at that time it is empty. So it is very quiet and I can think properly. Last spring I have a problem, because a company offered me a job in another city, and I don't know what to do about it. So I go there three evenings.

What I do is, I walk around the top floor two times. And then I stand in the corner and I speak the reasons loudly, like I am talking to another person. It is a little bit strange but it is helpful. Sometimes I make a list in my phone, sometimes not.

Why it helps me is because there is nothing there. In my flat there are many things and I am always thinking about other things. But there it is only concrete and the sky. Also the car park is closing at ten o'clock, so I cannot stay all night. In the end I decided to say no to the job. I felt good about this decision. So this is the place where I go when I have to decide something.

what_caps_it.point: The story slides into the present three times and one article is missing entirely.
Almost every sentence opens with 'so' or 'and', and the close repeats the card.
'Quiet', 'strange', 'helpful', 'good' — four flat adjectives carry the whole evaluation.

annotations.span: I go there in the evening, because at that time it is empty.
annotations.label: Gives a reason unprompted
annotations.why: Keep this habit — a 'because' clause after every fact is the cheapest upgrade there is.

annotations.span: It is car park near the market
annotations.label: Missing article
annotations.why: Say 'it's a car park'. Every singular countable noun needs a determiner in front of it.

annotations.span: Last spring I have a problem
annotations.label: Past story told in the present
annotations.why: Fix the tense in the first sentence of the story, then hold it to the end.

annotations.span: It is a little bit strange but it is helpful.
annotations.label: Two flat adjectives doing the evaluation
annotations.why: Swap for 'faintly ridiculous' and 'it does the job' — chunks, not adjectives.

annotations.span: the car park is closing at ten o'clock
annotations.label: Continuous used for a fixed fact
annotations.why: Say 'the car park closes at ten'. Scheduled facts take the present simple.

annotations.span: So this is the place where I go when I have to decide something.
annotations.label: Closes by reading the card back
annotations.why: End on a thought about places like it, not on the words of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the top floor of a multi-storey car park behind the market, which is about ten minutes from my flat on foot and is completely empty after about seven in the evening.

I don't go there for the view, exactly, though you can see most of the town from up there. I go when there's something I've been putting off deciding. Last spring, for instance, I'd been offered a job in another city, and I'd been going round in circles about it for the best part of a fortnight. I ended up going up there three evenings running.

What I actually do is fairly odd, I suppose. I walk two laps of the top level, and then I stand at the far corner and say the arguments out loud, one at a time, as if I were explaining them to somebody else. There's never anybody up there, so it doesn't matter how it looks.

As for why it helps — I think it's because the place has nothing at all to do with the decision. My flat is full of reminders, whereas up there there's nothing but concrete and sky, so the thing I'm weighing up is the only thing in front of me. There's also the fact that I can't stay indefinitely, because the barrier comes down at ten, and having a hard stop is what stops me mulling it over forever. I came down on the third evening having decided to turn the job down, and I've never really had second thoughts about it.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect for the background and 'as if I were' replace a flat run of past simples.
'Going round in circles', 'a hard stop', 'second thoughts' — chunks instead of adjectives.
Two spoken signposts give the turn a shape the listener can hear arriving.

annotations.span: I'll talk about the top floor of a multi-storey car park behind the market
annotations.label: Locates the place in one sentence
annotations.why: Give position and distance immediately; it saves you hunting for them later.

annotations.span: I don't go there for the view, exactly
annotations.label: Rules out the obvious answer first
annotations.why: Saying what it isn't buys a clause and sets up what it is.

annotations.span: I'd been going round in circles about it for the best part of a fortnight
annotations.label: Past perfect continuous for the run-up
annotations.why: Use it once per story to show something was already under way.

annotations.span: as if I were explaining them to somebody else
annotations.label: Unreal comparison with 'as if'
annotations.why: 'As if I were' is a ready-made subjunctive — keep it for any description of a habit.

annotations.span: As for why it helps
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet aloud
annotations.why: Naming the move out loud is the surest way not to skip the 'explain' bullet.

annotations.span: whereas up there there's nothing but concrete and sky
annotations.label: Contrast carried by 'whereas'
annotations.why: 'Whereas' joins two full clauses; 'but' would flatten the comparison.

annotations.span: having a hard stop is what stops me mulling it over forever
annotations.label: Two precise chunks in one clause
annotations.why: Reuse 'a hard stop' for any deadline that does you a favour.

annotations.span: I came down on the third evening having decided to turn the job down
annotations.label: Perfect participle compresses two events
annotations.why: 'Having decided' saves a whole clause and sounds entirely spoken.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place is the top deck of a car park behind the market — ten minutes on foot from my flat and, after about seven, completely deserted.

I go up there when something needs deciding and I've been dodging it. Last spring a firm in another city offered me a job, and I'd spent the better part of a fortnight going round in circles, so I took the whole thing up there on three consecutive evenings.

What I do is faintly ridiculous, admittedly. Two laps of the top level, then I plant myself in the far corner and argue the case out loud, one point at a time, as though somebody were standing there disagreeing with me. Not once have I met anybody up there, so there's nobody to explain myself to.

The reason it works, I think, is that the place has no stake in the outcome. Home is full of prompts — post on the table, the people I'd have to tell — whereas up there it's concrete, sky and one question. What also helps is the deadline: the barrier drops at ten, so there's a limit on how long I can sit on the fence. I walked down on the third evening having turned the job down in my head, and I haven't lost a night's sleep over it since. I suspect that's the real use of a place like that. It doesn't make you any wiser; it just stops you putting the thing off any longer.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion after 'not once' and a cleft with 'what also helps' replace ordinary word order.
'No stake in the outcome' and 'sit on the fence' land exactly where a native would put them.
The close abstracts to what such places are for instead of summing up the story.

annotations.span: Not once have I met anybody up there
annotations.label: Inversion after a negative adverbial
annotations.why: Same meaning as 'I've never met anybody', a register higher, still spoken.

annotations.span: the place has no stake in the outcome
annotations.label: One precise phrase carries the point
annotations.why: 'No stake in' is the shade of meaning that 'not related' cannot reach.

annotations.span: there's a limit on how long I can sit on the fence
annotations.label: Idiom used where a native would use it
annotations.why: Two idioms placed naturally beat six displayed ones.

annotations.span: concrete, sky and one question
annotations.label: Three-item list in one rhythmic run
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across the first two, then fall on the third.

annotations.span: It doesn't make you any wiser; it just stops you putting the thing off any longer.
annotations.label: Ends on a general claim
annotations.why: Lift the last line off your own story and the whole turn rises with it.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about a building which is very interesting for me. It is a water tower, at the end of the old railway yard, about one mile from my house.

The building is very tall, maybe five floors, and it is made from red brick. The brick is very old and in some places it is black now. On the top there is a big square part. This was the tank for the water, and it is much more wider than the tower under it. Somebody put big windows in this part, so in the night you can see a kitchen inside, with a light.

Before, it was for the steam trains, so nobody thinks about how it looks. After that it was empty for thirty years, I think. And then some people buy it and they make it into a house.

Why it is interesting is because it is different. The other buildings around are all normal, but this one is strange. Also I like that it was not built for beautiful, it was built for water. Every time when I pass I am looking up at the windows. So this is the building which I find very interesting to look at.

what_caps_it.point: A double comparative, a present-tense slip in the history, and one preposition error.
'Very tall', 'normal', 'strange', 'interesting' carry a whole description on their own.
Four sentences begin with 'so' or 'also', and the last line reads the card back.

annotations.span: The building is very tall, maybe five floors, and it is made from red brick.
annotations.label: Puts size and material together
annotations.why: Keep this — two physical facts in one sentence is exactly the right density.

annotations.span: it is much more wider than the tower under it
annotations.label: Double comparative
annotations.why: Say 'much wider'. 'More' and '-er' can never appear in the same phrase.

annotations.span: so nobody thinks about how it looks
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past history
annotations.why: Say 'nobody thought about how it looked' — the whole paragraph is past.

annotations.span: in the night you can see a kitchen inside
annotations.label: Wrong preposition of time
annotations.why: It is 'at night', always. Learn it as one fixed chunk.

annotations.span: it was not built for beautiful
annotations.label: Adjective used as a noun
annotations.why: Say 'it wasn't built to be looked at' — a clause, not a bare adjective.

annotations.span: So this is the building which I find very interesting to look at.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the prompt
annotations.why: Finish on an idea about buildings, not on the words of the card.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The building I want to describe is a Victorian water tower at the far end of the old railway yard, about a mile from where I live. It's been converted into a house by somebody with rather a lot of money, which is really what makes it worth a second look.

It's a plain square tower of dark red brick, five storeys or so, and the brick has weathered almost to black on one side. Sitting on top of it there's a much wider tank section, so the whole thing looks top-heavy, a bit like a hat two sizes too big. Somebody has cut a run of enormous windows into that tank, and at night you can see a lit kitchen up there, apparently floating above the car park below it.

It was put up in the 1880s to hold water for the steam engines, so nobody ever meant it to be looked at. Once the trains stopped it fell into disrepair and stood empty for about thirty years, and then a couple bought it and spent, apparently, the best part of a decade converting it.

As for why I find it interesting — it isn't the brickwork so much as the mismatch. It was designed by an engineer for a job that no longer exists, whereas everything around it was designed to be admired and mostly isn't worth looking at. There's something about a building that outlives its own purpose that I find genuinely moving, and I don't think that's just me being sentimental about trains. Every time I go past I catch myself looking up at those windows.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Weathered', 'top-heavy', 'fell into disrepair' replace four uses of 'very'.
Fronted 'sitting on top of it' and a clean passive history replace flat subject-verb order.
The description moves outside to top to inside, so the listener can follow the eye.

annotations.span: which is really what makes it worth a second look
annotations.label: Says why before describing
annotations.why: Give the listener a reason to care in sentence one; the description then lands.

annotations.span: the brick has weathered almost to black on one side
annotations.label: A verb doing the work of an adjective
annotations.why: 'Has weathered' beats 'is very old' and costs the same breath.

annotations.span: Sitting on top of it there's a much wider tank section
annotations.label: Fronted participle places the object
annotations.why: Start with the position and the listener builds the picture in order.

annotations.span: a bit like a hat two sizes too big
annotations.label: One comparison instead of three adjectives
annotations.why: A single homely simile does more than a list of dimensions.

annotations.span: it fell into disrepair and stood empty for about thirty years
annotations.label: The exact phrase for slow neglect
annotations.why: Reuse 'fell into disrepair' for any building, road or scheme left alone.

annotations.span: As for why I find it interesting
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Say the move out loud and you cannot forget to make it.

annotations.span: whereas everything around it was designed to be admired
annotations.label: Passive plus 'whereas' in one clause
annotations.why: The passive keeps the focus on the buildings, not on nameless architects.

annotations.span: I catch myself looking up at those windows
annotations.label: 'Catch myself' for an unplanned habit
annotations.why: Use it whenever you do something without deciding to.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The building I've picked is a Victorian water tower standing at the far end of the old railway yard, a mile or so from my flat and now, improbably, somebody's house.

It's a plain square tower of dark red brick, five storeys at a guess, weathered nearly to black on the side that takes the weather. Perched on top is the tank itself, far wider than the tower beneath it, which gives the whole thing a distinctly top-heavy look. Someone has cut a run of enormous windows into that tank, and after dark you can see a lit kitchen suspended above the car park below.

It went up in the 1880s to feed the steam engines, which is to say it was drawn by an engineer with no interest whatsoever in how it looked. Once the engines went, it stood empty for the better part of thirty years, slowly falling into disrepair, before a couple took it on and spent, by all accounts, a decade converting it.

What holds my attention isn't the brickwork; it's the mismatch. Here is a building that has outlived its own purpose and become, entirely by accident, the most striking thing for a mile in any direction. Everything around it was put up to be admired — the retail park, the new offices, the flats by the bridge — and almost none of it repays the effort. I think there's something in that about how buildings earn their looks — rarely, in my experience, by setting out to.

what_lifts_it.point: Inverted 'perched on top is the tank' and a cleft opening replace ordinary subject-first order.
'No interest whatsoever', 'repays the effort', 'outlived its own purpose' — precision, not rarity.
The close turns the tower into a claim about buildings in general.

annotations.span: Perched on top is the tank itself
annotations.label: Full inversion after a place phrase
annotations.why: Put the location first and invert; the listener builds the picture in order.

annotations.span: with no interest whatsoever in how it looked
annotations.label: 'Whatsoever' sharpens a negative
annotations.why: One emphatic word does more than three intensifiers in a row.

annotations.span: has outlived its own purpose
annotations.label: A precise verb for the whole idea
annotations.why: Choose the verb that carries the argument and the sentence shortens itself.

annotations.span: a mile or so from my flat and now, improbably, somebody's house
annotations.label: Parenthesis marked by pitch
annotations.why: Drop the pitch on 'improbably' and lift again after it.

annotations.span: rarely, in my experience, by setting out to
annotations.label: Ends on a hedged generalisation
annotations.why: Abstract away from your example in the final clause and the turn closes upward.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about the place where I go for exercise. It is the swimming pool in the leisure centre, near the park. The building is old, from 1930s I think, and it has a glass roof.

I go there three times in a week, in the morning before my work. Because if I go in the evening, I will not go, I know myself very well. I go since two years, because the doctor told me that my back is bad if I am sitting all the day.

What I do there is very simple. I swim forty lengths in the slow lane. It takes maybe twenty-five minutes and then I go out. I don't count very good, so I count eight and then eight again. There is one old man, he is always coming before me, but we never speak to each other.

Why I like this place is because I cannot say no to it. The pool is closing the lanes at eight o'clock, so I must go early. Also nobody can call me in the water, so it is very peaceful there. After that I am very tired but it is a good tired. So that is my place for the exercise and I am going there very often.

what_caps_it.point: 'Since two years', a continuous used for a fixed timetable, and one missing article.
'Simple', 'peaceful', 'a good tired' — the evaluation runs on three vague words.
Three sentences open with 'so' or 'also' and the final line repeats the card.

annotations.span: I don't count very good

annotations.why: Say 'I don't count very well'. Verbs take adverbs, not adjectives.

annotations.span: After that I am very tired but it is a good tired.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I want to describe is the swimming pool at the leisure centre on the other side of the park — a 1930s building with a glass roof, and at seven in the morning there's hardly anybody in it.

I go three mornings a week, always before work, because if I leave it until the evening I know perfectly well I won't go at all. I've been doing it for a couple of years now, ever since a physiotherapist told me my back would only get worse if I carried on sitting at a desk for nine hours a day.

What I actually do is unvarying to the point of being dull. Forty lengths, in the slow lane, in roughly the same twenty-five minutes, and then I'm out. I stopped counting properly a long time ago, so now I count in blocks of eight and lose my place at least twice. There's a man of about seventy who's always in before me and always finishes after me, and we've never once spoken.

The reason it suits me, I think, is that nothing about it is optional. The lanes close at eight, so there's no negotiating with myself about whether I'm going. And it's the one hour in the day when nobody can reach me, because you can't take a phone into the water, whereas in a gym I'd be checking mine between sets. I come out shattered, and I get more done on the mornings after a swim than on the ones I skip.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Ever since' plus a past narrative and a clean conditional replace the broken duration phrase.
'Unvarying', 'no negotiating with myself', 'shattered' land where four vague words were.
Each paragraph answers one bullet, so the listener always knows which one is running.

annotations.span: at seven in the morning there's hardly anybody in it
annotations.label: Adds the time of day to the place
annotations.why: A place at an hour is more specific than a place — and it costs four words.

annotations.span: because if I leave it until the evening I know perfectly well I won't go at all
annotations.label: First conditional giving a real reason
annotations.why: Use a conditional to justify a habit; it beats 'because it is better'.

annotations.span: ever since a physiotherapist told me my back would only get worse
annotations.label: Reported speech with backshift
annotations.why: 'Told me it would' is the natural past of 'it will' — practise the pair.

annotations.span: unvarying to the point of being dull
annotations.label: Owns the dullness instead of hiding it
annotations.why: Naming the flat bit of your own story sounds confident, not apologetic.

annotations.span: I stopped counting properly a long time ago
annotations.label: A small human detail inside the routine
annotations.why: One oddity makes a routine memorable; three make it a list.

annotations.span: The reason it suits me, I think, is that nothing about it is optional.
annotations.label: Opens the fourth bullet with the answer
annotations.why: State the reason first, then support it — don't build up to it.

annotations.span: whereas in a gym I'd be checking mine between sets
annotations.label: Hypothetical contrast with 'whereas'
annotations.why: Compare with the option you rejected and the choice starts to sound reasoned.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place is the pool at the leisure centre across the park — a 1930s building with a glass roof which, at seven in the morning, is more or less deserted.

I swim three mornings a week, always before work, on the principle that anything left until the evening simply doesn't happen. I've been at it a couple of years, ever since a physiotherapist pointed out that nine hours a day at a desk was only ever going to end one way.

What I do there is unvarying to the point of dullness: forty lengths in the slow lane, twenty-five minutes give or take, and out. I gave up counting properly long ago and now go in blocks of eight, losing my place at least twice on the way. Rarely do I see more than a handful of people at that hour, and one of them, a man of about seventy, has been in before me every single time without the two of us ever exchanging a word.

What makes it work is that none of it is up for discussion. The lanes close at eight, so there's no negotiating with myself on the way out of the door, and it's the one hour of the day when I'm genuinely unreachable — you can't take a phone into the water, whereas at a gym I'd be glancing at mine between sets. title: A noisy place you often have to spend time in

cue_card.topic: Describe a noisy place that you often have to spend time in.

target_words.note: Stress it when contrasting with sounds that stop.
Hit this word when setting it against machines.

whereas a voice pulls your attention
whether you want it to or not.

swap_slots.prompt: Your own place, with one number in it. A number makes a room specific instantly.

swap_slots.prompt: Your real frequency, and say what makes the exceptions happen.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now name three separate sources of noise in the street where you live and rank them by how much they bother you. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will describe the place where I am working, it is very noisy. It is a big office in the second floor with thirty desks, and there is no walls between them.

Why it is noisy is many reasons. First, the air conditioning is making a noise all the time, but after some time you don't hear it any more. Second, there are three sales teams and they are talking on the phone all the day. Also the coffee machine is near my desk, so many people are standing there and speaking. And under our building there is a shop for builders, so the lorries are coming at seven o'clock in the morning.

I am there five days in a week, sometimes four.

How I deal with the noise. I do the difficult work early, before ten o'clock, because at this time there are only some people. After that I put my headphones, but without music, because music is more bad. The thing I cannot accept is when people are speaking on the phone. A machine is ok but a voice is different. This is my noisy place.

what_caps_it.point: Habits told in the continuous, one plural agreement error and a broken comparative.
'First, second, also, and' is a list; the third bullet gets a single line.
'Noisy', 'different', 'ok' — no chunk anywhere to name what the noise is like.

annotations.span: I do the difficult work early, before ten o'clock
annotations.label: Names a real strategy
annotations.why: Keep this — a concrete tactic answers the bullet far better than a feeling.

annotations.span: It is a big office in the second floor
annotations.label: Wrong preposition with a floor
annotations.why: It is 'on the second floor'. Store the preposition with the phrase.

annotations.span: there is no walls between them
annotations.label: Singular verb with a plural noun
annotations.why: Say 'there aren't any walls between them'.

annotations.span: they are talking on the phone all the day
annotations.label: Continuous used for an everyday habit
annotations.why: Say 'they're on the phone all day' — habits take the simple form.

annotations.span: because music is more bad
annotations.label: Regular comparative on an irregular word
annotations.why: 'Bad' becomes 'worse'. There are only about six of these — learn them.

annotations.span: This is my noisy place.
annotations.label: Ends by labelling the card
annotations.why: Close on what the noise does to people, not on the title of the task.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'll describe is the office I work in, which is an open-plan room on the second floor with about thirty desks in it and no partitions of any kind. I'm there five days a week, or four if I can justify working from home on a Friday.

What makes it noisy isn't any one thing, and that's part of the problem. There's a constant hum off the air conditioning that you stop hearing after twenty minutes or so. On top of that, three sales teams sit behind me and they're on the phone from nine until six. The coffee machine happens to be at the end of my row, so there's a queue beside me from about half past nine. And the whole building sits above a builders' merchant, so lorries start reversing into the yard at seven.

As for how I deal with it, I've had to build the day round it rather than fight it. Anything that needs real thought I do before ten, when there are half a dozen people in. After that the headphones go on, though not with music, because music turns out to be worse — it's just noise I've chosen instead of noise I haven't.

If I'm honest, the part I've never got used to is other people's phone calls. You can tune out a machine, whereas a voice pulls your attention whether you want it to or not, and I don't think that's something you can train yourself out of.

what_lifts_it.point: The sources are separated and ranked instead of being listed as first, second, also.
'A constant hum', 'tune out', 'build the day round it' replace three uses of 'noise'.
Fronted objects and a clean relative clause carry structures the band-6 version never attempts.

annotations.span: What makes it noisy isn't any one thing, and that's part of the problem.
annotations.label: Frames the whole bullet before answering it
annotations.why: One framing sentence buys you time and organises everything after it.

annotations.span: There's a constant hum off the air conditioning
annotations.label: Names the type of sound, not its volume
annotations.why: 'Hum', 'clatter', 'drone' each say more than 'a big noise'.

annotations.span: On top of that
annotations.label: Adds without using 'also' again
annotations.why: Rotate your additive links; three 'alsos' is audible.

annotations.span: Anything that needs real thought I do before ten
annotations.label: Object fronted for emphasis
annotations.why: Put the important thing first and the sentence sounds deliberate.

annotations.span: it's just noise I've chosen instead of noise I haven't
annotations.label: A neat parallel does the arguing
annotations.why: Repeating a word with a twist is cheaper than a new clause and lands harder.

annotations.span: the part I've never got used to is other people's phone calls
annotations.label: Cleft plus present perfect
annotations.why: 'The part I've never got used to is…' works on any coping card.

annotations.span: You can tune out a machine, whereas a voice pulls your attention
annotations.label: Phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Tune out' is exactly the verb here; nothing formal improves on it.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place is the office I work in — open plan, second floor, thirty-odd desks and not a partition in sight. I'm in it five days a week, four if I can justify a Friday at home.

What makes it noisy is that no single thing does. There's a constant hum off the air conditioning which you stop registering within about twenty minutes; three sales teams sit behind me and are on the phone from nine until six; and the coffee machine sits, of all places, at the end of my row, so from half past nine there's a queue at my shoulder. Underneath all of it, the building sits above a builders' merchant, and the lorries begin reversing into the yard at seven.

I gave up fighting it a long time ago, which is the only approach that has ever worked. The thinking gets done before ten, when there are half a dozen people in and the place is almost civilised. After that the headphones go on — not music, though, because music is simply noise I've chosen rather than noise I haven't.

What I've never managed to tune out is other people's phone calls. Machines you can learn to ignore, whereas a human voice takes your attention whether you have given it permission or not. I've come round to thinking that isn't a failing on my part. We are built to listen to voices, and asking thirty of us to sit in one room and not listen is a fairly strange thing to expect.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft opener and a fronted object replace two plain statements from the band-7 version.
'Not a partition in sight', 'stop registering', 'come round to thinking' are exact rather than rare.
The close turns a personal irritation into a general claim about attention.

annotations.span: What makes it noisy is that no single thing does.
annotations.label: Cleft with an elliptical answer
annotations.why: The short second half does the work — resist the urge to explain it.

annotations.span: not a partition in sight
annotations.label: Idiomatic negative for absence
annotations.why: 'Not a … in sight' fits any place missing the obvious thing.

annotations.span: which you stop registering within about twenty minutes
annotations.label: One precise verb for a whole idea
annotations.why: 'Stop registering' says in two words what 'you don't hear it any more' needs six for.

annotations.span: Machines you can learn to ignore, whereas a human voice takes your attention
annotations.label: Fronting sets up the contrast
annotations.why: Front the thing you are contrasting and the listener hears the shape coming.

annotations.span: asking thirty of us to sit in one room and not listen is a fairly strange thing to expect
annotations.label: Closes on a general claim
annotations.why: Convert your complaint into an observation about people and the turn lifts.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about my hobby, it is gardening. But I don't have a garden, I have an allotment. It is a small piece of land which you can rent from the council, and it is fifteen minutes walking from my flat.

I am going there in the Saturday morning, and in summer also one or two times in the week, because it is light in the evening. It is a small plot but there is always some work to do. Usually I am alone. There is one woman in the next plot, she is there since thirty years, and she is always giving me advices about my vegetables.

How I started is a little bit funny. My neighbour was old and he was sick, so he asked me to take care of his plot for one summer. I never grow anything before, and in the first summer everything is dying. After he died in the winter, and I put my name in the list for my own plot.

I like it because you cannot do it fast. If I don't go for two weeks, the weeds are growing everywhere. And I can see the result of my work, this is a good feeling. So this is my outdoor activity.

what_caps_it.point: The origin story runs half in the present, and duration is expressed with 'since'.
'Advices' is not a word, and 'a good feeling' does the whole evaluation.
The talk ends on the card's own words and the third bullet gets one sentence.

annotations.span: How I started is a little bit funny.
annotations.label: Announces the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Keep this — naming the move stops you skipping the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: she is there since thirty years
annotations.label: Duration with the wrong tense and preposition
annotations.why: Say 'she's been there for thirty years'. Length of time takes 'for'.

annotations.span: she is always giving me advices
annotations.label: Plural on an uncountable noun
annotations.why: 'Advice' never takes -s. Count it as 'a piece of advice'.

annotations.span: I never grow anything before, and in the first summer everything is dying.
annotations.label: Past story told in the present
annotations.why: Say 'I'd never grown anything, and everything died'. Two past layers, both marked.

annotations.span: I put my name in the list
annotations.label: Wrong preposition with 'list'
annotations.why: You put a name 'on' a list. Store the preposition with the noun.

annotations.span: So this is my outdoor activity.
annotations.label: Ends by naming the task
annotations.why: Finish on why you still go, not on the label the examiner gave you.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The activity I'll talk about is gardening, though not in a garden of my own — I've got an allotment, which is a rented plot on a site about fifteen minutes' walk from my flat.

I go up there most Saturday mornings, and once or twice during the week in summer while it stays light. It's only a quarter of a plot, so it isn't very big, but it's easily enough to keep me busy for four or five hours at a time. Mostly I'm on my own, although there's a woman on the next plot who's been there thirty years and gives me advice whether I've asked for it or not.

How I got into it was almost accidental. My old neighbour had a plot and got too unwell to manage it, so he asked me to keep it going for a season while he recovered. I'd never grown anything in my life, and I killed most of what was already in the ground that first summer. He died the following winter, and by then I'd put my name down for one of my own without ever quite deciding to.

What keeps me going back is that none of it can be hurried. If I don't turn up for a fortnight, the weeds win, and there's no arguing with that. It's also the only thing I do all week where the results are visible — I can point at a row and say I put that there in March.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect twice, and the gear change from present habit to past story is clean.
'Keep it going', 'put my name down', 'the weeds win' replace flat verbs.
Each bullet gets a paragraph, and the origin story gets the longest one.

annotations.span: though not in a garden of my own
annotations.label: Corrects an assumption immediately
annotations.why: Heading off the obvious misunderstanding buys a clause and sounds precise.

annotations.span: gives me advice whether I've asked for it or not
annotations.label: Characterises a person in six words
annotations.why: One habit is worth more than three adjectives when describing somebody.

annotations.span: How I got into it was almost accidental.
annotations.label: Signposts and evaluates at once
annotations.why: Say what kind of story is coming before you tell it.

annotations.span: I'd never grown anything in my life
annotations.label: Past perfect for the earlier layer
annotations.why: Use it for what was already true when the story began.

annotations.span: by then I'd put my name down for one of my own without ever quite deciding to
annotations.label: Past perfect plus a trailing infinitive
annotations.why: 'Without ever quite deciding to' is a whole attitude in six words.

annotations.span: What keeps me going back is that none of it can be hurried.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the evaluation
annotations.why: Put the reason first; the evidence for it then has somewhere to go.

annotations.span: the weeds win, and there's no arguing with that
annotations.label: Plain words used with force
annotations.why: Short concrete language beats formal vocabulary in a spoken exam.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
What I do outdoors is grow vegetables, though not in a garden of my own: I rent a quarter-plot on an allotment site ten minutes up the hill from my flat.

I'm up there most Saturday mornings and, in summer, an evening or two in the week while the light holds. It's small enough to walk across in fifteen paces and quite big enough to keep me there half a day. I'm generally on my own, aside from the woman on the next plot, who has held it for thirty years and dispenses advice whether or not it has been asked for.

I fell into it entirely by accident. A neighbour of mine had the plot and became too ill to manage it, and he asked me to keep it ticking over for a season. I had never grown so much as a pot of herbs, and I lost most of what was already in the ground that first summer. He died that winter, and by then I had put my name down for one of my own without ever quite deciding to.

What keeps me going back is that none of it can be rushed. Miss a fortnight and the weeds have the run of the place; there is no negotiating with a season. It's also the only thing in my week whose results I can stand and point at — that row went in during March, and there it is. Precious little else I do leaves a mark like that.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative used as a conditional, plus a relative clause with 'whose', both new here.
'Keep it ticking over', 'dispenses advice', 'the run of the place' sit exactly right.
The final line generalises about the week rather than restating the hobby.

annotations.span: Miss a fortnight and the weeds have the run of the place
annotations.label: Imperative doing a conditional's job
annotations.why: 'Do X and Y happens' is faster and more spoken than 'if you do X'.

annotations.span: dispenses advice whether or not it has been asked for
annotations.label: One verb carries the whole character
annotations.why: 'Dispenses' is gently ironic — the precision is the joke.

annotations.span: keep it ticking over for a season
annotations.label: Idiom for minimum maintenance
annotations.why: Reuse it for a business, a project or a friendship you are just sustaining.

annotations.span: It's small enough to walk across in fifteen paces and quite big enough to keep me there half a day.
annotations.label: Balanced pair, stress on the contrast
annotations.why: Hit 'small' and 'big'; let everything between them stay level.

annotations.span: Precious little else I do leaves a mark like that.
annotations.label: Closes by widening to the whole week
annotations.why: One sentence that steps outside the anecdote is enough to lift the ending.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
For relaxing I do something which is maybe a bit strange. I wash the dishes with my hand. We have a dishwasher machine in the kitchen but I am not using it very much.

I do this after the dinner, so around eight o'clock, and it takes twenty minutes, or a little bit more if I cooked something big. I open the radio, not music but people who are talking. And I always do it in the same order, first the glasses, then the plates, and the pans at the end.

I know it is a strange answer for relax. But the reason is that it is finished. In my job nothing is finished, you close the computer and tomorrow it is the same again. But the sink is empty or it is not empty. This is a good feeling for me.

Also it is not difficult, so my hands are busy but my head is free. If I take my phone, after one hour I am thinking about work again. But with the dishes, when I finish, I am not thinking about work any more. My wife says I am strange. So this is what I do to relax.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
What I do to relax is probably the least exciting answer you'll get all day: I wash up. By hand, deliberately, even though there's a dishwasher about two feet away that I hardly ever use.

It happens after dinner, so usually somewhere between eight and half past, and it takes about twenty minutes from start to finish — a bit longer, obviously, if I've cooked something ambitious and there are pans involved. I put the radio on, talk rather than music, and I work through it in the same order every time: glasses first, then plates, pans last.

I'm aware of how that sounds as an answer to a question about relaxing. The reason it works, though, is that it's the only thing in my day with an obvious end to it. Most of what I do at work is unfinished — you close the laptop and it's still sitting there in the morning. The sink, on the other hand, is either empty or it isn't. There's something quite settling about a job you can complete in twenty minutes.

The other half of it is that it's just repetitive enough to occupy my hands and leave my head alone. If I sit down with my phone instead, I'm still turning the day over an hour later, whereas by the time the pans are done I've generally stopped. My partner thinks I'm strange about it, and I gave up trying to explain a while ago. I don't think it would work as an argument anyway.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Turning the day over', 'settling', 'occupy my hands' replace three approximate phrases.
Two reasons are announced and separated, so the argument is audible as an argument.
A concessive 'even though', a conditional and a clean 'whereas' all appear once each.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is possibly the dullest answer anybody will give you today: I do the washing-up. By hand, on purpose, with a perfectly good dishwasher standing two feet away.

It happens straight after dinner — eight o'clock, give or take — and takes twenty minutes from start to finish, appreciably longer if I've been ambitious with the cooking and there are pans to deal with. The radio goes on, talk rather than music, and I work through it in the same sequence every single time: glasses, plates, pans.

I'm aware of how that sounds. What makes it work, though, is that it's the one job in my day with a visible end to it. Almost everything at work is left half-done; you shut the laptop and it's waiting for you in the morning. A sink, by contrast, is either empty or it isn't, and there's something quietly settling about a task you can actually finish before nine.

The other half of it is that it occupies the hands and leaves the head alone. Pick up a phone instead and I'll still be going over the day an hour later; only once the pans are done do I generally stop. My partner finds the whole business baffling, and I gave up trying to explain it years ago. I've come to suspect that a good deal of what people call relaxing really amounts to this — finding one thing in the whole of the day that stays finished once you have finished it.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion after 'only once' and an imperative conditional replace two plain sentences.
'Give or take', 'finds the whole business baffling', 'amounts to' are exact and unforced.
The close turns a private habit into a claim about what relaxing is.

model_answers.transcript:
The skill I'll talk about is playing the piano, which I did as a child, gave up entirely at about fourteen, and picked it up again three years ago.

I practise first thing, before work — twenty minutes, five days a week, and never in the evening, because by then I'd rather not. It's always the same shape, and I don't vary it: five minutes of scales, which I hated as a child and have grudgingly come round to; then whatever piece I happen to be working on at the time; then five minutes of something I can already play from memory, so that I stop while I'm still enjoying it rather than when I've had enough.

I've been at it three years, which sounds longer than it feels. The first six months went on getting back what I'd already had at twelve, and that was oddly demoralising — I could hear exactly what it was meant to sound like, and my hands simply wouldn't do it.

The hardest part, though, hasn't been the technique. It's been accepting how slow the whole thing is. Progress on an instrument arrives in steps rather than a line: you do the same eight bars for a fortnight and nothing happens, and then one morning it's simply there. I've hit two long plateaus where I seriously considered giving the whole thing up, whereas as a child I never noticed a plateau at all, largely because nobody had ever told me that improvement was something to expect.

annotations.why: Use it once for what was already true before your story starts.

annotations.label: Rules out the expected answer
annotations.why: Say what the difficulty wasn't, and the real one lands harder.

annotations.why: A single metaphor is worth three sentences of explanation.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The skill is playing the piano — badly as a child, not at all between fourteen and my thirties, and then, three years ago, again.

I practise first thing, before work: twenty minutes, five mornings a week, never in the evening, because by then I've no patience for it. The shape never varies. Five minutes of scales, which I loathed at eight and have grudgingly come round to; then whatever piece is in front of me; then five minutes of something I can already play, purely so that I stop while I'm still enjoying myself.

Three years in, and most of the first six months went on recovering ground I'd already covered at twelve, which was more dispiriting than starting from nothing would have been. I knew precisely what the thing was meant to sound like, and my hands were having none of it.

What's been hardest, though, isn't the technique — it's the pace. Progress comes in steps rather than a line: a fortnight on the same eight bars with nothing to show for it, and then one morning it is there, as though it had been all along. Twice now I've hit a plateau long enough to make me think seriously about giving it up altogether. As a child I never noticed those, largely because nobody had told me improvement was something to expect — which may be the only real advantage of not knowing what you are doing.

what_lifts_it.point: An unreal 'as though' with the past perfect, and a comparative against a hypothetical clause.
'Having none of it', 'dispiriting', 'nothing to show for it' are exact, not decorative.
The close turns the plateau into a general point about learning as an adult.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe the journey which I do for visiting my mother. She is living in another town, about forty miles from my city.

I go by the train. If I catch the fast train it is twenty-five minutes, but if I don't catch it then I take the slow train, and it takes fifty minutes because it stops in every station. After that I walk twenty minutes from the station to her house, and it is up the hill. There is a bus also but I never take it. All together it is one hour and half.

I do this journey almost every Sunday. So I did it maybe hundred fifty times until now.

My feeling about this journey is mixed. On Saturday evening I am a little bit angry, because the Sunday is finished for other things. But when I am in the train it is fine, because I cannot do anything there, so I am just sitting and looking. And the walk is the best part, because when I arrive up the hill I know already what I want to say to her. So this is my regular journey.

what_caps_it.point: 'By the train', 'stops in', 'one hour and half' — three determiner and preposition slips.
'Angry', 'fine', 'the best part' carry every judgement in the answer.
The third bullet gets two short lines and the close repeats the card.

annotations.why: Keep this — mixed feelings hand you a reason clause on both sides for free.

annotations.why: Say 'she lives in another town'. Permanent facts take the simple form.

annotations.why: It's 'by train', 'by bus', 'on foot' — no article after 'by'.

annotations.why: Trains stop 'at' stations. Store the preposition with the noun.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The journey I'll describe is the one I make to see my mother, who lives about forty miles away in a town on the other side of the county.

I do it by train — twenty-five minutes on the fast service if I catch it, or nearer fifty if I don't and end up on the one that stops at every station. Then it's a twenty-minute walk from her station, up a hill, which I could perfectly well do by bus but for some reason never do. Door to door it comes to an hour and a half, and I make it most Sundays, so I've done it something like a hundred and fifty times by now.

How I feel about it is genuinely mixed, and I'd be lying if I said otherwise. On the Saturday night I usually resent it slightly — it takes the whole of the following day, and there's always something else that day could have been. Once I'm actually on the train, though, that goes completely. It's the one stretch of the week where there's nothing at all I can usefully do, and I've come to rely on it more than I'd have expected.

The walk, oddly enough, is the part I'd keep if I had to lose the rest of it. By the time I get to the top of the hill I've generally worked out what I want to say, which matters rather more with her than it happens to with most other people.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Resent it slightly', 'door to door', 'come to rely on' replace 'angry' and 'fine'.
A relative clause with 'which', a 'by the time' clause and a clean conditional all appear.
The two feelings are separated in time, so the answer has a shape rather than a list.

annotations.why: Naming the bit you would save is a stronger evaluation than praising all of it.

annotations.label: A slow change of attitude in one phrase
annotations.why: 'I've come to' expresses a shift you didn't decide on.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The journey is the one I make to my mother's, forty-odd miles away in a town on the far side of the county.

It's done by train: twenty-five minutes on the fast service if I make the connection, or the best part of an hour if I don't and end up on the stopping service. From her station it's twenty minutes on foot, uphill, which there is a perfectly good bus for and which I have never once taken. Door to door, an hour and a half; most Sundays; something in the region of a hundred and fifty times by now.

How I feel about it is genuinely mixed, and I'd be lying if I pretended otherwise. On a Saturday evening I resent it slightly — it accounts for the whole of the following day, and there is always something that day could otherwise have been. The moment the train pulls out, though, the resentment goes. It is the one stretch of the week in which there is nothing whatsoever I can usefully do, and I have come to depend on that far more than I would have predicted.

If I had to give up part of it, the walk would be the last thing to go. By the top of the hill I have generally worked out what I want to say, which matters rather more with her than it does with most people. That, I suspect, is what a regular journey quietly does: it makes a space nobody has to justify.

what_lifts_it.point: Two coordinated relative clauses, one with a stranded preposition, replace a simple statement.
'Accounts for', 'in the region of', 'nothing whatsoever' are exact rather than showy.
The close names what regular journeys do in general instead of summing up this one.

annotations.label: Two relatives, one preposition stranded
annotations.why: Ending a clause on 'for' is entirely natural in spoken English.

annotations.span: something in the region of a hundred and fifty times by now
annotations.label: Hedged number instead of a flat one
annotations.why: 'In the region of' says roughly without saying 'about' again.

annotations.span: The moment the train pulls out, though, the resentment goes.
annotations.label: Pinpoints the turn to a single second
annotations.why: The narrower the moment, the more convincing the change of feeling.

annotations.span: the walk would be the last thing to go
annotations.label: Ranks by what you would surrender
annotations.why: Ranking under a hypothetical loss is a strong way to show value.

annotations.span: it makes a space nobody has to justify
annotations.label: Ends on what such journeys are for
annotations.why: Generalise in the final clause and the whole turn rises with it.
