title: your home town

payload_json.topic: your home town
questions: Whereabouts is your home town?
How often do you get into the centre of it?
What's the best thing about living there?
Is it the kind of place people tend to move to, or move away from?
Would you say it's an easy place to live?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple to describe, present perfect for how long, 'tend to' for the claim
teaching.band_move: Give the place a shape in one sentence — size, position, feel — before you list what is in it.

questions.answer_shape: Name it, fix it on the map with a distance or a landmark, then say how big it is.
questions.extend_move: It's a smallish town about forty minutes north of the capital — sixty thousand people, give or take.

common_error.wrong: I come from a town which have sixty thousand people.
common_error.right: I come from a town which has about sixty thousand people.
common_error.why: The relative pronoun takes the verb of its singular noun.

questions.answer_shape: Say how often, add when you last went in, then one thing you do there.
questions.extend_move: Not as often as I used to — maybe a couple of times a month, usually on a Saturday.

common_error.wrong: I go there two times in a month.
common_error.right: I go there a couple of times a month.
common_error.why: Frequency phrases take 'a month', never 'in a month'.

questions.answer_shape: Name one thing you rate, give the reason, then a small concrete detail.
questions.extend_move: What I like most is that everything's walkable — I've never once needed a car there.

common_error.wrong: The best thing is the people is very friendly.
common_error.right: The best thing is that the people are very friendly.
common_error.why: A plural subject takes a plural verb after 'that'.

questions.answer_shape: Give the general trend with a quantifier, then name one group who go the other way.
questions.extend_move: Mostly people leaving, I'd say — a fair few of my old classmates are in the city now.

common_error.wrong: The most of people move away from there.
common_error.right: Most people move away from there.
common_error.why: 'Most' takes no article and no 'of' before a bare plural.

questions.probe: Why do you think that is?

questions.answer_shape: Take a side, give one reason, then say who it depends on.
questions.extend_move: Easy in some ways — it's cheap and it's quiet — though it depends what you want from a place.

common_error.wrong: It depends of the person really.
common_error.right: It depends on the person, really.
common_error.why: 'Depend' always keeps the preposition 'on'.

title: rain, snow and extreme weather

payload_json.topic: rain, snow and extreme weather
questions: What's the weather like where you live at this time of year?
Do you mind the rain?
Were the winters colder when you were a child?
Is there anything you'd change about the weather where you live?
Do you think people talk about the weather too much?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple now, 'used to' for childhood, second conditional for the change
teaching.band_move: Answer the small question small, then add one detail. Two sentences is a whole Part 1 answer.

questions.answer_shape: Name the season, describe it in one line, then say what that means for you.
questions.extend_move: It's the tail end of the wet season, so it's warm, but you never leave the house without a jacket.

common_error.wrong: The weather is very rain at the moment.
common_error.right: It's very wet at the moment.
common_error.why: 'Rain' is a noun; the adjective is 'wet' or 'rainy'.

questions.answer_shape: Say yes or no honestly, give the reason, then name the one exception.
questions.extend_move: I don't mind it at all, actually — it's only a nuisance when I'm carrying things.

common_error.wrong: I am not liking the rain very much.
common_error.right: I don't like the rain very much.
common_error.why: 'Like' is a state verb and takes no continuous form.

questions.answer_shape: Say whether it has changed, use 'used to' once, then one thing you remember.
questions.extend_move: They were, definitely — we used to get snow that sat there for a week.

common_error.wrong: When I was young it was snowing more.
common_error.right: When I was young it used to snow more.
common_error.why: Repeated past habits take 'used to', not the continuous.

questions.answer_shape: Name the one thing, wrap it in 'if I could', then justify the choice.
questions.extend_move: If I could get rid of one thing, it'd be the humidity — the heat I can live with.

common_error.wrong: If I can change it, I will make it more cool.
common_error.right: If I could change it, I'd make it cooler.
common_error.why: Imaginary changes take 'could' plus 'would'.

questions.answer_shape: Take a light position, give one reason, then hedge it slightly.
questions.extend_move: Probably, yes — although it's a safe thing to say to a stranger, so I do understand why.

common_error.wrong: People talks about weather everyday.
common_error.right: People talk about the weather every day.
common_error.why: Plural subject takes no -s; 'every day' is two words.

title: A time when the weather changed your plans

payload_json.topic: A time when the weather changed your plans

cue_card.topic: Describe a time when the weather made you change your plans.
bullets: what you had planned to do
where you were and who you were with
what the weather did
and explain whether the day turned out better or worse than the plan.
rounding_off: Would you make that plan again at the same time of year?
Do people where you live pay much attention to the forecast?

teaching.band_move: Let the weather be the subject of one sentence, then get straight back to what you did about it.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Take the first ruined day that comes to mind, even a small one. A cancelled picnic gives you as much language as a cancelled flight.

note_grid.cell: coast trip, 7am start, packed nite b4

prep_plan.trap: People describe the storm in loving detail and never reach whether the day turned out better.

time_plan.goal: Fix the season and say what was supposed to happen.
The plan and the people, four or five sentences.
What the weather did, and when you knew.
Better or worse than the plan, and why.
One line about plans and weather in general.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: what could you actually see or hear out of the window?
Say what the forecast had told you the night before, and whether you believed it.
Bring in whoever you were with — what did they want to do instead?
Say what would have happened if you'd gone ahead with it anyway.

error_watchlist.wrong: So we are packing the car and then the rain starts.
error_watchlist.right: We were packing the car when the rain started.
error_watchlist.why: Background takes past continuous; the interruption takes past simple.

error_watchlist.wrong: If we would go, we get stuck on the road.
error_watchlist.right: If we'd gone, we'd have got stuck on the road.
error_watchlist.why: Past might-have-beens need 'had' plus 'would have'.

error_watchlist.wrong: The whole day was very disappointed.
error_watchlist.right: The whole day was very disappointing.
error_watchlist.why: -ed describes the person; -ing describes the thing.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Weather words are cluster-heavy — storm, forecast, months — and a dropped ending swallows the plural.

target_words.note: Begin on /st/; don't put a vowel in front of the s.
/kt/ at the end, one syllable, not 'pack-ed'.
Stress falls on 'fore'; keep the final /st/ audible.
Aim for /nts/; 'mun' alone loses the plural.
Start with /kr/, not 'ker-'; two syllables only.

chunking_drill.sentence: I woke up at about six to rain hammering on the window, and by the time I got downstairs my aunt had already checked and the coast road was shut.
chunks: I woke up at about six
to rain hammering on the window,
and by the time I got downstairs
my aunt had already checked
and the coast road was shut.

minimal_pairs.contrast: short vowel against the long gliding one

teaching.examiner_note: You will not be interrupted once the minute is up. The examiner starts the clock, looks down and says nothing at all until the two minutes are gone.

swap_slots.span: last August
swap_slots.prompt: Your own time reference — a month or a season. One is plenty; two sounds rehearsed.

swap_slots.span: My aunt was going to drive, and my two cousins and I
swap_slots.prompt: Your own people: who they are to you, and how many. Never just 'my family'.

swap_slots.span: the coast road was shut
swap_slots.prompt: Your own obstacle — the exact thing the weather stopped, not 'the weather was bad'.

swap_slots.span: about six games of cards
swap_slots.prompt: What you really did instead, with a number or a detail attached to it.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now run the same three moves — the plan, what wrecked it, what you did instead — about a day something other than weather ruined. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about one day last year when we wanted to go to the beach. It was in the summer, and I planned it with my two cousins.

So the plan was, we go to the coast for the whole day. My aunt has a car and she said she can drive us there. We packed everything the night before, the food and the towels and all of this. We are very excited because we don't go there so much.

But then in the morning there is a big storm. I wake up and the rain is very heavy, and my aunt looked at her phone and she said the road to the coast is closed. So we cannot go. I felt very disappointing at that moment, and my cousins also.

So we stayed in the house. We cooked together and we played cards, and actually it was very nice. We talked a lot, more than normally. So in the end it was good, maybe better than the beach. If I know about the storm before, I don't pack everything. But anyway, this was the day when the weather changed my plan.

what_caps_it.point: Almost every sentence opens with 'so', 'and' or 'but', so the story flattens into a list.
The narrative slips into the present four times and the closing conditional collapses.
'Very nice', 'good', 'very excited', 'big storm' — four stock adjectives carry the whole evaluation.

annotations.span: I will talk about one day last year
annotations.label: Fixes the time straight away
annotations.why: Keep this — one time phrase in sentence one is worth more than any opener.

annotations.span: So the plan was, we go to the coast for the whole day.
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Say 'we were going to drive to the coast' and stay in the past from there.

annotations.span: the food and the towels and all of this
annotations.label: Vague list filler
annotations.why: 'Food, towels, the lot' says the same thing and sounds spoken.

annotations.span: I felt very disappointing at that moment
annotations.label: -ed and -ing adjectives swapped
annotations.why: You were disappointed; the day was disappointing. Learn them as a pair.

annotations.span: If I know about the storm before, I don't pack everything.
annotations.label: Third conditional collapses
annotations.why: Use 'If I'd known about the storm, I wouldn't have packed a thing.'

annotations.span: But anyway, this was the day when the weather changed my plan.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the card
annotations.why: Close on a thought about the day, not on the words of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same day, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a day last August, when the four of us were supposed to drive down to the coast and never got there.

The plan had been in the diary for weeks. My aunt was going to drive, and my two cousins and I had spent the previous evening loading the car — food, towels, the lot — so that we could leave at seven and get a full day out of it. We hardly ever manage to go anywhere together, so it had built up into a bit of an occasion.

What actually happened was that a storm came in overnight. I woke up at about six to rain hammering on the window, and by the time I got downstairs my aunt had already checked and the coast road was shut. There wasn't much to discuss, really. Nobody was going to drive two hours through that on the off chance it reopened.

As for how it turned out — better than the trip would have been, if I'm honest. We ended up in my aunt's kitchen for the whole day, cooking far more food than four people needed, and we got through about six games of cards. My cousins and I talked more in that one afternoon than we had in a year, and that wouldn't have happened on a crowded beach. If the weather had held, we'd have spent half the day in traffic and come home sunburnt and quiet.

Looking back, the weather did us a favour. The trip was only ever the excuse to be in the same room.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect carries the background and a third conditional carries the might-have-been.
'Hammering', 'on the off chance', 'did us a favour' — chunks where band 6 had adjectives.
Two spoken signposts and one very short sentence give the turn an audible shape.

annotations.span: a day last August
annotations.label: One time phrase, then the past holds
annotations.why: Say the month once and every verb after it knows which tense to be.

annotations.span: The plan had been in the diary for weeks.
annotations.label: Past perfect sets the background
annotations.why: Use it once per story to show two layers of time, not five.

annotations.span: What actually happened was that
annotations.label: Signposts the turn in the story
annotations.why: It buys a second of thinking time and tells the listener a change is coming.

annotations.span: rain hammering on the window
annotations.label: A precise verb instead of 'very heavy'
annotations.why: One accurate verb beats an adverb plus a flat adjective every time.

annotations.span: There wasn't much to discuss, really.
annotations.label: One short sentence changes the pace
annotations.why: Drop a five-word sentence in after a long one — it sounds thought, not recited.

annotations.span: on the off chance
annotations.label: A three-word chunk doing real work
annotations.why: Reuse it for any small hope you act on without expecting much.

annotations.span: As for how it turned out
annotations.label: Announces the fourth bullet out loud
annotations.why: Naming the move is how you stop forgetting the 'explain' bullet.

annotations.span: If the weather had held, we'd have spent half the day in traffic
annotations.label: Third conditional, used where it belongs
annotations.why: Any 'better or worse' bullet is an invitation to this structure.

annotations.span: food, towels, the lot
annotations.label: A three-item list, one rhythmic run
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level on the first two and fall on the third.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about a day last August that was meant to be spent at the coast and wasn't.

We'd had it planned for the best part of a month — my aunt driving, my two cousins and me, an early start so we'd get the whole day out of it. The car was loaded the night before, which tells you how seriously we were taking it. We're scattered all over the country now, so a day at the sea had quietly turned into something rather more than a day at the sea.

Then a storm blew in overnight. I was woken at six by rain coming down like gravel on the glass, and by the time I'd got downstairs my aunt had checked and the road was shut. Nobody argued about it. There's no sense in driving two hours into weather like that on the strength of a maybe.

What we did instead was very little, and that was rather the point. We stayed in the kitchen, cooked enough for twice our number, and played cards until it got dark. Had we made it to the coast, we'd have spent half of it queuing and the other half hunting for somewhere to park.

The odd thing is that I can't remember a single beach day from that whole decade, and I can remember that kitchen exactly. I've come round to the view that a plan is often just a pretext for getting everybody in the same room, and that the weather occasionally does you the favour of removing the pretext.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces 'if', and a passive opens the storm paragraph.
'Blew in', 'come round to the view', 'a pretext' — precision rather than display.
The close leaves the anecdote behind and states something general.

annotations.span: Had we made it to the coast
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if'
annotations.why: Same meaning as the third conditional, higher register, still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: a storm blew in overnight
annotations.label: The idiom a native would reach for
annotations.why: Two natural idioms in two minutes beat five decorative ones.

annotations.span: I've come round to the view that
annotations.label: A frame that signals a considered opinion
annotations.why: It implies you once thought otherwise — that alone sounds like real thinking.

annotations.span: The odd thing is that I can't remember a single beach day from that whole decade
annotations.label: Lifts the story into an observation
annotations.why: End on the pattern the story reveals, not on a summary of the story.

annotations.span: cooked enough for twice our number, and played cards until it got dark
annotations.label: Two clauses run as one breath group
annotations.why: Group them, hold the pitch, then fall on 'dark'.

title: Climate, seasons and the way people live

payload_json.topic: Climate, seasons and the way people live

part3_themes.title: how climate shapes daily life
questions: Why do people in hot countries organise their day so differently from people in cold ones?
How did your grandparents' generation deal with the weather compared with people now?
Do the seasons still mean much to people living in big cities?
part3_themes.counterpoint: heating and air conditioning have made climate more or less irrelevant to how people actually live
part3_themes.counter_probe: Isn't that only true for the people who can afford to ignore it?
part3_themes.concession_frame: There's something in that, though I'd still say ___

abstraction_ladder.concrete: Does the weather change what you do on a given day?
abstraction_ladder.local_general: Do the people you know plan around the weather much?
abstraction_ladder.societal_abstract: How far does a country's climate shape the way its people live?

question_notes.answer_shape: Name one cause, add a second, then say which of the two does more of the work.
question_notes.watch_out: Two causes ranked beats five causes listed. Stop at two.

question_notes.answer_shape: One 'used to' sentence, one 'these days' sentence, then name what actually changed.
question_notes.probe: Was that better in any way?
question_notes.watch_out: Don't romanticise the past — the examiner will push back on nostalgia.

question_notes.answer_shape: Say which group feels it more, give the mechanism, then concede the other side.
question_notes.probe: What about people who work outdoors?
question_notes.watch_out: 'People' with no quantifier turns a good point into an unearned claim.

part3_themes.title: getting ready for bad weather
questions: Whose job is it to get a town ready for severe weather — the people who live there, or the authorities?
Why do so many people ignore a warning even after they've heard it?
If extreme weather became far more common, how would towns have to change?
part3_themes.counterpoint: warning people is a waste of money, because they carry on regardless until something happens to them
part3_themes.counter_probe: So is there any point in spending public money on it at all?
part3_themes.concession_frame: I'd accept that up to a point, but ___

abstraction_ladder.concrete: Do you check a forecast before you make plans?
abstraction_ladder.local_general: Does your area handle bad weather well?
abstraction_ladder.societal_abstract: Where should the line fall between what residents prepare for and what the state prepares for?

question_notes.answer_shape: Split the job in two, give a part to each side, then justify where you drew the line.
question_notes.watch_out: Vary the modal. Three answers opening 'the government should' is one answer.

question_notes.answer_shape: Give the psychological reason, then the practical one, then say which is harder to fix.
question_notes.watch_out: Talking about yourself here drops the answer back to Part 1 altitude.

question_notes.answer_shape: Second conditional, one concrete change to buildings, one to how people behave.
question_notes.watch_out: 'Will' makes an imaginary scenario sound like a forecast. Use 'would'.

teaching.band_move: Give responsibility to two parties and say which gets the larger share — never stop at 'the government'.
teaching.bridge: That's one day the weather rearranged for you. Let's move away from that now and think about climate and the way people live more generally.

error_watchlist.wrong: The number of storms that hit the coast are rising.
error_watchlist.right: The number of storms that hit the coast is rising.
error_watchlist.why: The verb belongs to 'number', not to 'storms'.

error_watchlist.wrong: The people in the hot countries start work early.
error_watchlist.right: People in hot countries start work early.
error_watchlist.why: Drop 'the' when you mean people in general.

title: your home

payload_json.topic: your home
questions: What sort of place do you live in at the moment?
Do you spend much time at home during the week?
Is it very different from where you lived before?
Do you like having people round to your place?
Would you like to stay there for a while, or move on?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple to describe, present perfect for duration, 'would' for plans
teaching.band_move: Add one physical detail to every answer — a floor, a window, a street. Detail beats fluency here.

questions.answer_shape: Say house or flat, add one physical fact, then say who else is there.
questions.extend_move: A flat, second floor, two bedrooms — I share it with a friend from my course.

common_error.wrong: I live in flat with my friend.
common_error.right: I live in a flat with a friend.
common_error.why: Singular countable nouns always take a determiner.

questions.probe: Is it near where you work?

questions.answer_shape: Say how much, name the days, then one thing you do there.
questions.extend_move: Not really during the week — I'm out from eight until seven, so it's mainly for sleeping.

common_error.wrong: I stay at home usually in the evening.
common_error.right: I usually stay at home in the evening.
common_error.why: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb.

questions.answer_shape: Name the biggest difference, say which you prefer, then give one reason.
questions.extend_move: Completely — the old place was a house with a garden, so this feels quite closed in.

common_error.wrong: It is more small than my old house.
common_error.right: It's smaller than my old house.
common_error.why: Short adjectives take -er, never 'more'.

questions.probe: Do you miss the old one?

questions.answer_shape: Say yes or no, give the reason, then name what makes it easy or hard.
questions.extend_move: I do, though there's nowhere for everyone to sit, so it tends to be two or three people at most.

common_error.wrong: I enjoy to invite my friends there.
common_error.right: I enjoy inviting my friends there.
common_error.why: 'Enjoy' is followed by the -ing form.

questions.probe: When did you last do that?

questions.answer_shape: Give a rough horizon, then say what would push you out of there.
questions.extend_move: Another year or so, I'd think — after that I'd want somewhere with a bit more light.

common_error.wrong: I will stay maybe two years more.
common_error.right: I'll probably stay another two years.
common_error.why: 'Another' plus a number, not 'more' at the end.

title: rubbish and recycling

payload_json.topic: rubbish and recycling
questions: Do you separate your rubbish at home?
Who collects the rubbish where you live, and how often?
Did your family recycle when you were growing up?
Do most people in your area bother with it?
Do you think it makes much of a difference?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple routines, past simple for childhood, hedging on the final claim
teaching.band_move: Answer the small factual questions in two sentences and save your hedging for the last one.

questions.answer_shape: Say yes or no, name the categories, then say how much effort it is.
questions.extend_move: We do — paper, glass and everything else — although I get it wrong fairly regularly.

common_error.wrong: We are separating the rubbish every week.
common_error.right: We separate the rubbish every week.
common_error.why: A regular routine takes the present simple.

questions.answer_shape: Say who, say how often, then add one small local detail.
questions.extend_move: The council does it, twice a week, and you get fined if the bin's out on the wrong day.

common_error.wrong: They collect it in every Tuesday.
common_error.right: They collect it every Tuesday.
common_error.why: Day phrases with 'every' take no preposition.

questions.answer_shape: Say whether they did, use one past habit form, then contrast it with now.
questions.extend_move: Not at all, no — my grandmother reused everything, but that was thrift rather than recycling.

common_error.wrong: When I am a child we didn't recycle.
common_error.right: When I was a child we didn't recycle.
common_error.why: Both halves of a past sentence stay in the past.

questions.probe: Why do you think that was?

questions.answer_shape: Use a quantifier for the general picture, then name the group who don't.
questions.extend_move: Most households do, I'd say, though the flats behind us are noticeably worse at it.

common_error.wrong: In my country the people are recycling a lot.
common_error.right: Most people where I live recycle a fair amount.
common_error.why: Drop 'the' when you generalise about people.

questions.answer_shape: Give a hedged position, one reason, then say what would convince you either way.
questions.extend_move: A bit, probably — though I suspect what we buy matters far more than which bin it ends up in.

common_error.wrong: I am agree it makes difference.
common_error.right: I'd agree it makes a difference.
common_error.why: 'Agree' is a verb; it never follows 'am'.

title: buying second-hand things

payload_json.topic: buying second-hand things
questions: Have you ever bought anything second-hand?
Do you look at second-hand sites or shops very often?
Is buying used things common where you live?
Is there anything you wouldn't buy second-hand?
Do you think buying used things is becoming more acceptable?

teaching.tense_focus: present perfect for experience, present simple for habit and generalisation
teaching.band_move: Name the object and its price — 'a desk for fifteen pounds' — before you say why it was worth it.

questions.answer_shape: Say yes or no, name the item, then say where you got it.
questions.extend_move: Plenty of times — my desk came from a charity shop two streets away and cost almost nothing.

common_error.wrong: I buyed a desk in second hand.
common_error.right: I bought a desk second-hand.
common_error.why: 'Bought' is irregular; second-hand is the adverb.

questions.answer_shape: Give a frequency, then say what you tend to look for.
questions.extend_move: Every few weeks — mostly for furniture, because the new stuff falls apart.

common_error.wrong: I look the websites two times a month.
common_error.right: I look at the websites twice a month.
common_error.why: 'Look at' needs its preposition.

questions.answer_shape: Give a quantifier, name where it happens, then who does it most.
questions.extend_move: Increasingly, yes — there's a market on Sundays, and it's not just students any more.

common_error.wrong: In my city is very common to buy used things.
common_error.right: In my city, it's very common to buy used things.
common_error.why: Dummy 'it' is compulsory before 'is common'.

questions.answer_shape: Name the category, give the reason, then the one exception you'd make.
questions.extend_move: Anything electrical, really — you've no idea how hard it's been used, and there's no guarantee.

common_error.wrong: I never buy the electronics used.
common_error.right: I'd never buy electronics second-hand.
common_error.why: Drop 'the' for a general category.

questions.answer_shape: Take a position, name what shifted, then concede who still resists.
questions.extend_move: It is — nobody hides it now, whereas my parents' generation saw it as a bit shameful.

common_error.wrong: Now is more acceptable than before.
common_error.right: It's more acceptable now than it used to be.
common_error.why: Keep 'it'; compare with 'than it used to be'.

title: Something you own that you have repaired instead of replacing

payload_json.topic: Something you own that you have repaired instead of replacing

cue_card.topic: Describe something you own that you have repaired rather than replaced.
bullets: what the thing is
how long you have had it
what went wrong with it and how it was mended
and explain why you chose to repair it rather than buy a new one.
rounding_off: Is it as good now as it was before?
Do you know anybody else who gets things mended?

teaching.band_move: Get the duration out in the first ten seconds — present perfect, one number — then never mention it again.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Pick the object you can picture from across the room. If you can't see its scratches in your head, choose a different one.
prep_plan.trap: Almost nobody answers the last bullet honestly. 'To save money' is where most candidates stop.

time_plan.goal: Name the object and say how long you've had it.
Describe it properly, then where it came from.
What broke, and exactly how it got mended.
Two reasons for repairing, ranked.
One sentence about mending things generally.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: the colour, the weight, the marks it has picked up along the way.
Say what it was like when it was new, and what has changed since.
Contrast it with the version on sale now — what's different about that one?
Say whether you'd make the same choice with something far more expensive.

error_watchlist.wrong: I have them since nine years.
error_watchlist.right: I've had them for about nine years.
error_watchlist.why: 'For' takes a length; 'since' takes a starting point.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe my boots. They are walking boots, brown colour, and they are made from leather. I bought them maybe nine years ago because I was going to do a long walk in the mountains.

I have them since that time and I use them very much, not only for the mountains but also in winter for normal days. They are very good boots. After some years the bottom part, the sole, it was broken. There was a hole and my foot is wet every time I go outside.

So I take them to a small shop near the station. The man there said he can fix it. He put a new sole and it took one week. It cost me forty pounds. And after that I did the same thing again two years later.

Why I don't buy new one? First, because it is cheaper. New boots is very expensive, maybe one hundred and sixty pounds. And second, because these boots know my feet already. New boots always make problem in the beginning. Also I don't like to throw away things which are still good. So this is why I repaired my boots.

what_caps_it.point: Duration, subject–verb agreement and the past tense all break in the same three sentences.
'Very good', 'very expensive', 'make problem' — the description never leaves school vocabulary.
Reasons arrive as a numbered list, and every other sentence starts with 'and' or 'so'.

model_answers.label: The target — same object, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd like to talk about is a pair of walking boots — dark brown leather, quite heavy, the sort that take a fortnight to break in.

I've had them for about nine years now. I bought them for a walking trip I'd signed up to, and honestly I expected to wear them twice, but they've ended up being what I put on for most of the winter. There's a scar across the left toe from a loose stone, which I quite like, oddly enough.

What went wrong was the sole. It started letting water in about four years ago — nothing dramatic, just a damp sock at the end of a long day — and when I turned them over there was a split running the whole length of the seam. There's a cobbler in a railway arch near the station who resoled them for forty pounds, and he's done it once more since.

As for why I keep mending them rather than buying a new pair, part of it is the money, since a decent pair costs somewhere near a hundred and sixty. But the honest reason is that these ones fit. A new pair means a fortnight of blisters, whereas these already know exactly what my feet are like. And there's a third thing, which is that throwing out something that still works feels wrong to me, even when it turns out to be the cheaper option.

So that's the case for repair in a nutshell — it isn't really about money at all.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect holds the duration, and 'whereas' joins two clauses where band 6 used 'and'.
'Break in', 'letting water in', 'in a nutshell' — chunks the band 6 had no access to.
Three signposts and one concession make the reasoning audible instead of listed.

annotations.why: 'Let water in' beats 'was broken' on any container or piece of clothing.

annotations.span: As for why I keep mending them rather than buying a new pair

annotations.why: Naming the move is what stops you forgetting the 'explain' bullet.

annotations.span: whereas these already know exactly what my feet are like
annotations.label: 'Whereas' linking two full clauses
annotations.why: Reach for 'whereas' the second time you would have said 'but'.

annotations.span: And there's a third thing, which is that
annotations.label: Counts the reasons as they arrive
annotations.why: Numbering out loud buys thinking time and sounds organised, not listed.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'll take a pair of walking boots — dark brown leather, heavier than anything anyone sells now, and on their third sole.

They came into my life about nine years ago, for a trip I'd been talked into, and I assumed they'd go straight to the back of a cupboard afterwards. Instead they've become the thing I reach for from October onwards. There's a gouge across the left toe from a loose stone, which I've never had the slightest wish to hide.

The sole was the first thing to go. It began quietly — a damp sock, nothing you'd call a leak — and by the time I turned them over there was a split running the length of the seam. A cobbler works out of a railway arch near the station, and he resoled them for forty pounds without once suggesting I buy something else. He has done it again since.

Now, why not simply replace them? Money comes into it, of course; a comparable pair runs to something like a hundred and sixty. But that isn't what decides it. What decides it is that these have already made every adjustment a boot can make to one particular pair of feet, and no new pair arrives pre-worn.

If I'm honest there's a stubbornness in it too. Nothing about them has stopped working, and I have never been able to see the argument for replacing something on the grounds that it has merely got older.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft sentence carries the main reason, and a passive quietly removes the persuader.
'On their third sole', 'talked into', 'runs to' — compression, not extra words.
The close states a principle that the boots only happen to illustrate.

annotations.span: What decides it is that these have already made every adjustment
annotations.label: Cleft sentence fronting the real reason
annotations.why: 'What decides it is…' puts your best point in the strongest position.

annotations.span: for a trip I'd been talked into
annotations.label: Passive idiom in five words
annotations.why: It tells us somebody persuaded him without naming or explaining them.

annotations.span: on their third sole
annotations.label: Four words instead of a sentence
annotations.why: Compression like this is what band 8 sounds like, not rare words.

annotations.span: It began quietly — a damp sock, nothing you'd call a leak —
annotations.label: Parenthesis delivered at lower pitch
annotations.why: Drop the pitch inside the dashes, then come back up. It sounds unrehearsed.

annotations.span: I have never been able to see the argument for replacing something on the grounds that it has merely got older
annotations.label: Ends on a principle, not a summary
annotations.why: State the rule your story is an example of, then stop talking.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a problem in my area. It is about the road near the primary school. There is no crossing there, only some white lines on the road.

The problem is that the cars go very fast on this road. And also many cars park on both sides, so when you want to cross you cannot see anything. It is dangerous. Every morning many children go to the school from that side, so they must cross exactly there.

The people who suffer are mostly the children and their parents. Also old people, because they walk slowly. My neighbour is eighty and she is afraid to cross there alone.

About what they did — two years ago some parents made a petition and gave to the council. After that they painted the lines and put one sign. But they don't put a light, so nothing really change.

I think it is important because it is not expensive to fix. They only need a light. And if they wait more, maybe one day there is accident, and then they will do it, but it is too late. So for me this problem must be first in the list.

model_answers.label: The target — same case, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The problem I'd choose is the junction at the end of my road, right outside a primary school, where there's no proper crossing at all.

It's a fairly narrow road with cars parked hard against the kerb on both sides, and drivers come round the bend faster than they should, because there's nothing there to slow them down. If you're standing at the kerb with a child, you can't actually see what's coming until you're already halfway out. There are white lines painted on the tarmac and one sign, and that is the extent of it.

The people it hits hardest are the ones with the least room for error — small children walking in on their own from about the age of seven, parents pushing prams, and a few older neighbours. One of them, who's in her eighties, told me she'd started going the long way round rather than risk it, which is a fifteen-minute detour on a road she has lived on all her life.

Something was attempted, to be fair. A group of parents got a petition together a couple of years ago, and the response was the paint and the sign — a stopgap, essentially, and nothing that changes what a driver can see.

As for why it should be a priority, the fix is cheap, it's a set of lights, and everybody involved already knows that. What worries me is that these things tend to get done after somebody is hurt rather than before, and there's no good reason for that to be how it works.

'Hard against the kerb', 'room for error', 'a stopgap' — precision where band 6 said 'dangerous'.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is the junction at the end of my road, immediately outside a primary school, which has never had a crossing on it.

It's a narrow street with cars wedged against the kerb on both sides, and since there's nothing to slow anybody down, drivers take the bend at a speed the road was never built for. Stand at that kerb holding a child's hand and you are effectively blind until you have already committed. What exists by way of protection is some paint and a sign.

The people carrying the risk are the ones least able to absorb it — seven-year-olds walking in alone, parents with prams, and a handful of neighbours in their eighties. One of them told me she now walks the long way round, a quarter of an hour's detour on a street she has lived on since she was married.

In fairness, something was tried. Parents put a petition in a couple of years back, and the paint and the sign were what came of it. Nobody involved would call that a solution; it is what gets done when a solution has been deferred.

What makes it worth pushing is that none of it is difficult. It needs a set of lights, and everybody knows as much. Had that junction sat outside a hospital or a courthouse, it would have been dealt with years ago. The problem isn't cost or complexity — it's that the people it endangers are the ones least able to make a fuss.

title: A public place in your town where people meet

payload_json.topic: A public place in your town where people meet

cue_card.topic: Describe a public place in your town where people go to meet each other.

who you see there, and when

teaching.band_move: Attach a relative clause to every feature you name. A row of 'there is' sentences is the flat-listing trap.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Pick the place you could walk to with your eyes shut. Familiarity is what gives you detail at the ninety-second mark.

note_grid.cell: old market sq, top of high st
free, dry, on route, nobody asks

prep_plan.trap: Half of all candidates describe the buildings for two minutes and never mention a single person.

time_plan.goal: Name the place and say where it sits.
Position it, then two things you can actually see.
Who is there, and at which time of day.
Why there rather than the obvious alternative.
One line about what such places are for.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: the surface underfoot, the noise level, what people are sitting on.
Say what it looked like five years ago, or on the day it was built.
Contrast it with the shopping centre — what does that place get wrong?

error_watchlist.wrong: It is in the top of the high street.
error_watchlist.right: It's at the top of the high street.
error_watchlist.why: 'At' fixes a point; 'in' encloses a space.

error_watchlist.wrong: In the middle there is fountain.

error_watchlist.why: Every singular countable noun needs 'a', 'the' or 'my'.

error_watchlist.wrong: There are many benchs and a lot of peoples.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Describing a place produces long noun phrases, and one pause inside a phrase makes the listener restart.

target_words.note: One syllable; /skw/ runs straight into the vowel.
Stress first; the second syllable nearly disappears.
Two syllables, and the ending is barely a vowel.
First syllable; the second reduces to a schwa.
Three syllables, and the beat is on the last.

chunking_drill.sentence: It's a wide open space paved in cobbles, with a stone fountain in the middle that hasn't run for years, and a set of broad steps that people treat as seating.
chunks: It's a wide open space paved in cobbles,
with a stone fountain in the middle
that hasn't run for years,
and a set of broad steps
that people treat as seating.

minimal_pairs.contrast: long vowel against short; the meaning changes entirely

teaching.examiner_note: The card stays on the table for the whole two minutes. Glancing down at it is expected; reading the bullets aloud one by one is not.

swap_slots.span: the old market square
swap_slots.prompt: Your own place: what it's called and what kind of space it actually is.

swap_slots.span: two minutes from the bus station
swap_slots.prompt: One distance from one landmark, so a stranger could find it from your words.

teaching.transfer_drill: Now describe a second place, indoors this time, using position, two visible details, the people, then why there. Forty-five seconds.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about the market square in my town. It is in the centre, in the top of the high street, near to the bus station.

The square is very old. There is fountain in the middle and around it there are some steps. The ground is not normal ground, it is small stones, I think in English it is called cobbles. There is also an old building with a big roof, so when it rains the people can stay under it.

Many kinds of people go there. In the morning there are old men and they play chess on the stone tables. After the school, about four o'clock, the teenagers sit on the steps and they talk very loud. On Sunday there are families with small children.

Why people choose this place? First because it is free. In the shopping centre you must buy something, but here nobody says anything to you. And second because everybody knows it, so it is easy to say 'meet me at the fountain'. Also it is in the way to everywhere. So this is the place where the people in my town meet.

what_caps_it.point: Three prepositions and two articles go wrong inside the description alone.
'Very old', 'very loud', 'not normal ground' — the square is described by what it isn't.
Every feature gets its own 'there is' sentence, so nothing is ever subordinated.

annotations.span: so it is easy to say 'meet me at the fountain'
annotations.label: Backs a reason with a real sentence
annotations.why: Keep this — quoting what people actually say is worth ten adjectives.

annotations.span: in the top of the high street
annotations.label: Wrong preposition for a point
annotations.why: 'At the top of'. 'In' would put you inside the street itself.

annotations.span: There is fountain in the middle
annotations.label: Article missing before a countable noun
annotations.why: 'There's a fountain'. This is the single most frequent slip in place cards.

annotations.span: The square is very old.
annotations.label: Age given instead of a description
annotations.why: Say what makes it look old — the cobbles, the stone, the worn steps.

annotations.span: it is in the way to everywhere
annotations.label: Wrong partner inside the phrase
annotations.why: 'On the way to'. 'In the way' means it is blocking you.

annotations.span: So this is the place where the people in my town meet.
annotations.label: Closes by repeating the card
annotations.why: Say what a place like that is for, then stop.

model_answers.label: The target — same square, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd pick is the old market square, right at the top of the high street, about two minutes from the bus station.

It's a wide open space paved in cobbles, with a stone fountain in the middle that hasn't run for years, and a set of broad steps that people treat as seating. On one side there's the market hall, which is basically a roof on pillars, so there's somewhere dry to stand when it rains — and that matters more than it sounds, given the weather we get.

Who you find there depends entirely on the hour. First thing, it's older men playing chess on the two stone tables under the hall roof, and they're out there almost regardless of the temperature. From about four it belongs to teenagers, who sit along the steps in a row and are audible from the far end of the street on a quiet afternoon. Sundays it fills up with families, mostly because the fountain is the one thing small children can be trusted around.

As for why people choose it over anywhere else, the honest answer is that it costs nothing and nobody moves you on. In the shopping centre you're expected to be buying something, whereas nobody in the square has ever asked me what I'm doing there. And it's on the way to everything, so meeting there isn't a detour for anybody.

I think that's what a public space actually is — somewhere you can turn up without a reason.

what_lifts_it.point: Two relative clauses and one 'whereas' subordinate what band 6 left as separate sentences.
'Treat as seating', 'moves you on', 'belongs to' — the square is described by use, not size.
Each paragraph opens by naming its subject, so all four bullets are audible.

annotations.span: The place I'd pick is the old market square
annotations.label: Chooses out loud in eight words
annotations.why: Commit in the first sentence and the remaining time has somewhere to go.

annotations.span: a stone fountain in the middle that hasn't run for years
annotations.label: Relative clause carrying a second fact
annotations.why: One clause gives you the object and its history in a single breath.

annotations.span: that people treat as seating
annotations.label: Describes the thing by its use
annotations.why: Use beats measurement — it tells the listener about the town, not the stone.

annotations.span: Who you find there depends entirely on the hour.
annotations.label: Organises the whole third bullet
annotations.why: One organising sentence saves you from listing people at random.

annotations.span: From about four it belongs to teenagers
annotations.label: Ownership used figuratively
annotations.why: 'Belongs to' says occupation and atmosphere in two words.

annotations.span: whereas nobody in the square has ever asked me what I'm doing there
annotations.label: 'Whereas' plus embedded question order
annotations.why: Note 'what I'm doing', not 'what am I doing' — statements keep normal order.

annotations.span: nobody moves you on
annotations.label: Four words for a whole social rule
annotations.why: Reuse it anywhere staff ask people to leave a space.

annotations.span: As for why people choose it over anywhere else
annotations.label: Signposts the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Naming the bullet out loud is the cheapest insurance against forgetting it.

annotations.span: somewhere you can turn up without a reason
annotations.label: Defines the category, then stops
annotations.why: A definition is a stronger ending than a summary of what you said.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'll take the old market square, at the top of the high street and a couple of minutes' walk from the bus station.

It's a wide cobbled space with a stone fountain at its centre, dry for as long as I can remember, and a run of shallow steps that everybody uses as seating without anyone ever having decided they should. Along one edge stands the market hall — a roof held up on pillars, essentially — which gives you somewhere to stand out of the rain, and in a town with our weather that is not a small thing.

The square changes hands through the day. Early on it belongs to a few older men who play chess on the stone tables and appear entirely unbothered by the cold. By four it has passed to the teenagers, arranged along the steps and audible from the other end of the street. On Sundays the families arrive, largely because a dry fountain is the one feature a small child cannot come to any harm on.

Why there and not somewhere else? Because nothing about it asks anything of you. In a shopping centre your presence is conditional on spending; in the square nobody has ever enquired what I was doing. It also happens to lie on the route to everywhere, so choosing it costs nobody a detour.

Which is, I suspect, the whole definition of a public place — the last sort of place where turning up needs no justification.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted adverbial with inversion, and a contrast made without any conjunction at all.
'Changes hands', 'conditional on spending', 'unbothered' — one word for band 7's clause.
The close defines the category the place belongs to rather than praising the place.

annotations.span: Along one edge stands the market hall
annotations.label: Fronted adverbial with inversion
annotations.why: Put the location first and the verb before its subject; it sounds written and is not.

annotations.span: The square changes hands through the day.
annotations.label: One metaphor organises a whole paragraph
annotations.why: Find the verb that describes the pattern, then hang the examples off it.

annotations.span: your presence is conditional on spending
annotations.label: Abstract precision in five words
annotations.why: Naming the rule beats describing three times somebody enforced it.

annotations.span: a roof held up on pillars, essentially
annotations.label: Aside delivered at lower pitch
annotations.why: Drop your pitch inside the dashes and come back up; it sounds like thinking.

annotations.span: the last sort of place where turning up needs no justification
annotations.label: Ends on a definition, not a verdict
annotations.why: Say what kind of thing it is, and the examiner hears an abstract gear change.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to speak about one time when I need a doctor. It was in February. I move to a new city for my work, and my ear was very painful three days.

The problem is I am not registered in a doctor there. So I cannot make an appointment. My colleague said there is a walk-in centre near the sport centre, so I go there in the morning.

I arrive at eight o'clock and there is already many people in the queue. I wait two hours. Then the lady in the reception said, today we are full, sorry. I was very angry. And also worried, because my ear is really bad.

But then this lady, she start to call other doctors. After fifteen minutes she find one for four o'clock. And they gave me the medicine the same day.

The past is stated once and then abandoned; nine verbs afterwards sit in the present.
'Very painful', 'really bad', 'very angry', 'very grateful' — every judgement is an intensifier plus a basic adjective.

annotations.span: And they gave me the medicine the same day.
annotations.label: The one verb marked correctly for tense
annotations.why: Keep this. 'Gave' is right. Now do the same to the other nine verbs.

annotations.span: my ear was very painful three days

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about the time when I needed a doctor. It was in February. I just moved to a new city for my job, and my ear was very painful for three days.

The problem is I am not registered in any doctor there. So I could not make appointment. My colleague told me about a walk-in centre near the leisure centre, so I went there in the morning.

I arrive there at eight o'clock and there is already a big queue outside. I waited during two hours. And then at ten the lady at the desk said they are full for today. I was very angry, and also worried, because my ear is really bad.

But then the lady, she saw my face I think, and she started to call other places. She called three or four surgeries. And after fifteen minutes she found one place who can see me at four o'clock. They gave me the medicine the same day.

So I felt very grateful for this lady. The system was not good but she was very good. This is my experience with a public service.

what_caps_it.point: The story starts in the past and slides into the present four separate times.
'Very painful', 'very angry', 'very good' — three different ideas all delivered by 'very'.
The actual point arrives flatly in the last two sentences and is then abandoned.

annotations.span: The system was not good but she was very good.
annotations.label: Separates the system from the person
annotations.why: Keep this idea and give it better words — it is the whole point of the story.

annotations.span: I am not registered in any doctor there
annotations.label: Wrong tense and wrong preposition
annotations.why: 'I hadn't registered with a surgery.' You register 'with' a practice.

annotations.span: I could not make appointment
annotations.label: Article missing before a countable noun
annotations.why: 'Make an appointment'. Learn the article as part of the phrase.

annotations.span: I arrive there at eight o'clock and there is already a big queue outside.
annotations.label: Past narrative slips into the present
annotations.why: 'I got there at eight and there was already a queue.'

annotations.span: I waited during two hours.
annotations.label: Wrong preposition for a duration
annotations.why: 'For two hours'. 'During' needs a named period like 'the meeting'.

annotations.span: she found one place who can see me at four o'clock
annotations.label: Wrong relative pronoun, wrong tense
annotations.why: 'A place that could see me at four.' 'Who' is for people only.

model_answers.label: The target — same morning, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the time I needed to see a doctor, which was in February, a few weeks after I'd moved cities for work.

I'd had earache for about three days and it had got to the point where I couldn't sleep on that side. The trouble was that I hadn't registered with a surgery yet, so there was no appointment for me to book in the first place. A colleague mentioned a walk-in centre next to the leisure centre, and that looked like the only option left.

I got there just before eight and there was already a queue down the side of the building. I waited about two hours, and then the woman on the desk announced that they'd reached capacity for the day. Which, honestly, was the point at which I nearly gave up and went home.

What she did instead was pick up the phone. She rang round three or four surgeries in the area, explained the situation each time, and found one that would take me at four that afternoon. It took her about fifteen minutes, and none of it was her job.

As for how I felt about it — grateful to her personally, and fairly cross with everything around her. That's what I took away from it, really. The service was clearly stretched to breaking point, whereas the person inside it went out of her way for somebody she'd never met. Those two facts sat side by side all morning, and I don't think one cancels out the other.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect sets up the backstory and a pseudo-cleft fronts the one thing that mattered.
'Got to the point where', 'rang round', 'went out of her way' — chunks instead of 'very'.
Two feelings are held apart rather than collapsing into one flat verdict.

annotations.span: a few weeks after I'd moved cities for work
annotations.label: Past perfect anchoring the backstory
annotations.why: One past perfect early on tells the listener there are two time layers.

annotations.span: it had got to the point where I couldn't sleep on that side
annotations.label: A chunk that measures severity
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever a problem crossed a line: 'it got to the point where…'.

annotations.span: The trouble was that
annotations.label: Names the obstacle out loud
annotations.why: Four words tell the listener the story is about to turn.

annotations.span: Which, honestly, was the point at which I nearly gave up and went home.
annotations.label: A deliberate fragment for pace
annotations.why: Spoken English allows this; it sounds like thought rather than recital.

annotations.span: What she did instead was pick up the phone.
annotations.label: Fronts the turning point of the story
annotations.why: 'What she did was…' throws the weight onto the action that follows.

annotations.span: rang round three or four surgeries
annotations.label: The phrasal verb a native would use
annotations.why: 'Ring round' means calling several people to solve one problem.

annotations.span: none of it was her job
annotations.label: Evaluates without leaving the story
annotations.why: A short judgement inside the narrative is worth more than a summary later.

annotations.span: As for how I felt about it
annotations.label: Announces the fourth bullet
annotations.why: Say the bullet aloud and you cannot arrive at 2:00 having skipped it.

annotations.span: whereas the person inside it went out of her way for somebody she'd never met
annotations.label: 'Whereas' carrying the central contrast
annotations.why: Use 'whereas' when both halves matter equally; 'but' subordinates one.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about needing a doctor in February, a few weeks into a move I'd made for work.

I'd been carrying an earache around for three days by then, and it had reached the stage where lying on that side was out of the question. Having only just arrived, I wasn't registered anywhere, which meant there was no appointment for me to book at all. A colleague pointed me towards a walk-in centre beside the leisure centre, and I went on the basis that it was that or nothing.

I was there shortly before eight, behind a queue that already ran the length of the building. Two hours later the woman on the desk announced that they had hit capacity for the day, which is roughly when I decided to write the morning off.

Rather than leave it there, she picked up the phone. She worked through three or four surgeries, explaining the whole thing again each time, and found one prepared to see me at four. Fifteen minutes of her day, and not a second of it was anything she was obliged to do.

What stays with me is how easily those two things sat together. The service itself was visibly running on empty; the person staffing it went well past anything anyone could have asked for. It would be neat to conclude that the second redeems the first, and I have never quite managed to believe that it does.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause opens a sentence where band 7 needed a full subordinate one.
'Hit capacity', 'running on empty', 'write the morning off' — idiom used, not displayed.
It declines the tidy conclusion, which is both harder and more honest.

annotations.span: Having only just arrived, I wasn't registered anywhere
annotations.label: Participle clause replacing 'because'
annotations.why: Front the reason as an -ing clause and the sentence gains a gear.

annotations.span: they had hit capacity for the day
annotations.label: The institution's own vocabulary
annotations.why: Borrowing the phrase the place itself would use reads as precision.

annotations.span: The service itself was visibly running on empty
annotations.label: One idiom carrying a whole judgement
annotations.why: Place your best idiom on your most important sentence, not at random.

annotations.span: Fifteen minutes of her day
annotations.label: Fronted phrase with a pause after
annotations.why: Say it, stop, then finish the sentence. The pause does the emphasis.

annotations.span: It would be neat to conclude that the second redeems the first, and I have never quite managed to believe that it does.
annotations.label: Refuses the tidy ending
annotations.why: Naming the obvious conclusion and rejecting it sounds like real thinking.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
February, three or four weeks after I'd moved here for a job, and I needed to see a doctor.

I'd had earache for three days and had reached the point of not being able to lie on that side. Because the move was so recent I hadn't registered with a practice, so there was nothing for me to book — as far as the system was concerned I didn't exist. Somebody at work mentioned a walk-in centre next to the leisure centre, and I went because the alternative was nothing.

I was outside it before eight, at the back of a queue that already went round the corner of the building. Two hours on, the woman at the desk came out and said they'd taken as many as they could take that day, at which point I gave the morning up as lost.

She then picked up a telephone. Three or four practices, the whole story explained from scratch each time, and eventually one that would fit me in at four that afternoon. It took a quarter of an hour of her working day, and not one minute of it was anything her job required.

What I've kept from that morning is how comfortably the two facts sat together. An institution with visibly nothing left in the tank, and inside it somebody doing considerably more than anyone was entitled to expect. The tempting conclusion is that the second cancels out the first, and I've given up trying to believe it: if a service only works because whoever is on the desk goes beyond their job, then it doesn't work.

what_lifts_it.point: 'At which point' and a fused-relative conditional, both arriving with no change of pace.
'Nothing left in the tank', 'tempting conclusion', 'gave the morning up' — spoken and exact.
The close states a test the service fails, where band 8 left an unresolved feeling.

annotations.span: at which point I gave the morning up as lost
annotations.label: 'At which point' links two sentences
annotations.why: A relative that refers back to the whole clause, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.span: if a service only works because whoever is on the desk goes beyond their job, then it doesn't work
annotations.label: Conditional with a fused-relative subject
annotations.why: 'Whoever' is subject and object at once, which saves you an entire clause.

annotations.span: with visibly nothing left in the tank
annotations.label: An idiom about people applied to an institution
annotations.why: Move a familiar idiom onto an organisation and it does new work.

annotations.span: The tempting conclusion
annotations.label: Names the easy answer before rejecting it
annotations.why: Admitting the neat answer is attractive is what makes rejecting it convincing.

annotations.span: not one minute of it was anything her job required
annotations.label: Separates the person from the role
annotations.why: Say what her job did not require; it praises her without praising the system.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Add what happened at four o'clock and afterwards. The end of the story is missing.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Choose one tense for the whole account and mark every verb. Nine verbs here have no tense at all.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Give one sentence to the system and one to the person. Keeping them apart is what this card rewards.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Turn the two facts into a test: if it only works because somebody goes beyond their job, then it doesn't work.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a rule in the trains in my country. In every long train there is one carriage which is called the quiet carriage. In this carriage you cannot make phone call and you cannot listen music loud.

The rule is only in this one carriage, not in the whole train. There is a sign in the window and also a small sign inside, near the door. I think it is always the first or the last one.

About how people follow it, I would say quite good. Sometimes somebody forget and takes a call, but then all the people look at him and he goes outside to the corridor. The staff never say nothing about it, it is the passengers who do it.

I think this rule is good because it is not expensive for the company. They only put a sign. And for the passengers it is very relaxing, you can sleep or read. Of course some people think it is not fair because maybe they must call for their work. But they can go in another carriage. So for me it is a good rule.

annotations.span: Sometimes somebody forget and takes a call

annotations.why: 'Somebody forgets and takes a call.' Both verbs share the subject.

annotations.label: Two negatives in one clause
annotations.why: 'The staff never say anything.' English allows one negative per clause.

model_answers.label: The target — same rule, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The rule I'd like to talk about is the quiet carriage on the trains here — no phone calls, no music out loud, and conversation kept fairly low.

It only applies to one carriage on each of the longer trains, usually the one at the very front or the very back. There's a sticker on the outside of the window and another one by the door, so you can't board it by accident and claim you didn't know. Everywhere else on the train you can do more or less as you please.

How strictly it's followed is the interesting part, because it's almost entirely self-policing. The staff don't enforce it at all — I've never once seen a guard say a word. What happens instead is that somebody takes a call, and within about ten seconds half the carriage has looked up, and the person concerned is on their feet and heading for the door, still talking. Nobody has to say anything. It works far better than a fine would.

As for why it does more good than harm, I'd accept straight away that it's an inconvenience if you genuinely need to be reachable — but nothing forces you to sit there. That's the whole point of it: it's a choice rather than a ban. It costs the operator nothing beyond two stickers, and it gives you an hour when nobody can get hold of you, which is harder to come by than it used to be.

The best rules seem to be the ones nobody has to enforce.

what_lifts_it.point: A pseudo-cleft and a comparative with ellipsis replace band 6's run of simple clauses.
'Self-policing', 'come by', 'get hold of you' — chunks doing what adjectives did before.
The objection is raised and answered inside the turn instead of left hanging.

annotations.span: The rule I'd like to talk about is the quiet carriage
annotations.label: States the rule in one clause
annotations.why: Get the subject out first; explanation is easier once it has a name.

annotations.span: it's almost entirely self-policing
annotations.label: One word instead of a paragraph
annotations.why: Find the term for the pattern and the examples become illustrations.

annotations.span: How strictly it's followed is the interesting part
annotations.label: Signposts the third bullet
annotations.why: Announce which bullet you are on and you never lose your place.

annotations.span: What happens instead is that somebody takes a call
annotations.label: Pseudo-cleft fronting the real behaviour
annotations.why: 'What happens is…' promises a payoff, so the listener stays with you.

annotations.span: It works far better than a fine would.
annotations.label: Comparative with the verb left out
annotations.why: Ending on the bare auxiliary is natural spoken English and shows control.

annotations.span: As for why it does more good than harm
annotations.label: Announces the fourth bullet
annotations.why: The evaluative bullet carries the band. Say its name out loud.

annotations.span: I'd accept straight away that it's an inconvenience
annotations.label: Concedes before defending
annotations.why: Give the objection first and your defence sounds considered rather than blind.

annotations.span: harder to come by than it used to be
annotations.label: A chunk about scarcity
annotations.why: Reuse 'hard to come by' for anything that has become rare.

annotations.span: The best rules seem to be the ones nobody has to enforce.
annotations.label: Generalises out of the example
annotations.why: One sentence about the whole category is the strongest possible close.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The rule I'd choose is the quiet carriage on our intercity trains — no calls, no music aloud, conversation at a murmur.

It covers exactly one carriage per train, generally the one at either end, and it's announced by a sticker on the window and a second one inside the door. Nobody ends up in there by mistake; if they do, they have walked past two warnings to manage it. The rest of the train is left entirely alone, and always has been.

What interests me is that nothing enforces it. In all the years I've been using those trains I have never seen a guard intervene. Somebody's phone goes, they answer it, and inside ten seconds a carriage of strangers has looked up in unison — at which point the offender is on their feet and heading for the door, still talking. Not a word is exchanged. No penalty ever devised would work that fast.

Does it cost anybody anything? Certainly, if you need to be reachable — though nothing compels you to sit there, and that is precisely what makes it defensible. It is opt-in. Against that, it costs the operator two stickers and hands passengers an hour in which they cannot be found, which is a scarcer commodity every year.

I've come to think that's the mark of a rule worth having: it survives on the strength of what everybody already believes, and the enforcement is only ever a formality.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative fronting and a bare passive replace band 7's ordinary subject-verb order.
'At a murmur', 'in unison', 'a scarcer commodity' — words picked for shade, not size.
The close generalises about rules as a category rather than defending this one.

annotations.span: Not a word is exchanged.
annotations.label: Negative fronting plus passive
annotations.why: Four words. Put the negative first and the sentence lands like a full stop.

annotations.span: conversation at a murmur
annotations.label: A noun where most say an adverb
annotations.why: 'At a murmur' fixes the volume exactly; 'quietly' does not.

annotations.span: which is a scarcer commodity every year
annotations.label: Economic word applied to time
annotations.why: Moving a word across fields is precision; piling on rare words is not.

annotations.span: a carriage of strangers has looked up in unison
annotations.label: One breath group across the whole clause
annotations.why: Run it without a pause and the suddenness is audible, not just described.

annotations.span: it survives on the strength of what everybody already believes
annotations.label: Defines what a good rule is
annotations.why: End by saying what the category needs, and the anecdote becomes evidence.

error_watchlist.why: Set the scene with 'was -ing', then move to past simple.
