model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about the time when I helped in a running event in my village. It is every year in May, and many people from other places come also.

I helped because my neighbour asked me. Two days before, she called me and she said one person cannot come, so they need somebody. I said okay because I have nothing special to do that day.

My job was the water. I was in the table at four kilometres. Before the start I filled the cups with water, maybe four hundred cups, it took long time. And then when the runners come, I give them the cup. It was very busy for one hour. Some people take the cup and throw it on the ground, and after we must pick up everything.

What I got from this? I think two things. First, now I know many people in my village. Before I only know my neighbours. And second, I understand that somebody must do the boring job. It is not interesting but without this the event cannot happen. So I was happy to help.

what_caps_it.point: Four verbs slip into the present tense, and two nouns lose their article.
'Very busy', 'boring', 'happy' — two hours of work described in three words.
'First' and 'second' are the only cohesion; nothing else links one sentence to the next.

annotations.span: somebody must do the boring job
annotations.label: A real conclusion, not a summary
annotations.why: Keep the idea and give it better words — this is what the bullet was asking for.

annotations.span: I want to tell about the time
annotations.label: Wrong verb for the opening
annotations.why: 'Tell' needs a person: 'I'll tell you about…' or simply 'I'd like to talk about…'.

annotations.span: I was in the table at four kilometres
annotations.label: Wrong preposition for a position
annotations.why: 'On the table' if it's an object, 'at the table' if it's your post.

annotations.span: it took long time
annotations.label: Article missing before a time phrase
annotations.why: 'It took a long time.' The article is not optional here.

annotations.span: when the runners come, I give them the cup
annotations.label: Past story told in the present
annotations.why: 'When the runners came, I handed them a cup.' Fix the tense once, early.

annotations.span: So I was happy to help.
annotations.label: A flat verdict closing the turn
annotations.why: You had a better ending two sentences earlier. Move it to the end.

model_answers.label: The target — same morning, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll tell you about the village fun run, which happens on the first Saturday in May and pulls in a few hundred people from the surrounding area.

I ended up involved almost by accident. My neighbour rang me on the Thursday evening to say that somebody had pulled out, and would I mind covering a water station. I'd never done anything like it before, but it was two hours on a Saturday morning, so it was quite hard to think of a reason not to.

What I actually did was less glamorous than it sounds. I was on the table at the four-mile mark, and the first job was filling cups — about four hundred of them, poured out in advance and lined up in rows, which took the best part of an hour before anybody had even set off. Then the runners came through in waves for about seventy minutes, and after that we spent half an hour picking cups out of the hedge.

What I got out of it wasn't what I expected. I'd assumed it would be a pleasant enough morning and nothing more. In fact the useful part is that I now recognise about forty people in the village that I'd only have nodded at before, which changes what walking to the shop feels like. The other thing, slightly less comfortably, is that I'd never once thought about who does the dull jobs at events I've enjoyed for years.

Somebody had always been filling those cups.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a reported question replace band 6's flat run of past simples.
'Pulls in', 'the best part of an hour', 'less glamorous than it sounds' — chunks, not adjectives.
Every paragraph names the bullet it is answering, and the last line carries the point.

annotations.span: I ended up involved almost by accident.
annotations.label: Answers the second bullet in six words
annotations.why: Say how you got involved before you say what you did; it explains the whole story.

annotations.span: somebody had pulled out, and would I mind covering a water station
annotations.label: Past perfect plus a reported question
annotations.why: Dropping the reporting verb — 'and would I mind' — is very natural spoken English.

annotations.span: pulls in a few hundred people
annotations.label: A verb that measures an event
annotations.why: 'Pull in' is what events do to crowds; reuse it for a festival or a match.

annotations.span: What I actually did was less glamorous than it sounds.
annotations.label: Signposts the third bullet
annotations.why: Announcing the bullet buys a second and stops you drifting off it.

annotations.span: which took the best part of an hour before anybody had even set off
annotations.label: Relative clause with a past perfect inside
annotations.why: Two time layers in one clause is exactly the range examiners are listening for.

annotations.span: picking cups out of the hedge
annotations.label: The detail that proves you were there
annotations.why: One unglamorous specific does more than any adjective for credibility.

annotations.span: What I got out of it wasn't what I expected.
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluative bullet
annotations.why: This is the bullet that carries the band. Never let it arrive unannounced.

annotations.span: I'd assumed it would be a pleasant enough morning
annotations.label: Past perfect for a mistaken expectation
annotations.why: 'I'd assumed…' sets up a contrast the listener is now waiting for.

annotations.span: Somebody had always been filling those cups.
annotations.label: One short sentence as the ending
annotations.why: End short. A six-word close after a long paragraph lands hard.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is the village fun run — first Saturday in May, a few hundred entrants, and rather more spectators than the village strictly has residents.

I was drafted in rather than volunteering, if I'm honest about it. My neighbour phoned on the Thursday to say somebody had dropped out and to ask whether I'd take a water station, and two hours of a Saturday is not something you can refuse without sounding as though you have better things to do.

The work itself was as unglamorous as it gets. I had the table at four miles, and the first hour went entirely on filling cups — four hundred of them, poured and lined up before a single runner had left the start. Then seventy minutes of holding one out and having it taken, over and over, while people I had never met said thank you without breaking stride. Afterwards, half an hour retrieving cups from a hedge.

What I took from it was not the warm feeling I had been expecting. It was, first, that I now recognise perhaps forty faces I would previously have walked straight past, which quietly alters the business of going out for bread. And second, less comfortably, that I had spent years enjoying events of that kind without once wondering who filled the cups. Somebody always had.

I've done it every May since. Not out of virtue, particularly — more because, having once seen the machinery, it is quite difficult to unsee it.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause and the elliptical 'Somebody always had' do work band 7 spelled out.
'Drafted in', 'without breaking stride', 'the machinery' — one image, chosen rather than decorative.
The reason for going back is given last and undercuts itself, which sounds unrehearsed.

annotations.span: having once seen the machinery, it is quite difficult to unsee it
annotations.label: Participle clause carrying the reason
annotations.why: Front the cause as an -ing clause and the sentence stops sounding like a list.

annotations.span: I was drafted in rather than volunteering
annotations.label: One passive verb, whole situation
annotations.why: 'Drafted in' says asked, needed and not entirely willing, in two words.

annotations.span: as unglamorous as it gets
annotations.label: A superlative built from an idiom
annotations.why: 'As … as it gets' is the natural spoken superlative; use it once per turn.

annotations.span: holding one out and having it taken, over and over
annotations.label: Repetition delivered as one flat run
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across the repeat; the monotony is the meaning.

annotations.span: Somebody always had.
annotations.label: Three words, whole point
annotations.why: Ellipsis at the end of a paragraph is the most controlled ending available.

teaching.tense_focus: present simple to describe, second conditional to change, 'would like' ahead
teaching.band_move: Say what you do in the room, not just which room it is. The activity is what makes it yours.

questions.answer_shape: Name the room, say what you do there, then say why not another one.

common_error.right: I spend most of my time in the kitchen.
common_error.why: 'Most of my time', and the room takes 'the'.

common_error.right: There isn't much light in my flat.
common_error.why: 'Light' is uncountable when you mean brightness.

common_error.wrong: If I have money, I will buy new furniture.
common_error.right: If I had the money, I'd buy new furniture.
common_error.why: An imagined situation takes past form plus 'would'.

common_error.right: I don't like tidying up every day.
common_error.why: 'Every day' is singular and takes no -s.

common_error.right: I'd like to live in the countryside to have a garden.

title: Something people in your country spend a lot of money on

payload_json.topic: Something people in your country spend a lot of money on

cue_card.topic: Describe something that people in your country spend a lot of money on.
bullets: what it is
who spends the most on it
why it costs as much as it does
and explain whether you think it is money well spent.
rounding_off: Have you spent much on it yourself?
Was it the same twenty years ago?

teaching.band_move: Put one number into the first thirty seconds. A spending card with no figure in it is just an opinion.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: You're describing a country, not yourself, so pick something you've watched other people pay for — weddings, cars, schooling, phones.

note_grid.cell: no: 1 day vs 3 yrs of repayments

prep_plan.trap: The third bullet asks why it costs so much, and most candidates answer 'because it is expensive'.

time_plan.goal: Name the thing and attach one number.
What it is, then exactly who pays for it.
Two reasons the price is what it is.
Worth it or not, and your narrow reason.
One line on what the money is really for.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in: list what the money actually goes on, item by item.
Say what the same thing cost when your parents' generation did it.
Bring in one couple you know — what did they cut, and what wouldn't they?
Contrast it with a country where people spend far less on the same thing.

error_watchlist.wrong: They spend too much moneys on the party.
error_watchlist.right: They spend far too much money on the party.
error_watchlist.why: 'Money' is uncountable and never takes a plural -s.

error_watchlist.wrong: The amount of money people spend on weddings are rising.
error_watchlist.right: The amount of money people spend on weddings is rising.
error_watchlist.why: The verb belongs to 'amount', not to 'weddings'.

error_watchlist.right: It costs three times as much as it did.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Money talk is plural and third-person throughout, and a dropped -s costs you grammar as well as clarity.

target_words.note: /sts/ is the hardest ending in the language.
The -es here is a whole extra syllable.
/ndz/ — finish the entire cluster.
/ndz/ again; don't stop at 'thousan'.
/sts/, and the u is silent throughout.

teaching.examiner_note: You may be asked about your country without being expected to know any statistics. A clearly reasoned impression is exactly what is wanted.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I want to talk about is the weddings. In my country a wedding is very very expensive, more than people can pay I think.

Who spends the most? Normally the family of the bride pays for the biggest part, but now also the couple pay themselves, especially if they are older, maybe thirty or thirty-five.

Why it is so expensive? First because everybody invites so many guest. Two hundred, three hundred people is normal. And the food for this is a lot of money. Also the place, the hotel, they know the date is fixed, so they don't reduce the price. My cousin married last year and it cost more than fifteen thousand, only for one day.

Is it money well spent? For me, no. Because after one day it is finished, but the loan is not finished. They pay for three years. Of course the family is happy and the photos are nice. But I think it is too much. So this is something people spend a lot of money on in my country.

what_caps_it.point: A plural is dropped, a plural subject takes a singular verb, and 'the' opens a generalisation.
'Very very expensive', 'a lot of money', 'too much' — one idea wearing three costumes.
Each bullet is read out as a question and answered separately; the answers never join up.

annotations.span: they know the date is fixed, so they don't reduce the price
annotations.label: Explains the price properly
annotations.why: Keep this — it answers 'why does it cost so much' with a mechanism, not an adjective.

annotations.span: The thing I want to talk about is the weddings.
annotations.label: Article on a plural generalisation
annotations.why: 'Weddings', with no 'the'. Plural generalisations drop the article.

annotations.span: very very expensive
annotations.label: Intensifier repeated for emphasis
annotations.why: Repeating 'very' adds nothing. 'Eye-watering' or a number adds a lot.

annotations.span: everybody invites so many guest
annotations.label: Plural -s missing after a quantifier
annotations.why: 'So many guests'. 'Many' guarantees the noun is plural.

annotations.span: Two hundred, three hundred people is normal.
annotations.label: Plural subject, singular verb
annotations.why: 'Two hundred people are normal' — or better, 'is a normal number'.

annotations.span: So this is something people spend a lot of money on in my country.
annotations.label: Closes by reading the card back
annotations.why: Finish on what the spending is for. The prompt does not need repeating.

model_answers.label: The target — same subject, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd pick is weddings, which have got extraordinarily expensive here over the last twenty years or so.

Traditionally it was the bride's family who paid for most of it, and to a large extent that's still the case, though couples now tend to be older — often well into their thirties — and end up funding a fair chunk of it themselves. So it's usually two households and one couple all contributing, which is part of why nobody ever quite adds up the total.

As for why it costs what it does, I'd say there are two reasons. The obvious one is the guest list: two or three hundred people is normal, and once you're feeding that many, everything else scales with it. The less obvious one is that the date gets fixed months in advance, so the venue and the caterer know perfectly well you can't walk away. Nobody haggles over a wedding. A cousin of mine got married last spring and the whole thing came to somewhere over fifteen thousand, for a single day.

Is it money well spent? Honestly, I don't think it is — although I'd want to be careful here, because it clearly matters enormously to the people doing it. My objection is narrower than that. The day lasts twelve hours and the borrowing lasts three years, and I've watched more than one couple start married life in debt to impress relatives they see twice a decade.

If it were really about the marriage, nobody would need the flowers.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect for the change and a second conditional for the close, where band 6 had neither.
'A fair chunk', 'scales with it', 'haggles' — precision instead of three kinds of 'expensive'.
The two reasons are ranked out loud, and the judgement is hedged before it is delivered.

annotations.span: which have got extraordinarily expensive here over the last twenty years
annotations.label: Present perfect for a change
annotations.why: Any 'how things are now' card wants one present perfect in its first sentence.

annotations.span: end up funding a fair chunk of it themselves
annotations.label: Two chunks in one clause
annotations.why: 'End up -ing' and 'a fair chunk' are both reusable anywhere money is discussed.

annotations.span: As for why it costs what it does, I'd say there are two reasons.
annotations.label: Signposts and counts at once
annotations.why: Promising two reasons obliges you to give two, which stops you drifting.

annotations.span: everything else scales with it
annotations.label: One verb explains the arithmetic
annotations.why: 'Scales with' says 'goes up in proportion' in three words.

annotations.span: The less obvious one is that
annotations.label: Ranks the second reason above the first
annotations.why: Saying which reason is better is analysis; listing two is not.

annotations.span: Nobody haggles over a wedding.
annotations.label: Five words, delivered as a full stop
annotations.why: A short sentence after a long one resets the listener's attention.

annotations.span: although I'd want to be careful here
annotations.label: Hedges before criticising
annotations.why: It signals you know real people are involved, and it costs you nothing.

annotations.span: My objection is narrower than that.
annotations.label: Narrows the claim on purpose
annotations.why: A precise small objection is far harder to argue with than a sweeping one.

annotations.span: If it were really about the marriage, nobody would need the flowers.
annotations.label: Second conditional closing the turn
annotations.why: End on a conditional and the examiner hears grammar and judgement together.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'd choose weddings, which within my lifetime have gone from expensive to something close to absurd.

The money still comes largely from the bride's family, by custom, but the picture has blurred. People marry later now, often well into their thirties, and a couple who have both been earning for a decade end up carrying a good deal of it themselves. Three sets of pockets, one bill, and nobody with a complete view of the total.

Why so much? Partly arithmetic. Invite three hundred people and every other decision is multiplied by three hundred before you have even made it. But the sharper reason is that the date is set long before the money is spent, and everybody selling into that day knows it. There is no walking away from a booked venue six weeks out, and the prices reflect precisely that, as everyone in the trade understands. A cousin married last spring for something north of fifteen thousand, which bought one afternoon.

Well spent? I'd say not, though I want to be careful, because for the people involved it plainly is. What I object to is narrower: the celebration lasts an afternoon and the repayments last three years, and I have watched couples begin a marriage in debt in order to impress relatives they will next see at a funeral.

Strip out everything nobody would notice was missing, and what you'd have left is the part that was actually the wedding.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative used as a conditional, and a verbless sentence carrying a paragraph's whole point.
'North of', 'three sets of pockets', 'arithmetic' — compression rather than extra vocabulary.
The close proposes a test instead of a verdict, and lets the listener finish it.

annotations.span: Invite three hundred people and every other decision is multiplied by three hundred
annotations.label: Imperative doing a conditional's job
annotations.why: 'Do X and Y happens' is a conditional without the 'if'. Very natural, very spoken.

annotations.span: something north of fifteen thousand
annotations.label: An approximator that sounds native
annotations.why: 'North of' means 'more than' and signals you're estimating, not quoting.

annotations.span: Three sets of pockets, one bill
annotations.label: A verbless sentence doing real work
annotations.why: Cut the verb when the nouns alone carry the idea. It sounds thought, not read.

annotations.span: Why so much? Partly arithmetic.
annotations.label: Question and fragment, tight rhythm
annotations.why: Ask your own question, answer it in two words, then expand. It resets the pace.

annotations.span: Strip out everything nobody would notice was missing
annotations.label: Ends by proposing a test
annotations.why: Give the listener a way to check your claim and the claim sounds earned.

I want to talk about one app that I am using every day. It is a transport app and it shows the bus times.

So it is very simple. You open it and you can see when the bus is coming. It is very useful because sometimes the bus is late and you don't know. So this app tells you.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is a small transport app that shows live bus times — nothing clever, it simply tells you where the bus actually is rather than where the timetable claims it should be. It opens on a single screen and there's no account to sign into, which is half the appeal.

I came across it completely by accident. I was standing at a stop one evening and a colleague had it open at the stop while we were both getting soaked, and I remember thinking it was slightly absurd that I'd been using that route for years without knowing such a thing existed. I installed it the same night and I've stuck with it ever since.

As for when I use it, it's mainly first thing in the morning, before I've even put my coat on, because it saves me standing outside for eleven minutes in February. I check it again on the way home, and occasionally at weekends if I'm going somewhere I don't know.

Why I've kept it rather than switching — I suppose it's that it does one thing well. I did try one of the big all-in-one travel apps, and it was crammed with features I'd never touch, whereas this one opens straight onto the stop nearest me. It also loads fast, which sounds trivial until you're doing it in the rain with cold hands. Honestly, the test for me with anything on my phone is whether I'd notice it going, and I'd notice this one within a day.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The app I'd single out is an unglamorous little thing that tracks live bus times — it doesn't plan your journey or sell you anything, it just tells you where the bus has actually got to. One screen, no login, and it has quietly become part of leaving the house.

I stumbled on it years ago in the least romantic circumstances imaginable: a colleague had it open at a stop in the rain while the two of us stood there guessing. What struck me wasn't the app so much as how long I'd put up with not knowing. I had it installed before I got home.

These days I check it before I've got my coat on, again somewhere around six, and at weekends if I'm heading anywhere unfamiliar. It's become entirely automatic — I couldn't tell you when I last decided to open it. It's the sort of habit you only notice yourself having when somebody asks you about it.

As for why it survived and its rivals didn't, I think it's simply that it knows what it isn't. The all-in-one travel apps I tried were stuffed with things I'd never use, and every extra feature bought a fraction of a second of loading time. Rarely does a piece of software win by doing less, but this one does. And that, I suspect, is the real test of anything you use daily — not whether it impresses you, but whether you'd notice the hole it left.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one that comes to mind is a documentary about the people who clean office buildings at night. It isn't dramatic in the slightest — there's no narrator and no music, it simply follows one crew through a single shift, from about ten in the evening until five, and lets them talk while they work.

I came to it more or less by accident. I couldn't sleep, it was on late, and I only meant to give it ten minutes. In the end I sat through the whole thing with the sound turned right down so I wouldn't wake anybody up, which is not how I usually watch anything.

I was on my own, and I think that mattered — there was nobody there to make a joke and break the spell. I did talk about it the next day with my sister, who works in a hospital, and she said it was exactly the same on her wards: an entire shift of people the daytime staff essentially never meet.

As for what it changed — it changed who I notice. Before that I'd have walked straight past the man mopping the lobby without registering him at all, not out of rudeness, but because the whole arrangement is designed to keep that work out of sight. Now I catch myself wondering when a place was cleaned, and by whom, which sounds like a small thing until you realise it applies to nearly everything you use. And the programme never says any of that. It films people doing their jobs and lets you get there yourself.

model_answers.transcript:
The programme I keep coming back to is a documentary about night cleaners in office blocks. It has almost nothing in the way of technique — no narration, no score, no arc to speak of. It follows one crew from ten at night until five in the morning and simply refuses to look away.

I found it by accident, in the way you find most things at one in the morning. I gave it ten minutes out of politeness to nobody in particular and ended up watching the lot with the volume at a whisper.

I watched it alone, which I now think was the point. There was no one to lighten it with a comment. What I did do was ring my sister the following day — she's a nurse — and she was entirely unsurprised: on her wards there is a whole population of staff the day shift never lays eyes on.

What changed wasn't my opinion of anything, it was my attention. Never had it occurred to me to wonder who cleans the building I work in, and that isn't carelessness so much as design: the work is scheduled precisely so that nobody has to see it. That, I think, is what the better documentaries do. They don't hand you an argument. They rearrange what you happen to notice, and the argument arrives on its own about a week later, by which point it feels like something you worked out yourself.

annotations.span: What changed wasn't my opinion of anything, it was my attention.

annotations.why: Naming the wrong answer before the right one sharpens both.

annotations.span: simply refuses to look away
annotations.label: Personification doing real work
annotations.why: Giving the film the verb is more precise than 'it shows everything'.

annotations.span: the work is scheduled precisely so that nobody has to see it
annotations.label: Passive chosen for the agent's absence
annotations.why: The passive is right when who does it is exactly the missing information.

annotations.span: They rearrange what you happen to notice, and the argument arrives on its own
annotations.label: Two beats, second one lower
annotations.why: Let the pitch fall across the second clause so the ending sounds deliberate.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
There's a documentary about the people who clean office buildings overnight that has stayed with me longer than it had any right to. It does almost nothing that documentaries usually do — nobody narrates it, there's no music, and it has no shape to speak of. A single crew, ten at night until five in the morning, and a camera that declines to look elsewhere.

I came across it the way you come across anything at one in the morning, which is to say by not sleeping. I gave it ten minutes as a courtesy to no one, and watched the remaining eighty with the sound almost off so the flat stayed asleep.

Watching it by myself was probably the whole thing. Had anybody been in the room, one comment would have punctured it. I did ring my sister about it the next day — she's a nurse — and she couldn't see why I was surprised. Her hospital runs an entire shift of people the daytime staff wouldn't recognise in the street.

What shifted wasn't a belief. It was where my eyes go. It had genuinely never crossed my mind to ask who cleans the building I sit in five days a week, and that's not indifference, it's scheduling: the work is deliberately placed in the hours when nobody is there to see it. That, I suspect, is the difference between a good documentary and a persuasive one. A good one doesn't argue. It moves what you notice, and the argument shows up a week later feeling like your own idea.

what_lifts_it.point: An inverted third conditional and an extraposed subject, neither of them slowing the delivery.
'Scheduling', 'punctured', 'no shape to speak of' — precise, and never reaching for effect.
The close separates a good documentary from a persuasive one, which band 8 merged.

annotations.span: Had anybody been in the room, one comment would have punctured it.
annotations.label: Inverted third conditional
annotations.why: Drop 'if' and invert. Same meaning, and it never sounds written down.

annotations.span: It had genuinely never crossed my mind to ask who cleans the building I sit in
annotations.label: Extraposed subject with 'it'
annotations.why: 'It never crossed my mind to ask' puts the long part where it belongs, at the end.

annotations.span: as a courtesy to no one
annotations.label: A stock phrase completed wrongly on purpose
annotations.why: Take a fixed phrase and finish it against expectation. That is the joke.

annotations.span: that's not indifference, it's scheduling
annotations.label: One noun replaces the whole explanation
annotations.why: 'Scheduling' says it was arranged; 'at night' says nothing at all.

annotations.span: the argument shows up a week later feeling like your own idea
annotations.label: Gives the abstract claim a timescale
annotations.why: Attach a duration to an idea and it sounds observed rather than argued.

ladder_note.from_5_to_6: Say what changed. 'Now I think about it' is the start of bullet four, not the answer to it.
ladder_note.from_6_to_7: Describe the content in the present simple and your watching of it in the past. Never mix the two.
ladder_note.from_7_to_8: Explain why you didn't notice before. 'Not carelessness so much as design' is the sentence this card wants.
ladder_note.from_8_to_9: Put a timescale on the abstract claim. 'A week later' makes an idea sound observed rather than argued.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will describe one account that I am following on social media. It is about the history of my city.

Every morning they are posting one old photo of the city. And under the photo there is small text, two lines, where it is and which year. I think one man is doing it, a teacher, but I am not sure.

I follow it since three years. My cousin shared one photo and then I saw it, and after that I clicked follow.

The photos are different. Sometimes it is a street, sometimes a shop or a bus. Some of them I know the place and some I don't know. And many people are writing comments under it, and they are discussing which street it is.

Why I don't unfollow it. Because it is not annoying. Many accounts I unfollowed because they are posting too much and they want to sell something. But this one is very simple and it is only one photo. So it is a good account and I like it very much.

what_caps_it.point: Continuous forms for habits throughout, and 'since' used with a length of time.
Each bullet gets roughly the same time, so the reason at the end is the thinnest part.
'Good', 'simple', 'not annoying', 'like it very much' — evaluation with no precision.

annotations.span: under the photo there is small text, two lines, where it is and which year
annotations.label: Describes an actual post
annotations.why: Keep this — one concrete post is worth more than any summary of the account.

annotations.span: I follow it since three years.
annotations.label: 'Since' with a duration
annotations.why: Say 'I've been following it for three years'. 'For' takes a length.

annotations.span: Every morning they are posting one old photo
annotations.label: Continuous used for a routine
annotations.why: A daily habit is present simple: 'he posts one old photo'.

annotations.span: Some of them I know the place and some I don't know.
annotations.label: Two structures collided
annotations.why: Choose one: 'I recognise some of them, and others I don't.'

annotations.span: So it is a good account and I like it very much.
annotations.label: Closes on the flattest words available
annotations.why: End on what it gives you, not on 'good' and 'like'.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd talk about is a local history account that posts one old photograph of my city every morning, with two or three lines underneath saying roughly where it was taken and when. It's run by a retired teacher, as far as I can tell, working entirely on his own and with no apparent interest in being noticed.

I've been following it for about three years now. It turned up in my feed because a cousin had shared one of the pictures, and I stayed as much for the comments as for the photographs — half the city seems to appear underneath, arguing about which street it actually is.

What it posts is quite narrow, and that's the appeal. One picture, one caption, no opinion about anything. Some mornings it's a tram on a road that doesn't exist any more; other mornings it's a shopfront that has since become a phone repair shop. Every so often he'll put the modern view beside it, and that's when the comments really take off.

As for why I've kept it when I've cleared out almost everything else — I think it's because it asks nothing of me. There's no outrage in it, nothing is trying to sell me a course, and the whole thing takes about eleven seconds. It's also taught me a fair amount about the place I live in, which I certainly hadn't signed up for. If more of what I followed behaved like that, I'd spend a lot less time wishing I were off my phone.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect continuous for duration, a past perfect, and one clean second conditional.
'Take off', 'cleared out', 'asks nothing of me' replace the flat adjectives.
Two concrete posts are described, so the account stops being an abstraction.

annotations.span: I've been following it for about three years now.
annotations.label: Present perfect continuous with 'for'
annotations.why: This is the tense the bullet is asking for. Say it once, early, and move on.

annotations.span: It turned up in my feed because a cousin had shared one of the pictures
annotations.label: Past perfect for the earlier event
annotations.why: Two past events in one sentence: the earlier one goes into 'had'.

annotations.span: What it posts is quite narrow, and that's the appeal.
annotations.label: Turns a limitation into the point
annotations.why: Naming a weakness and then defending it reads as genuine judgement.

annotations.span: a tram on a road that doesn't exist any more
annotations.label: One post, described exactly
annotations.why: Specifics do the work adjectives cannot. Give two, never a list of five.

annotations.span: that's when the comments really take off
annotations.label: Phrasal verb used precisely
annotations.why: 'Take off' says suddenly-increase in two ordinary words.

annotations.span: As for why I've kept it when I've cleared out almost everything else
annotations.label: Announces the explain bullet
annotations.why: Signposting the fourth bullet is the cheapest insurance against skipping it.

annotations.span: it asks nothing of me
annotations.label: Four words carrying the judgement
annotations.why: Reuse this shape for anything you value because it makes no demands.

annotations.span: which I certainly hadn't signed up for
annotations.label: Dry aside, dropped in pitch
annotations.why: Lower the voice slightly on an aside so it reads as a comment, not a claim.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The account I'd pick is a quiet local history page that puts up a single archive photograph of my city each morning, captioned with a street name and an approximate year. It appears to be one retired teacher, working alone, with no interest whatsoever in growing.

I've had it in my feed for three years or so. A cousin shared one of the pictures, I followed on impulse, and unlike almost everything else I acquired that year it survived. What kept me there initially wasn't the photographs at all but the argument underneath them: half the city turns up to insist that the corner in question is not the corner he says it is.

The format never varies. One image, two lines, no commentary. A tram on a street that was flattened decades ago; a bakery that is now a phone repair shop. Nothing is ever explained and nothing is ever argued for. Occasionally he sets the modern view alongside, at which point the comments become genuinely heated.

What has kept it, when I've stripped out practically everything else, is that it wants nothing from me. No outrage, no course to buy, eleven seconds and gone. I look at it before I'm properly awake and I have never once resented it. And it has taught me more about this city than I ever set out to learn, which I suspect is the only way anybody learns anything now — sideways, from something they were only half looking at.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted cleft and 'unlike' as a sentence adverbial, where band 7 used plain clauses.
'On impulse', 'stripped out', 'genuinely heated' — precise choices rather than displayed rarity.
The close abstracts into a claim about how people learn, not a summary.

annotations.span: What kept me there initially wasn't the photographs at all but the argument underneath them
annotations.label: Cleft with a corrective 'but'
annotations.why: State the expected answer, reject it, then give the real one.

annotations.span: unlike almost everything else I acquired that year it survived
annotations.label: Fronted comparison
annotations.why: Putting 'unlike X' first sets the contrast before the clause arrives.

annotations.span: with no interest whatsoever in growing
annotations.label: Emphatic negative, understated
annotations.why: 'Whatsoever' after a negative noun phrase is natural and easy to reuse.

annotations.span: it wants nothing from me
annotations.label: The judgement, compressed
annotations.why: Short sentence after long ones — the contrast is what makes it land.

annotations.span: sideways, from something they were only half looking at
annotations.label: Pause before the final phrase
annotations.why: A short break before the last idea marks it as the point.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about one time when I saw something on the internet and it was not true.

It was a message in our family group. The message says that one food can stop a very serious illness, and there is a photo of a laboratory, so it looks very official. My aunt sent it. She is not a stupid person, but she believed it.

And many people in the group answered, thank you, this is very useful. So I also thought maybe it is true.

But then I read it again and something is strange. It writes the name of a university. So I searched this university and I found the study. And the study is real, but it is about a different thing completely. The number in the message is from another place.

After that I was thinking what to do. If I write in the group, my aunt will feel bad in front of everybody. So I sent her a private message and I sent the study, and I said I also almost believed it. And after one hour she deleted it herself. So I was happy about this, and I think it was the good decision.

what_caps_it.point: The narrative slides into the present five times and the conditional never backshifts.
'And', 'so' and 'but' carry every join; nothing is subordinated to anything.
'Very official', 'very useful', 'strange', 'happy', 'the good decision' — flat throughout.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
This happened a couple of years ago, in one of those family groups on a messaging app that you can never quite leave. Somebody had forwarded a message claiming that a particular food could prevent a fairly serious illness, with a photograph of a laboratory attached to make it look official.

It reached us through my aunt, who is not a foolish woman at all. She'd been sent it by a friend, who'd been sent it by somebody else, and by the time it arrived nobody had any idea where it had started. Three or four relatives had already replied saying how useful it was, so my first instinct, honestly, was to assume it was fine.

What made me look properly was the wording. It named a university, so I searched for the study — and the study did exist. It simply didn't say anything remotely like what the message claimed. It was about something else entirely, and the figure it quoted had been lifted from a completely different table.

As for what I did, that's the part I still think about. I didn't correct it in the group, because I could see exactly how that would go: my aunt would have been shown up in front of everybody and she'd have dug her heels in. So I messaged her privately, sent her the actual paper, and told her I'd nearly believed it myself, which was true. She deleted it an hour later without being asked. Looking back, if I'd said it publicly I'm fairly sure that message would still be circulating.

what_lifts_it.point: Three past perfects layer the timeline, and the third conditional lands where regret belongs.
'Dug her heels in', 'shown up', 'lifted from' replace the plain reporting verbs.
The decision gets the most time, which is what the fourth bullet actually asks for.

annotations.span: This happened a couple of years ago
annotations.label: Time fixed in four words
annotations.why: One time phrase up front commits the whole turn to the past tense.

annotations.span: She'd been sent it by a friend, who'd been sent it by somebody else
annotations.label: Past perfect passive, twice
annotations.why: Chaining 'had been sent' shows a history without any dates at all.

annotations.span: my first instinct, honestly, was to assume it was fine
annotations.label: Admits being taken in
annotations.why: Conceding your own error early makes the rest sound honest rather than smug.

annotations.span: What made me look properly was the wording.
annotations.label: Cleft opening the third bullet
annotations.why: 'What made me…' announces a turn in the story and buys a beat of thinking time.

annotations.span: had been lifted from a completely different table
annotations.label: Precise verb for misuse of data
annotations.why: 'Lifted' says taken-without-permission in one ordinary word.

annotations.span: she'd have dug her heels in
annotations.label: Idiom used exactly right
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever someone refuses to move once challenged.

annotations.span: if I'd said it publicly I'm fairly sure that message would still be circulating
annotations.label: Mixed conditional, past to present
annotations.why: Past cause, present result — this is the structure regret actually takes.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This was two or three years back, in one of those family groups nobody has the nerve to leave. A message had been forwarded round claiming that a particular food headed off a fairly serious illness, and it came with a stock photograph of a laboratory, which is apparently all it takes.

It reached me through an aunt of mine — a sharp woman, not remotely gullible. She'd had it from a friend, who'd had it from somebody else, and its origins had long since vanished. Several relatives had already thanked her for it, and I'll admit my own first reaction was to let it go.

What snagged on me was the wording. It named a university, so I went looking, and the paper turned out to be perfectly real — it simply had nothing to do with the claim. Different subject, different question, and the figure in the message had been quietly borrowed from an unrelated table.

Then came the awkward part. Had I posted the correction in the group, my aunt would have been humiliated in front of thirty relatives and would have defended it to the last. So I went to her privately, sent the paper, and said I'd very nearly fallen for it myself — which happened to be true. She took it down within the hour. What I took from that is that being right is only half of it; the other half is leaving somebody a way to change their mind.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion with 'had I posted' replaces the standard third conditional band 7 used.
'Headed off', 'snagged on me', 'fallen for it' — idiom used, not exhibited.
The close turns the anecdote into a principle about how corrections actually work.

annotations.span: Had I posted the correction in the group
annotations.label: Inversion for the third conditional
annotations.why: Drop the 'if' and invert. Higher register, still perfectly speakable.

annotations.span: which is apparently all it takes
annotations.label: Dry aside carrying a judgement
annotations.why: A short trailing comment evaluates without a single evaluative adjective.

annotations.span: the figure in the message had been quietly borrowed from an unrelated table
annotations.label: One adverb does the accusing
annotations.why: 'Quietly' implies deliberate concealment without you having to claim it.

annotations.span: being right is only half of it; the other half is leaving somebody a way to change their mind
annotations.label: Anecdote lifted into a principle
annotations.why: End on the general rule you drew, never on a summary of events.

annotations.span: Different subject, different question
annotations.label: Parallel phrases, matched rhythm
annotations.why: Two short phrases in the same shape make the contrast audible.

I want to tell about the time when I repaired a tap in my kitchen. It was dripping for many weeks and it was very annoying because I can hear it from the other room.

So I decided to repair it myself. I don't want to pay a plumber for such a small thing. I searched on the internet and I found a video. In the video there is a man in a garage and he does everything in four minutes. Also there was a text guide from a shop but I only looked it quickly.

The repair is not difficult. You remove the handle, you open the top, you change one small rubber piece and you close everything. But the problem is I don't stop the water first. The man says it in the beginning but I jumped this part because I want to see the important part.

So when I opened the top, all the water came on my face. It was very shocking. And after that I was searching the valve on the floor for five minutes.

Next time I will watch all the video from the start. This is the lesson. But actually it was good because now I know how to do it and I repaired two more taps after.

model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the time I tried to fix a dripping tap in my kitchen. It had been going for weeks and had reached the stage where I could hear it from the next room, so it was that or lose my mind.

The instructions came from a video, inevitably. I'd searched for the make of the tap and found a man in a garage who got through the whole job in about four minutes, with the camera propped on a paint tin. There was a written guide on a hardware shop's site as well, which I skim-read and, in hindsight, should have read properly.

How it went is the interesting part. The repair itself is straightforward: you take the handle off, unscrew the top, replace a small rubber washer, and put it all back. What I hadn't done was turn the water off at the mains, because the video mentions it in the first fifteen seconds and I'd skipped ahead to the section that looked useful. So the moment I loosened the top I got a face full of cold water, and spent the next five minutes on the kitchen floor hunting for a valve I'd never once thought about.

What I'd do differently is embarrassingly obvious — watch the whole thing before touching anything. Although I'd also say the panic taught me more than the video did. If it had gone smoothly I'd have forgotten it by the weekend, whereas I now know exactly where that valve is, and I've fixed two more since.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect, a fronted 'what I hadn't done was', and one clean third conditional.
'Skim-read', 'got through', 'hunting for' replace the plain verbs of the band-6 version.
The mistake is announced as the interesting part, so the listener knows what to wait for.

annotations.span: It had been going for weeks and had reached the stage where I could hear it from the next room
annotations.label: Past perfect sets up the trigger
annotations.why: Show how long the problem ran before the story starts. One sentence is enough.

annotations.span: so it was that or lose my mind
annotations.label: Exaggeration used for judgement
annotations.why: A light overstatement evaluates without any evaluative adjective.

annotations.span: How it went is the interesting part.
annotations.label: Flags the bullet and the payoff
annotations.why: Telling the listener what matters next buys you a second to organise it.

annotations.span: What I hadn't done was turn the water off at the mains
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect
annotations.why: This shape names an omission far more sharply than 'I forgot to'.

annotations.label: Cause given before the effect

annotations.span: What I'd do differently is embarrassingly obvious

annotations.why: Naming the fourth bullet aloud is the cheapest way to guarantee you cover it.

annotations.label: Third conditional, used naturally
annotations.why: Regret and near-misses are exactly where this structure belongs.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick is the afternoon I decided to deal with a tap in my kitchen that had been dripping since roughly the previous autumn and had got audible from two rooms away.

My instructions came, as everybody's now do, from a video: a man in a garage, camera balanced on a paint tin, the entire job dispatched in four minutes flat. There was a written version on a hardware chain's site as well, which I skimmed in the way one skims a safety card on an aeroplane.

The job itself could hardly be simpler. Handle off, top unscrewed, a rubber washer the size of a coin swapped out, everything back. What I had failed to do — and it is mentioned inside the first fifteen seconds, which tells you how far I'd skipped ahead — was turn the water off at the mains. Loosening that top produced a jet of cold water straight into my face and five undignified minutes crawling about looking for a valve whose existence had never crossed my mind.

What would I change? Watch the thing through, obviously. But had it gone to plan, I'd have forgotten the whole business by Sunday. As it is, I could find that valve in the dark, and I've since done two more taps without incident. There's a case for saying that nothing you get right first time ever really sticks, and that the useful part of any instruction is the step you were too impatient to watch.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion with 'had it gone to plan' replaces the standard conditional band 7 used.
'Dispatched in four minutes', 'undignified', 'without incident' — precision, not display.
The close states a general claim about learning rather than summarising the story.

annotations.span: had it gone to plan, I'd have forgotten the whole business by Sunday
annotations.label: Inverted third conditional
annotations.why: Drop 'if' and invert. It sounds considered rather than formal.

annotations.span: which I skimmed in the way one skims a safety card on an aeroplane
annotations.label: Comparison doing the evaluating
annotations.why: An analogy tells the listener how carelessly, without you saying 'carelessly'.

annotations.span: Handle off, top unscrewed, a rubber washer the size of a coin swapped out
annotations.label: Verbless list, even rhythm
annotations.why: Clip the steps and keep them level in pitch, then fall on the last one.

annotations.span: a valve whose existence had never crossed my mind
annotations.label: Relative clause with 'whose'
annotations.why: 'Whose' works for things too, and saves you a whole extra clause.

annotations.span: nothing you get right first time ever really sticks
annotations.label: Generalises out of the anecdote
annotations.why: End on the rule your story illustrates, not on what happened next.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about the thing that I do for keeping contact with my friend. Every Sunday I am sending her a long voice message, and she sends me one back on Monday usually.

She is my friend from the university. She moved to another country six years ago. There is five hours difference between us, so it is not easy.

In the beginning we are trying to call. But it was always a problem. When I am free she is sleeping, and when she is free I am working. And also when we finally called, we prepared many things to say in the week, and then we said nothing. It was strange.

So after that we started the voice messages. They are very long, maybe ten minutes, and they are about nothing important. What she ate, some problem in her office, a book. I record mine when I walk home so there is a lot of noise.

Why this one continues. Because there is no appointment. Nobody must be free in one exact time, so nobody feels bad. And I think now I know her daily life more than before, when we lived in the same city. So it is a very nice habit.

what_caps_it.point: Continuous forms used for habits throughout, and 'since'-style duration never appears.
'Not easy', 'strange', 'nice', 'important' — the whole judgement rests on four flat words.
'So' and 'and' open six sentences, so the reasoning is stated but never subordinated.

annotations.why: Keep this — a short list of specifics beats any general description.

annotations.label: Continuous for a weekly routine
annotations.why: Say 'every Sunday I send her'. Habits take the present simple.

annotations.span: In the beginning we are trying to call.
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: 'At first we tried calling' — fix the tense and hold it.

annotations.span: Nobody must be free in one exact time
annotations.label: Wrong modal and preposition
annotations.why: 'Nobody has to be free at a particular time.' 'Must not' means forbidden.

annotations.label: Closes on the flattest adjective

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd describe isn't remotely impressive: I send a long voice message to a friend of mine every Sunday evening, and she sends one back, usually on the Monday.

We were at university together and she moved abroad about six years ago, which put five hours between us. We tried calling for a while and it was hopeless — either I was at work or she was asleep, and on the rare occasions we managed it we'd both spent the whole week storing things up and then said none of them.

So at some point we gave up on calls altogether. The messages are about ten minutes long, which sounds excessive, and they're almost entirely about nothing: what she had for lunch, an argument with a colleague, whatever she happens to be reading. I record mine walking home, so there's traffic all over the recording, and neither of us edits anything or, as far as I know, ever listens back to their own.

As for why this one has lasted when every other habit I started that year has fallen by the wayside — I think it's because there's no arrangement to break. Nobody has to be free at a particular hour, nobody feels guilty for missing one, and if I'm honest it's easier to say something real into a phone than across a video call where you spend the time watching your own face. Six years on, I probably know more about her ordinary week than I ever did in the two years we lived in the same building.

what_lifts_it.point: Frequency adverbs land correctly, and 'we'd spent … and then said' holds one past frame.
'Storing things up', 'fallen by the wayside', 'no arrangement to break' carry the meaning.
The reason bullet is the longest section, and it gives a mechanism rather than a feeling.

annotations.label: Lowers the stakes immediately
annotations.why: Saying the subject is ordinary frees you to describe it precisely.

annotations.label: Distance expressed as time
annotations.why: Six words replace a whole clause about time zones.

annotations.span: on the rare occasions we managed it
annotations.label: Frequency inside a noun phrase
annotations.why: 'On the rare occasions' is more precise than 'sometimes' and sounds spoken.

annotations.span: we'd both spent the whole week storing things up and then said none of them
annotations.label: Past perfect then past simple
annotations.why: Two layers of past in one sentence, with no dates required.

annotations.span: As for why this one has lasted
annotations.label: Signposts the explain bullet
annotations.why: Name the fourth bullet out loud and you will not skip it.

annotations.span: there's no arrangement to break
annotations.label: A mechanism, not a feeling
annotations.why: Explaining how something works beats saying how much it means.

annotations.span: where you spend the time watching your own face
annotations.label: Stress falls on 'own'
annotations.why: Put the emphasis on the contrasting word and the joke lands.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
What I do is almost aggressively unremarkable. Every Sunday evening I record a rambling voice message for a friend from university, and one arrives back from her, generally on the Monday.

She went abroad six years ago, which put five hours and a working week between us. We persevered with calls for a while and they were a disaster: whenever I was free she was asleep, and the handful we did manage had the peculiar quality of two people who had saved up a fortnight of news and then couldn't think of a word of it.

So the calls quietly stopped. What replaced them runs to about ten minutes a side and concerns nothing whatsoever — lunch, a colleague who has annoyed her, three pages of a book. Mine are recorded walking home, traffic and all. Neither of us has ever edited one, and I doubt either of us listens back.

What has kept it alive, when every other habit from that year fell by the wayside, is precisely that there is nothing to break. No hour to be free at, no apology owed for a missed week. And there is something about talking into a phone in the dark that people simply do not manage on a video call. Not for the first time, the version that asked least of us turned out to be the one that lasted, which is probably worth remembering the next time I plan something ambitious.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted 'what has kept it alive' cleft and a 'not for the first time' inversion opener.
'Persevered', 'peculiar quality', 'aggressively unremarkable' — precision rather than rarity.
The close states a general rule about habits instead of summing up the friendship.

annotations.label: Cleft with an interruption inside
annotations.why: Hold the subject open across a clause, then land the answer.

annotations.span: almost aggressively unremarkable
annotations.label: Adverb sharpening an ordinary word
annotations.why: One unexpected adverb outperforms a rare adjective every time.

annotations.span: two people who had saved up a fortnight of news and then couldn't think of a word of it
annotations.label: A situation described, not labelled
annotations.why: Describing the behaviour is stronger than naming the feeling.

annotations.span: No hour to be free at, no apology owed for a missed week.
annotations.label: Two matched fragments
annotations.why: Same shape twice, falling both times — it sounds settled rather than clipped.

annotations.span: the version that asked least of us turned out to be the one that lasted
annotations.label: Closes on a general principle
annotations.why: Lift the last line out of your story and into a claim about habits.

model_answers.label: Below the target — the first rung
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe my first phone. It was grey and small, with buttons. The screen was very small, like a stamp.

It was not new. My brother use it two years and after he give it to me. Two buttons had no colour because he use it very much.

I get it in the summer. I am fourteen. My parents said I must pay the credit, so normally there is no credit inside.

But it was very strong. One time it fall in the stairs and nothing happen. I use it for messages. There was one game also, with a line, and I play it every time in the queue. The camera was very bad, you cannot see nothing in the photos.

Before, I must call the house of my friend and speak with the mother. With the phone, no. So it was very good for me. That is my first phone.

what_caps_it.point: The bullet asking what difference it made gets three words, and the turn ends at eighty seconds.
Past and present alternate inside the same paragraph; the hand-me-down needs a past perfect and gets none.
Outside the stamp comparison, everything is 'very small', 'very strong', 'very bad', 'very good'.

annotations.span: The screen was very small, like a stamp.
annotations.label: One comparison beats three adjectives
annotations.why: Keep this. Comparing an object to a familiar thing is the fastest description there is.

annotations.span: My brother use it two years and after he give it to me.
annotations.label: Two past verbs left unmarked
annotations.why: Say "My brother had used it for two years and then handed it down."

annotations.span: I get it in the summer. I am fourteen.
annotations.label: The story slips into the present
annotations.why: Say 'I got it the summer I turned fourteen.' Join them and keep both past.

annotations.span: you cannot see nothing in the photos
annotations.label: Double negative
annotations.why: Say "you couldn't see anything." English allows one negative per clause.

annotations.span: With the phone, no.
annotations.label: The fourth bullet is answered in three words
annotations.why: This bullet carries the band. Say what you could suddenly arrange on your own.

annotations.span: So it was very good for me.
annotations.label: The evaluation is one flat adjective
annotations.why: Say what changed: 'nobody's mother stood between me and a Saturday.'

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe my first phone. It was a small grey phone with buttons, and the screen was very small, like a stamp.

It was not new. My brother is using it two years before, and after he bought a new one he gives it to me. Two buttons had no paint on them because he used it very much.

I got it in the summer when I am fourteen years old. My parents said I must pay the credit myself, so most of the time there is no credit in it.

But it was very strong. One time it fell down the stairs and nothing happened. I used it for messages mostly. There was also one game, you move a line on the screen and you must not touch yourself, and I played it in every queue. The camera was there but the photos were terrible, you cannot see anything.

The difference was that before I must call the house of my friend and speak with his mother. With the phone I can arrange everything alone. For a boy of fourteen this was a big thing. Now my phone does everything, and that one did almost nothing, but it was my first one and it was special.

what_caps_it.point: Present tense keeps invading the narrative, and 'must' is used where 'had to' belongs.
'Very small', 'very strong', 'terrible', 'a big thing', 'special' — evaluation without precision.
The final bullet is answered in two sentences and then closes by repeating the card.

annotations.span: you move a line on the screen and you must not touch yourself
annotations.label: Explains rather than names
annotations.why: Keep this — describing a thing you cannot name is a genuinely useful skill.

annotations.span: My brother is using it two years before
annotations.label: Present continuous for a past period
annotations.why: 'My brother had had it for two years' puts it properly in the past.

annotations.span: My parents said I must pay the credit myself
annotations.label: Modal not backshifted
annotations.why: After a past reporting verb use 'had to': 'said I had to pay'.

annotations.span: With the phone I can arrange everything alone.
annotations.label: Present ability inside a past story
annotations.why: 'I could arrange everything myself' keeps the whole passage in the past.

annotations.span: it was my first one and it was special
annotations.label: Closes on an empty adjective
annotations.why: Say what it let you do that nothing before it had.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The first one I actually owned was a small grey phone with actual buttons and a screen about the size of a stamp. It wasn't new — my brother had had it for two years and handed it down when he upgraded, and by then the paint had worn off two of the keys.

I got it the summer I turned fourteen, on the condition that I paid for the credit myself, which meant it was almost permanently out of credit. It was solid, though. You could drop it down a flight of stairs and it would carry on working, which I happen to know because I did.

What I used it for was texting, almost exclusively. There was a game on it as well — you steered a line round the screen and tried not to run into yourself — and I played that in every queue I stood in for about three years. Photographs weren't really an option: there was a camera, technically, but the pictures came out looking like weather maps.

The difference it made was less about the phone than about who I had to go through. Before that, arranging anything meant ringing somebody's house and speaking to their mother first. Suddenly I could organise my own Saturday without a single adult being involved, which at fourteen felt enormous. Compared with what I carry around now it did practically nothing — but it was the first object I'd owned that made me feel like somebody with arrangements of my own.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect for the object's earlier life, plus 'would' for repeated past capability.
'Handed it down', 'out of credit', 'looking like weather maps' replace flat adjectives.
The last bullet reframes the question — who I had to go through — instead of listing features.

annotations.span: my brother had had it for two years and handed it down when he upgraded
annotations.label: Past perfect for the object's past
annotations.why: An object with a history before you owned it needs 'had'.

annotations.span: You could drop it down a flight of stairs and it would carry on working
annotations.label: 'Would' for repeated past capability
annotations.why: Use 'would' for what used to happen, not only for conditionals.

annotations.span: which I happen to know because I did
annotations.label: Aside that supplies the evidence
annotations.why: A trailing clause adds a fact and a joke in six words.

annotations.span: the pictures came out looking like weather maps
annotations.label: Comparison instead of an adjective
annotations.why: One image beats 'very bad quality' and is far more memorable.

annotations.span: The difference it made was less about the phone than about who I had to go through.
annotations.label: Reframes the final bullet
annotations.why: Answering a slightly better question than the one asked is a band-7 habit.

annotations.span: arranging anything meant ringing somebody's house and speaking to their mother first
annotations.label: Shows the old world concretely
annotations.why: Describe the procedure that disappeared and the change explains itself.

annotations.span: which at fourteen felt enormous
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'enormous'
annotations.why: Put the beat on the evaluative word and the sentence does its job.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The first device that was genuinely mine was a squat grey phone with rubber buttons and a screen roughly the area of a postage stamp. It arrived second-hand: my brother had carried it about for two years, and the paint had gone from the two keys he used most.

It came to me the summer I turned fourteen, with one condition attached — the credit was my problem. Which is why it spent most of its life with nothing on it. Sturdy, though. It went down a full flight of stairs at one point and simply carried on, a claim I have not been able to make about anything I have owned since.

Its uses were texting and, when there was no credit, a game in which you steered a line around the screen and tried not to collide with yourself. I must have played that in every queue in the city. There was nominally a camera; the results looked like weather maps.

What it changed had very little to do with the phone. Until then, making any plan at all meant telephoning somebody's house and getting past their mother. Overnight, my Saturdays became mine to arrange. Set against what sits in my pocket now it could do almost nothing at all — and yet nothing since has felt quite so much like being handed the keys to something. I suspect that is what people are really remembering when they get sentimental about old machines.

what_lifts_it.point: Fronted 'set against what sits in my pocket now' and a fragment used deliberately for rhythm.
'Squat', 'sturdy', 'getting past their mother' — one exact word doing a clause of work.
The close reaches for a metaphor about independence rather than restating the comparison.

annotations.span: Set against what sits in my pocket now it could do almost nothing at all
annotations.label: Fronted comparison, no 'compared'
annotations.why: Putting the comparison first raises the register without lengthening it.

annotations.span: a claim I have not been able to make about anything I have owned since
annotations.label: Reduced relative summing up a clause
annotations.why: 'A claim I…' lets you comment on the whole sentence you just said.

annotations.span: getting past their mother
annotations.label: Three words containing the whole ordeal
annotations.why: 'Getting past' implies an obstacle without you naming one.

annotations.span: Sturdy, though.
annotations.label: Two-word sentence for contrast
annotations.why: Drop a fragment between long sentences and the rhythm carries the meaning.

annotations.span: nothing since has felt quite so much like being handed the keys to something
annotations.label: Closes on an image, not a summary
annotations.why: A final metaphor lifts the answer out of the specification list.

model_answers.label: The top rung — effortless and exact
model_answers.transcript:
The first device that was genuinely mine was a squat grey phone with rubber buttons and a screen roughly the area of a postage stamp. It came second-hand: my brother had carried it about for two years, and the paint had gone from the two keys he used most, which told you everything about what he did with it.

It reached me the summer I turned fourteen, with one condition attached — the credit was my problem. Which is why it spent most of its life with nothing on it. Sturdy, though. It went down a full flight of stairs at one point and simply carried on, a claim I've not been able to make about anything I've owned since.

Its uses were texting and, when the credit ran out, a game in which you steered a line around the screen and tried not to run into yourself. I must have played that in every queue in the city. There was nominally a camera. The results looked like weather maps.

What it changed had almost nothing to do with the phone. Until then, making any plan at all meant ringing somebody's house and getting past their mother first. Overnight, my Saturdays became mine to arrange, and at fourteen that is not a small transfer of power. Set against what sits in my pocket now it could do practically nothing — and yet nothing since has felt quite so much like being handed a set of keys. Which is, I suspect, what people are actually being sentimental about when they get sentimental about old machines.

what_lifts_it.point: A modal perfect and stacked present perfects, both used to measure the object against now.
'Nominally', 'squat', 'transfer of power' — three exact choices where band 8 was already good.
The close names the general behaviour the anecdote illustrates, not the feeling it produced.

annotations.span: I must have played that in every queue in the city.
annotations.label: Modal perfect for a deduction about the past
annotations.why: 'Must have' says you are inferring, not remembering. It sounds like genuine recall.

annotations.span: a claim I've not been able to make about anything I've owned since
annotations.label: Two present perfects in one reduced relative
annotations.why: Stacking perfects links a past object to now without a single 'and'.

annotations.span: There was nominally a camera.
annotations.label: One adverb carries the whole joke
annotations.why: 'Nominally' means in name only. It replaces a sentence of explanation.

annotations.span: not a small transfer of power
annotations.label: Understatement plus an abstract noun
annotations.why: Naming what actually changed — power — is more exact than 'freedom'.

annotations.span: what people are actually being sentimental about when they get sentimental about old machines
annotations.label: Generalises out of the object at the end
annotations.why: Close on what the story is an example of, not on the object itself.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a photo that I don't share in the end.

It was in the spring, I am going home in the train. And there is a man in front of me and he is sleeping in a very funny position. His head is back, his mouth is open, and he is holding a sandwich in his hand.

So I took a photo. I wanted to put it in one group that I have with my university friends, about forty people. Everybody puts this kind of thing there. I already wrote the text under the photo.

But then I see something. He has a card on his neck from his company, and you can read his name very clear. And I thought, in forty people maybe somebody knows him. And also I thought, if this is me, I will be very angry.

So I deleted it. I think it was correct. But honestly, one part is because I am afraid, not only because it is wrong. Now I am thinking more before I put something. Many people take photos of strangers and they don't think about this person at all. So this is my story.

'Very funny', 'very clear', 'correct', 'wrong' — the judgement has no shading at all.
Closes by announcing that the story is over, which restates the card and adds nothing.

annotations.why: 'Clearly' modifies the verb. The -ly is doing real work here.
